Components.exp: Components are the fundamental building blocks of Angular apps, each consisting of a TypeScript class, HTML template, and optional CSS styles. They control a view via a decorated class with @Component metadata.

Modules.exp: NgModules organize an Angular app into cohesive blocks of functionality by declaring components, importing dependencies, and providing services. Every app has a root module (AppModule) as the entry point.

Templates.exp: Angular templates extend HTML with custom syntax including interpolation ({{ }}), property binding ([ ]), event binding (( )), and structural directives (*ngIf, *ngFor) for dynamic views.

Dependency Injection.exp: Angular's dependency injection system provides dependencies to classes via constructor parameters. The injector hierarchy creates singleton or per-component instances of services automatically.

Services.exp: Services are singleton classes decorated with @Injectable that encapsulate business logic, data access, or cross-cutting concerns. They are the recommended way to share logic between components.

Providers.exp: Providers configure the injector with dependency recipes, controlling how services are created and scoped. They can be registered at module level, component level, or using providedIn: 'root' for tree-shaking.

Router.exp: Angular Router enables navigation between views in SPAs with URL-based routing, nested routes, lazy-loaded modules, and route parameters. It integrates with the browser's history API.

Lazy Loading.exp: Lazy loading loads feature modules on demand when the user navigates to their routes, reducing initial bundle size. Use loadChildren in route config to point to a module imported via dynamic import.

Guards.exp: Route guards control navigation using interfaces like CanActivate, CanDeactivate, and Resolve. They prevent unauthorized access, prompt for unsaved changes, and pre-fetch data before a route activates.

Template-driven.exp: Template-driven forms rely on directives in the template like ngModel for two-way data binding. They are simpler but less scalable than reactive forms, suitable for basic form use cases.

Reactive.exp: Reactive forms provide a model-driven approach with form control instances created programmatically, offering more predictability, testability, and advanced validation capabilities.

Validation.exp: Angular forms support built-in validators (required, minLength, pattern) and custom async validators. Validation state is exposed through CSS classes (ng-valid, ng-invalid) and component properties.

HttpClient.exp: HttpClient is Angular's built-in HTTP client with typed request/response, interceptors, and automatic JSON parsing. Methods return Observables supporting RxJS operators for transformations.

Interceptors.exp: Interceptors sit between the application and the backend, transforming outgoing requests or incoming responses. Common use cases include adding auth tokens, logging, and error handling.

Error Handling.exp: Error handling in HTTP requests is done via RxJS catchError operator, retrying failed requests, or displaying user-friendly error messages. Global error handling can be centralized in interceptors.

Directives.exp: Angular offers three types of directives: components, structural directives (alter DOM layout), and attribute directives (change appearance or behavior). Custom directives encapsulate reusable DOM manipulation.

Pipes.exp: Pipes transform data in templates for display, such as formatting dates, currencies, or filtering lists. Angular provides built-in pipes and you can create custom pure or impure pipes.

Custom Decorators.exp: Decorators are TypeScript features used extensively in Angular for metadata. Custom decorators can extend component behavior, add logging, or transform class properties at design time.

Jasmine.exp: Jasmine is a behavior-driven development framework for testing JavaScript code with a clean, readable syntax. It provides describe/it blocks, matchers (toEqual, toContain), and spies.

Karma.exp: Karma is a test runner that executes tests in real browsers, providing fast feedback loops and reporting. It's the default test runner in Angular CLI projects via ng test.

TestBed.exp: TestBed is Angular's primary testing utility for configuring and creating component test environments. It manages module compilation, dependency injection, and provides ComponentFixture for interaction.

Change Detection.exp: Angular's default change detection checks every component in the tree when any data changes, ensuring consistency. It uses zone.js to patch browser APIs and trigger checks automatically.

OnPush.exp: OnPush change detection strategy reduces unnecessary checks by only running detection when input references change, events fire, or observables emit. It's essential for large lists and performance-critical views.

Code Splitting.exp: Angular supports code splitting through lazy-loaded modules and ES dynamic imports. The CLI generates separate chunks per lazy route, and the router loads them on demand when the user navigates.

Standalone API.exp: Standalone components, directives, and pipes are self-contained without needing NgModules. Created with the standalone: true flag, they import dependencies directly and can be lazy-loaded via the router.

Bootstrap Standalone.exp: Applications can bootstrap directly from a standalone component instead of NgModule. The main.ts calls bootstrapApplication with the root component and optional provider configuration.

Routing Standalone.exp: Standalone components load lazily with loadComponent in the route config, eliminating the need for feature modules. Each route points directly to a component with its own imports.

Writable Signals.exp: Signals are reactive primitives that notify consumers when their value changes. Writable signals created with signal() expose get/set/update methods for synchronous state management.

Computed Signals.exp: Computed signals derive values from other signals with lazy evaluation and caching. They only recompute when dependent signals change, replacing manual ChangeDetectorRef calls.

Effects.exp: Effects run side effects automatically when their signal dependencies change. They are used for syncing state to localStorage, logging, or triggering imperative DOM operations.

Signal Inputs.exp: Signal-based inputs replace @Input with input() and input.required(), providing reactive input values without lifecycle hooks. They integrate natively with the change detection system.

ng generate.exp: The Angular CLI generates components, directives, pipes, services, modules, and more using ng generate. Schematics customize generation with options for style, inline template, and routing.
ng generate.code:
ng generate component dashboard --standalone --inline-style --skip-tests
ng generate service api/data
ng generate module admin --route admin --module app

Custom Schematics.exp: Custom schematics automate project scaffolding by generating files, modifying existing code, and installing dependencies. They are published as npm packages and run with ng generate.

Angular Builders.exp: Builders extend the Angular CLI build pipeline with custom build, test, or deploy logic. They replace Angular's default builder to support custom tooling like custom webpack configs.

@defer.exp: Deferrable views (introduced in Angular 17) lazy-load component dependencies with @defer blocks. They improve initial bundle size by deferring heavy components until a specified trigger.

Defer Triggers.exp: Defer triggers control when lazy content loads: on viewport (enters viewport), on interaction (user clicks), on immediate, on idle (browser idle), or on a custom timer.

Defer Dependencies.exp: Deferred components and their transitive dependencies are split into separate JavaScript chunks. Angular loads these chunks asynchronously when the trigger condition is met, reducing initial payload.

inject().exp: The inject() function provides a programmatic alternative to constructor-based dependency injection. It can be called in the class body, making DI more flexible and reducing boilerplate.

Injection Context.exp: inject() must be called within an injection context such as a constructor, class field initializer, or factory function. Outside these contexts it throws, ensuring predictable DI resolution.

AWS Account & Root User.exp: Create an AWS account at aws.amazon.com. Root user has full unrestricted access — enable MFA immediately. Never use root for daily tasks. Create IAM users and roles instead. Set up billing alerts. Use AWS Organizations to manage multiple accounts centrally. Enable CloudTrail in all regions.
AWS Account & Root User.code:
# AWS CLI setup
aws configure
# Access Key ID / Secret Access Key / Region / Output

# Check caller identity
aws sts get-caller-identity

# List available regions
aws ec2 describe-regions

# Enable CloudTrail
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket-name my-logs
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name my-trail

IAM Users, Groups & Roles.exp: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls access. Users are individuals. Groups organize users with shared permissions. Roles are assumed by services (EC2, Lambda) or federated users. Policies are JSON documents with Allow/Deny effects. Follow least privilege. Use managed policies when possible.
IAM Users, Groups & Roles.code:
# Create IAM user
aws iam create-user --user-name devops
aws iam create-access-key --user-name devops

# Add user to group
aws iam create-group --group-name admins
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name devops --group-name admins

# Attach managed policy
aws iam attach-group-policy \
  --group-name admins \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess

# Create IAM role for EC2
aws iam create-role --role-name ec2-s3-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json

IAM Policies Deep.exp: IAM policies have: Version (2012-10-17), Statement list with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (service:operation), Resource (ARN), and optional Condition (IP, time, MFA, tags). Use policy variables ${aws:username}. Managed policies vs inline. Permission boundaries limit max permissions. Service Control Policies (SCP) in Organizations.

AWS Organizations & SCPs.exp: AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple accounts. Root OU contains all accounts. Create OUs for structure (Production, Staging, Sandbox). Service Control Policies (SCPs) restrict max permissions across accounts. Consolidate billing for volume discounts. Use AWS SSO for user access across accounts.

Regions, AZs & Edge Locations.exp: AWS has 30+ regions worldwide (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1, etc.). Each region has 3-6 Availability Zones (AZs) — isolated data centers. Edge Locations are CDN endpoints (400+). Use multiple AZs for HA. Choose region based on latency, compliance, cost, and service availability. Some services are global (IAM, Route53, CloudFront).
Regions, AZs & Edge Locations.code:
# List AZs for a region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1

# Check service availability per region
# aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /aws/service/global-infrastructure/regions

# Recommended regions
# us-east-1: N. Virginia (most services, lowest cost)
# eu-west-1: Ireland (EU presence)
# ap-southeast-1: Singapore (Asia)
# sa-east-1: Sao Paulo (South America)

EC2 Instances Deep.exp: EC2 provides virtual machines. Instance families: general (t3, m6i), compute (c6i), memory (r6i, x2gd), storage (i3, d2), GPU (p4, g5). Purchase options: On-Demand (pay per hour/sec), Reserved (1-3yr, up to 72% off), Spot (up to 90% off, interruptible), Dedicated Host. User data runs at boot. Placement groups control instance placement for low latency or HA.
EC2 Instances Deep.code:
# Launch EC2
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.medium \
  --key-name my-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-xxx \
  --subnet-id subnet-xxx \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=ec2-s3-role \
  --block-device-mappings "DeviceName=/dev/xvda,Ebs={VolumeSize=50,VolumeType=gp3}"

# Spot instance
aws ec2 request-spot-instances \
  --spot-price "0.05" \
  --instance-count 2 \
  --launch-specification file://spot-spec.json

EC2 Networking & Security Groups.exp: Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached to ENIs. Rules: allow only (no deny), evaluate all rules. NACLs are stateless firewalls at subnet level (allow/deny, rule numbers). Elastic IPs are static public IPs. ENIs are virtual network cards. VPC Flow Logs capture traffic metadata.
EC2 Networking & Security Groups.code:
# Create security group
aws ec2 create-security-group \
  --group-name web-sg \
  --description "Web server SG" \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxx

# Add rules
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 10.0.0.0/8

# Allocate Elastic IP
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 associate-address --instance-id i-xxx --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx

EC2 Auto Scaling.exp: Auto Scaling maintains desired instance count. Launch template specifies instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking (e.g., keep CPU at 50%), step scaling, scheduled scaling. Health checks replace unhealthy instances. Cooldown periods prevent rapid scaling. Lifecycle hooks run custom actions during scale events.
EC2 Auto Scaling.code:
# Create launch template
aws ec2 create-launch-template \
  --launch-template-name web-template \
  --launch-template-data file://template.json

# Create Auto Scaling group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=web-template \
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-xxx,subnet-yyy" \
  --target-group-arns arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...

# Target tracking policy
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name cpu-target \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration file://cpu-target.json

Elastic Load Balancing.exp: ALB (Application LB): HTTP/HTTPS, path-based routing, host-based routing, WebSockets. NLB (Network LB): TCP/UDP/TLS, ultra-low latency, static IP. Gateway LB: transparent inspection of traffic. Target groups route to instances, IPs, or Lambda. Sticky sessions via cookies. Health checks detect failures. Cross-zone load balancing distributes evenly.
Elastic Load Balancing.code:
# Create ALB
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
  --name my-alb \
  --subnets subnet-xxx subnet-yyy \
  --security-groups sg-xxx \
  --scheme internet-facing

# Create target group
aws elbv2 create-target-group \
  --name web-tg \
  --protocol HTTP --port 80 \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxx \
  --health-check-path /health

# Add target
aws elbv2 register-targets \
  --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:... \
  --targets Id=i-xxx Id=i-yyy

# Create listener
aws elbv2 create-listener \
  --load-balancer-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:... \
  --protocol HTTPS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:... \
  --default-actions Type=Forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...

AWS Lambda.exp: Lambda runs code without servers. Runtimes: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, custom (provided.al2). Triggers: API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, Kinesis. Max execution 15 min, max memory 10GB, max ephemeral storage 10GB. Concurrency limit per account (1000 default). Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm. Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations.
AWS Lambda.code:
# Create Lambda function
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name my-function \
  --runtime python3.12 \
  --role arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/lambda-role \
  --handler index.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --memory-size 512 \
  --timeout 30

# Add S3 trigger
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
  --function-name my-function \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket \
  --events s3:ObjectCreated:*

# Python function code
# import json
# def handler(event, context):
#     return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps({'message': 'Hello!'})}

ECS, EKS & Fargate.exp: ECS runs Docker containers at scale. Launch types: Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage) and EC2 (control over instances). EKS is managed Kubernetes. ECR stores container images. Task definitions describe containers (CPU, memory, ports, env vars). Services maintain desired task count with load balancer integration.
ECS, EKS & Fargate.code:
# ECS task definition
{ "family": "web-app",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "app",
    "image": "nginx:alpine",
    "memory": 512,
    "cpu": 256,
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 80, "protocol": "tcp"}],
    "environment": [{"name": "NODE_ENV", "value": "production"}]
  }],
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512"
}

# Create ECS service
aws ecs create-service \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --service-name web-service \
  --task-definition web-app:1 \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
  --desired-count 3 \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-xxx],securityGroups=[sg-xxx]}"

Elastic Beanstalk.exp: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — upload code, AWS handles provisioning, load balancing, auto scaling, monitoring. Platforms: Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Go, Docker. Environments: Web tier (ALB + ASG) and Worker tier (SQS + background jobs). Customize with .ebextensions config files. Easy for MVPs and standard web apps.
Elastic Beanstalk.code:
# Initialize EB project
pip install awsebcli
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
eb init -p node.js-20 my-app --region us-east-1

# Create environment
eb create production --cname my-app-prod

# Deploy
eb deploy

# Open in browser
eb open

# .ebextensions/options.config
option_settings:
  aws:autoscaling:asg:
    MinSize: '2'
    MaxSize: '6'
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:environment:
    EnvironmentType: LoadBalanced
  aws:autoscaling:launchconfiguration:
    InstanceType: t3.small

EC2 Image Builder & AMIs.exp: EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation. Pipeline steps: source image, build components (install packages), test components (validate), distribute to regions. Golden AMIs ensure consistent instances. Systems Manager Parameter Store tracks latest AMI IDs. Automate AMI refresh in Auto Scaling via lifecycle hooks.
EC2 Image Builder & AMIs.code:
# Create Image Builder pipeline
# Console or SDK — configures:
# - Source: Amazon Linux 2023
# - Build component: Install packages, harden
# - Test component: Run security scans
# - Distribute: us-east-1, eu-west-1

# Systems Manager parameter for AMI
aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /ami/web-app \
  --value ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --type String

# AMI cleanup lifecycle
autoscaler:
  - Create new AMI via Image Builder
  - Update SSM parameter
  - Launch new instance via ASG instance refresh

S3 Deep Dive.exp: Amazon S3 is object storage with 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. Storage classes: Standard (frequent access), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-cost optimization), Standard-IA (infrequent), One Zone-IA (lower cost, single AZ), Glacier Instant (archival, ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min retrieval), Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, 12hr retrieval). Versioning protects against deletes. Lifecycle policies transition between classes. S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda/SQS/SNS.
S3 Deep Dive.code:
# Create bucket
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket --region us-east-1

# Enable versioning
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Lifecycle policy
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# lifecycle.json: transition to IA after 30d, Glacier after 90d, expire after 365d
{
  "Rules": [{
    "Id": "archive-rule",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 365 }
  }]
}

# Pre-signed URL (temporary access)
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/private.txt --expires-in 3600

S3 Security & Encryption.exp: S3 security: Block Public Access (account/bucket level). Bucket policies (resource-based). IAM policies (identity-based). ACLs (legacy). Encryption: SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS managed), SSE-KMS (KMS keys, audit trail), SSE-C (customer provided key), client-side encryption. Object Lock (WORM — write once read many). S3 Access Points simplify managing access for large datasets.
S3 Security & Encryption.code:
# Block public access
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# Bucket policy (allow CloudFront only)
{ "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::cloudfront:user/CloudFront Origin Access Identity E1A2B3C4D5E6" },
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
  }]
}

# Enable default encryption
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'

EBS & Instance Storage.exp: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage for EC2. Volume types: gp3 (baseline 3000 IOPS, 125 MB/s, max 16000 IOPS), io2 (provisioned IOPS, 99.999% durability), st1 (throughput optimized, HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). Snapshots are incremental backups to S3. EBS Multi-attach for clustered workloads. EBS Fast Snapshot Restore for instant snapshot hydration. Instance Store is ephemeral (data lost on stop/terminate).
EBS & Instance Storage.code:
# Create EBS volume
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type gp3 \
  --size 100 \
  --iops 5000 \
  --throughput 250 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a

# Attach to EC2
aws ec2 attach-volume \
  --volume-id vol-xxx \
  --instance-id i-xxx \
  --device /dev/xvdf

# Create snapshot
aws ec2 create-snapshot \
  --volume-id vol-xxx \
  --description "Pre-upgrade backup"

# Enable Fast Snapshot Restore
aws ec2 enable-fast-snapshot-restores \
  --availability-zones us-east-1a us-east-1b \
  --source-snapshot-id snap-xxx

EFS & FSx.exp: EFS is managed NFS for Linux. Elastic — grows/shrinks automatically. Performance modes: General Purpose (default, latency-sensitive) and Max I/O (high-throughput, parallel). Throughput modes: Bursting and Provisioned. Lifecycle management moves files to EFS IA after N days. EFS Replication for cross-region DR. FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, AD integration) and FSx for Lustre (high-performance, HPC/AI).
EFS & FSx.code:
# Create EFS
aws efs create-file-system \
  --performance-mode generalPurpose \
  --throughput-mode bursting \
  --creation-token my-efs

# Create mount target (one per AZ)
aws efs create-mount-target \
  --file-system-id fs-xxx \
  --subnet-id subnet-xxx \
  --security-groups sg-xxx

# Mount on EC2
sudo mount -t nfs4 -o nfsvers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2,noresvport fs-xxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs

# FSx for Lustre (HPC)
# aws fsx create-file-system --file-system-type LUSTRE --storage-capacity 1200 --subnet-ids subnet-xxx

CloudFront CDN.exp: CloudFront is a global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, Lambda Function URL, HTTP server. Behaviors route by path pattern. Price classes: All, 200 (most), NA+EU only. SSL/TLS termination via ACM. Geo-restriction (whitelist/blacklist countries). Lambda@Edge for custom logic. OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. Real-time logs to Kinesis. WAF integration for DDoS protection.

RDS Deep Dive.exp: RDS manages relational databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Multi-AZ: synchronous standby replica in another AZ for HA (failover is automatic). Read replicas: async replication for read scaling (up to 15). Automated backups with point-in-time recovery (up to 35 days). Manual snapshots persist beyond retention. Enhanced Monitoring (CloudWatch metrics per second). Performance Insights for query analysis. RDS Proxy for connection pooling.
RDS Deep Dive.code:
# Create RDS PostgreSQL
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --engine postgres \
  --engine-version 16.3 \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 200 \
  --storage-type gp3 \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret \
  --multi-az \
  --backup-retention-period 35 \
  --enable-performance-insights \
  --enable-cloudwatch-logs-exports '["postgresql"]'

# Create read replica
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb-ro \
  --source-db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --region us-west-2

Aurora.exp: Amazon Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with cloud-native architecture. 6-way replication across 3 AZs — only 1/6 of data written (quorum). Auto-scaling storage from 10GB to 128TB. Aurora Serverless v2 scales to 0 ACUs (pay per second). Global Database: 1 primary region, up to 5 secondary regions with <1s replication. Backtrack: rewind DB to a specific time without restore. Parallel Query pushes analytics to storage layer.
Aurora.code:
# Create Aurora cluster
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --engine-version 16.4 \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-pg \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret

# Add writer instance
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier aurora-pg-writer \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-pg

# Serverless v2
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=128 \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-serverless

# Backtrack (MySQL Aurora only)
aws rds backtrack-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-mysql \
  --backtrack-to "2025-12-01T00:00:00Z"

DynamoDB.exp: DynamoDB is fully managed NoSQL key-value/document DB. Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Primary key: partition key (HASH) or composite (HASH + RANGE). Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, auto-scales) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, auto-scaling). DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Global Tables are multi-region, multi-writer (active-active). Streams capture changes for Lambda triggers or Kinesis. TTL auto-expires items.
DynamoDB.code:
# Create table
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name Users \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S AttributeName=email,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=email,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

# Put item
aws dynamodb put-item \
  --table-name Users \
  --item '{ "id": {"S": "user1"}, "name": {"S": "Alice"}, "age": {"N": "30"} }'

# Query (must use partition key)
aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name Users \
  --key-condition-expression "id = :id" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{ ":id": {"S": "user1"} }'

# Enable TTL
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live \
  --table-name Sessions \
  --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt

ElastiCache & MemoryDB.exp: ElastiCache provides managed Redis and Memcached. Redis: multi-AZ, replication, persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets, streams, Lua scripting. Memcached: simple, multi-threaded, no persistence. Cluster Mode shards data across nodes (up to 500 shards). Global Datastore for cross-region replication. MemoryDB is Redis-compatible, durable (write-ahead log), for microservices requiring both speed and durability. Use cases: session store, caching, rate limiting, leaderboards, message queues.
ElastiCache & MemoryDB.code:
# Create Redis cluster
aws elasticache create-cache-cluster \
  --cache-cluster-id redis-cluster \
  --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large \
  --engine redis \
  --num-cache-nodes 1 \
  --multi-az-enabled \
  --automatic-failover-enabled

# Create Redis with cluster mode
aws elasticache create-replication-group \
  --replication-group-id redis-sharded \
  --replication-group-description "Sharded Redis" \
  --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large \
  --engine redis \
  --num-node-groups 3 \
  --replicas-per-node-group 1

# Connect via redis-cli
# redis-cli -h my-cluster.xxxxx.clustercfg.use1.cache.amazonaws.com -p 6379

Redshift & Data Analytics.exp: Redshift is cloud data warehouse (petabyte-scale). Columnar storage, massively parallel (MPP). Node types: DC (dense compute), DS/RA3 (managed storage). Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN. Sort keys define data order per block. Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 without loading. Automatic workload management (WLM) prioritizes queries. Concurrency Scaling handles burst queries. Materialized views for pre-computed aggregates. Unload data to S3 for analysis.
Redshift & Data Analytics.code:
# Create Redshift cluster
aws redshift create-cluster \
  --cluster-identifier dw-cluster \
  --node-type dc2.large \
  --number-of-nodes 4 \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret

# Unload to S3
UNLOAD ('SELECT region, SUM(sales) FROM sales GROUP BY region')
TO 's3://my-bucket/unload/'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/redshift-s3'
PARQUET
PARTITION BY (region);

# External table (Spectrum)
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE spectrum.sales (
  id INT, amount DECIMAL, region VARCHAR(50)
)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.parquet.serde.ParquetHiveSerDe'
LOCATION 's3://my-bucket/sales-parquet/';

VPC Design.exp: VPC is your isolated network in AWS. CIDR block defines IP range (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide the VPC (public for internet-facing, private for internal). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway (IGW) for public internet access. NAT Gateway for private subnets to reach internet (outbound only). VPC Peering connects VPCs within or across accounts. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-prem. Endpoints (Gateway: S3/DynamoDB; Interface: other services) provide private access without IGW.
VPC Design.code:
# Create VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1b

# Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx

# NAT Gateway
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-xxx --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx

# VPC Peering
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-xxx --peer-vpc-id vpc-yyy

# VPC Endpoint (Gateway type)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-xxx --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-xxx

Route53 DNS.exp: Route53 is a DNS service (authoritative + resolver). Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verify), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources — free, works at zone apex). Routing policies: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-value. Health checks monitor endpoint health and route away from failures. Private hosted zones for internal DNS. DNSSEC for security.

AWS WAF & Shield.exp: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that protects HTTP endpoints. Rule groups: IP set, SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo-match, regex patterns. Managed rule groups from AWS (Core, SQL DB, Admin Protection, Known Bad Inputs). Shield Standard is free, protects against DDoS (L3/L4). Shield Advanced ($3k/mo) adds L7 DDoS protection, cost protection, DRT (DDoS Response Team). WAF integrates with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync.
AWS WAF & Shield.code:
# Create WAF IP set
aws wafv2 create-ip-set \
  --name allowed-ips \
  --scope CLOUDFRONT \
  --ip-address-version IPV4 \
  --addresses '["203.0.113.0/24", "198.51.100.0/24"]'

# Create WAF ACL
aws wafv2 create-web-acl \
  --name web-acl \
  --scope CLOUDFRONT \
  --default-action Allow={} \
  --rules file://waf-rules.json \
  --visibility-config SampledRequestsEnabled=true,CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName=web-acl-metric

# Associate with CloudFront
# aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn arn:aws:wafv2:... --resource-arn arn:aws:cloudfront::...distribution/xxx

AWS KMS & Secrets Manager.exp: KMS manages encryption keys. Customer managed keys vs AWS managed keys. Automatic annual key rotation. Envelope encryption: generate a data key to encrypt data, encrypt the data key with a KMS key. Key policies control who can use/administer keys. Grant allows temporary access. Secrets Manager stores secrets (DB passwords, API keys) with automatic rotation via Lambda. Parameter Store (free) stores config data and secrets.
AWS KMS & Secrets Manager.code:
# Create KMS key
aws kms create-key --description "My app encryption key"
aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/my-app-key --target-key-id xxx

# Encrypt with KMS
aws kms encrypt \
  --key-id alias/my-app-key \
  --plaintext fileb://secret.txt \
  --output text --query CiphertextBlob | base64 --decode > encrypted.txt

# Secrets Manager
aws secretsmanager create-secret \
  --name prod/db/password \
  --secret-string '{"username":"admin","password":"P@ssw0rd"}'

# Get secret
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password

# Parameter Store
aws ssm put-parameter --name /app/db-url --value "postgresql://..." --type String --tier Standard

CloudFormation.exp: CloudFormation is IaC (Infrastructure as Code) on AWS. Templates written in YAML/JSON. Resources define AWS components. Parameters allow customization at deploy time. Outputs export values for cross-stack references. Change sets preview changes before applying. Nested stacks compose complex infrastructure. Drift detection checks if real-world resources match the template. StackSets deploy across accounts/regions via Organizations. DeletionPolicy controls resource retention on stack delete.
CloudFormation.code:
# Template structure
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Web application infrastructure
Parameters:
  EnvName:
    Type: String
    Default: production
    AllowedValues: [production, staging]
Resources:
  WebServer:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    Properties:
      InstanceType: t3.micro
      ImageId: ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0
      SecurityGroups:
        - !Ref WebSecurityGroup
  WebSecurityGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: HTTP access
      SecurityGroupIngress:
        - IpProtocol: tcp
          FromPort: '80'
          ToPort: '80'
          CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0
Outputs:
  InstanceId:
    Value: !Ref WebServer
    Export:
      Name: !Sub "${AWS::StackName}-InstanceId"

# Deploy
aws cloudformation deploy --template-file template.yaml --stack-name my-stack --parameter-overrides EnvName=production

CI/CD with CodePipeline.exp: CodePipeline automates build-test-deploy. Source: CodeCommit, GitHub, Bitbucket, S3. Build: CodeBuild (managed build server, pay per minute). Deploy: CodeDeploy (EC2, Lambda, ECS), Elastic Beanstalk, CloudFormation. Stages run sequentially with manual approval gates. Artifacts stored in S3. CloudWatch Events trigger pipelines on source changes.
CI/CD with CodePipeline.code:
# Buildspec (CodeBuild)
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 20
    commands:
      - npm install
  build:
    commands:
      - npm run build
  post_build:
    commands:
      - npm test
artifacts:
  files:
    - 'dist/**/*'
  discard-paths: yes

# Appspec (CodeDeploy)
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /var/www/app
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/stop_server.sh
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/start_server.sh
      timeout: 300

CloudWatch Monitoring.exp: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms. Metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network, custom metrics. Alarms: threshold-based, composite (multiple conditions), anomaly detection. Logs: agent collects from EC2, streams to log groups. Logs Insights queries logs with SQL-like syntax. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors (IPs, endpoints). Synthetics (Canaries) monitor endpoints with Node.js scripts. ServiceLens traces requests across services (X-Ray integration). Dashboards visualize metrics in one place.
CloudWatch Monitoring.code:
# Put custom metric
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --metric-name ActiveUsers \
  --namespace MyApp \
  --value 42 \
  --unit Count

# Create alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name HighCPU \
  --alarm-description "CPU > 80% for 5 min" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

# Query logs
# fields @timestamp, @message
# | filter @message like /ERROR/
# | sort @timestamp desc
# | limit 20

EventBridge & Step Functions.exp: EventBridge is a serverless event bus. Sources: AWS services, SaaS (Datadog, Zendesk), custom apps. Rules filter events and route to targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions). Pipes connects sources to targets with filtering and enrichment. Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows (visual state machine). Standard Workflows (up to 1-year duration) vs Express (up to 5-min, high volume). States: Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait, Succeed, Fail. Error handling with retries and catch.

AWS Budgets & Cost Control.exp: AWS Budgets track spending and send alerts. Types: Cost budget, Usage budget, Savings Plans budget, Reservation budget. Budget actions can apply IAM policy or stop EC2 instances when threshold is exceeded. Cost Explorer visualizes spend. Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing. Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) offer discounts for commitment. Trusted Advisor checks cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits. Consolidated billing aggregates usage across accounts.
AWS Budgets & Cost Control.code:
# Create cost budget
aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id 123456789012 \
  --budget file://budget.json

# budget.json
{ "BudgetName": "monthly-budget",
  "BudgetType": "COST",
  "BudgetLimit": { "Amount": "1000", "Unit": "USD" },
  "TimePeriod": { "Start": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" },
  "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
  "CostFilters": { "Service": ["EC2", "RDS"] }
}

# Cost Explorer query
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=2025-01-01,End=2025-12-31 \
  --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics "BlendedCost" "UnblendedCost" \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE

VPC Deep Dive.exp: VPC is the foundation of AWS networking. Subnets (public/private) segment IP ranges. Route tables direct traffic to IGW (public) or NATGW (private). NAT Gateway enables outbound internet for private subnets — costs ~$0.045/hr + data processed. VPC Peering connects VPCs directly (no transitive peering). Security Groups (stateful, allow-only) vs NACLs (stateless, allow/deny, rule numbers). Common mistake: forgetting NACL rules are stateless — must configure both inbound and outbound rules separately. VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata for analysis. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs/on-prem via a hub. Use VPC endpoints for private access to S3/DynamoDB without NAT/IGW.
VPC Deep Dive.code:
# Create VPC with public/private subnets
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a

# Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx

# NAT Gateway (costs money! ~$0.045/hr + data)
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-public --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx

# Route tables
aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id vpc-xxx
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-xxx --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id igw-xxx
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id rtb-xxx --subnet-id subnet-public

# Security Group (stateful — return traffic allowed automatically)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-xxx --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# NACL (stateless — need both inbound AND outbound rules)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx --ingress --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --port-range From=443,To=443 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx --egress --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --port-range From=1024,To=65535 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow

# VPC Peering
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-main --peer-vpc-id vpc-peer
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxx

Route53 & DNS.exp: Route53 is AWS's DNS service. Hosted zones contain DNS records for a domain. Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (cannot be used at zone apex), MX (mail), TXT (verification), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources, works at zone apex, free). Routing policies: Simple (single record), Weighted (A/B testing), Latency (best performance), Failover (active-passive DR), Geolocation (by user location), Geoproximity (by resource location). Health checks monitor endpoints. Common mistake: using CNAME at zone apex — use Alias instead. Enable DNSSEC for DNS spoofing protection.

CloudFront & CDN.exp: CloudFront is AWS's global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Distributions define content delivery configuration. Origins: S3 buckets, ALBs, EC2, custom HTTP servers. Behaviors route by URL path pattern. Lambda@Edge executes code at edge locations (viewer/origin request/response) — use for A/B testing, URL rewrites, authentication. Price classes: Price Class All (all edges), Price Class 200 (most, cheaper), Price Class 100 (US+Europe, cheapest). Invalidations clear edge caches (charged per path). OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. WAF integration for DDoS. Common mistake: caching sensitive data — set appropriate Cache-Control and Cookie/QueryString forwarding policies.

DynamoDB.exp: DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with single-digit ms latency. Tables contain items (up to 400KB each). Primary key: Partition Key (HASH) alone or Composite (HASH + RANGE/Sort Key). GSIs (Global Secondary Indexes) have different partition/sort keys — eventually consistent, add after table creation. LSIs (Local Secondary Indexes) same partition key, different sort key — created only at table creation, strongly consistent. DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is an in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, best for variable traffic) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, cheaper for predictable traffic). Streams capture changes for 24h. TTL auto-expires items. Common mistake: scanning instead of querying — always Query with a partition key.
DynamoDB.code:
# Create table with GSI
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name Orders \
  --attribute-definitions \
    AttributeName=CustomerId,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=OrderDate,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=Status,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
    AttributeName=CustomerId,KeyType=HASH \
    AttributeName=OrderDate,KeyType=RANGE \
  --global-secondary-indexes '[
    {
      "IndexName": "StatusIndex",
      "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName": "Status", "KeyType": "HASH"}, {"AttributeName": "OrderDate", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
      "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "ALL"}
    }
  ]' \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

# Query (efficient — uses partition key)
aws dynamodb query --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression "CustomerId = :cid AND OrderDate BETWEEN :start AND :end" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":cid": {"S": "cust-123"}, ":start": {"S": "2025-01-01"}, ":end": {"S": "2025-12-31"}}'

# Scan (expensive — avoid in production!)
aws dynamodb scan --table-name Orders --filter-expression "Status = :s"

# DAX (cache for microsecond reads)
aws dynamodb create-cluster --cluster-name my-dax --node-type dax.r5.large --replication-factor 3 --iam-role-arn arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/dax-role

# Enable TTL
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name Sessions --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=ttl

SQS & SNS.exp: SQS is fully managed message queuing. Standard queues: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queues: exactly-once processing, first-in-first-out, 3000 msg/s max (with batching). Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after maxReceiveCount retries. Visibility timeout hides messages during processing — set longer than your processing time. Long polling reduces empty responses and costs. SNS is pub/sub messaging. Topics fan out messages to subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS). Fan-out pattern: SNS sends to multiple SQS queues for parallel processing. Message filtering with filter policies. Common mistake: forgetting to delete messages from SQS after processing (they reappear after visibility timeout!).
SQS & SNS.code:
# Create standard queue
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue --attributes '{
  "VisibilityTimeout": "30",
  "MessageRetentionPeriod": "345600",
  "ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds": "20"
}'

# Create DLQ and set redrive policy
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue-dlq
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue \
  --attributes '{
    "RedrivePolicy": "{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:xxx:my-queue-dlq\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"3\"}"
  }'

# Send and receive
aws sqs send-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue --message-body "Hello"
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue
aws sqs delete-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue --receipt-handler xxx

# FIFO queue (exactly-once, ordered)
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue.fifo --attributes '{"FifoQueue": "true", "ContentBasedDeduplication": "true"}'

# SNS topic
aws sns create-topic --name my-topic

# Subscribe SQS to SNS (fan-out)
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:my-topic --protocol sqs \
  --notification-endpoint arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:xxx:my-queue

# Publish message
aws sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:my-topic --message "Hello"

# Filter policy (receive only specific event types)
# Subscription attribute: {"event": ["order_created", "order_shipped"]}

Step Functions & Workflows.exp: Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows as state machines. Standard Workflows: up to 1-year duration, exactly-once execution, billed per state transition. Express Workflows: up to 5-min duration, at-least-once, billed by execution time/memory. State types: Task (invoke Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SQS), Choice (if/else), Parallel (fan-out), Map (iterate array), Wait (delay), Succeed/Fail (terminate). Error handling: Retry (exponential backoff, maxAttempts) and Catch (redirect to fallback state). Timeouts prevent stuck executions. Heartbeats for long-running tasks. Common mistake: not setting appropriate timeouts — workflows can hang indefinitely.

CloudWatch & Monitoring.exp: CloudWatch is the single source of truth for AWS observability. Metrics: AWS service metrics (CPU, requests, latency) and custom metrics (up to 15-second granularity). Alarms: threshold-based, anomaly detection (ML-based), composite alarms (combine multiple conditions). Alarm actions trigger SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 stop/reboot. Logs Insights queries logs with a SQL-like query language. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors. Synthetics Canaries monitor endpoints. Dashboards combine metrics, logs, and alarms. Common mistake: not setting dimension combinations on custom metrics (each unique combination is a separate metric). Best practice: use structured JSON logging for easier Logs Insights queries. Set log retention to avoid accumulating costs.
CloudWatch & Monitoring.code:
# Put custom metric with dimensions
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --namespace "MyApp" \
  --metric-name "OrderCount" \
  --dimensions "Environment=Production,Service=Checkout" \
  --value 42 --unit Count

# Anomaly detection alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name "AnomalousCPU" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average \
  --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

# Composite alarm (combine conditions)
aws cloudwatch put-composite-alarm --alarm-name "HighCPUOrHighLatency" \
  --alarm-rule "ALARM(HighCPU) OR ALARM(HighLatency)" \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

# Logs Insights (structured JSON logging)
# fields @timestamp, @message
# | filter @message like /ERROR/
# | parse @message '{"level": "*", "requestId": "*", "error": "*"}' as level, requestId, error
# | stats count() by error
# | sort @timestamp desc
# | limit 20

# Set retention policy
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/lambda/my-function --retention-in-days 30

# Dashboard
aws cloudwatch put-dashboard --dashboard-name MyDashboard --dashboard-body '{"widgets": [{"type": "metric", "x": 0, "y": 0, "width": 12, "height": 6, "properties": {"metrics": [["AWS/EC2", "CPUUtilization"]], "period": 300, "region": "us-east-1", "title": "EC2 CPU"}}]}'

Azure Account & Portal.exp: Create an Azure account at portal.azure.com. Free tier: $200 credit for 30 days + 55+ always-free services. Azure Portal is the web UI. Azure CLI for command-line management. PowerShell Az module for scripting. Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management layer. Every resource belongs to a resource group. Subscriptions group resource groups with billing boundaries. Management groups organize subscriptions hierarchically. Azure Blueprints for compliance.
Azure Account & Portal.code:
# Install Azure CLI
# curl -sL https://aka.ms/InstallAzureCLIDeb | bash

az login

# List subscriptions
az account list --output table

# Set active subscription
az account set --subscription "MySubscription"

# Create resource group
az group create --name my-rg --location eastus

# List regions
az account list-locations --output table

Azure Regions & Availability.exp: Azure has 60+ regions worldwide, more than any other cloud provider. Region pairs (e.g., East US + West US) are 300+ miles apart for DR. Availability Sets (up to 3 fault domains + 5 update domains) for VMs. Availability Zones (3+ per region) are physically separate data centers within a region. Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to a secondary region for disaster recovery. Proximity Placement Groups reduce VM-to-VM latency.
Azure Regions & Availability.code:
# List VMs by region
az vm list-sizes --location eastus --output table

# Check if region supports availability zones
az vm list-availability-zones --location eastus

# Region pairs:
# East US <-> West US
# UK South <-> UK West
# Southeast Asia <-> East Asia
# North Europe <-> West Europe

Azure Resource Manager & RBAC.exp: ARM manages all resources via declarative JSON/Bicep templates. Every resource has a unique ARM ID. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): roles are assignments of permissions at a scope (subscription, resource group, resource). Built-in roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator. Custom roles define granular permissions. Managed Identities give Azure resources an identity in Entra ID without managing credentials. Azure Policy enforces rules across resources.
Azure Resource Manager & RBAC.code:
# ARM resource ID format
# /subscriptions/{sub}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/{provider}/{type}/{name}

# RBAC role assignment
az role assignment create \
  --assignee user@example.com \
  --role Reader \
  --resource-group my-rg

# Create custom role
az role definition create --role-definition '{
  "Name": "VM Operator",
  "Description": "Can start/stop VMs",
  "Actions": [
    "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action",
    "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action"
  ],
  "AssignableScopes": ["/subscriptions/xxx"]
}'

# Azure Policy: enforce tag
az policy assignment create --policy "require-tag" --parameters '{"tagName":{"value":"Environment"}}'

Azure Entra ID (formerly Active Director.exp: Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service. Previously Azure AD. Tenants represent organizations. Users and Groups manage access. App registrations for OAuth2/OIDC authentication. Service principals are identities for applications. Managed identities for Azure resources (system-assigned or user-assigned). Conditional Access policies enforce MFA, device compliance, location. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) provides just-in-time admin access. Identity Protection detects compromised credentials.
Azure Entra ID (formerly Active Director.code:
# List users
az ad user list --output table

# Create group
az ad group create --display-name "Developers" --mail-nickname developers

# Add member
az ad group member add --group Developers --member-id xxx

# Create app registration
az ad app create --display-name "my-app"

# Managed identity for VM
az vm identity assign --resource-group my-rg --vm-name my-vm

# Conditional Access (via Portal or Graph API)
# Requires Microsoft Graph - not available via Azure CLI

Azure VMs Deep.exp: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS compute. VM series: General purpose (B-series burstable, D-series balanced), Compute optimized (F-series), Memory optimized (E-series, M-series), Storage optimized (L-series), GPU (NC, ND, NV). Availability Sets distribute VMs across fault/update domains (99.95% SLA). Availability Zones provide 99.99% SLA. Azure Dedicated Host for compliance. VM Scale Sets automatically manage identical VMs with autoscaling. Proximity Placement Groups reduce inter-VM latency.
Azure VMs Deep.code:
# Create VM
az vm create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name my-vm \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --size Standard_B2s \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --availability-zone 1 \
  --public-ip-sku Standard

# Resize VM
az vm resize --resource-group my-rg --name my-vm --size Standard_D4s_v5

# Deallocate (stops billing)
az vm deallocate --resource-group my-rg --name my-vm

# VM Scale Set
az vmss create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name web-vmss \
  --instance-count 3 \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --size Standard_B2s \
  --upgrade-policy-mode automatic

# Autoscale rule
az monitor autoscale create --resource web-vmss --resource-group my-rg --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets \
  --condition "Percentage CPU > 75 avg 5m" --scale-out 2
  --condition "Percentage CPU < 30 avg 5m" --scale-in 1

Azure App Service.exp: App Service is PaaS for web apps, REST APIs, and mobile backends. Supports .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Docker containers. Plans define pricing tier: Free/Shared (dev), Basic (custom domain, manual scale), Standard (auto-scale, staging slots), Premium (private endpoints, increased scale). Deployment Slots enable staging (swap with zero downtime). Auto-scale based on metrics or schedule. Built-in authentication (Entra ID, Google, Facebook). Hybrid Connections connect to on-prem resources. App Service Environment (ASE) is fully isolated, dedicated.
Azure App Service.code:
# Create App Service plan
az appservice plan create \
  --name my-plan \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku S1 \
  --is-linux

# Create web app
az webapp create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --plan my-plan \
  --name my-app \
  --runtime "NODE:20-lts"

# Deploy from GitHub
az webapp deployment source config \
  --name my-app \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --repo-url https://github.com/user/my-app \
  --branch main

# Create staging slot
az webapp deployment slot create \
  --name my-app \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --slot staging

# Swap slots
az webapp deployment slot swap \
  --name my-app \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --slot staging --target-slot production

Azure Functions.exp: Azure Functions is serverless compute. Triggers: HTTP (API), Timer, Blob Storage, Queue Storage, Event Grid, Cosmos DB, Service Bus. Hosting plans: Consumption (pay per execution, auto-scale to zero), Premium (pre-warmed instances, VNet integration, unlimited execution), Dedicated (on App Service plan). Durable Functions for stateful workflows (function chaining, fan-out/fan-in, human interaction). Supports C#, JavaScript, Python, Java, PowerShell, TypeScript. Managed dependencies with PowerShell.
Azure Functions.code:
# Create Function App
az functionapp create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --consumption-plan-location eastus \
  --runtime python \
  --runtime-version 3.11 \
  --functions-version 4 \
  --name my-func \
  --storage-account mystorage

# Python HTTP trigger
