#     name = req.params.get('name')
#     return func.HttpResponse(f"Hello {name}!")

# Deploy
func azure functionapp publish my-func

# Durable Functions (C#)
# [FunctionName("ProcessOrder")]
# public async Task ProcessOrder(
#     [OrchestrationTrigger] IDurableOrchestrationContext ctx)
# {
#     var order = ctx.GetInput<Order>();
#     await ctx.CallActivityAsync("ValidatePayment", order);
#     await ctx.CallActivityAsync("UpdateInventory", order);
#     await ctx.CallActivityAsync("SendConfirmation", order);
# }

Azure Container Apps & AKS.exp: Azure Container Apps (ACA): serverless containers, auto-scaling (including scale to zero), HTTP ingress, revisions, Dapr integration, KEDA scaling. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS): managed Kubernetes, automated upgrades, node pools, Azure AD integration, Azure Policy for Gatekeeper, advanced networking (Calico/Cilium). Azure Container Instances (ACI): simple single-pod containers, fast startup, no orchestration. Azure Container Registry (ACR): private Docker registry, geo-replication, task automation.
Azure Container Apps & AKS.code:
# Create Container App
az containerapp create \
  --name my-app \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --environment my-env \
  --image nginx:alpine \
  --target-port 80 \
  --ingress external

# Create AKS cluster
az aks create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name my-aks \
  --node-count 3 \
  --enable-cluster-autoscaler \
  --min-count 1 --max-count 10 \
  --enable-oidc-issuer \
  --enable-workload-identity

# Get credentials
az aks get-credentials --resource-group my-rg --name my-aks

# ACR
az acr create --resource-group my-rg --name myregistry --sku Basic
az acr build --registry myregistry --image web-app:v1 .

Azure Batch & HPC.exp: Azure Batch runs large-scale parallel and HPC workloads. Creates and manages a pool of VMs, installs applications, schedules tasks. Auto-scale pool size based on queue depth. Low-priority VMs for up to 80% cost savings (can be preempted). Integration with Azure Storage for input/output. Azure CycleCloud for HPC cluster management. Useful for rendering, financial modeling, genomics, and Monte Carlo simulations.
Azure Batch & HPC.code:
# Create Batch account
az batch account create \
  --name my-batch \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus

# Create pool
az batch pool create \
  --account-name my-batch \
  --id my-pool \
  --vm-size Standard_D2s_v3 \
  --target-dedicated-nodes 10 \
  --image canonical:ubuntuserver:22_04-lts-gen2:latest \
  --node-agent-sku-id batch.node.ubuntu 22.04

# Submit job
az batch job create --account-name my-batch --id my-job --pool-id my-pool

# Submit task
az batch task create --account-name my-batch --job-id my-job --task-id task1 --command-line "echo Hello"

Azure Blob Storage.exp: Azure Blob Storage is object storage for unstructured data. Access tiers: Hot (frequent, lowest access cost), Cool (infrequent, 30-day min), Cold (rare, 90-day min), Archive (offline, 180-day min, hours to retrieve). Storage types: Block blobs (general objects, up to 4.7TB), Append blobs (logs), Page blobs (VHDs, up to 8TB). Lifecycle management auto-tiers data. Immutable storage (WORM) for compliance. Soft delete protects against accidental deletion. Azure Files is managed SMB/NFS file shares. Static websites can be hosted directly from blob storage.
Azure Blob Storage.code:
# Create storage account
az storage account create \
  --name mystorageaccount \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --sku Standard_GRS \
  --kind StorageV2 \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2

# Upload blob
az storage blob upload \
  --account-name mystorageaccount \
  --container-name data \
  --name myfile.txt \
  --file ./myfile.txt

# Generate SAS token
az storage blob generate-sas \
  --account-name mystorageaccount \
  --container-name data \
  --name myfile.txt \
  --permissions r \
  --expiry 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z

# Lifecycle policy (via JSON)
az storage account management-policy create \
  --account-name mystorageaccount \
  --policy @policy.json
# policy.json: tier to Cool after 30d, Archive after 90d, delete after 365d

Azure Disk Storage.exp: Azure Managed Disks are block storage for VMs. Types: Ultra Disk (sub-ms latency, provisioned IOPS), Premium SSD v2 (high performance, cost-optimized), Premium SSD (production workloads), Standard SSD (dev/test), Standard HDD (backup, non-critical). Disk roles: OS disk (up to 4TB), data disks (up to 32TB per disk). Encryption at rest: SSE (platform-managed) or customer-managed keys (Azure Key Vault). Azure Disk Encryption via BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux). Shared disks (Windows Server Failover Cluster, Linux Pacemaker). Incremental snapshots for backup.
Azure Disk Storage.code:
# Create managed disk
az disk create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name data-disk \
  --size-gb 256 \
  --sku PremiumSSD_LRS \
  --zone 1

# Attach to VM
az vm disk attach \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --vm-name my-vm \
  --name data-disk

# Create snapshot
az snapshot create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name data-snapshot \
  --source data-disk

# Create disk from snapshot
az disk create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name data-disk-restored \
  --source data-snapshot

# Resize disk
az disk update --resource-group my-rg --name data-disk --size-gb 512

Azure Files & NetApp Files.exp: Azure Files provides fully managed SMB and NFS file shares. Accessible from Windows, Linux, macOS via standard file protocols. SMB Multichannel for performance. Azure File Sync caches shares on Windows Servers (hybrid). Identity-based auth (Entra ID DS or AD DS). Azure NetApp Files (ANF): enterprise-grade, high-performance NFS/SMB, on bare metal, sub-ms latency, up to 100GB/s throughput. Multiple service levels: Standard, Premium, Ultra. Cross-region replication for DR.
Azure Files & NetApp Files.code:
# Create file share
az storage share create \
  --account-name mystorageaccount \
  --name myshare \
  --quota 100

# Mount on Linux
sudo mount -t cifs //mystorageaccount.file.core.windows.net/myshare /mnt/files \
  -o vers=3.0,username=mystorageaccount,password=xxx,dir_mode=0777,file_mode=0777

# Create NetApp account and volume
az netappfiles account create --resource-group my-rg --name my-netapp --location eastus
az netappfiles pool create --resource-group my-rg --account-name my-netapp --name my-pool --size 4 --service-level Premium
az netappfiles volume create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --account-name my-netapp \
  --pool-name my-pool \
  --name my-volume \
  --file-path my-unique-path \
  --usage-threshold 100 \
  --subnet /subscriptions/.../subnets/default \
  --protocol-types NFSv3

Azure CDN & Front Door.exp: Azure CDN is a global CDN with point-of-presence (POP) locations. Profiles: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (rules engine), Verizon (advanced HTTP), Akamai (real-time stats). Azure Front Door (AFD) is a modern cloud CDN with: global HTTP load balancing, TLS termination, web application firewall (WAF), URL rewrite/redirect, path-based routing, latency-based routing, caching acceleration. Front Door operates at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). WAF policies protect against SQL injection, XSS, bots, DDoS. Private link support for origin access.
Azure CDN & Front Door.code:
# Create Front Door profile
az afd profile create \
  --profile-name my-afd \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor

# Create endpoint
az afd endpoint create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --profile-name my-afd \
  --endpoint-name my-app \
  --enabled-state Enabled

# Add origin group
az afd origin-group create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --profile-name my-afd \
  --origin-group-name app-servers \
  --probe-request-type GET \
  --probe-protocol Http \
  --probe-interval-in-seconds 30

# Add route
az afd route create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --profile-name my-afd \
  --endpoint-name my-app \
  --forwarding-protocol MatchRequest \
  --link-to-default-domain Enabled \
  --origin-group app-servers \
  --supported-protocols Http Https \
  --patterns "/*"

Azure SQL Database.exp: Azure SQL Database is fully managed SQL Server (PaaS). Service tiers: General Purpose (serverless or provisioned, 5-99.99% HA), Business Critical (always-on, 99.995% HA), Hyperscale (up to 100TB, fast scaling). Elastic Pools share resources among multiple databases (cost-effective for many DBs with spiky usage). Geo-replication for DR (readable secondaries in other regions). Auto-failover groups for transparent failover. Azure SQL Managed Instance (SQL MI) is near-100% SQL Server compatible, with full network isolation. Advanced data security: vulnerability assessment, data discovery, threat detection.
Azure SQL Database.code:
# Create SQL Database server
az sql server create \
  --name my-sql-server \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --admin-user admin \
  --admin-password P@ssw0rd!

# Create database
az sql db create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --server my-sql-server \
  --name my-db \
  --service-objective GP_Gen5_2

# Elastic pool
az sql elastic-pool create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --server my-sql-server \
  --name my-pool \
  --edition GeneralPurpose \
  --capacity 4 --max-capacity 16

# Add DB to pool
az sql db create --resource-group my-rg --server my-sql-server --name db2 --elastic-pool my-pool

# Geo-replication
az sql db replica create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --server my-sql-server \
  --name my-db \
  --partner-server my-secondary-server --partner-resource-group my-rg

Azure Database for MySQL & PostgreSQL.exp: Flexible Server (recommended) vs Single Server (legacy). Flexible Server features: zone-redundant HA, stop/start, burstable SKUs, private networking (VNet), up to 16TB storage, 35-day backup retention. Read replicas (up to 10). Azure Database for PostgreSQL: supports PostgreSQL 16+, pg_cron, pg_hint_plan, PostGIS, and other extensions. Built-in connection pooling with PgBouncer. Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL (formerly Hyperscale, Citus) distributes data across shards for multi-tenant apps. Azure Database Migration Service simplifies migration from on-prem.
Azure Database for MySQL & PostgreSQL.code:
# Create PostgreSQL Flexible Server
az postgres flexible-server create \
  --name my-pg-server \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --admin-user admin \
  --admin-password P@ssw0rd! \
  --sku-name Standard_D2s_v3 \
  --tier GeneralPurpose \
  --version 16 \
  --high-availability ZoneRedundancy \
  --storage-size 128

# Create MySQL Flexible Server
az mysql flexible-server create \
  --name my-mysql-server \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --admin-user admin \
  --admin-password P@ssw0rd! \
  --version 8.0 \
  --tier Burstable \
  --sku-name Standard_B1ms

# Create read replica
az postgres flexible-server replica create \
  --replica-name my-replica \
  --source-name my-pg-server \
  --resource-group my-rg

Azure Cosmos DB.exp: Cosmos DB is globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database. APIs: NoSQL (native document), MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Cassandra, Gremlin (graph), Table (key-value). Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Multi-region writes (active-active) for 99.999% availability. Automatic and instant scaling (RU/s — Request Units per second). Analytical store for HTAP (hybrid transactional/analytical processing). Change Feed triggers Azure Functions. Point-in-time backup (continuous backup mode). Dedicated gateway for query routing. SLA-backed 99.999% read availability globally.
Azure Cosmos DB.code:
# Create Cosmos DB account
az cosmosdb create \
  --name my-cosmos \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --kind GlobalDocumentDB \
  --locations regionName=eastus failoverPriority=0 \
  --locations regionName=westus failoverPriority=1 \
  --enable-multiple-write-locations true \
  --default-consistency-level Session

# Create database and container
az cosmosdb sql database create --account-name my-cosmos --resource-group my-rg --name my-db
az cosmosdb sql container create \
  --account-name my-cosmos \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --database-name my-db \
  --name users \
  --partition-key-path "/userId" \
  --throughput 1000

# Query (NoSQL API)
# SELECT * FROM users u WHERE u.city = 'NYC'
# SELECT u.id, u.name FROM users u ORDER BY u.createdAt OFFSET 10 LIMIT 20

Azure Cache for Redis.exp: Azure Cache for Redis is managed Redis. Tiers: Basic (single node, dev/test, no SLA), Standard (replicated, 99.9% SLA), Premium (persistence, clustering, VNet, 99.95% SLA), Enterprise (Redis Enterprise, active geo-replication, modules: RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries, RedisBloom), Enterprise Flash (tiered storage, lower cost). Redis Cluster splits data across shards. Persistence: RDB (snapshots) or AOF (write-ahead log). Data eviction policies (LRU, TTL, LFU, random). Geo-replication for DR. Private endpoint for secure access.
Azure Cache for Redis.code:
# Create Redis cache
az redis create \
  --name my-redis \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --sku Premium \
  --vm-size P1 \
  --enable-non-ssl-port \
  --minimum-tls-version 1.2

# Get connection string
az redis show --name my-redis --resource-group my-rg --query "hostName"

# Connect via redis-cli
# redis-cli -h my-redis.redis.cache.windows.net -p 6380 -a AccessKey --tls

# Enterprise (RediSearch)
# FT.CREATE idx ON HASH PREFIX 1 "product:" SCHEMA name TEXT price NUMERIC
# FT.SEARCH idx "@name:laptop*" SORTBY price DESC LIMIT 0 10

Azure Virtual Network.exp: Azure VNet is your isolated network in Azure. Address space defined by CIDR. Subnets segment the VNet; each subnet can have a Network Security Group (NSG) with allow/deny rules. Azure Bastion provides RDP/SSH without public IPs. Service Endpoints connect PaaS services privately via Microsoft backbone. Private Link exposes services privately from your VNet (like your own service behind a private IP). VNet Peering connects VNets within same region (low latency). Global VNet Peering connects across regions. VPN Gateway connects on-premises via IPsec. ExpressRoute is dedicated private connection to Azure.
Azure Virtual Network.code:
# Create VNet
az network vnet create \
  --name my-vnet \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16 \
  --subnet-name web-subnet \
  --subnet-prefix 10.0.1.0/24

# Create additional subnet
az network vnet subnet create \
  --vnet-name my-vnet \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --name data-subnet \
  --address-prefix 10.0.2.0/24

# NSG with rules
az network nsg create --name web-nsg --resource-group my-rg
az network nsg rule create --nsg-name web-nsg --resource-group my-rg --name AllowHTTPS \
  --priority 100 --destination-port-ranges 443 --protocol Tcp --access Allow

# VNet Peering
az network vnet peering create --name peer1 --resource-group my-rg --vnet-name my-vnet --remote-vnet vnet-yyy --allow-vnet-access

# Private Link (for PaaS)
az network private-link-service create --name my-pls --resource-group my-rg --vnet-name my-vnet --subnet data-subnet

Azure Load Balancer & Traffic Manager.exp: Azure Load Balancer (L4): distributes TCP/UDP traffic across VMs. SKUs: Basic (no HA, no SLA) and Standard (99.99% SLA, availability zones, HA ports, outbound rules). Inbound NAT rules for direct VM access. Backend pools: VMs, VMSS, IP addresses. Health probes check endpoint health. Azure Application Gateway (L7): HTTP/HTTPS load balancer with WAF, URL-based routing, SSL termination, session affinity, rewrite rules. Traffic Manager: DNS-based traffic routing (performance, geographic, priority, weighted, multi-value). Azure DNS hosts domains.
Azure Load Balancer & Traffic Manager.code:
# Create Standard Load Balancer
az network lb create \
  --name my-lb \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku Standard \
  --frontend-ip-name my-frontend \
  --backend-pool-name my-backend \
  --public-ip-address my-pip

# Health probe
az network lb probe create --lb-name my-lb --resource-group my-rg --name http-probe --protocol Tcp --port 80

# Load balancing rule
az network lb rule create --lb-name my-lb --resource-group my-rg --name http-rule \
  --protocol Tcp --frontend-port 80 --backend-port 80 \
  --frontend-ip-name my-frontend --backend-pool-name my-backend \
  --probe-name http-probe

# Application Gateway (L7)
az network application-gateway create --name my-appgw --resource-group my-rg --sku WAF_v2 \
  --capacity 2 --vnet-name my-vnet --subnet appgw-subnet \
  --frontend-port 443 --http-settings-port 80 --http-settings-protocol Http \
  --public-ip-address my-pip

# Traffic Manager
az network traffic-manager profile create --name my-tm --resource-group my-rg --routing-method Performance

Azure DNS & Private DNS.exp: Azure DNS hosts domains and provides name resolution. Authoritative DNS — no need to buy a separate DNS provider. Alias records map to Azure resources (free, zone apex support). Private DNS zones resolve names within VNets without public DNS. Auto-registration of VMs in Private DNS. Conditional forwarding for hybrid networks. Azure DDoS Protection (Basic: free, automatic; Standard: $3k/mo, advanced mitigation, analytics, DRT). Network Watcher monitors and diagnoses network issues (topology, IP flow verify, next hop, packet capture, VPN troubleshoot, connection monitor).
Azure DNS & Private DNS.code:
# Create DNS zone
az network dns zone create --resource-group my-rg --name example.com

# Create record
az network dns record-set a add-record \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --zone-name example.com \
  --record-set-name www \
  --ipv4-address 203.0.113.10

# Alias record (points to Azure resource)
az network dns record-set a create --resource-group my-rg --zone-name example.com --name api --target-resource /subscriptions/.../frontdoors/my-afd

# Private DNS zone
az network private-dns zone create --resource-group my-rg --name internal.contoso.com
az network private-dns link vnet create --zone-name internal.contoso.com --name my-link --virtual-network my-vnet --registration-enabled true

# Network Watcher (flow logs)
az network watcher flow-log create --nsg web-nsg --resource-group my-rg --workspace my-workspace --traffic-analytics true

Azure Security Center & Defender.exp: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center + Defender for Cloud) provides unified security management. Defender plans: Defender for Servers, Databases, Storage, Containers, Key Vault, App Service, SQL, DNS, Resource Manager. Key Vault stores secrets, keys, and certificates with HSM option. Access policies vs RBAC. Soft delete and purge protection. Azure Policy for compliance (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001). Sentinel is cloud-native SIEM (Microsoft's Splunk alternative). Secure Score measures security posture. Just-in-Time (JIT) VM access for temporary admin.
Azure Security Center & Defender.code:
# Key Vault
az keyvault create --name my-kv --resource-group my-rg --location eastus --sku Standard

# Store secret
az keyvault secret set --vault-name my-kv --name db-password --value "P@ssw0rd!"

# Grant VM access via managed identity
az keyvault set-policy --name my-kv --object-id $(az vm show --name my-vm --resource-group my-rg --query identity.principalId -o tsv) --secret-permissions get list

# Enable Defender for Cloud (via Portal)
# - Go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud
# - Enable Defender plans
# - Configure email notifications
# - Review Secure Score

# Just-in-Time VM access
az security jit-policy create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --vm-name my-vm \
  --port 22 --protocol Tcp --max-request-access-duration 3h --allowed-source-address-prefixes "203.0.113.0/24"

ARM & Bicep.exp: ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep (DSL, compiles to ARM) are Azure's IaC. Bicep is simpler: concise syntax, module support, intellisense, idempotent deployments. Resources reference each other via symbolic names. Modules decompose infrastructure into reusable files. Parameters, variables, outputs. Conditions and loops for conditional/count-based resources. Deployment scopes: resource group, subscription, management group. What-If shows changes before applying. Deployment stacks manage groups of resources as a single unit.
ARM & Bicep.code:
# Bicep template (main.bicep)
param location string = resourceGroup().location
param envName string = 'production'

var uniqueName = 'app-${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}'

resource storage 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-01-01' = {
  name: uniqueName
  location: location
  kind: 'StorageV2'
  sku: { name: 'Standard_GRS' }
  tags: { Environment: envName }
}

output storageEndpoint string = storage.properties.primaryEndpoints.blob

# Deploy
az deployment group create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters envName=staging

# What-If (preview changes)
az deployment group what-if --resource-group my-rg --template-file main.bicep

# Module (storage.bicep)
# resource stg ...
# output endpoint string = stg.properties.primaryEndpoints.blob
# 
# main.bicep: module stg 'storage.bicep' = { name: 'storageDeploy' }

Azure DevOps Pipelines.exp: Azure DevOps provides CI/CD with Pipelines (build/test/deploy), Repos (Git), Boards (work tracking), Test Plans, Artifacts (package feeds). YAML pipelines define stages (sequential), jobs (parallel per stage), steps (tasks). Multi-stage: Build → Test → Deploy to staging → Approve → Deploy to production. Environments track deployments with approvals and checks. Service connections to Azure, GitHub, Docker, etc. Self-hosted agents run in your network. Variable groups and library for secrets. Integration with GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab.
Azure DevOps Pipelines.code:
# azure-pipelines.yml
trigger:
  branches:
    include: [main]

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

stages:
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: BuildJob
    steps:
    - task: NodeTool@0
      inputs:
        versionSpec: '20.x'
    - script: |
        npm install
        npm run build
      displayName: 'Build app'
    - task: PublishBuildArtifacts@1
      inputs:
        PathtoPublish: 'dist'
        ArtifactName: 'drop'

- stage: Deploy
  jobs:
  - deployment: DeployToWeb
    environment: 'production'
    strategy:
      runOnce:
        deploy:
          steps:
          - task: AzureWebApp@1
            inputs:
              azureSubscription: 'my-connection'
              appName: 'my-app'
              package: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop/**/*.zip'

Azure Monitor.exp: Azure Monitor collects and analyzes telemetry from Azure resources. Log Analytics workspaces store logs and metrics. Kusto Query Language (KQL) queries logs (like SQL for logs). Application Insights monitors live web apps (request rates, response times, failure rates, dependency tracking, distributed tracing, user behavior analytics). Smart detection highlights anomalies. Metrics Explorer visualizes numeric data. Alerts: metric, log, activity log, smart groups. Action groups send email, SMS, webhook, ITSM. Workbooks are interactive reports (parameterized, multi-visualization). Managed Grafana for dashboards.
Azure Monitor.code:
# Create Log Analytics workspace
az monitor log-analytics workspace create \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --workspace-name my-logs

# Application Insights
az monitor app-insights component create \
  --app my-app \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --kind web

# KQL queries (run in Log Analytics)
# // VM CPU over 90% in last hour
# InsightsMetrics
# | where Name == 'Percentage CPU'
# | where Val > 90
# | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Val
# | sort by TimeGenerated desc

# // Failed requests in last 24h
# requests
# | where timestamp > ago(24h)
# | where success == false
# | summarize failureCount=count() by name, resultCode
# | top 10 by failureCount desc

Azure Automation & Logic Apps.exp: Azure Automation automates repetitive tasks: VM start/stop, patch management, configuration management. Runbooks (PowerShell, Python) execute on schedule or via webhook. Update Management assesses and installs OS updates. Change Tracking detects configuration changes. Desired State Configuration (DSC) enforces VM config state. Logic Apps are serverless workflows (visual designer, 400+ connectors). Triggers: HTTP, schedule, Azure services. Actions: condition, switch, parallel branches, loops. Enterprise integration: AS2, EDIFACT, X12, RosettaNet.

Azure DevOps.exp: Azure DevOps provides CI/CD with Pipelines (build/test/deploy), Repos (Git), Boards (work tracking), Test Plans, Artifacts (package feeds). YAML pipelines define stages (sequential), jobs (parallel per stage), steps (tasks). Multi-stage: Build to Test to Deploy with manual approval gates. Environments track deployments with approvals and checks. Service connections to Azure, GitHub, Docker. Self-hosted agents run in your network for custom dependencies. Variable groups and library for secrets. Common mistake: hardcoding secrets in pipelines — use Azure Key Vault integration or variable group secrets.
Azure DevOps.code:
# azure-pipelines.yml (multi-stage)
trigger:
  branches:
    include: [main]

variables:
  - group: production-vars
  - name: buildConfig
    value: Release

stages:
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: BuildJob
    steps:
    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      inputs:
        command: build
        arguments: --configuration $(buildConfig)
    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      inputs:
        command: test
    - task: PublishBuildArtifacts@1
      inputs:
        PathtoPublish: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)'
        ArtifactName: 'drop'

- stage: DeployStaging
  dependsOn: Build
  condition: succeeded()
  jobs:
  - deployment: DeployToStaging
    environment: staging
    strategy:
      runOnce:
        deploy:
          steps:
          - task: AzureWebApp@1
            inputs:
              azureSubscription: 'my-connection'
              appName: 'my-app-staging'
              package: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop/**/*.zip'

- stage: DeployProduction
  dependsOn: DeployStaging
  condition: succeeded()
  jobs:
  - deployment: DeployToProduction
    environment: production
    strategy:
      rolling:
        deploy:
          steps:
          - task: AzureWebApp@1
            inputs:
              azureSubscription: 'my-connection'
              appName: 'my-app'
              package: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop/**/*.zip'

Azure Key Vault.exp: Key Vault stores secrets, encryption keys, and certificates. Soft delete (enabled by default) retains deleted items for retention period (90 days default). Purge protection prevents permanent deletion. Managed Identities (system-assigned or user-assigned) let Azure resources (VMs, App Services, Functions) authenticate to Key Vault without credentials. RBAC for Key Vault uses Azure RBAC (data plane) — preferred over access policies for modern setups. Key Vault Firewall restricts access by IP and VNet. Key rotation can be automated with Event Grid + Functions. Common mistake: storing secrets in code or config files instead of Key Vault. Enable diagnostics logs to audit secret access.
Azure Key Vault.code:
# Create Key Vault with RBAC authorization
az keyvault create --name my-kv --resource-group my-rg --location eastus --sku Standard --enable-rbac-authorization

# Assign role (grant VM access to secrets)
az role assignment create \
  --assignee $(az vm show --name my-vm --resource-group my-rg --query identity.principalId -o tsv) \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/my-kv

# Store and retrieve a secret
az keyvault secret set --vault-name my-kv --name db-password --value "P@ssw0rd!"
az keyvault secret show --vault-name my-kv --name db-password

# Create and import a key
az keyvault key create --vault-name my-kv --name my-rsa-key --protection software
# az keyvault key import --vault-name my-kv --name my-key --byok-file ./key.pem

# Certificate operations
az keyvault certificate create --vault-name my-kv --name my-cert --policy @policy.json

# Enable soft delete and purge protection
az keyvault update --name my-kv --enable-soft-delete true --enable-purge-protection true

# Diagnostics (send logs to workspace)
az monitor diagnostic-settings create --resource my-kv --workspace my-logs --metrics '[{"category": "AllMetrics", "enabled": true}]'

Azure Logic Apps.exp: Logic Apps are serverless workflows with a visual designer and 400+ connectors. Triggers: HTTP request, schedule (recurrence), Azure services (Blob created, Event Grid), SaaS (Salesforce, Slack). Actions: condition, switch, parallel branches, loops (forEach, until), compose/parse JSON. Managed connectors: Office 365, SharePoint, Dynamics 365, Service Bus, SQL Server. Integration Account for enterprise B2B (AS2, EDIFACT, X12, RosettaNet). Built-in connectors run natively for higher performance. Common mistake: not handling transient failures — configure retry policies on actions. Consumption plan (pay per action) vs Standard plan (dedicated, better performance, VNet integration).

Azure Event Grid.exp: Event Grid is a fully managed event routing service. Events are JSON payloads describing what happened. Topics: system topics (Azure service events like Blob Created, VM Deleted) and custom topics (your own events). Subscriptions: push to Event Handlers (Functions, Webhooks, Service Bus, Queue Storage, Hybrid Connections, Logic Apps). Event filtering by event type, subject prefix/suffix, or advanced filters (numeric ranges, boolean, string contains). Retry policy: exponential backoff (up to 30 days). Dead-letter destination for failed events. Common mistake: forgetting to validate webhook endpoints (Event Grid requires endpoint validation handshake). Up to 10M events/sec per region.
Azure Event Grid.code:
# Create custom topic
az eventgrid topic create --name my-topic --resource-group my-rg --location eastus

# Create subscription (Event Hub endpoint)
az eventgrid event-subscription create \
  --name my-sub \
  --source-resource-id /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.EventGrid/topics/my-topic \
  --endpoint-type eventhub \
  --endpoint /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.EventHub/namespaces/my-eh/eventhubs/my-hub

# Create subscription with advanced filtering
az eventgrid event-subscription create \
  --name filtered-sub \
  --source-resource-id /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.EventGrid/topics/my-topic \
  --endpoint-type webhook \
  --endpoint https://my-app.azurewebsites.net/api/events \
  --advanced-filter data.orderStatus stringin shipped delivered \
  --advanced-filter data.total numberinrange 100 10000 \
  --deadletter-endpoint /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/my-storage/blobServices/default/containers/deadletter

# Publish custom event
az eventgrid event-subscription create --name my-sub --source-resource-id /subscriptions/xxx/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.EventGrid/topics/my-topic \
  --endpoint https://my-app.azurewebsites.net/api/events

# Publish event (using curl)
# curl -X POST https://my-topic.eastus-1.eventgrid.azure.net/api/events \
#   -H "aeg-sas-key: xxx" \
#   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
#   -d '[{"id": "1", "eventType": "order.created", "subject": "orders/123", "data": {"orderId": "123", "total": 99.99}, "dataVersion": "1.0"}]'

# Webhook endpoint validation (must respond)
# Return validation code in response body: {"validationResponse": "<code>"}

API Management.exp: API Management (APIM) publishes APIs to external and internal consumers. Products group APIs with access rules and rate limits. Subscriptions: product access keys for developers. Policies: XML-based transformation, validation, rate limiting, CORS, caching, IP filtering, JWT validation. Policy scopes: global, product, API, operation. Versioning: URL-based or header-based version schemes. Multiple deployment regions for low latency. Self-hosted gateway for on-prem/hybrid. Developer portal for API documentation and testing. Common mistake: exposing backend implementation details — use policies to transform requests/responses. Enable diagnostic logging for monitoring API usage and errors.
API Management.code:
# Create APIM instance
az apim create --name my-apim --resource-group my-rg --location eastus --publisher-name MyCompany --publisher-email admin@company.com --sku-name Developer

# Import API from OpenAPI/Swagger
az apim api import --resource-group my-rg --service-name my-apim \
  --path /api --api-id my-api \
  --specification-format OpenApi --specification-url https://my-app.azurewebsites.net/swagger/v1/swagger.json

# Create product
az apim product create --resource-group my-rg --service-name my-apim \
  --product-id gold-tier --product-name "Gold Tier" --description "Premium API access" \
  --subscription-required true --approval-required true --subscriptions-limit 5 --state published

# Add API to product
az apim product api add --resource-group my-rg --service-name my-apim --product-id gold-tier --api-id my-api

# Policy example (rate limiting + CORS)
# <policies>
#   <inbound>
#     <cors allow-credentials="true">
#       <allowed-origins><origin>https://myapp.com</origin></allowed-origins>
#       <allowed-methods><method>GET</method><method>POST</method></allowed-methods>
#     </cors>
#     <rate-limit calls="100" renewal-period="60" />
#     <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401">
#       <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/xxx/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
#     </validate-jwt>
#   </inbound>
#   <backend>
#     <base />
#   </backend>
#   <outbound>
#     <base />
#   </outbound>
# </policies>

# Set policy on API
# az apim api policy set --resource-group my-rg --service-name my-apim --api-id my-api --policy-format xml --policy-path @policy.xml

How the Internet Works.exp: The internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standardized protocols. Data is broken into packets, routed through multiple nodes, and reassembled at the destination. Key concepts include IP addresses, DNS, TCP/IP, and the client-server model.

What is HTTP.exp: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of data communication on the web. It's a request-response protocol where clients send requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to servers, which return status codes (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error) and response bodies.

DNS & How It Works.exp: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (142.250.190.46). It's a hierarchical system with root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative nameservers. DNS resolution involves recursive queries that cache results for performance.

What is Hosting.exp: Web hosting is a service that stores your website files on a server and makes them accessible via the internet. Types include shared hosting (multiple sites on one server), VPS (virtual private server), dedicated hosting (physical server for one client), and cloud hosting (scalable resources across multiple servers).

Browsers & How They Work.exp: Browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) are user agents that fetch, render, and display web content. The browser engine parses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, constructs the DOM and CSSOM trees, performs layout calculations, and paints pixels to screen. Key components include the rendering engine, JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey), and networking stack.

What is a Domain Name.exp: A domain name is a unique, human-readable address that identifies a website on the internet. Domain structure includes TLD (top-level domain like .com, .org), second-level domain (the name you choose), and subdomains (like www or blog). Domains are registered through registrars and must be renewed periodically.

Git Basics.exp: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code during development. It allows multiple developers to work simultaneously, maintains a complete history of changes, and enables branching/merging. Key concepts: repositories, commits, branches, staging area, and remote tracking.
Git Basics.code:
git init                    # Initialize a new repo
git add .                    # Stage all changes
git commit -m "message"     # Commit staged changes
git branch feature          # Create a branch
git checkout feature        # Switch to branch
git merge feature           # Merge branch into current
git log --oneline           # View commit history

GitHub.exp: GitHub is a cloud-based platform for hosting Git repositories. It provides collaboration features like pull requests, code reviews, issue tracking, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, GitHub Pages for static hosting, and project management tools. It's the largest host of source code worldwide, owned by Microsoft.
GitHub.code:
# Typical GitHub workflow:
# 1. Fork a repository
# 2. Clone to local machine
# 3. Create a feature branch
# 4. Make changes and commit
# 5. Push to your fork
# 6. Open a Pull Request
# 7. Code review and discussion
# 8. Merge to main branch

GitLab.exp: GitLab is a DevOps platform that provides Git repository management, CI/CD pipelines, container registry, and project planning tools. It offers both cloud-hosted (GitLab.com) and self-managed (GitLab CE/EE) options. Key differentiators: built-in CI/CD with .gitlab-ci.yml, auto DevOps, and integrated monitoring.
GitLab.code:
// .gitlab-ci.yml example:
stages:
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm install
    - npm test

build-image:
  stage: build
  script:
    - docker build -t myapp .

Repo Hosting Services.exp: Beyond GitHub and GitLab, other repository hosting services include Bitbucket (Atlassian, integrates with Jira), SourceForge (one of the oldest), and self-hosted options like Gitea and Gogs. Each offers varying features for code review, access control, and integrations with CI/CD and project management tools.
Repo Hosting Services.code:
# Choosing a hosting service:
# GitHub:   Largest community, Actions, Pages
# GitLab:   Built-in CI/CD, self-hostable
# Bitbucket: Jira integration, free private repos
# Gitea:    Lightweight, self-hosted, open source

PostgreSQL.exp: PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source object-relational database known for reliability, feature robustness, and performance. It supports advanced data types, full-text search, JSON/JSONB, indexing (B-tree, Hash, GiST, GIN), transactions with ACID compliance, and extensibility through custom functions and extensions like PostGIS.

MySQL.exp: MySQL is a widely-used open-source relational database management system, popular for web applications (especially with LAMP/LEMP stacks). It offers InnoDB (transactional, foreign keys) and MyISAM (full-text search) storage engines, replication support, and strong performance for read-heavy workloads.
MySQL.code:
-- MySQL example
CREATE TABLE products (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    category_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (category_id) REFERENCES categories(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Index for fast lookup
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category
ON products(category_id);

SQL & Querying.exp: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing relational databases. Core operations include SELECT (retrieve), INSERT (add), UPDATE (modify), DELETE (remove). Advanced features include JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL), subqueries, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG), GROUP BY, HAVING, and window functions.
SQL & Querying.code:
-- Advanced SQL query
SELECT
    u.name,
    COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
    SUM(o.total) AS total_spent,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(o.total) DESC) AS rank
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id, u.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 5
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

Normalization.exp: Database normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. Normal forms include 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependencies), 3NF (no transitive dependencies), and BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Denormalization is sometimes used for read performance optimization.
Normalization.code:
-- Normalization example
-- UNNORMALIZED (0NF):
-- Orders: order_id, customer_name, items (comma-separated)

-- 1NF: Atomic values
-- OrderItems: order_id, customer_name, item_name

-- 2NF: Remove partial dependencies
-- Orders: order_id, customer_name
-- OrderItems: order_id, item_name

-- 3NF: Remove transitive dependencies
-- Orders: order_id, customer_id
-- Customers: customer_id, customer_name
-- OrderItems: order_id, item_name

ACID Transactions.exp: ACID is a set of properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data persists). Isolation levels range from Read Uncommitted (dirty reads) to Serializable (full isolation).

Database Indexes.exp: Indexes are data structures (B-tree, Hash, GiST) that speed up data retrieval at the cost of slower writes and increased storage. A primary key automatically gets a unique index. Composite indexes (multiple columns) must follow leftmost prefix rule. Use EXPLAIN to analyze query plans and find missing indexes.
Database Indexes.code:
-- Index creation strategies
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email);

-- Composite index (column order matters!)
CREATE INDEX idx_state_city
ON addresses(state, city);

-- This query uses the index:
SELECT * FROM addresses
WHERE state = 'CA' AND city = 'SF';

-- This might NOT use the index:
SELECT * FROM addresses
WHERE city = 'SF';  -- skips leftmost column

Sharding & Scaling.exp: Database scaling strategies include vertical scaling (more powerful hardware) and horizontal scaling (distributing data across multiple servers). Sharding partitions data across databases based on a shard key (e.g., user_id hash). Other approaches include read replicas for read-heavy workloads, and connection pooling for managing many concurrent connections.
Sharding & Scaling.code:
-- Sharding strategies:
-- Range-based: users 1-10000 on Shard A, 10001-20000 on Shard B
-- Hash-based: shard = hash(user_id) % N
-- Directory-based: lookup table maps keys to shards
-- Geographic: users in US on Shard US, EU on Shard EU

-- Challenges:
-- Cross-shard queries are expensive
-- Rebalancing when adding shards is hard
-- JOINs across shards require app-level logic

Database Design & Modeling.exp: Database design involves creating an efficient schema that represents the problem domain. Start with an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD), identify entities, attributes, and relationships (1:1, 1:M, M:N). Consider query patterns, access paths, and use cases. Tools like draw.io, dbdiagram.io, and MySQL Workbench help visualize schemas.
Database Design & Modeling.code:
-- Database design process:
-- 1. Requirements analysis
-- 2. Conceptual design (ERD)
-- 3. Logical design (schema)
-- 4. Physical design (indexes, partitions)
-- 5. Normalization review
-- 6. Performance optimization

-- Key questions:
-- What queries will be most frequent?
-- What's the read/write ratio?
-- What are the data growth patterns?

MongoDB.exp: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It uses a sharded cluster architecture for horizontal scaling, replica sets for high availability, and the aggregation pipeline for data processing. Best suited for flexible schemas, rapid iteration, and hierarchical data.

Redis.exp: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker. It supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and streams. Key features: sub-millisecond latency, pub/sub messaging, Lua scripting, persistence (RDB/AOF), and built-in replication. Ideal for caching, session storage, and real-time analytics.
Redis.code:
// Redis commands
SET user:1 '{"name":"Alice"}'
GET user:1
EXPIRE user:1 3600  # TTL 1 hour

// Data structures
LPUSH queue task1        # List
SADD tags:1 'backend'    # Set
ZADD leaderboard 1000 'Alice'  # Sorted Set

// Pub/Sub
SUBSCRIBE notifications
PUBLISH notifications 'New message'

Cassandra.exp: Apache Cassandra is a distributed NoSQL database designed for high availability and linear scalability with no single point of failure. It uses a peer-to-peer architecture, tunable consistency levels, and the Cassandra Query Language (CQL). Best for write-heavy workloads, time-series data, and applications requiring multi-region deployment.
Cassandra.code:
-- Cassandra CQL
CREATE TABLE user_timeline (
    user_id UUID,
    tweet_id TIMEUUID,
    content TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, tweet_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (tweet_id DESC);

-- Consistency levels:
-- ONE:        Fast but might read stale data
-- QUORUM:     Majority of replicas must respond
-- ALL:        All replicas must respond (slowest)
-- LOCAL_QUORUM: Quorum within a datacenter

Elasticsearch.exp: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It provides near-real-time full-text search, structured search, aggregations, and analytics. Data is stored as JSON documents in indexes, which are sharded across nodes. Commonly used for log analysis (ELK stack), application search, and observability.

REST APIs.exp: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources identified by URLs. REST APIs should be stateless, use proper HTTP status codes, and support pagination, filtering, and versioning.
REST APIs.code:
// REST API design
GET    /api/users          # List users
POST   /api/users          # Create user
GET    /api/users/:id      # Get user by ID
PUT    /api/users/:id      # Replace user
PATCH  /api/users/:id      # Update user fields
DELETE /api/users/:id      # Delete user

// Response
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com"
}

GraphQL.exp: GraphQL is a query language for APIs developed by Meta. Clients request exactly the data they need, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching. A single endpoint (/graphql) handles all operations. Type system defines the schema, resolvers fetch data from various sources. Supports queries, mutations, and subscriptions for real-time data.

gRPC.exp: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework by Google that uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport. It supports bidirectional streaming, flow control, and multiplexing. Service definitions are written in .proto files, generating client and server code in multiple languages. Ideal for microservices communication.

WebSockets.exp: WebSockets provide full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time data exchange. Unlike HTTP request-response, the server can push data to clients. Used for chat apps, live notifications, collaborative editing, and gaming. Libraries like Socket.IO add fallback transports and room management.

OpenAPI / Swagger.exp: OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a standard for describing REST APIs using a YAML or JSON specification. It defines endpoints, request/response schemas, authentication, and error codes. Tools like Swagger UI generate interactive documentation, and code generators create client SDKs and server stubs automatically.
OpenAPI / Swagger.code:
# OpenAPI 3.0 specification
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: List all users
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful response
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'

JWT (JSON Web Tokens).exp: JWT is a compact, URL-safe token format for transmitting claims between parties. It consists of three parts: header (algorithm, type), payload (claims like user_id, role, exp), and signature (verified with a secret or key pair). JWTs are stateless — the server doesn't need to store session data, but they can't be revoked without a blocklist.

OAuth 2.0.exp: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows third-party apps to access user data without sharing passwords. It involves authorization server, resource server, and client. Grant types include Authorization Code (most common), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), Implicit (legacy), and Refresh Token. Used by Google, GitHub, and Facebook login systems.

Basic Authentication.exp: Basic Authentication is the simplest HTTP authentication method. The client sends the username and password encoded in Base64 in the Authorization header. It's insecure over plain HTTP (easily decoded) and should only be used over HTTPS. Typically paired with session tokens or API keys for modern applications.

Session & Cookie Auth.exp: Session-based authentication uses server-side sessions identified by a cookie. When a user logs in, the server creates a session, stores it (in memory, Redis, or database), and sends the session ID as a cookie. The browser sends the cookie with each request. Provides easy revocation (delete the session) but requires server-side storage.

API Security Best Practices.exp: API security involves multiple layers: rate limiting (prevent abuse), input validation (sanitize all inputs), HTTPS everywhere, proper authentication/authorization (least privilege principle), CORS configuration, request size limits, SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries), XSS protection, CSRF tokens, and security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options).
API Security Best Practices.code:
# API security checklist:
# [ ] HTTPS enforced (HSTS header)
# [ ] Rate limiting (100 req/min per user)
# [ ] Input validation & sanitization
# [ ] Parameterized queries (no raw SQL)
# [ ] CORS whitelist (not *)
# [ ] Authentication on all endpoints
# [ ] Role-based access control (RBAC)
# [ ] Audit logging
# [ ] Security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options)
# [ ] Request size limits

Caching Strategies.exp: Caching stores frequently accessed data in a fast storage layer to reduce latency and database load. Common strategies include: Cache-Aside (application checks cache first), Read-Through (cache layer fetches from DB on miss), Write-Through (write to cache AND DB simultaneously), Write-Behind (async write to DB), and Cache Eviction policies (LRU, TTL, FIFO).

Redis as Cache.exp: Redis is the most popular caching solution due to its in-memory performance and rich data structures. Common caching patterns include: session storage, database query result caching, page caching (full HTML), rate limiting counters, leaderboards, and distributed locks. Redis Cluster provides automatic sharding for large-scale deployments.

Content Delivery Networks.exp: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a distributed network of servers that delivers cached static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) from locations geographically closer to users. Leading providers include Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, and Akamai. CDNs reduce latency, offload origin servers, and provide DDoS protection. Dynamic content can also be accelerated through edge computing.
Content Delivery Networks.code:
# CDN workflow:
# 1. User requests example.com/image.png
# 2. DNS resolves to nearest CDN edge server
# 3. Edge server checks cache
# 4. Cache HIT -> Serve directly
# 5. Cache MISS -> Fetch from origin, cache, serve
# 6. Subsequent requests are fast!

# Cache-Control headers control behavior:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

HTTP Caching.exp: HTTP caching allows browsers and proxies to store responses and reuse them. Cache-Control directives (max-age, no-cache, no-store, public, private) and ETags/Last-Modified headers control caching behavior. Conditional requests with If-None-Match (ETag) or If-Modified-Since allow servers to return 304 Not Modified instead of full responses, saving bandwidth.
HTTP Caching.code:
# HTTP caching headers

# Strong caching (browser caches for 1 year)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Validate with server each time
Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: "abc123"

# Never cache sensitive data
Cache-Control: no-store, private

# Conditional request (browser sends)
If-None-Match: "abc123"
# Server responds:
# 304 Not Modified (no body) -- or --
# 200 OK with new content

Nginx.exp: Nginx is a high-performance web server, reverse proxy, load balancer, and HTTP cache. It uses an event-driven, asynchronous architecture that handles thousands of concurrent connections with low memory usage. Common use cases: serving static files, reverse proxying to application servers, SSL termination, rate limiting, and as a gateway for microservices.

Apache.exp: Apache HTTP Server is one of the oldest and most widely-used web servers. It uses a process-based (prefork) or threaded (worker/event) MPM architecture. Configuration is done through .htaccess files (per-directory) and httpd.conf. Supports modules for rewrites (mod_rewrite), SSL (mod_ssl), authentication, caching, and proxying.
Apache.code:
# Apache virtual host
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    Redirect permanent / https://example.com/
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html

    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/ssl/certs/example.crt
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/private/example.key

    <Directory /var/www/html>
        AllowOverride All
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>

Reverse Proxy.exp: A reverse proxy sits between clients and backend servers, forwarding requests and returning responses. Benefits include: load balancing across multiple servers, SSL termination (offloading encryption), caching static content, compression, rate limiting, and hiding backend server topology. Both Nginx and HAProxy are common reverse proxy solutions.

Unit Testing.exp: Unit testing validates individual components (functions, methods, classes) in isolation. Tests should be fast, deterministic, and independent. Follow the AAA pattern: Arrange (set up), Act (execute), Assert (verify). Mock external dependencies. Aim for high coverage on critical business logic. Use test runners like Jest, pytest, JUnit, or Go test.

Integration Testing.exp: Integration testing verifies that different components work together correctly — database queries, API endpoints, file I/O, and third-party service interactions. Unlike unit tests, integration tests use real (or containerized) dependencies. Test the boundary between your code and external systems. Use test databases and clean up data between tests.

API / E2E Testing.exp: End-to-end testing validates the entire system from the user's perspective. For backend APIs, this means sending real HTTP requests and verifying responses, status codes, headers, and side effects. Tools like Supertest (Node.js), pytest + requests (Python), REST Assured (Java), and Postman/Newman automate API testing.

Docker.exp: Docker packages applications and dependencies into lightweight, portable containers that run consistently across environments. Images are built from Dockerfiles using layered filesystems. Key concepts: Dockerfile (build instructions), images (read-only templates), containers (running instances), volumes (persistent data), networks (container communication), and Docker Compose (multi-container apps).
Docker.code:
# Dockerfile example
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

Docker Compose.exp: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file. Each service specifies its image, ports, volumes, environment variables, and dependencies. Compose handles network creation, service discovery, and startup ordering. Essential for local development environments with multiple services (app + database + cache + queue).
Docker Compose.code:
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/myapp

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  pgdata:

Kubernetes Basics.exp: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Key concepts: Pods (smallest deployable unit), Deployments (declarative updates), Services (networking abstraction), ConfigMaps/Secrets (configuration), and Ingress (external access). Kubectl is the command-line tool.
Kubernetes Basics.code:
# Kubernetes manifests
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: myapp
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000

RabbitMQ.exp: RabbitMQ is a message broker implementing AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). Producers send messages to exchanges, which route them to queues based on bindings and routing keys. Consumers process messages from queues. Supports multiple exchange types: direct, topic, fanout, and headers. Offers message durability, acknowledgments, and dead-letter queues for reliability.

Apache Kafka.exp: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant data pipelines. Topics are partitioned and replicated across brokers. Producers write events, consumers read from offsets. Unlike RabbitMQ, Kafka persists all messages for a configurable retention period. Used for event sourcing, log aggregation, stream processing, and data integration at scale.
Apache Kafka.code:
# Kafka concepts
# Topic:  A category/feed name (e.g., "orders")
# Partition: Ordered, immutable sequence of records
# Offset:  Unique ID of a record within a partition
# Broker:  A Kafka server in the cluster
# Consumer Group: Group of consumers sharing work

# CLI commands
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders
kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders --from-beginning --group my-group

Message Queue Patterns.exp: Common messaging patterns include: Work Queues (competing consumers distribute tasks), Pub/Sub (one-to-many broadcast), RPC (request-response over queue), Event Sourcing (storing events as authoritative state), CQRS (separate read/write models), Saga Pattern (distributed transactions via compensating actions), and Dead Letter Queues (failed message handling).
Message Queue Patterns.code:
# Common messaging patterns

# 1. Work Queue (Task distribution)
# Multiple consumers compete for messages
# Each message processed exactly once

# 2. Pub/Sub (Broadcast)
# One message -> multiple consumers
# Each consumer gets every message

# 3. Saga (Distributed transaction)
# Order Service: Create order -> publish OrderCreated
# Payment Service: Consume -> process payment -> publish PaymentProcessed
# Inventory Service: Consume -> reserve items -> publish InventoryReserved
# If any step fails, compensating events undo previous steps

Logging.exp: Logging records application events for debugging, auditing, and monitoring. Structured logging (JSON format) enables machine parsing and search. Log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) control verbosity. Centralized logging with tools like ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Loki + Grafana aggregates logs from multiple services. Avoid logging sensitive data.

Metrics & Monitoring.exp: Metrics are numerical measurements of system health and performance collected over time. Key categories: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources. Common metrics: request latency (p50, p95, p99), error rates, throughput, CPU/memory usage, and database query times. Prometheus collects metrics; Grafana visualizes them.
Metrics & Monitoring.code:
# RED Method for services:
# Rate:     Requests per second
# Errors:   Failed requests / total requests
# Duration: Latency distribution (p50, p95, p99)

# USE Method for resources:
# Utilization:  % time resource is busy
# Saturation:   Queue length / contention
# Errors:       Count of error events

# Prometheus query examples:
# Request rate: rate(http_requests_total[5m])
# Error ratio:  sum(rate(http_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# P99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

Distributed Tracing.exp: Distributed tracing tracks requests as they flow through multiple services in a microservices architecture. Each request gets a trace ID, and each span represents a unit of work. Tools like Jaeger, Zipkin, and OpenTelemetry provide end-to-end visibility. Helpful for identifying latency bottlenecks, error propagation, and service dependencies.

Application Performance Monitoring.exp: APM tools provide comprehensive monitoring of application performance, including transaction traces, dependency maps, error tracking, and real-user monitoring. Popular solutions include Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, and open-source alternatives like SigNoz and Grafana Faro. APM helps identify slow queries, memory leaks, N+1 problems, and external service degradation.
Application Performance Monitoring.code:
# What APM tracks:
# - Transaction traces (end-to-end request paths)
# - Database query performance
# - External API call latencies
# - Error rates and stack traces
# - Memory and CPU profiles
# - Garbage collection patterns
# - Slow code paths (hotspots)
# - Service dependency maps
# - Real user experience (RUM)

Continuous Integration.exp: CI automatically builds and tests every code change to detect integration issues early. Developers merge changes frequently (multiple times daily) into a shared branch. CI servers run automated tests, linting, type checking, and security scans. Failures are reported immediately. Tools include GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, and Travis CI.
Continuous Integration.code:
# GitHub Actions CI workflow
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

Continuous Deployment.exp: CD automatically deploys validated code changes to production (or staging) environments. The deployment pipeline includes building artifacts, running integration tests, deploying to staging, running smoke tests, and promoting to production with strategies like blue-green (two identical environments) or canary (gradual rollout). Rollbacks should be fast and reliable.
Continuous Deployment.code:
# CD deployment strategies

# Blue-Green:
# Blue = current production
# Green = new version
# Switch load balancer from Blue to Green
# Rollback: switch back to Blue

# Canary:
# Route 5% of traffic to new version
# Monitor error rates and latency
# Gradually increase to 25%, 50%, 100%
# Rollback: route 0% to canary

# Rolling:
# Update instances one-by-one
# Keep some running during update
# Rollback: redeploy previous version

Infrastructure as Code.exp: IaC manages infrastructure (servers, networks, databases) through machine-readable definition files, enabling version control, reproducibility, and automation. Tools include Terraform (multi-cloud provisioning), AWS CloudFormation, Pulumi (general-purpose languages), and Ansible (configuration management). IaC eliminates manual server configuration and drift between environments.

Microservices.exp: Microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, independent services that communicate over a network. Each service owns its data (database-per-service), can be deployed independently, and is built around a business capability. Benefits include: independent scaling, technology diversity, and smaller codebases. Challenges include: distributed complexity, data consistency, and service discovery.
Microservices.code:
# Microservices principles:
# - Single Responsibility (one business capability)
# - Database per Service (no shared databases)
# - API-first design (REST/gRPC for communication)
# - Independent deployability
# - Decentralized governance (teams choose tech)
# - Resilience (circuit breakers, retries)
# - Observability (logging, metrics, tracing)
# - Automation (CI/CD for each service)

Load Balancing.exp: Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to ensure reliability and performance. Types: DNS load balancing (round-robin), hardware load balancers (F5), software load balancers (HAProxy, Nginx), and cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/ELB, Google Cloud LB). Algorithms include round-robin, least connections, IP hash, and weighted distribution.

Database Scaling.exp: Scaling databases involves read replicas (offload read queries to copies), connection pooling (manage DB connections efficiently), caching layers (Redis/Memcached), partitioning (vertical/horizontal), and sharding. Read replicas improve read throughput but introduce eventual consistency. Connection poolers like PgBouncer manage thousands of concurrent connections efficiently.
Database Scaling.code:
# Database scaling strategies

# 1. Read Replicas
# Primary handles writes, replicas handle reads
# Eventually consistent (replication lag)

# 2. Connection Pooling
# PgBouncer: Lightweight connection pooler
# Maintains persistent connections to DB
# Apps borrow/release connections

# 3. Vertical Scaling
# Bigger instance (more CPU, RAM, IOPS)
# Simpler but has upper limits

# 4. Sharding
# Split data across multiple databases
# Each shard handles subset of data

Caching Architecture.exp: Multi-layer caching architecture: browser cache (private), CDN (edge cache), reverse proxy/load balancer (Nginx cache), application cache (in-memory), and database cache (buffer pool). Cache invalidation strategies include TTL-based (time to live), write-through (update cache and DB), write-behind (async), and event-driven invalidation (publish cache invalidation events).
Caching Architecture.code:
# Multi-layer caching
# Browser:         Cache-Control, ETag, Service Worker
# CDN:              Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront
# Reverse Proxy:    Nginx, Varnish (microcaching)
# Application:      Redis, Memcached
# Database:         InnoDB buffer pool, Query cache

# Cache invalidation strategies:
# TTL:        "This data expires in 5 minutes"
# Write-through: "Write to cache AND database"
# Write-behind:  "Write to cache, async write to DB"
# Event-based:   "Publish event when data changes, cache subscribes"

AI-Assisted Coding.exp: AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) use large language models to generate, refactor, and explain code. They integrate with IDEs and support context-aware completions, test generation, bug fixing, and code review. Best practices: provide clear context, review generated code, never blindly accept, and treat AI as a pair programmer, not a replacement.
AI-Assisted Coding.code:
# AI-assisted coding best practices:
# - Write clear comments and function names
# - Provide examples in the context
# - Break complex tasks into smaller prompts
# - Review generated code for correctness
# - Write tests first (AI generates implementations)
# - Use AI for boilerplate, refactoring, and docs
# - Never paste sensitive data into AI tools
# - Understand what AI generates - don't black-box

Building AI Features.exp: Backend developers integrate AI capabilities through API calls to LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) or self-hosted models (Llama, Mistral). Patterns include: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation — search documents + ask LLM), embeddings for semantic search, streaming responses for real-time chat, function calling for structured outputs, and AI agents for multi-step tasks.

Prompt Engineering.exp: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing input prompts to get desired outputs from LLMs. Techniques include: few-shot prompting (providing examples), chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning), system prompts (setting behavior/role), structured output constraints (JSON mode), and temperature control (creativity vs precision). Key for building reliable AI-powered backend features.
Prompt Engineering.code:

# System message (sets behavior)
You are a code reviewer. Analyze the following
code for bugs, security issues, and performance
problems. Respond in JSON format.

# Few-shot prompting (examples)

SQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 18
MQL: db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 18 } })

MQL:

Let's think step by step about whether this
query will use the index...

What is Bootstrap.exp: Bootstrap is the world's most popular front-end component library, providing a responsive grid system, pre-built UI components, and utility classes. It uses a mobile-first approach with 12-column grid, five responsive breakpoints (xs, sm, md, lg, xl), and Sass variables for customization. Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery dependency and uses vanilla JavaScript for interactive components.
What is Bootstrap.code: Hello, Bootstrap!

Grid System.exp: Bootstrap's grid uses flexbox with 12 columns across five breakpoints. Rows are wrappers for columns; columns specify width via col-{breakpoint}-{size}. Equal-width columns use col. Auto-layout with col-{breakpoint} adjusts per breakpoint. Nest rows inside columns. Offsets push columns right. Gutters control spacing via g-* classes.

What is C.exp: C is a low-level, statically typed language developed by Dennis Ritchie in 1972. It provides direct memory access, minimal runtime, and is the foundation for most operating systems, embedded systems, and virtually every modern language.

Hello World.exp: Every C program starts execution in `main()`. `#include <stdio.h>` brings in the standard I/O library. `printf()` prints formatted text. `return 0` signals success to the OS.

C Syntax & Structure.exp: C programs consist of functions. `main()` is the entry point. Statements end with semicolons. Blocks are enclosed in braces. `#include` directives include header files. C is case-sensitive and whitespace-insensitive.

Compilation Process.exp: C source code goes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking. `gcc` (GNU C Compiler) is the standard compiler. Use `-o` to name the output, `-Wall` for warnings, `-g` for debug symbols.
Compilation Process.code:
gcc -Wall -g -o program program.c
./program
# Or with multiple files
gcc -Wall -o program main.c helper.c -lm

Data Types.exp: Basic types: `int`, `char`, `float`, `double`, `void`. Modifiers: `short`, `long`, `signed`, `unsigned`. `sizeof()` returns bytes. Type sizes vary by platform (int is usually 4 bytes, char is always 1).

Comments.exp: C supports `//` single-line comments (C99+) and `/* */` multi-line comments. Comments are stripped by the preprocessor. Use comments to explain why, not what.

Variables & Assignment.exp: Variables must be declared with a type before use. Naming rules: letters, digits, underscores; cannot start with digit. Convention uses snake_case. Uninitialized local variables contain garbage values.

Constants & Literals.exp: Constants are fixed values that cannot be changed. Use `const` keyword or `#define` preprocessor. Integer, floating-point, character, and string literals. Suffixes: L (long), U (unsigned), F (float).

Scope & Lifetime.exp: Scope determines where a variable is accessible. Block scope `{}`, file scope (global), function scope. Lifetime: automatic (stack) vs static (program duration). Variables shadow outer scopes.

Storage Classes.exp: `auto` (default for locals), `register` (suggest CPU register), `static` (persists lifetime, limits scope), `extern` (declares variable defined elsewhere). `static` on globals limits to file.

Type Qualifiers.exp: `const` makes variable read-only. `volatile` tells compiler value may change externally (hardware registers, signal handlers). `restrict` promises no other pointer aliases the same memory.

Type Conversion.exp: Implicit conversion (type coercion) happens automatically: `int` -> `float` -> `double`. Explicit conversion (casting) uses `(type)` syntax. Promotion rules: values are promoted to the larger type.

typedef.exp: `typedef` creates type aliases for cleaner code. Commonly used with structs, function pointers, and complex types. Doesn't create new types — just aliases.

Arithmetic Operators.exp: Standard math: `+` addition, `-` subtraction, `*` multiplication, `/` division, `%` modulo (remainder). Integer division truncates toward zero. Mixing types causes implicit conversion.

Relational & Logical Operators.exp: Relational: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical: `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), `!` (NOT). C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. Short-circuit evaluation for && and ||.

Bitwise Operators.exp: Manipulate individual bits: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `~` NOT, `<<` left shift, `>>` right shift. Used for flags, hardware control, and performance optimization.
Bitwise Operators.code:
unsigned int a = 5;   // 0101
unsigned int b = 3;   // 0011
unsigned int c = a & b;  // 0001 = 1
unsigned int d = a | b;  // 0111 = 7
unsigned int e = a ^ b;  // 0110 = 6
unsigned int f = a << 1; // 1010 = 10

Assignment Operators.exp: Compound assignments: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`. More concise and can be more efficient than separate operation and assignment.
Assignment Operators.code:
int x = 10;
x += 5;   // x = 15
x *= 2;   // x = 30
x %= 7;   // x = 2

unsigned int flags = 0;
flags |= 0x01;  // set bit 0
flags &= ~0x01; // clear bit 0

sizeof, Ternary & Comma.exp: `sizeof` returns size in bytes (type or expression). Ternary `?:` is a compact if-else. Comma `,` evaluates both operands, returns the second. Useful in `for` loops.

Operator Precedence.exp: Precedence determines evaluation order. Postfix > Unary > Multiplicative > Additive > Shift > Relational > Equality > Bitwise AND > XOR > OR > Logical AND > OR > Ternary > Assignment > Comma. Use parentheses to clarify.

if / else if / else.exp: Conditional branching with `if`, `else if`, `else`. Conditions must be in parentheses. C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. No boolean type in early C — use `<stdbool.h>` for `bool`.

Switch Statement.exp: `switch` branches on integer/enum values. Each `case` must end with `break` to prevent fallthrough. `default` handles unmatched values. C23 allows `switch` on expression with multiple cases per label.

Loops: for, while, do-while.exp: `for` when count is known (init; condition; increment). `while` when condition-based. `do-while` runs body at least once. All loops can be nested. Watch for infinite loops and off-by-one errors.

break & continue.exp: `break` exits the innermost loop or switch immediately. `continue` skips rest of current iteration and goes to next. In nested loops, break only exits the innermost one.

goto & Labels.exp: `goto` jumps to a labeled statement in the same function. Generally discouraged for structured flow, but useful for breaking out of deeply nested loops or centralized error cleanup.

Infinite Loops & Pitfalls.exp: Common loop bugs: off-by-one (`<=` vs `<`), missing braces causing unintended body, using assignment `=` instead of comparison `==`, forgetting increment, and semicolon after `for` or `while`.

Function Declaration & Definition.exp: Functions must be declared before use (prototype) or defined first. Return type, name, parameter list with types. `void` for no return value or no parameters. K&R style is obsolete.

Pass by Value.exp: C passes arguments by value — functions receive copies. To modify variables in the caller, pass pointers. Arrays decay to pointers when passed. Structs are copied unless passed by pointer.

Return Values.exp: Functions return a value matching their declared return type. No value needed for `void`. Returned value can be ignored by caller. Never return pointer to local variable — use `static` or dynamic allocation.

Recursion.exp: A recursive function calls itself. Must have a base case to terminate. Stack memory is used for each call — deep recursion can cause stack overflow. Example: factorial, Fibonacci, tree traversal.

Inline Functions.exp: `inline` suggests the compiler replace function calls with the body code to avoid call overhead (C99). Compiler may ignore. Static inline in headers is common. Modern compilers auto-inline better than programmers.

Variadic Functions.exp: Functions with variable arguments use `<stdarg.h>`: `va_list`, `va_start()`, `va_arg()`, `va_end()`. At least one named parameter is required. No type safety — caller must provide correct types.

main() Arguments.exp: `int main(int argc, char *argv[])` receives command-line arguments. `argc` is argument count (program name is argv[0]). `argv` is array of strings. `getopt()` for parsing flags.

Pointer Basics.exp: Pointers store memory addresses. `&` gets address of variable. `*` dereferences (accesses value at address). `NULL` is a safe pointer value. Always initialize pointers. Size is platform-dependent (4 or 8 bytes).

Pointer Arithmetic.exp: Incrementing a pointer moves to the next element of its type: `ptr + n` adds `n * sizeof(type)` bytes. Arrays and pointers are closely related. Subtraction gives the number of elements between two pointers.

Pointers & Arrays.exp: Array name decays to pointer to first element. `arr[i]` is equivalent to `*(arr + i)`. The `[]` operator works on pointers too. But `sizeof(arr)` differs from `sizeof(ptr)` — arrays remember their size at compile time.

Pointer to Pointer.exp: `int **pp` stores address of an `int*`. Used for dynamic 2D arrays, modifying pointer arguments in functions, and arrays of strings. Can be chained arbitrarily deep.

Void Pointers.exp: `void*` is a generic pointer that can hold any address. Must be cast to a specific type before dereferencing. Used in generic functions like `malloc()`, `qsort()`, `memcpy()`. No pointer arithmetic on void*.

Function Pointers.exp: Function pointers store addresses of functions. Used for callbacks, strategy patterns, and dynamic dispatch. Syntax: `returnType (*name)(params)`. `qsort()` takes a comparator function pointer.

Dynamic Memory Allocation.exp: `malloc()` allocates on heap, `free()` releases it. `calloc()` allocates and zero-initializes. `realloc()` resizes. Always check for NULL return. Free to avoid leaks. Include `<stdlib.h>`.

Memory Leaks & Debugging.exp: A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is never freed. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`), leak sanitizer. Common issues: forgetting to free, losing the pointer, double free, use-after-free.

One-Dimensional Arrays.exp: Contiguous memory blocks of the same type. Fixed size determined at compile time. Index from 0. No bounds checking — buffer overflows are dangerous and a common security vulnerability.

Multidimensional Arrays.exp: Arrays of arrays stored in row-major order. `int matrix[rows][cols]`. Access with `matrix[r][c]`. Can be passed to functions with all dimensions except first specified.
