Array Initialization & Bounds.exp: Arrays can be initialized with `= {values}`. Designated initializers (C99): `int arr[5] = {[0]=1, [4]=5}`. C has no runtime bounds checking — accessing out of bounds causes undefined behavior: crashes or security holes.

Strings as char Arrays.exp: C strings are null-terminated char arrays (`\0` marks end). String literals are `char*` pointing to read-only memory. Always ensure buffer is large enough for the null terminator.

String Library.exp: `<string.h>` provides: `strlen()` (length), `strcpy()` (copy), `strncpy()` (bounded copy), `strcat()` (append), `strncat()` (bounded append), `strcmp()` (compare), `strchr()` (find char), `strstr()` (find substring). Always prefer bounded versions.

Array of Strings.exp: An array of strings is a 2D char array or array of char pointers. `char names[5][20]` — fixed size. `char *names[5]` — flexible, each string can differ in length. Both have different memory layouts.

Character Classification.exp: `<ctype.h>` provides: `isalpha()`, `isdigit()`, `isalnum()`, `isspace()`, `islower()`, `isupper()`, `tolower()`, `toupper()`. Functions work with `int` (EOF-safe). Very efficient — lookup-table based.

Structs.exp: Structures group related data of different types. Define with `struct`. Access members with `.` (dot) operator. Use `->` with pointers to structs. Structs can be copied by assignment.

Unions.exp: Unions store different types in the same memory location (size = largest member). Only one member can hold a value at a time. Useful for variant types, register access, and memory-efficient design. Type punning is common but can be undefined behavior.

Bit Fields.exp: Bit fields pack multiple values into a single integer, specifying exact bits. Used in device drivers, network protocols, and embedded systems. Can't take address of a bit field. Order and alignment are implementation-defined.

enum.exp: Enums define named integer constants (default: 0, 1, 2...). Can specify explicit values. Enums improve code readability and type safety (some compilers warn on switch missing cases). C23 allows `enum` with type specifier.

Struct Padding & Alignment.exp: Compilers may add padding bytes between struct members for alignment. Reorder members from largest to smallest to minimize padding. `offsetof()` from `<stddef.h>` gets member offset. Packed structs with `__attribute__((packed))`.

Flexible Array Members.exp: A struct can have an incomplete array as its last member (C99). Allows variable-length data without pointers. The struct is allocated with extra space for the array. Common in network protocols and variable-length records.

Nested & Self-Referential Structs.exp: Structs can contain other structs as members. Self-referential structs (containing pointer to same type) are used for linked data structures: linked lists, trees, graphs. Forward declaration with `struct Name;`.

Opening & Closing Files.exp: `fopen()` opens a file: `r` read, `w` write (truncates), `a` append, `r+` read/write, `w+` read/write (truncates), `a+` read/append. `fclose()` closes. Always check return value for NULL. Binary mode: append `b` (e.g. `rb`, `wb`).

Reading & Writing Text.exp: Character: `fgetc()`, `fputc()`. Line: `fgets()` (safe, includes newline), `fputs()`. Block: `fread()`, `fwrite()`. `fgets()` reads at most n-1 chars and adds null terminator. `getline()` is POSIX, not standard C.

Formatted I/O.exp: `fprintf()` writes formatted output to a file. `fscanf()` reads formatted input from a file. Format specifiers: `%d` int, `%f` float, `%s` string, `%c` char, `%x` hex. `sscanf()` / `sprintf()` work with strings.

Binary I/O.exp: `fread()` and `fwrite()` read/write raw binary data. Parameters: pointer to data, size of each element, count, file pointer. Binary files are more compact and precise but not portable across endianness. Use `"rb"` / `"wb"` modes.

File Positioning.exp: `fseek(fp, offset, whence)` moves file position: `SEEK_SET` (beginning), `SEEK_CUR` (current), `SEEK_END` (end). `ftell()` returns current position. `rewind()` resets to beginning. `feof()` checks for end-of-file.

Error Handling.exp: File operations set `errno` on failure. `perror()` prints a descriptive error message to stderr. `strerror()` returns the error string. `ferror()` checks if a file stream has an error. Always check return values of I/O functions.

Macros (#define).exp: The preprocessor runs before compilation. `#define` creates macros (constants or function-like). Use parentheses to avoid precedence bugs. No type checking. Convention: UPPER_CASE names.
Macros (#define).code:
#define PI 3.14159
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

printf("%f\n", SQUARE(5 + 1));  // (6*6) = 36
printf("%d\n", MAX(3, 7));

Conditional Compilation.exp: `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else`, `#elif`, `#endif` control which code gets compiled. Used for platform-specific code, debug builds, feature toggles. `defined()` operator works in `#if`.

Header Files & Guards.exp: Header files (`.h`) declare functions, macros, and types. Use include guards (`#ifndef`) to prevent double inclusion. `#pragma once` is a modern alternative (non-standard but widely supported).

#pragma & #error.exp: `#error` emits a compiler error with a custom message — stops compilation. `#pragma` provides compiler-specific instructions: `#pragma once` (header guard), `#pragma pack(push, 1)` (packing), `#pragma GCC optimize`. Non-standard.
#pragma & #error.code:
#ifndef REQUIRED_FEATURE
    #error "REQUIRED_FEATURE must be defined"
#endif

#pragma once  // modern header guard
#pragma pack(push, 1)  // pack structs tightly
#pragma GCC optimize("O3")

Predefined Macros.exp: Standard predefined macros: `__FILE__` (current file), `__LINE__` (current line), `__DATE__` (compilation date), `__TIME__` (compilation time), `__STDC__` (1 if standard C), `__STDC_VERSION__` (C version: 199901L, 201112L, 202311L).

Stringification & Token Pasting.exp: `#` converts macro parameter to string literal. `##` concatenates two tokens into one. Useful for generating repetitive code patterns and creating type-generic macros.

Variadic Macros.exp: Macros with variable arguments using `__VA_ARGS__` (C99). Named variadic argument in C23 (`__VA_OPT__` for trailing comma handling). Useful for debug logging and generic printing.

stdlib.h Utilities.exp: `atoi()` / `atol()` / `atof()` parse strings to numbers. `itoa()` is non-standard — use `sprintf()`. `rand()` / `srand()` for pseudo-random numbers. `qsort()` for sorting. `abs()` / `labs()` for absolute value. `div()` / `ldiv()` for quotient and remainder.

math.h Functions.exp: Mathematical functions: `sqrt()`, `sin()`, `cos()`, `tan()`, `asin()`, `acos()`, `atan2()`, `pow()`, `exp()`, `log()`, `log10()`, `floor()`, `ceil()`, `fabs()`, `fmod()`. Link with `-lm`. Angles in radians.

time.h Functions.exp: `time()` gets current time. `clock()` gets CPU time. `difftime()` calculates difference. `strftime()` formats time. `localtime()` / `gmtime()` convert to struct. `mktime()` converts back. `clock_gettime()` for nanosecond precision (POSIX).

assert.h & setjmp.h.exp: `assert(expr)` aborts if expr is false (debug builds). Disable with `#define NDEBUG`. `setjmp()` / `longjmp()` provide non-local jumps (like try/catch). Save state with `jmp_buf`. Limited, use sparingly — complicates resource cleanup.

signal.h Handling.exp: `signal()` sets a handler for OS signals: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGTERM (termination), SIGSEGV (segfault), SIGFPE (divide by zero). Handler must be `void handler(int sig)`. Some signals (SIGKILL, SIGSTOP) cannot be caught.

stddef.h & Limits.exp: `<stddef.h>`: `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `NULL`, `offsetof()`. `<limits.h>`: integer limits (INT_MIN, INT_MAX, LONG_MAX, CHAR_BIT). `<float.h>`: floating limits (FLT_MAX, DBL_EPSILON). `<stdint.h>`: fixed-width types (int32_t, uint64_t).

Linked Lists.exp: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node points to the next. Singly linked: `next` pointer. Doubly linked: `prev` and `next`. Operations: insert, delete, traverse, search. O(1) insert/delete given pointer, O(n) access by index.

Debugging with GDB.exp: GDB is the GNU debugger. Compile with `-g` for debug symbols. Commands: `run`, `break`, `next`, `step`, `print`, `backtrace`, `watch`, `continue`. Set breakpoints on functions or lines. Inspect variables and memory.
Debugging with GDB.code:
# Compile with debug symbols
gcc -g -o program program.c

# GDB commands:
# gdb ./program
# (gdb) break main
# (gdb) run
# (gdb) print x
# (gdb) next
# (gdb) continue
# (gdb) backtrace
# (gdb) quit

Memory Debugging (Valgrind).exp: Valgrind detects memory leaks, invalid accesses, and use-after-free. Run with `valgrind ./program`. Tools: `memcheck` (default), `callgrind` (profiling), `helgrind` (race conditions). Focus on errors = definitely lost bytes.
Memory Debugging (Valgrind).code:
# Compile with -g for better output
gcc -g -o program program.c

# Check for memory errors
valgrind --leak-check=full ./program

# Typical output:
# HEAP SUMMARY:
#     definitely lost: 40 bytes in 2 blocks
# ERROR SUMMARY: 3 errors

Build Systems (Make).exp: Make automates compilation. Rules: `target: dependencies`, then tab-indented commands. Variables: `CC=gcc`, `CFLAGS=-Wall`. Automatic variables: `$@` (target), `$<` (first dep), `$^` (all deps).
Build Systems (Make).code:
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g
LDFLAGS = -lm

program: main.o helper.o
	$(CC) -o $@ $^ $(LDFLAGS)

main.o: main.c helper.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $<

helper.o: helper.c helper.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $<

.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f *.o program

Multithreading (pthreads).exp: POSIX threads (`<pthreads.h>`) create concurrent execution. `pthread_create()`, `pthread_join()`, `pthread_mutex_lock/unlock()`, `pthread_cond_wait/signal()`. Data races cause undefined behavior. Always synchronize shared data.

Network Programming (Sockets).exp: Berkeley sockets (`<sys/socket.h>`) for networking. Steps: `socket()`, `bind()`, `listen()`, `accept()` (server) or `connect()` (client). `send()` / `recv()` for data. Use `inet_pton()` for IP addresses. Compile with `-lsocket` on some systems.

Atomics & _Generic (C11).exp: `<stdatomic.h>` (C11) provides portable atomic operations: `atomic_int`, `atomic_store()`, `atomic_load()`, `atomic_fetch_add()`, `atomic_compare_exchange_weak()`. `_Generic` (C11) enables type-generic macros like built-in overloads.

Interactive I/O (getchar/putchar).exp: K&R-style character I/O with `getchar()` and `putchar()`. EOF is a macro (-1 on most systems). Ctrl+D (Unix) / Ctrl+Z (Windows) sends EOF. `getchar()` returns `int`, not `char`, to accommodate EOF. Classic book-copying program.

Low-Level I/O (UNIX System Interface).exp: `<unistd.h>` provides `read()`, `write()`, `open()`, `close()`, `lseek()`. Lower-level than stdio — no buffering, direct file descriptors (ints). Used in systems programming, signal handlers, and performance-critical code. K&R Chapter 8 covers this.

Storage Allocator (K&R Chapter 8).exp: K&R builds a `malloc()`-like allocator using a free list of headers. Each block has a header with size and pointer to next free block. `sbrk()` grows the program break. Real allocators are more sophisticated (thread caches, slab allocators, buddy system).

Complex Declarations (Right-Left Rule).exp: Read C declarations spirally: start at identifier, go right, then left, then right again (spiral rule). `int *(*fp)(int)` is pointer-to-function taking int returning pointer-to-int. Practice with `signal()`: `void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int)`.

Variable-Length Arrays (C99).exp: VLA syntax: `int arr[n]` where `n` is not a compile-time constant. Memory on stack (auto duration). `sizeof` on VLA computed at runtime. No VLA in file scope or structs. Support is optional in C11 (most compilers still provide it).

Complex Numbers (C99).exp: `<complex.h>` provides `complex` type, `I` (imaginary unit), `creal()`, `cimag()`, `cabs()`, `carg()`, `conj()`, `csqrt()`, `cexp()`. Types: `float complex`, `double complex`, `long double complex`. Link with `-lm`.

Defensive Programming.exp: From Learn C the Hard Way: always check return values, validate pointers before dereferencing, assert invariants in debug builds, and enable all compiler warnings. Use `const` for read-only parameters. Never trust user input or buffer sizes.

Three Common Bugs.exp: Learn C the Hard Way drills these: 1) Off-by-one: loop runs one iteration too many/few. 2) Buffer overflow: writing past allocated space. 3) Use-after-free: accessing freed heap memory. Detect with `-fsanitize=address` and Valgrind.

Safe String Handling.exp: C string functions are inherently unsafe. Prefer bounded versions: `strncpy()`, `strncat()`, `snprintf()` (always null-terminates). For POSIX: `strlcpy()` / `strlcat()`. Better yet, use a string struct with explicit length field.

Pointer Pitfalls.exp: From Absolute Beginner's Guide: 1) Uninitialized pointers hold garbage — always init to NULL. 2) Dangling pointers reference freed memory — NULL after free. 3) Null dereference crashes. 4) Pointer arithmetic past bounds is UB. 5) Alignment violations on cast.

Debugging Strategies.exp: Layer your approach: 1) Compiler warnings (`-Wall -Wextra`). 2) `assert()` to catch invariants. 3) `printf()` / `fprintf(stderr)` for tracing. 4) GDB for interactive debugging. 5) Valgrind for memory leaks. 6) AddressSanitizer for fast memory checking.

Working with Multiple Files.exp: Split code across `.h` (declarations with include guards) and `.c` (definitions). `static` functions/variables are file-private. `extern` references names defined in other files. Compile all `.c` files and link them into one executable.

What is CI/CD.exp:
CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment. It is a method of frequently delivering apps to customers by introducing automation into the stages of app development. CI/CD bridges the gap between development and operations teams by automating build, test, and deployment processes.

Continuous Integration ensures every code change is automatically built and tested, catching bugs early. Continuous Delivery extends CI by automatically deploying code to production-like environments for testing. Continuous Deployment takes it further — every change that passes all stages of the pipeline is automatically released to production.

Pipeline Architecture.exp:
A CI/CD pipeline is a series of automated steps that code goes through from commit to deployment. The typical stages are:

  • Source — code is pushed to version control (Git)
  • Build — code is compiled and dependencies are resolved
  • Test — automated tests (unit, integration, e2e) are run
  • Analyze — static analysis, linting, and security scanning
  • Package — artifacts (binaries, containers) are built and stored
  • Deploy — artifacts are deployed to staging or production

Each stage must pass before the next begins — this is called a gated pipeline. Modern pipelines run stages in parallel where possible for speed.

Benefits of CI/CD.exp:
Adopting CI/CD brings several key benefits:

  • Faster releases — automate manual steps to ship code multiple times a day
  • Reduced risk — catch bugs early with automated testing in every commit
  • Higher quality — consistent testing and code analysis standards
  • Developer productivity — less time spent on manual deployments and debugging
  • Auditability — every change is tracked, tested, and logged
  • Team confidence — automated validation means safer deployments

Companies practicing CI/CD deploy code 208x more frequently than those that don't (DORA State of DevOps report).

Git Hooks.exp:
Git hooks are scripts that run automatically before or after Git events like commit, push, or merge. They are stored in the .git/hooks directory and can enforce policies locally before code reaches the remote repository.

Common CI/CD use cases include:

  • pre-commit — run linters, format code, check for secrets
  • pre-push — run unit tests before pushing
  • commit-msg — enforce conventional commit format
  • post-merge — install new dependencies after pulling

Tools like Husky and lint-staged make managing hooks easier across teams.

Branching Strategies.exp:
CI/CD pipelines work hand-in-hand with branching strategies. Common approaches include:

  • GitFlow — main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches. Good for scheduled releases but complex.
  • GitHub Flow — single main branch with feature branches and pull requests. Simpler, ideal for continuous deployment.
  • Trunk-based Development — short-lived feature branches merged to main multiple times a day. Best for CI/CD with automated testing.

CI/CD pipelines typically trigger on push to specific branches (e.g., main) and on pull requests for validation before merge.

Pull Request Workflows.exp:
Pull requests (PRs) are at the heart of modern CI/CD. A typical PR workflow:

  1. Developer creates a feature branch, commits changes, and pushes
  2. PR is opened, triggering a CI pipeline that runs tests and analysis
  3. PR checks report status (pass/fail) directly in the PR view
  4. Team reviews code; additional commits trigger re-runs
  5. Once approved and all checks pass, the PR is merged
  6. Merge triggers a CD pipeline to build and deploy

Tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Azure DevOps integrate PR checks natively with status badges and required checks.

Build Automation.exp:
Build automation is the process of automating the compilation of source code into executable artifacts. Every commit should produce a build to verify the code compiles correctly.

Common build tools by language:

  • JavaScript/TypeScript — npm, yarn, pnpm, vite, webpack
  • Java — Maven, Gradle
  • Python — setuptools, poetry, pipenv
  • Go — go build
  • Rust — cargo build
  • C/C++ — CMake, Make, GCC

The build stage should be fast (under 5 minutes) to provide quick feedback. Cache dependencies between builds to speed up execution.

Automated Testing.exp:
Testing is the heart of CI. Every pipeline should run multiple levels of tests:

  • Unit tests — test individual functions and methods (fastest, most coverage)
  • Integration tests — test interactions between components (database, API, services)
  • End-to-end tests — test the full system from user perspective (slowest, least coverage)

The test pyramid suggests many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few e2e tests. Tests should be deterministic — always pass or fail the same way given the same code. Flaky tests undermine CI trust.

Code Quality & Linting.exp:
Automated code quality checks are essential in CI/CD. These include:

  • Linters — ESLint (JS/TS), Ruff/Flake8 (Python), Clippy (Rust), golangci-lint (Go)
  • Formatters — Prettier, Black, gofmt, rustfmt
  • Static analysis — SonarQube, CodeQL, Coverity
  • Type checking — TypeScript (tsc), mypy (Python), Flow

These checks should fail the pipeline if thresholds are not met (e.g., code coverage < 80%, lint errors, type errors). Many teams enforce formatting with pre-commit hooks and reserve CI for deeper analysis.

GitHub Actions.exp:
GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. Workflows are defined as YAML files in .github/workflows/. It offers deep GitHub integration, a large marketplace of pre-built actions, and supports Linux, macOS, Windows, and containers.

Key concepts: workflows (automated processes), jobs (sets of steps), steps (individual tasks), runners (execution environments). GitHub provides free minutes for public repositories and paid minutes for private ones.

Jenkins.exp:
Jenkins is the most widely used open-source automation server. It supports hundreds of plugins for building, deploying, and automating projects. Jenkins pipelines can be defined as code using Jenkinsfile with Declarative or Scripted pipeline syntax.

Strengths: extreme flexibility, massive plugin ecosystem, mature community. Weaknesses: requires server management, UI can feel dated, plugin compatibility issues. Best for complex enterprise environments needing fine-grained control.

CircleCI.exp:
CircleCI is a cloud-native CI/CD platform known for speed and reliability. Pipelines are configured in a .circleci/config.yml file. CircleCI supports parallelism, caching, and Orbs — reusable configuration packages that simplify complex pipelines.

Key features: Docker layer caching, SSH debugging for troubleshooting, dynamic configuration via pipeline parameters, and optimized resource classes (CPU/RAM per job). CircleCI offers a generous free tier for individual developers and open-source projects.

Azure DevOps.exp:
Azure DevOps is Microsoft's full DevSecOps platform providing a complete toolchain: Azure Pipelines (CI/CD), Azure Boards (work tracking), Azure Repos (Git repos), Azure Artifacts (package management), and Azure Test Plans (testing).

Azure Pipelines supports any language, platform, and cloud. Key strengths: deep Azure integration, deployment groups for multi-machine rollouts, Kubernetes integration, and YAML or classic editor pipeline definitions. Free tier includes 1,800 minutes per month.

GitLab CI/CD Overview.exp:
GitLab CI/CD is GitLab's built-in continuous integration, delivery, and deployment system. Pipelines are defined declaratively in a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the repository root. GitLab CI/CD is deeply integrated into the GitLab platform, providing a unified experience for source control, CI/CD, container registry, package registry, and deployment.

Key strengths: single application for the entire DevOps lifecycle, built-in auto-scaling runners, review apps for per-branch environments, and a generous free tier for both public and private repositories.

GitLab CI Pipeline Configuration.exp:
GitLab CI pipelines are defined in YAML with these core concepts:

  • Stages — groups of jobs that run in order (e.g., build, test, deploy). Jobs in the same stage run in parallel.
  • Jobs — define what to run (script, image, dependencies). Each job belongs to a stage.
  • Runners — agents that execute jobs. GitLab provides shared runners (Linux, Windows, macOS) and you can register your own.
  • Variables — environment variables for configuration. Can be set at project, group, or instance level.
  • Cache & Artifacts — cache speeds up dependency installs; artifacts pass build outputs between stages.

Example pipeline: lint → test → build → deploy. Jobs can run conditionally based on branch, tags, or changes to specific files.

GitLab Auto DevOps.exp:
Auto DevOps is GitLab's zero-configuration CI/CD pipeline. When enabled, GitLab automatically detects your application language and builds a complete pipeline including:

  • Code quality analysis (SonarQube)
  • SAST and Dependency Scanning
  • Container scanning and DAST
  • License compliance review
  • Automatic deployment to staging and production
  • Review Apps (temporary environments per merge request)
  • Performance testing and browser testing

Auto DevOps uses a Dockerfile or buildpack to build your app. It's ideal for teams new to CI/CD who want instant value without writing pipeline config.

GitLab Runners & Scaling.exp:
GitLab Runners are the agents that execute CI/CD jobs. Types include:

  • Shared runners — GitLab-hosted, available to all projects (Linux, Windows, macOS)
  • Group runners — available to all projects in a group
  • Project runners — dedicated to a single project
  • Specific runners — locked to specific projects or tags

Scaling strategies: use Docker autoscaling with Docker Machine or Kubernetes with the GitLab Runner Helm chart to spin up runners dynamically based on job demand. GitLab Runner supports executors including Docker, Kubernetes, SSH, and VirtualBox.

Deployment Strategies.exp:
Different deployment strategies balance risk, speed, and user impact:

  • Rolling Update — gradually replaces instances of the old version with the new one. Zero downtime, easy rollback.
  • Blue/Green — run two identical environments. Switch traffic from blue (current) to green (new) instantly. Instant rollback by switching back.
  • Canary — route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, then gradually increase. Real user validation with minimal risk.
  • Feature Flags — deploy code hidden behind toggles, then enable for specific users. Separates deployment from release.

Modern CD pipelines use a combination of these strategies depending on the application and risk tolerance.

Rollback & Recovery.exp:
Even the best pipelines can fail in production. CD systems must support fast, reliable rollback:

  • Automated rollback — if health checks fail after deployment, automatically revert to the last known-good version
  • Database rollbacks — use reversible migrations (up/down) to safely revert schema changes
  • Version pinning — always tag deployed versions (git tags, container tags) for easy identification
  • Audit trail — every deployment should log who deployed what, when, and the result

The golden rule: if it hurts, do it more often. Frequent, small deployments are easier to roll back than rare, large ones.

Release Management.exp:
Release management in CI/CD coordinates how changes move through environments:

  • Environment promotion — code flows: dev → staging → production, with gates at each stage
  • Semantic versioning — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.1.0) based on change impact
  • Changelogs — auto-generated from conventional commits
  • Release branches — for scheduled releases, create a release branch from main
  • Approval gates — manual approval steps before production deployment (compliance, QA sign-off)

Tools like Release Please, Semantic Release, and Changesets automate versioning and changelog generation.

Terraform in CI/CD.exp:
Applying Infrastructure as Code (IaC) through CI/CD brings infrastructure changes under the same governance as application changes.

Terraform CI/CD best practices:

  • Run terraform fmt and terraform validate in CI to check formatting and syntax
  • Use terraform plan in PRs to show infrastructure changes without applying them
  • Store state remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud) with state locking
  • Apply only after PR approval and plan review
  • Use workspaces or directories for environment separation

The terraform plan output in a PR comment is one of the most valuable CI/CD practices for infrastructure teams.

Configuration Management.exp:
Configuration management tools maintain consistent system state across environments:

  • Ansible — agentless, push-based, YAML playbooks. Great for app deployment and server configuration.
  • Chef — Ruby-based DSL, pull-based with Chef Client and Server. Good for large-scale server fleets.
  • Puppet — declarative DSL, pull-based. Strong in enterprise environments.

In CI/CD, run config management as part of the deployment stage to ensure servers match the desired state after deployment.

Policy as Code.exp:
Policy as Code (PaC) enforces rules automatically in the pipeline:

  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) — general-purpose policy engine. Enforce rules like "all S3 buckets must be encrypted" before apply.
  • Sentinel — HashiCorp's policy framework for Terraform and Vault.
  • Checkov — static analysis for IaC to find misconfigurations (open ports, hardcoded secrets).
  • Conftest — test configuration files against OPA policies in CI.

PaC shifts security left — catching policy violations before infrastructure is provisioned.

Docker Build Pipelines.exp:
Container-based CI/CD pipelines use Docker throughout the pipeline:

  • Build stage produces a Docker image with the application and all dependencies
  • Tag images with commit SHA, branch name, and semantic version
  • Push to a container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, GHCR)
  • Use multi-stage builds to minimize image size
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Snyk, Docker Scout)

The same image built in CI is deployed everywhere — no "works on my machine" problems. Images are immutable and versioned.

Kubernetes Deployments.exp:
Deploying to Kubernetes from CI/CD involves:

  • Update the deployment manifest (YAML) with the new image tag
  • Use kubectl set image or patch the deployment
  • Apply with kubectl apply to trigger rolling update
  • Use Helm for templated releases — pass the image tag as a value
  • Monitor rollout with kubectl rollout status

Advanced setups use ArgoCD or Flux (GitOps) where the CD system watches a Git repository for manifest changes and synchronizes the cluster automatically.

GitOps.exp:
GitOps is a deployment model where the Git repository is the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure. Changes are made via PRs, and an operator synchronizes the live environment to match the repository state.

Key tools:

  • ArgoCD — Kubernetes-native CD tool. Syncs clusters to a Git repository with automatic or manual sync policies.
  • Flux — GitOps operator from Weaveworks. Supports multi-tenancy, image updates, and Kustomize/Helm.

Benefits: complete audit trail (every change is a Git commit), easy rollback (revert commit), and a single workflow for both dev and ops.

SAST & DAST.exp:
Security testing should be integrated into every pipeline:

  • SAST (Static Application Security Testing) — analyzes source code for vulnerabilities without running it. Tools: SonarQube, CodeQL, Semgrep, Checkmarx. Runs early in the pipeline (build stage).
  • DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) — tests running applications for vulnerabilities. Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Runs against staging environments later in the pipeline.

SAST catches issues early (shift left), while DAST catches runtime vulnerabilities. Both should be gated — fail the pipeline on high-severity findings.

Secret Scanning.exp:
Accidentally committing secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens) is one of the most common CI/CD security issues. Prevent and detect with:

  • Pre-commit hooks — tools like talisman, git-secrets, and detect-secrets scan before commits
  • CI scanning — GitHub Secret Scanning, GitLab Secret Detection, TruffleHog scan in the pipeline
  • Secret managers — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager

CI/CD configs should reference secrets from the CI platform's built-in secrets store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Jenkins credentials), never hardcode them.

SBOM & Supply Chain.exp:
Software supply chain security is critical in 2026:

  • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — a machine-readable inventory of all components in your software. Generated by tools like CycloneDX and Syft.
  • Dependency scanning — Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk automatically detect and update vulnerable dependencies
  • Artifact signing — sign container images and binaries with Cosign to verify authenticity
  • Attestations — create signed metadata about how and where artifacts were built

AI-generated code increases the importance of SBOM scanning. Every CI/CD pipeline should generate and verify SBOMs before deployment.

Pipeline Metrics.exp:
Track these key metrics to measure CI/CD pipeline health:

  • Pipeline duration — time from commit to deployment. Target: under 15 minutes total.
  • Build failure rate — percentage of builds that fail. Target: under 10%.
  • Deployment frequency — how often you deploy to production. Elite teams deploy multiple times per day.
  • Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) — time from detecting a failure to recovery. Target: under 1 hour.
  • Change failure rate — percentage of deployments causing incidents. Target: under 5%.

These are the DORA metrics — the industry standard for measuring DevOps and CI/CD performance.

Pipeline Notifications.exp:
Keep teams informed about pipeline status with automated notifications:

  • Slack/Discord — send messages on failure, success, or deployment events. Include links to the pipeline run.
  • Email — send summaries for failed pipelines or approval requests
  • Status badges — embed pipeline status (passing/failing) in README files
  • PR comments — post test results, coverage changes, and deployment URLs directly in PRs

Most CI/CD platforms have built-in notification integrations. Focus on actionable alerts — don't spam teams with every successful build.

Incident Response.exp:
When a CI/CD pipeline failure or production incident occurs, a structured response process is essential:

  1. Detect — automated monitoring and alerts detect the failure
  2. Stop the bleeding — rollback the deployment or block the pipeline
  3. Triage — determine severity, impact, and affected teams
  4. Investigate — review logs, metrics, and pipeline output to find root cause
  5. Remediate — fix the issue and push the fix through the same CI/CD pipeline
  6. Review — post-mortem to prevent recurrence

CI/CD pipelines themselves should be treated as critical infrastructure with their own monitoring, redundancy, and incident response plans.

What is Cloud Computing.exp: Cloud computing delivers computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet. Key benefits: pay-as-you-go, elastic scaling, reduced maintenance, global reach.
What is Cloud Computing.code:
# Cloud service models
# IaaS: Infrastructure (AWS EC2, GCP Compute)
# PaaS: Platform (Heroku, Google App Engine)
# SaaS: Software (Gmail, Office 365)
# FaaS: Functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions)

Deployment Models.exp: **Public cloud:** shared infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP). **Private cloud:** dedicated to one org. **Hybrid cloud:** mix of public and private. **Multi-cloud:** using multiple providers. **Community cloud:** shared by several orgs.
Deployment Models.code:
# Deployment comparison
# Public: scalable, cost-effective
# Private: secure, compliant
# Hybrid: best of both worlds
# Multi-cloud: avoid vendor lock-in

Cloud Providers Overview.exp: **AWS:** market leader, 200+ services. **Azure:** Microsoft ecosystem, enterprise focus. **GCP:** Google tools, data/AI strength. **DigitalOcean:** simple, developer-friendly. **Linode/Vultr:** budget options.
Cloud Providers Overview.code:
# AWS: aws.amazon.com
# Azure: azure.microsoft.com
# GCP: cloud.google.com
# DO: digitalocean.com

Regions & Availability Zones.exp: **Regions** are geographic areas (us-east-1, eu-west-2). **Availability Zones (AZs)** are isolated data centers within a region. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability. Choose regions close to users.
Regions & Availability Zones.code:
# AWS Regions
# us-east-1: N. Virginia
# eu-west-1: Ireland
# ap-southeast-1: Singapore
# Deploy in 3+ AZs for HA

Virtual Machines (EC2).exp: **AWS EC2** provides virtual servers. Choose instance types (general, compute, memory optimized). AMIs define OS/software. Security groups control traffic. Elastic IPs for static addresses.
Virtual Machines (EC2).code:
# Launch EC2
aws ec2 run-instances 
  --image-id ami-xxxx 
  --instance-type t3.micro 
  --key-name my-key 
  --security-group-ids sg-xxx

Serverless (Lambda).exp: **AWS Lambda** runs code without provisioning servers. Triggers: HTTP (API Gateway), S3 events, scheduled (CloudWatch), SQS. Supports Node.js, Python, Go, Java, C#, Ruby. Pay per execution + duration.

Containers (ECS/EKS).exp: **ECS** (Elastic Container Service) runs Docker containers. **EKS** is managed Kubernetes. **Fargate** runs containers without managing servers. Use ECR for container image registry.

App Engine (GCP).exp: **Google App Engine** is a PaaS that auto-scales apps. Standard environment (sandboxed, faster) vs Flexible (Docker, more features). Supports Go, Python, Java, Node.js, PHP, Ruby.
App Engine (GCP).code:
# app.yaml (GAE Standard)
 runtime: python312
 entrypoint: gunicorn -b :$PORT main:app
 automatic_scaling:
   min_instances: 1
   max_instances: 10

Object Storage (S3).exp: **AWS S3** is object storage with 99.999999999% durability. Buckets hold objects. Storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier (archive). Versioning, lifecycle policies, static website hosting.
Object Storage (S3).code:
# S3 CLI
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket
aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/
aws s3 sync ./folder s3://my-bucket/folder
# Lifecycle rule (archive after 30d)
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration ...

Block Storage (EBS).exp: **EBS** provides block-level storage volumes for EC2. Types: gp3 (general), io2 (high-performance), st1 (throughput). Snapshots back up to S3. Can be encrypted. Attach to one instance at a time.
Block Storage (EBS).code:
# Create EBS
aws ec2 create-volume \n  --volume-type gp3 \n  --size 100 \n  --availability-zone us-east-1a
# Snapshot
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-xxx

CDN (CloudFront).exp: **CloudFront** is a CDN that caches content at edge locations. Origins: S3, HTTP server, ALB. Price classes determine edge coverage. Supports Lambda@Edge for custom logic at edge. SSL/TLS termination.
CDN (CloudFront).code:
# CloudFront distribution
aws cloudfront create-distribution \n  --origin-domain-name my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com \n  --default-root-object index.html

File Storage (EFS).exp: **EFS** is a scalable, elastic NFS file system for Linux. Grows/shrinks automatically. Accessed by multiple EC2 instances simultaneously. Lifecycle management moves files to Infrequent Access tier.
File Storage (EFS).code:
# Mount EFS on EC2
sudo mount -t nfs4 \n  fs-xxxxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs
# Automatic in fstab
fs-xxxxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs nfs4 defaults,_netdev 0 0

RDS (Relational).exp: **RDS** manages relational databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Features: Multi-AZ (HA), Read Replicas, automated backups, automated patching, encryption at rest.
RDS (Relational).code:
# Create RDS MySQL
aws rds create-db-instance 
  --engine mysql 
  --db-instance-identifier mydb 
  --db-instance-class db.t3.micro 
  --master-username admin 
  --master-user-password secret 
  --allocated-storage 20

DynamoDB (NoSQL).exp: **DynamoDB** is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database. Single-digit millisecond performance. Auto-scaling, DAX (caching), Global Tables (multi-region), On-Demand capacity.
DynamoDB (NoSQL).code:
# Create DynamoDB table
aws dynamodb create-table 
  --table-name Users 
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S 
  --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH 
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

MongoDB Atlas.exp: **MongoDB Atlas** is the official managed MongoDB service. Deploy across AWS/Azure/GCP. Features: auto-scaling, backups, BI Connector, Atlas Search, Serverless instances, global clusters.
MongoDB Atlas.code:
# Atlas connection
mongosh "mongodb+srv://cluster.abcde.mongodb.net/"
# Create free cluster
# atlas clusters create --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 --tier M0

Firestore (GCP).exp: **Firestore** is a flexible, scalable NoSQL database for mobile/web apps. Real-time updates via listeners. Automatic multi-region replication. Strong consistency. Serverless — no provisioning needed.

Cloud SQL.exp: **Cloud SQL** is GCP's managed relational database. Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server. Features: automatic replication, backups, failover, encryption, private network access. Up to 30TB storage.
Cloud SQL.code:
# Create Cloud SQL
gcloud sql instances create my-instance 
  --database-version POSTGRES_15 
  --tier db-f1-micro 
  --region us-central1 
  --root-password secret

Cosmos DB (Azure).exp: **Cosmos DB** is Azure's globally distributed NoSQL database. Multi-model: document, key-value, graph, column-family. SLA-backed 99.999% availability. Single-digit ms latency anywhere in the world.
Cosmos DB (Azure).code:
# Cosmos DB CLI
az cosmosdb create 
  --name my-cosmos-db 
  --resource-group my-rg 
  --kind GlobalDocumentDB

VPC (Virtual Private Cloud).exp: **VPC** is a logically isolated network in AWS. Subnets divide IP ranges (public/private). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway for public access. NAT Gateway for private subnets.
VPC (Virtual Private Cloud).code:
# Create VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx

Load Balancers.exp: **ALB** (Application LB) routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic. **NLB** (Network LB) handles TCP/UDP. **ELB** (Classic) is legacy. Target groups route to instances. Health checks detect failures. Auto Scaling integrates with LBs.
Load Balancers.code:
# Create ALB
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer 
  --name my-alb 
  --subnets subnet-xxx subnet-yyy 
  --security-groups sg-xxx
aws elbv2 create-target-group --name my-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id vpc-xxx

IAM (Identity & Access).exp: **IAM** manages users, groups, roles, and policies. Policies are JSON documents defining permissions (Allow/Deny). Least privilege principle. Roles for EC2/Lambda to access services. MFA for extra security.

Security Best Practices.exp: Use IAM roles (not keys). Enable CloudTrail for auditing. Encrypt data at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Security groups as firewalls. WAF for web attacks. Shield for DDoS. Regular security audits.
Security Best Practices.code:
# Enable CloudTrail
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket-name my-logs
# KMS encryption
aws kms create-key
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket my-bucket --server-side-encryption-configuration ...

CI/CD Pipelines.exp: Automate build, test, deploy with CI/CD. **AWS CodePipeline** + CodeBuild + CodeDeploy. **GitHub Actions** for simpler workflows. **GitLab CI** with built-in registry. Test in staging before production.
CI/CD Pipelines.code:
# GitHub Actions workflow
name: Deploy
on: push to main
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm install && npm test
      - run: aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-bucket

Infrastructure as Code.exp: Manage cloud resources with code. **Terraform:** multi-cloud, declarative HCL. **CloudFormation:** AWS-native JSON/YAML. **Pulumi:** code in Python/TS/Go. Version control your infrastructure!

Monitoring & Logging.exp: **CloudWatch:** metrics, logs, alarms. **X-Ray:** distributed tracing. **Prometheus + Grafana:** open-source monitoring. **ELK Stack:** Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana for log analysis. Set up alerts for critical metrics.
Monitoring & Logging.code:
# CloudWatch alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm 
  --alarm-name CPUHigh 
  --metric-name CPUUtilization 
  --namespace AWS/EC2 
  --threshold 80 --period 300 
  --evaluation-periods 2 
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:xxx

Auto Scaling.exp: **Auto Scaling** adjusts compute capacity based on demand. Launch template defines instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking, step scaling, scheduled. Health checks replace unhealthy instances.
Auto Scaling.code:
# Create Auto Scaling group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group 
  --auto-scaling-group-name my-asg 
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=my-template 
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 
  --vpc-zone-identifier subnet-xxx,subnet-yyy

Microservices Architecture.exp: Microservices decompose an app into small, independent services. Each service has its own database, API, and deployment pipeline. API Gateways (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, GCP Apigee) route requests, handle auth, rate limiting. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul) manages service-to-service communication with mTLS, traffic splitting, observability. Circuit breakers (Resilience4j, Hystrix) prevent cascading failures — fail fast and degrade gracefully. Common mistake: premature decomposition — start with a monolith, extract services when needed. Anti-pattern: shared databases between services (tight coupling). Use eventual consistency and saga patterns for distributed transactions.
Microservices Architecture.code:
# Service decomposition example
# Monolith breaking into services:
# User Service - /users/* (PostgreSQL)
# Order Service - /orders/* (DynamoDB)
# Payment Service - /payments/* (RDS)
# Notification Service - async (SQS/SNS)

# API Gateway route (e.g., AWS)
# aws apigateway create-rest-api --name my-api
# aws apigateway create-resource --rest-api-id xxx --parent-id yyy --path-part orders

# Circuit breaker (pseudo-code)
# const circuitBreaker = new CircuitBreaker(fetchPaymentService, {
#   failureThreshold: 5,
#   successThreshold: 2,
#   timeout: 10000
# });
# const result = await circuitBreaker.call(request);

# Service mesh sidecar injection (K8s)
# kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled
# istioctl install --set profile=demo

Cloud Security Best Practices.exp: Shared Responsibility Model: provider secures the cloud (physical, network, hypervisor), you secure what's in the cloud (data, IAM, OS, app config). IAM least privilege: grant only required permissions — use service-specific roles, not admin. Encryption at rest: all cloud providers offer server-side encryption (SSE-S3, Azure SSE, GCP CSEK). Encryption in transit: enforce TLS 1.2+ everywhere, use HTTPS-only listeners. Secret management: store secrets in provider-native vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) — never in code or config files. Common mistake: over-permissive IAM policies (using wildcards). Enable CloudTrail/Audit Logs and set up anomaly alerts. Rotate keys and credentials regularly. Enable MFA for all human users.
Cloud Security Best Practices.code:
# IAM least privilege structure
# AWS: arn:aws:iam::xxx:policy/S3ReadOnly
# { Effect: Allow, Action: ['s3:GetObject'], Resource: 'arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*' }

# Enforce TLS
# aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn xxx --protocol HTTPS --port 443

# Secret retrieval at runtime (never hardcode)
# AWS: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password
# Azure: az keyvault secret show --vault-name my-kv --name db-password
# GCP: gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret my-secret

# Enable audit logging
# aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket my-logs
# az monitor diagnostic-settings create --resource xxx --workspace my-logs
# gcloud logging buckets create my-bucket --location global

# KMS/CMEK for encryption at rest
# aws kms create-key --description 'app-key'
# az keyvault create --name my-kv
# gcloud kms keys create my-key --keyring my-keyring --location global --purpose encryption

Cost Optimization.exp: Right-sizing: match instance size to workload needs — analyze utilization metrics and downsize over-provisioned resources. Reserved instances / Committed use discounts: 1yr or 3yr commitment saves 30-70% for predictable workloads. Spot/Preemptible instances: 60-90% discount for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads (batch, ML training, CI/CD). Storage tiers: move infrequent data to cheaper tiers (S3 IA/Glacier, Azure Cool/Archive, GCP Nearline/Archive). Tagging strategy: tag all resources (Environment, Team, Project, Cost Center) for cost allocation and chargeback. Common mistake: leaving unused resources running (orphaned EBS volumes, idle load balancers, unattached IPs). Use budgets and alerts to track spending. Review and delete unused resources monthly.
Cost Optimization.code:
# AWS: right-size EC2 with Compute Optimizer
# aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations

# AWS: buy reserved instances
# aws ec2 purchase-reserved-instances-offering --offering-id xxx --instance-count 3

# Azure: reserved VM instances
# az reservation calculate --sku Standard_D2s_v3 --location eastus --quantity 3

# GCP: committed use discounts
# gcloud compute commitments create --region us-central1 --plan 12-month --resources vcpu=8,memory=32GB

# Tagging strategy
# aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-xxx --tags Key=Environment,Value=production Key=CostCenter,Value=123
# az tag create --resource-id /subscriptions/xxx --tags Environment=production CostCenter=123
# gcloud compute instances add-labels my-vm --labels=environment=production,cost-center=123

# Storage lifecycle (auto-tier to cheaper storage)
# AWS S3: transition to Glacier after 30 days
# Azure Blob: tier to Cool after 30 days
# GCS: set Nearline after 30 days

# Budget alert
# aws budgets create-budget ...
# az consumption budget create --amount 1000 --time-grain monthly
# gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account xxx --amount 1000 --currency USD

High Availability & Disaster Recovery.exp: Multi-AZ: deploy across multiple availability zones in one region for resilience against AZ failure. Multi-region: deploy across geographic regions for region-level disaster recovery. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): max acceptable data loss (e.g., 1 hour = hourly backups). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): max acceptable downtime (e.g., 4 hours = time to restore). Backup strategies: automated snapshots, cross-region replication, point-in-time recovery. Failover patterns: Active-Passive (one region active, other on standby — Route53 failover), Active-Active (both regions serve traffic — Route53 latency routing, DynamoDB Global Tables, Cosmos DB multi-region writes). Common mistake: testing DR only once a year — automate DR drills. Use infrastructure as code to rebuild environments quickly.
High Availability & Disaster Recovery.code:
# Multi-AZ RDS
# aws rds create-db-instance --multi-az --engine postgres --db-instance-identifier mydb

# Cross-region snapshot copy
# aws rds create-db-cluster-snapshot --db-cluster-identifier aurora-cluster
# aws rds copy-db-cluster-snapshot --source-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:xxx:snapshot:xxx --target-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier my-snapshot-copy --destination-region us-west-2

# Route53 failover routing (active-passive DR)
# Create two records: primary (with health check) and secondary (with failover type)

# DynamoDB Global Tables (active-active multi-region)
# aws dynamodb create-global-table --global-table-name Orders --replication-group region-names us-east-1 us-west-2

# Azure Site Recovery (DR)
# az site-recovery vault create --name my-vault --resource-group my-rg --location eastus

# GCP: configure multi-region Cloud Storage
# gsutil mb -l US gs://my-bucket  # multi-region US

# Backup automation with lifecycle
# 1. Automated daily snapshot (retained 30 days)
# 2. Weekly snapshot (retained 3 months)
# 3. Monthly snapshot (retained 1 year)
# 4. Cross-region copy to DR region

Infrastructure as Code.exp: IaC manages cloud resources through code (declarative or imperative). Terraform: multi-cloud, state management (local or remote like S3/Terraform Cloud), HCL syntax, modules for reusability. CloudFormation: AWS-native, YAML/JSON, StackSets for multi-account, drift detection. Pulumi: code in TypeScript, Python, Go, C# — full programming language power (loops, functions, conditionals). State management: store state remotely (S3 + DynamoDB locking for Terraform, Pulumi Cloud, CloudFormation managed by AWS). Modular design: break infrastructure into reusable modules (vpc, compute, database) with versioning. Common mistake: storing state locally or not using state locking. Never manually modify resources outside of IaC (drift). Use pre-commit hooks for formatting. Validate templates before apply.
Infrastructure as Code.code:
# Terraform: module structure
# modules/
#   vpc/
#   compute/
#   database/
# environments/
#   dev/
#     main.tf
#     terraform.tfvars
#   prod/
#     main.tf
#     terraform.tfvars

# Terraform example
# provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }
# module "vpc" {
#   source = "../../modules/vpc"
#   cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
#   environment = var.environment
# }

# Terraform commands
# terraform init
# terraform plan
# terraform apply -auto-approve
# terraform destroy

# Pulumi (TypeScript)
# import * as aws from "@pulumi/aws";
# const bucket = new aws.s3.Bucket("my-bucket", {
#   acl: "private",
#   versioning: { enabled: true }
# });
# export const bucketName = bucket.id;

# CloudFormation
# aws cloudformation deploy --template-file template.yaml --stack-name my-stack

# Pre-commit hook (terraform fmt)
# git add .
# terraform fmt -recursive
# git commit -m "infra: update VPC configuration"

What is C++.exp: C++ is a powerful, statically-typed systems programming language that extends C with object-oriented, generic, and functional features. It gives fine-grained control over memory and performance.

C++ Versions.exp: Major standards: C++98 (original), C++11 (modern), C++14, C++17, C++20, C++23. Each adds features. Compile with -std=c++17, -std=c++20, etc. Always check compiler support.

Compilers & Build.exp: Major compilers: GCC (g++), Clang, MSVC. Build systems: CMake (most common), Make, Ninja, Bazel. CMake generates build files for your platform.
Compilers & Build.code:
// Single file compile
// g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o app main.cpp

# CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(MyApp LANGUAGES CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
add_executable(app main.cpp utils.cpp)
target_include_directories(app PRIVATE include)

Project Structure.exp: Typical layout: src/ for .cpp, include/ for .hpp/.h, lib/ for dependencies, tests/ for unit tests. Use header guards (#pragma once) to prevent double inclusion.
Project Structure.code:
my-project/
  CMakeLists.txt
  src/
    main.cpp
    utils.cpp
  include/
    mylib/
      utils.hpp
  tests/
    test_utils.cpp
  lib/
  README.md

// include/mylib/utils.hpp
#pragma once
int add(int a, int b);

Namespaces.exp: Namespaces prevent name collisions. `std` is the standard library namespace. Nested namespaces (C++17): `namespace A::B::C {}`. Never `using namespace` in headers.

Basic Syntax.exp: Semicolons terminate statements. Blocks use braces. `//` single-line, `/* */` multi-line comments. `std::cout` output, `std::cin` input. `#include` for headers.

auto & decltype.exp: `auto` deduces type from initializer (C++11). `decltype` yields the type of an expression. `auto&` deduces reference, `const auto&` deduces const reference.
auto & decltype.code:
auto a = 42;        // int
auto b = 3.14;      // double
auto c = &a;        // int*
const int x = 5;
auto y = x;         // int (const dropped)
auto& z = x;        // const int&

decltype(x) w = 10; // const int
decltype(a + b) d;  // double (promotion)

Type Deduction Rules.exp: `auto` strips references and top-level const (unless you use `auto&` or `const auto&`). `decltype(auto)` preserves exact type (C++14). Template deduction follows similar rules.

nullptr & Fixed-Width Types.exp: `nullptr` (C++11) is the type-safe null pointer. `<cstdint>` provides `int32_t`, `uint64_t`, etc. with guaranteed sizes. `size_t` for sizes/indices.

const & constexpr.exp: `const` for runtime constants. `constexpr` (C++11) for compile-time constants. `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization. `consteval` (C++20) produces compile-time only.

Arithmetic & Logical.exp: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (modulo). `++`, `--` (pre/post). `&&`, `||`, `!` short-circuit. Compound: `+=`, `-=`, etc. Integer division truncates toward zero.
Arithmetic & Logical.code:
int a = 10, b = 3;
int sum = a + b;   // 13
int div = a / b;   // 3 (truncation)
int rem = a % b;   // 1

bool cond = (a > 5) && (b < 10); // true

int x = 5;
int y = ++x;    // x=6, y=6
int z = x++;    // x=7, z=6

Bitwise & Shift.exp: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift). Useful for flags, bitfields, low-level protocols.

Overloaded Operators Basics.exp: Operators can be overloaded for user types. `operator+`, `operator<<`, `operator[]`, `operator()`, etc. Keep semantics intuitive. Some cannot be overloaded (::, ., ?:, sizeof).

User-Defined Literals.exp: Suffixes for literals (C++11). `operator""_suffix`. Common: `std::string` literal `s` (C++14), `std::chrono` literals. Must begin with underscore for user-defined.

if / else.exp: Conditional branching. C++17 added `if constexpr` for compile-time branching in templates. C++17 init-statements: `if (init; cond)`.

Switch.exp: Switch on integral/enum types. Each case needs `break` or `return`. `[[fallthrough]]` suppresses warnings. C++20 added init-statement for switch.

Loops.exp: `for`, `while`, `do-while`. `break` exits, `continue` skips iteration. Classic for uses init;cond;incr pattern.

Range-Based For.exp: Simplified iteration over containers (C++11). Works with arrays, STL containers, and anything with begin/end. Use `auto&` to avoid copies, `const auto&` for read-only.

if constexpr.exp: Compile-time conditional (C++17). Unused branch is discarded, not compiled. Essential for template metaprogramming. Replaces SFINAE in many cases.

Structured Bindings.exp: Decompose tuples, pairs, arrays, structs into individual variables (C++17). Works with `auto`, `auto&`, `const auto&`.

Init-Statements.exp: Variables scoped to if/switch/for (C++17). Reduces scope, improves safety. Combined with structured bindings for powerful patterns.

Declaration & Definition.exp: Declaration (prototype) tells compiler about name/return/params. Definition has the body. Default arguments go in declaration. `void` means no return.

Overloading & Default Args.exp: Multiple functions with the same name but different parameters (overloading). Default arguments must be at the end. Resolved at compile time.

Lambda Expressions.exp: Anonymous functions (C++11). `[]` capture by value, `[&]` by reference. Generic lambdas (C++14): `[](auto x)`. `mutable` allows modifying captured values.

Trailing Return Type.exp: `auto func() -> type` (C++11). Useful when return type depends on parameter types. `decltype` in trailing return enables complex type computation.

noexcept.exp: `noexcept` declares function won't throw. Optimizer can skip exception handling. `noexcept(condition)` for conditional noexcept. `noexcept` is part of function type.

consteval / constinit.exp: `consteval` (C++20) forces compile-time evaluation (immediate function). `constinit` (C++20) guarantees static initialization order. Both complement constexpr.

Function Try Blocks.exp: Function-level try block catches exceptions from constructor initializer lists and function bodies. Primarily useful in constructors for logging/re-throwing.

std::string.exp: Dynamic, safe string from `<string>`. Methods: `length()`, `substr()`, `find()`, `rfind()`, `replace()`, `append()`, `insert()`, `erase()`. Concatenate with `+`.

String Views.exp: `std::string_view` (C++17) is a non-owning reference to a string. Zero-copy. Perfect for function parameters. No null terminator guarantee.

Raw String Literals.exp: Raw literals (C++11) preserve backslashes and newlines. `R"(text)"`. Delimiter optional: `R"delim(text)delim"`. Great for regex, file paths, JSON.

String Conversion.exp: Convert between strings and numbers. `std::to_string()`, `std::stoi`, `stol`, `stod`, `stof`. `std::stringstream` for flexible formatting.

UTF-8 Support.exp: C++11 added `u8"..."` for UTF-8 strings. C++20 made `char8_t` a distinct type. `<codecvt>` is deprecated. Use ICU or platform APIs for full Unicode support.

Classes & Objects.exp: Classes bundle data and methods. Access specifiers: `public`, `private`, `protected`. Constructors with initializer lists. `this` points to current instance.

Inheritance & Polymorphism.exp: Derived classes inherit from base. `virtual` functions enable dynamic dispatch. `override` keyword ensures correct override (C++11). Base class should have virtual destructor.

Virtual Destructors.exp: Base class must have virtual destructor to ensure derived destructors run when deleting through base pointer. `= default` for compiler-generated version.

Pure Virtual & Abstract Classes.exp: Pure virtual `= 0` makes class abstract (cannot instantiate). Derived classes must override. Interface-style classes have only pure virtual methods.

Virtual Inheritance.exp: Solves diamond problem where multiple bases share a common ancestor. `virtual` in inheritance specifier ensures only one copy of base subobject.

Copy & Swap Idiom.exp: Provide strong exception safety for copy-assignment. Implement copy constructor and destructor normally. Assignment operator takes by value (copy) then swaps.

Rule of Five.exp: If you define any of destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment, define all five. Or =default/=delete.

Move Semantics.exp: Move transfers resources without copying (C++11). `std::move` casts to rvalue. Move constructor/assignment use `&&`. After move, source is in valid but unspecified state.

RAII.exp: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. Constructor acquires, destructor releases. Smart pointers, `std::fstream`, `std::lock_guard`, `std::thread` all follow RAII.

std::vector.exp: Dynamic array with O(1) amortized push_back, O(n) insert/erase. Contiguous memory. Methods: `push_back`, `pop_back`, `emplace_back`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`.

std::map & std::set.exp: Ordered associative containers (red-black tree). O(log n) lookup. `map<K,V>` key-value, `set<T>` unique values. Iterate in sorted order.

std::unordered_map / set.exp: Hash-based containers (C++11). O(1) average lookup. Keys need hash function. No order guarantees. `reserve()` for pre-allocation.

std::deque.exp: Double-ended queue. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Non-contiguous memory (chunks). Slightly slower than vector for index access.

std::list & forward_list.exp: `std::list` doubly-linked, `std::forward_list` singly-linked (C++11). O(1) insert/erase anywhere with iterator. No random access. Higher per-element overhead.

Container Adaptors.exp: `std::stack` (LIFO), `std::queue` (FIFO), `std::priority_queue` (max-heap). Built on underlying container (default deque or vector).

std::array.exp: Fixed-size array wrapper (C++11). Stack-allocated. Knows its size. Safer than C arrays. `at()` for bounds checking. Compatible with STL algorithms.

sort, find, transform.exp: Core algorithms from `<algorithm>`. `sort()`, `stable_sort()`, `find()`, `find_if()`, `transform()`, `for_each()`, `copy_if()`. Work on iterator pairs.

lower_bound & binary_search.exp: Binary search on sorted ranges (O(log n)). `lower_bound` returns first >= value. `upper_bound` returns first > value. `binary_search` returns bool. `equal_range` returns both.

partial_sort & nth_element.exp: `partial_sort` sorts first N elements, rest unsorted. `nth_element` places N-th element in correct position, partition around it. Both O(n log k) or O(n).

accumulate & iota.exp: `std::accumulate` (<numeric>) sums/reduces a range. `std::iota` fills with incrementing values. `std::inner_product`, `std::adjacent_difference`, `std::partial_sum`.

count_if & for_each.exp: `count_if` returns count matching predicate. `for_each` applies callable to each element. C++17: `for_each_n`. `all_of`, `any_of`, `none_of` for boolean checks.

Function & Class Templates.exp: Templates parameterize types and values. `typename` or `class` for type params. Non-type params: `int N`. `auto` non-type params (C++17). Template specialization.

Template Specialization.exp: Full specialization provides specific implementation for particular types. Partial specialization for some parameters. Used for type-specific optimization.

Template Template Parameters.exp: Template parameter that is itself a template. Allows passing container templates. `template<typename> class Container`. Works with template template arguments.

Variadic Templates.exp: Templates with variable number of arguments (C++11). `typename... Args`. Pack expansion with `...`. `sizeof...(Args)` for count. Recursive or fold-based processing.

Fold Expressions.exp: Unary and binary folds over parameter packs (C++17). `(... op args)` unary right fold. `(args op ...)` unary left fold. `(init op ... op args)` binary fold.

SFINAE & enable_if.exp: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error. `std::enable_if` controls template overload resolution. `<type_traits>` provides type predicates. Largely replaced by concepts in C++20.

Concepts.exp: Compile-time constraints on template parameters (C++20). Standard: `std::integral`, `std::floating_point`, `std::ranges::range`, `std::convertible_to`. Custom with `concept`.

Ranges Library.exp: Composable, lazy range algorithms (C++20). Pipe syntax `|` for composition. Views: `filter`, `transform`, `take`, `drop`, `reverse`, `join`. `std::views` namespace.

Coroutines.exp: Stackless coroutines (C++20). `co_await`, `co_yield`, `co_return`. Compiler generates state machine. Need library support (cppcoro, or custom promise/awaiter).

Modules.exp: Modern replacement for headers (C++20). `export module`, `import`. Faster compilation, no header guards, better encapsulation. Not all compilers fully support.

Spaceship Operator <=>.exp: Three-way comparison operator (C++20). Returns `std::strong_ordering`, `std::weak_ordering`, `std::partial_ordering`. `= default` generates all six comparison operators.

Views & Lazy Evaluation.exp: `std::views` provide lazy, composable transformations. No allocations. `std::span` is a non-owning view over contiguous memory (C++20). `std::string_view` for strings.

std::expected.exp: Error handling with either a value or an error (like Rust's Result). From `<expected>`. No exception overhead. Functional chaining with `and_then`, `or_else`, `transform`.

Deducing This.exp: Deduce the reference qualifier of `this` for member functions. Allows lambda-like syntax for member functions. Eliminates need for const/non-const overload pairs.

flat_map & flat_set.exp: Contiguous-storage associative containers. `std::flat_map<K,V>` sorted vector<pair>. Faster iteration, less memory, but O(n) insertion. From `<flat_map>`.

mdspan.exp: Multidimensional array view (C++23). Non-owning, layout-polymorphic. Supports strides, extents, subspan. From `<mdspan>`. Replaces manual index calculation.

std::unique_ptr.exp: Exclusive ownership. Non-copyable, movable. `std::make_unique` (C++14). Custom deleter as template parameter. Automatic memory management with zero overhead.

std::shared_ptr.exp: Reference-counted shared ownership. `std::make_shared` allocates control block and object together (one allocation). Thread-safe ref count.

std::weak_ptr.exp: Non-owning reference to shared_ptr. Breaks circular references. Lock to get temporary shared_ptr. `expired()` checks if object still exists.

enable_shared_from_this.exp: CRTP base class that lets object safely create shared_ptrs to itself. Requires object is already managed by shared_ptr. `shared_from_this()` method.

Custom Deleters.exp: Smart pointers accept custom deleters (callable). For non-memory resources: file handles, sockets, C resources. Stored in control block (shared_ptr) or as part of unique_ptr type.

std::thread.exp: OS thread wrapper. `join()` blocks until completion. `detach()` lets run independently (careful with dangling). `std::this_thread::sleep_for`, `get_id`.

Mutex & Locks.exp: `std::mutex` protects shared data. `std::lock_guard` RAII lock. `std::unique_lock` more flexible (defer, try, timed). `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) reader-writer.

Async & Futures.exp: `std::async` launches async tasks. `std::future<T>` gets result once. `std::promise<T>` manually sets value/exception. `std::packaged_task` wraps callable.

std::jthread.exp: Joining thread (C++20). Automatically joins on destruction. Cooperative cancellation via `get_stop_token()`, `request_stop()`.

std::latch & std::barrier.exp: `std::latch` (C++20) single-use countdown. `std::barrier` (C++20) reusable synchronization point. Both from `<latch>` and `<barrier>`.

std::counting_semaphore.exp: Signaling mechanism (C++20). `std::counting_semaphore<max>` with `acquire()`, `release()`. Binary semaphore alias `std::binary_semaphore`. Good for producer-consumer.

std::fstream Basics.exp: File streams: `ifstream` (read), `ofstream` (write), `fstream` (read+write). RAII: closes in destructor. Open modes: `app`, `binary`, `in`, `out`, `trunc`.

std::filesystem.exp: Filesystem library (C++17). Path manipulation, directory iteration, file status. `std::filesystem::path`, `directory_iterator`, `file_status`. Cross-platform.

std::stringstream.exp: In-memory string I/O. `std::stringstream`, `std::istringstream`, `std::ostringstream`. Works with `<<` and `>>`. Useful for parsing and formatting.

Binary I/O.exp: Reading/writing raw bytes. `read()`, `write()` on streams. `reinterpret_cast` for type punning. Endianness and portability concerns.

Exceptions.exp: Exception handling with `try`, `catch`, `throw`. Stack unwinding calls destructors. Catch by reference. `catch(...)` catches all. Re-throw with `throw;`.

noexcept Specifier.exp: `noexcept` promises no exception. `noexcept(condition)` conditional. `noexcept` operator checks. Violation calls `std::terminate`. Optimizer can improve code.

std::exception Hierarchy.exp: Standard exception classes from `<stdexcept>`. Base: `std::exception`. Derived: `logic_error`, `runtime_error`, `bad_alloc`, `bad_cast`, etc.

Error Codes & std::error_code.exp: Lightweight error handling without exceptions. `<system_error>`: `std::error_code`, `std::error_category`. `std::errc` for standard POSIX errors.

CMake Deep.exp: Modern CMake (3.x): targets, properties, generator expressions. `target_link_libraries`, `target_include_directories`, `INTERFACE/PUBLIC/PRIVATE`. FetchContent for dependencies.
CMake Deep.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(MyLib VERSION 1.0.0 LANGUAGES CXX)

# C++ standard
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

# Library target
add_library(mylib
    src/core.cpp
    src/utils.cpp
)
target_include_directories(mylib
    PUBLIC include
    PRIVATE src
)
target_compile_options(mylib PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)

# Executable
add_executable(myapp src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE mylib)

# FetchContent for dependencies
include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(
    fmt
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt
    GIT_TAG 10.1.0
)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt)
target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE fmt::fmt)

# Install
install(TARGETS mylib myapp DESTINATION lib)
install(FILES include/mylib.hpp DESTINATION include)

vcpkg.exp: C++ package manager by Microsoft. Manifest mode (`vcpkg.json`). Integrates with CMake via toolchain file. Ports for 2000+ libraries.
vcpkg.code:
# vcpkg.json
{
    "name": "my-project",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "dependencies": [
        "fmt",
        "boost-asio",
        "nlohmann-json",
        {
            "name": "imgui",
            "features": ["opengl3", "glfw-binding"]
        }
    ]
}

# Install dependencies
# vcpkg install

# CMake integration
# cmake -B build -S . -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=/path/to/vcpkg.cmake

# In CMakeLists.txt (after find_package)
find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)
find_package(nlohmann_json CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE fmt::fmt nlohmann_json::nlohmann_json)

Conan.exp: Decentralized C/C++ package manager. `conanfile.txt` or `conanfile.py`. Supports multiple generators (CMake, MSBuild, etc.). Profiles for configurations.
Conan.code:
# conanfile.txt
[requires]
fmt/10.1.0
boost/1.84.0
nlohmann_json/3.11.2

[generators]
CMakeDeps
CMakeToolchain

[options]
boost/*:shared=False

# Install dependencies
# conan install . --output-folder=build --build=missing

# CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(MyApp)

find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)
find_package(nlohmann_json CONFIG REQUIRED)

add_executable(app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE fmt::fmt nlohmann_json::nlohmann_json)

# Or with conanfile.py for complex logic
# from conans import ConanFile
# class MyConan(ConanFile):
#     requires = "fmt/10.1.0"
#     generators = "CMakeDeps"

Build Tools Overview.exp: Ninja (fast parallel builds), Make (classic), Bazel (monorepo), Meson (Python-based). C++20 modules require build system support.
Build Tools Overview.code:
# Ninja (generated by CMake)
# cmake -B build -G Ninja
# ninja -C build

# Make (traditional)
CXX = g++
CXXFLAGS = -std=c++20 -Wall -O2

app: main.cpp utils.cpp
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -o $@ $^

clean:
	rm -f app *.o

# Bazel BUILD file
# cc_binary(
#     name = "app",
#     srcs = ["main.cpp", "utils.cpp"],
#     deps = ["//lib:mylib"],
# )

# Meson
# project('myapp', 'cpp', version: '1.0')
# executable('app', 'main.cpp', 'utils.cpp')

Qt Framework.exp: Cross-platform framework for GUI, networking, SQL, etc. Key modules: QtWidgets, QtCore, QtNetwork, QtQml, QtQuick. Signal-slot mechanism for communication.

Boost Libraries.exp: Peer-reviewed, portable C++ library collection. Key: Boost.Asio (networking), Boost.Beast (HTTP/WebSocket), Boost.Filesystem, Boost.Test, Boost.PropertyTree, Boost.ProgramOptions.

Unreal Engine C++.exp: UE uses C++ with reflection macros: `UCLASS`, `USTRUCT`, `UPROPERTY`, `UFUNCTION`. Gameplay classes, Actors, Components, GameplayAbilitySystem.

Google Test & Benchmark.exp: Testing and benchmarking. GTest: `TEST`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. GMock for mocking. Google Benchmark for performance measurement.

std::optional (C++17).exp: `std::optional<T>` holds a value or nothing. Avoids sentinel values (-1, nullptr, empty string). `has_value()`, `value()` (throws `std::bad_optional_access` on empty), `value_or(default)`. Monadic ops in C++23: `and_then`, `transform`, `or_else`.

std::variant (C++17).exp: Type-safe union from `<variant>`. Holds one of several types at a time. `std::visit()` dispatches based on current type. `index()` returns which alternative is active. No undefined behavior unlike raw unions. `std::monostate` for empty variant.

std::any (C++17).exp: Type-erased container (like `void*` but type-safe). From `<any>`. `any_cast<T>()` throws `std::bad_any_cast` on type mismatch. `has_value()`, `type()` for RTTI. Prefer `variant` when types are known at compile time.

Type Traits & Metaprogramming.exp: `<type_traits>` provides compile-time queries: `is_integral`, `is_floating_point`, `is_pointer`, `is_same`, `remove_reference`, `decay`, `enable_if`. `static_assert` for compile-time checking. `if constexpr` (C++17) simplifies template code.

Inline Variables (C++17).exp: C++17 extends `inline` to variables, allowing header-only definitions without ODR violations. Previously, static class members and global constants needed a `.cpp` definition. `inline constexpr` works too. All translation units share one address.

[[nodiscard]] & [[maybe_unused]].exp: `[[nodiscard]]` (C++17) warns if return value is discarded. C++20 adds `[[nodiscard("reason")]]`. `[[maybe_unused]]` suppresses unused warnings. Essential for error-returning functions, RAII guards, and stub/hook points.

std::clamp / std::gcd / std::lcm (C++17).exp: `std::clamp(v, lo, hi)` from `<algorithm>` constrains a value to [lo, hi]. `std::gcd` / `std::lcm` from `<numeric>` compute greatest common divisor and least common multiple. All are constexpr-friendly.

Parallel STL Algorithms (C++17).exp: Execution policies from `<execution>`: `seq` (sequential), `par` (parallel threads), `par_unseq` (parallel + SIMD), `unseq` (C++20, vectorized single-thread). Apply to `sort`, `transform`, `for_each`, `reduce`, etc. Backend: Intel TBB or compiler-specific.

Code Organization (PIMPL Idiom).exp: PIMPL (Pointer to Implementation) hides private members from the header, reducing recompilation dependencies. The header only has a forward-declared struct pointer (`Impl*` or `unique_ptr<Impl>`). The .cpp file defines the implementation struct.

Design Patterns: Strategy & Observer.exp: Strategy: encapsulate algorithms behind a common interface, selected at runtime. Observer: one-to-many notification on state change. C++ supports both via virtual interfaces, `std::function`, and smart pointers for ownership management.

Testing with Catch2 & GTest.exp: Catch2: header-only (v2) or compiled library (v3), BDD-style with SECTIONs. GTest: xUnit-style, `TEST()`, `EXPECT_EQ`, `ASSERT_TRUE`. Both support matchers, fixtures, and parameterized tests. Integrate with CMake: `enable_testing()` + `add_test()`.

Performance Optimization.exp: From Professional C++: 1) Move semantics avoid deep copies. 2) Reserve vector capacity upfront. 3) Pass by const reference, not value. 4) CRTP avoids virtual dispatch in hot paths. 5) Profile first (Google Benchmark, perf). 6) Small-string optimization.

References.exp: A reference (`T&`) is an alias to an existing object. Cannot be null, must be initialized, cannot be rebound. Used for function parameters (pass by reference) and return values.

Raw Pointers.exp: Pointers hold memory addresses. Declared as `T*`. Dereference with `*`, get address with `&`. Can be null (`nullptr`). Support pointer arithmetic.

new & delete.exp: Dynamic memory allocation. `new` allocates + constructs, `delete` destructs + deallocates. Array forms: `new[]`, `delete[]`. Prefer smart pointers in modern C++.

Memory Leakage.exp: Memory allocated with `new` that is never `delete`d. Causes: lost pointers, exception before delete, circular shared_ptr. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer.

Memory Model.exp: C++ memory model defines how threads interact through memory. `std::memory_order` for atomics. Sequential consistency, acquire/release, relaxed.

Object Lifetime.exp: Objects are created (constructor), live, then destroyed (destructor). Storage durations: automatic (stack), static, thread, dynamic (heap).

static_cast.exp: Compile-time cast between related types. Numeric conversions, upcasts/downcasts in class hierarchies, `void*` to typed pointer.

dynamic_cast.exp: Runtime-checked cast for polymorphic types. Requires at least one virtual function. Returns null for pointers on failure.

const_cast.exp: Adds or removes `const`/`volatile` qualification. Modifying a const object through const_cast is UB.

reinterpret_cast.exp: Unsafe cast that reinterprets the bit pattern. No type checking. Used for serialization, hardware access.

RTTI & typeid.exp: Run-Time Type Information. `typeid` returns `std::type_info`. `dynamic_cast` also uses RTTI. Disabled with `-fno-rtti`.

Undefined Behavior.exp: UB: program can do anything. Common: null dereference, buffer overflow, signed overflow, use-after-free, data races.

ADL.exp: Argument-Dependent Lookup (Koenig lookup): searches namespaces of argument types when calling a function.

Name Mangling.exp: Compilers encode function signatures into linker symbols. Different across compilers => no ABI compatibility. `extern "C"` disables mangling.

Macros.exp: Preprocessor directives (`#define`, `#ifdef`, `#pragma`). Text substitution before compilation. Modern C++ prefers `constexpr`, templates.
Macros.code:
#define PI 3.14159
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#ifndef MY_HEADER_H
#define MY_HEADER_H
#endif
#ifdef DEBUG
#define LOG(x) std::cerr << x << std::endl
#else
#define LOG(x)
#endif
std::cout << __FILE__ << ":" << __LINE__ << std::endl;
#define STR(x) #x
#define CONCAT(a,b) a ## b

Forward Declaration.exp: Declaring a symbol before its full definition. Reduces compilation dependencies, breaks circular references.

Scope & Storage Duration.exp: Scope controls name visibility. Storage duration: automatic (stack), static, thread, dynamic (heap). `::` for global scope.

Multiple Inheritance.exp: A class can inherit from multiple base classes. Syntax: `class D : public A, public B`. Can lead to diamond problem.

Diamond Inheritance.exp: Two classes share a common base. Virtual inheritance (`virtual public`) creates one shared subobject.

Virtual Tables.exp: Each polymorphic class has a vtable. Each object has a vptr. `virtual` function calls dispatch through vtable at runtime.

Dynamic Polymorphism.exp: Runtime polymorphism via virtual functions and base pointers/references. Enables substitutability.

GDB Basics.exp: GNU Debugger: step through code, inspect variables, backtrace. Commands: `run`, `break`, `next`, `step`, `print`, `backtrace`.
GDB Basics.code:
# g++ -g -O0 -o app main.cpp
# gdb ./app
# (gdb) break main
# (gdb) run
# (gdb) next
# (gdb) step
# (gdb) print x
