# (gdb) backtrace
# (gdb) continue
# (gdb) quit

Debugging Symbols.exp: `-g` flag embeds debug info (DWARF on Linux, PDB on Windows). Levels: `-g0` none, `-g3` extra.
Debugging Symbols.code:
# g++ -g -O2 -o app main.cpp
# g++ -g3 -O0 -o app main.cpp
# objcopy --only-keep-debug app app.debug
# strip app
# nm -C app
# readelf -w app

Sanitizers.exp: Google sanitizers catch memory errors and UB. `-fsanitize=address` (ASan), `-fsanitize=undefined` (UBSan).

Performance Profiling.exp: Profiling measures where time is spent. `perf` (Linux), Google Benchmark, `gprof`.
Performance Profiling.code:
# perf record -g ./app
# perf report
# g++ -pg -O2 -o app main.cpp
# ./app
# gprof app gmon.out > report

Compiler Stages.exp: Four stages: 1) Preprocessing, 2) Compilation (C++ -> assembly), 3) Assembly (asm -> .o), 4) Linking.
Compiler Stages.code:
# g++ -E main.cpp -o main.i
# g++ -S main.cpp -o main.s
# g++ -c main.cpp -o main.o
# g++ main.o utils.o -o app

GCC & Clang.exp: GCC (`g++`): mature, extensive optimization. Clang (`clang++`): faster, better error messages, great tooling.
GCC & Clang.code:
# g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -O2 -o app main.cpp
# g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -march=native -flto -o app main.cpp
# clang++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -O2 -o app main.cpp
# clang-tidy src/main.cpp
# clang-format -i src/*.cpp

MSVC.exp: Microsoft Visual C++: Windows-only, `/std:c++latest`. MinGW: GCC port for Windows.
MSVC.code:
# cl /std:c++latest /EHsc /W4 /O2 main.cpp
# cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 /O2 /Fe:app.exe main.cpp
# g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -o app.exe main.cpp
# x86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -std=c++20 -o app.exe main.cpp
# clang-cl /std:c++20 /EHsc main.cpp

Linkers & LTO.exp: Linker combines object files into executable/library. Link-Time Optimization enables cross-TU inlining.
Linkers & LTO.code:
# g++ main.o utils.o -o app -static
# g++ -shared -o libmylib.so mylib.cpp
# g++ main.cpp -L. -lmylib -o app
# g++ -flto -O2 main.cpp utils.cpp -o app
# clang++ -flto -O2 main.cpp utils.cpp -o app
# nm -C app.o
# ldd app

CRTP.exp: Curiously Recurring Template Pattern: derived class passes itself as template parameter to base. Static polymorphism, no vtable overhead.

Non-Copyable Idiom.exp: Delete copy operations to prevent unintended duplication. Essential for RAII wrappers owning unique resources.

Erase-Remove Idiom.exp: `remove`/`remove_if` moves elements to end, returns new logical end. Pair with `erase`. C++20 `std::erase` simplifies.

Copy on Write.exp: Defer copying until a write is attempted. Less beneficial with move semantics.

std::chrono.exp: Type-safe time library. `duration`, `time_point`, `clock`. C++20 adds calendar and time zones.

Random Number Generation.exp: C++11 `<random>`: engines (mt19937) and distributions (uniform_int, normal). Better than `rand()`.

Iterator Categories.exp: Five categories: Input, Output, Forward, Bidirectional, Random Access. Higher categories support more algorithms.

fmtlib.exp: Fast, safe formatting library. Basis for C++20 `std::format`. Type-safe, extensible.

spdlog.exp: Fast, header-only logging library. Async logging, rotating files, multiple sinks.

Protobuf & gRPC.exp: Protocol Buffers: language-agnostic serialization. gRPC: RPC framework using protobuf + HTTP/2.

What is .NET?.exp: .NET is a free, cross-platform, open-source developer platform. It includes .NET Core (modern), .NET Framework (Windows-only legacy), and .NET 5+ (unified). Choose the right runtime for your scenario.

Project Types & Templates.exp: .NET provides project templates via `dotnet new`: console, classlib, web (ASP.NET Core), mvc, webapi, blazor, xunit, maui, worker, and more. Each generates the right .csproj structure.
Project Types & Templates.code:
dotnet new list                      # List all templates
dotnet new console -n MyConsole       # Console app
dotnet new webapi -n MyApi            # Web API
dotnet new classlib -n MyLib          # Class library
dotnet new xunit -n MyTests           # Test project

IDE & Editor Choices.exp: C# development works in Visual Studio (full IDE), Visual Studio Code (lightweight with C# Dev Kit), JetBrains Rider (cross-platform), or the CLI with any editor. The .NET CLI is universal.
IDE & Editor Choices.code:
# VS Code with C# Dev Kit
dotnet build          # Build all projects
dotnet test           # Run all tests
dotnet publish -c Release  # Publish for production
dotnet format         # Auto-format code

Top-Level Statements.exp: C# 9+ top-level statements eliminate boilerplate Program class and Main method. The compiler generates them automatically, enabling script-like entry points.

File-Scoped Namespaces.exp: C# 10 file-scoped namespaces remove one level of indentation. Use `namespace X;` syntax at the top of the file instead of a block. All declarations in the file belong to that namespace.

Primitive Types.exp: C# has built-in value types: integral (byte, short, int, long), floating-point (float, double, decimal), character (char), boolean (bool). Each maps to a .NET struct in System namespace.

var & Implicit Typing.exp: The `var` keyword tells the compiler to infer the type from the right-hand expression. It is strongly typed at compile time. Use it when the type is obvious from context, but prefer explicit types for public APIs.

object & dynamic.exp: `object` is the universal base type (requires casting). `dynamic` bypasses compile-time type checking and resolves at runtime. Use `dynamic` sparingly — it sacrifices safety for flexibility (COM, JSON, DLR scenarios).

Nullable Value Types.exp: Value types (structs) can be made nullable with the `?` suffix (e.g., int?, bool?). Nullable<T> wraps the value with HasValue/Value properties. Use null-conditional operators to handle null safely.

Nullable Reference Types.exp: C# 8+ nullable reference types enable compile-time null-state analysis. Types are non-nullable by default; use `?` suffix to allow null. Enable via `#nullable enable` or in .csproj. The compiler emits warnings for unsafe dereferences.

Null-Forgiving Operator.exp: The `!` postfix operator (null-forgiving / dammit operator) suppresses nullable warnings when you know a value isn't null despite the compiler's analysis. Use cautiously.

Constants & Readonly.exp: `const` is a compile-time constant (implicitly static, no modifiers). `readonly` is a runtime constant set in the constructor. `static readonly` is like a constant that can be computed at runtime.

Tuple Types.exp: C# 7+ tuples provide lightweight multi-value grouping with named fields. ValueTuple structs avoid heap allocation. Tuples are great for internal use; prefer records for public APIs.

Arithmetic & Assignment.exp: Standard arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) work on numeric types. Assignment can be combined (+=, -=, etc.). The increment (++) and decrement (--) operators have prefix/postfix forms with different evaluation order.
Arithmetic & Assignment.code:
int a = 10, b = 3;
Console.WriteLine(a + b);  // 13
Console.WriteLine(a - b);  // 7
Console.WriteLine(a * b);  // 30
Console.WriteLine(a / b);  // 3 (integer division)
Console.WriteLine(a % b);  // 1

int x = 5;
Console.WriteLine(x++);     // 5 (post-increment)
Console.WriteLine(++x);     // 7 (pre-increment)
x += 10; Console.WriteLine(x); // 17

Comparison & Equality.exp: Comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) work on value types. For reference types, == compares references by default; override Equals and == for value semantics. Records have built-in value equality.

Logical & Bitwise.exp: Logical operators (&&, ||, !) short-circuit. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) operate on integer bits. Use `&&` instead of `&` and `||` instead of `|` for boolean logic to benefit from short-circuit evaluation.
Logical & Bitwise.code:
bool a = true, b = false;
Console.WriteLine(a && b);  // False (short-circuits)
Console.WriteLine(a || b);  // True (short-circuits)
Console.WriteLine(!a);      // False

int x = 0b1100, y = 0b1010;
Console.WriteLine(x & y);   // 1000 (8)
Console.WriteLine(x | y);   // 1110 (14)
Console.WriteLine(x ^ y);   // 0110 (6)
Console.WriteLine(~x);      // ...0011
Console.WriteLine(x << 2);  // 110000 (48)

Null-Conditional Operator.exp: The `?.` operator safely accesses members of a possibly-null expression. It short-circuits to null if the left operand is null. Chain multiple `?.` or combine with `??` for fallback values.

Null-Coalescing Operators.exp: `??` returns the left operand if it's not null, otherwise the right operand. `??=` (C# 8+) assigns the right operand to the left only if the left is null. Both short-circuit.

Switch Expressions.exp: C# 8+ switch expressions provide concise, expression-based pattern matching. Unlike switch statements, they produce a value. Supports type patterns, when guards, property patterns, discards, and relational patterns.

Conditional Operator.exp: The ternary `?:` operator evaluates a boolean condition and returns one of two expressions. Use for inline conditional values; avoid nesting for readability.

if / else if / else.exp: Standard conditional branching. Use `if` for boolean conditions, chain with `else if` for multiple paths, and `else` as the fallback. Can use pattern matching in conditions with `is` expressions.

Switch Statement.exp: Switch statements evaluate an expression against multiple case patterns. C# 7+ added type patterns, when guards, and the `_` discard. Cases can fall through with `goto case`, but typically each case has a `break`.

Pattern Matching.exp: C# pattern matching includes type patterns, property patterns, positional patterns (with deconstruction), var patterns, discard patterns, relational patterns (`<`, `>`, `>=`), and logical patterns (`and`, `or`, `not`).

for Loop.exp: The classic `for` loop uses an initializer, condition, and iterator. Perfect for indexed iteration, reverse loops, and scenarios where the iteration count is known. Declare the counter variable inline for scoped access.

foreach Loop.exp: `foreach` iterates over any type implementing IEnumerable or IEnumerable<T>. The iterator variable is read-only inside the loop. For arrays, the compiler optimizes with a `for` loop internally.

while & do-while.exp: `while` checks the condition before each iteration (zero or more runs). `do-while` checks after (always runs at least once). Use when the iteration count isn't known upfront.

break, continue, goto.exp: `break` exits the current loop. `continue` skips to the next iteration. `goto` jumps to a labeled statement (use rarely). `return` exits the method entirely. Use `break` in loops and switch cases.

using Declaration.exp: C# 8+ using declarations automatically dispose resources when the variable goes out of scope. Eliminates the nesting of traditional `using` statements. Works with IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable.

Method Basics.exp: Methods encapsulate reusable logic. They have a signature (name, return type, parameters), a body, and an access modifier. C# supports method overloading (same name, different parameters). Methods can be static or instance.

Parameter Modifiers (ref, in, out).exp: `ref` passes a reference to the variable (read-write). `in` passes by reference but is read-only (avoids copying for large structs). `out` passes by reference for returning values; the method must assign it before returning.

params Keyword.exp: The `params` keyword allows a variable number of arguments. The parameter must be a single-dimensional array and must be the last parameter. The compiler generates the array automatically.

Optional & Named Parameters.exp: Optional parameters have default values and can be omitted. Named arguments let you specify parameters by name, enabling skipping optional ones and improving readability for boolean/optional parameters.

Expression-Bodied Members.exp: C# 6+ expression-bodied members use `=>` for concise single-expression methods, properties, and operators. Available for methods, get-only properties, constructors, finalizers, and operators.

Local Functions.exp: C# 7+ local functions are nested methods inside another method. They capture variables from the enclosing scope, support generics, async, and even attributes. Great for helper logic that shouldn't leak.

Return Values & Multiple Returns.exp: Methods return a single value. Return multiple values using tuples, out parameters, or a custom class/record. Tuples are lightweight; records are better for public APIs. Use `ValueTuple` for zero-allocation returns.

Classes & Objects.exp: Classes are reference types that serve as blueprints for objects. They encapsulate data (fields, properties) and behavior (methods). Use `new` to create instances. Classes support inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.

Fields & Properties.exp: Fields store internal state. Properties expose fields with get/set accessors, enabling validation, computed values, and lazy initialization. Auto-properties generate backing fields automatically (C# 3+).

Init Setters & Required Members.exp: C# 9 `init` setters enable object initializer-only property assignment (immutable after construction). C# 11 `required` members force callers to provide a value during initialization. Both support object/collection initializer patterns.

Primary Constructors.exp: C# 12 primary constructors allow parameter declaration directly on the class/struct/record. Parameters are in scope throughout the class body. For classes, they don't auto-generate properties (unlike records). Capture them explicitly if needed.

Record Types.exp: C# 9 records provide value semantics by default: positional construction, immutable properties (with init), value-based equality, `with` expressions for non-destructive mutation, and concise deconstruction. Use `record class` (reference) or `record struct` (value).

Inheritance.exp: C# supports single class inheritance. Use `:` to derive, `virtual` for overridable methods, `override` for specialization, `abstract` for forced implementation, `sealed` to prevent further inheritance. Base class constructors chain via `: base()`.

Polymorphism.exp: Polymorphism allows derived types to be treated as base types. Virtual method dispatch calls the most derived override at runtime. Interface polymorphism enables unrelated types to share contracts. Use `is` and `as` for type-safe casting.

Abstract Classes & Sealed.exp: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated, serving as base types with partial implementation. `abstract` members have no body and must be overridden. `sealed` on a class prevents inheritance entirely; on a method it stops further overriding.

Static Members & Classes.exp: Static classes contain only static members and cannot be instantiated. Static members belong to the type, not instances. Static constructors run once per type before any static member access. Extension methods must be in static classes.

Object Initializers.exp: Object initializers set properties/fields at creation without requiring a constructor. Collection initializers add items inline. Works with `init` setters and `required` members (C# 11+).

Interface Basics.exp: Interfaces define contracts with methods, properties, events, and indexers. A class/struct can implement multiple interfaces. Interfaces enable loose coupling, polymorphism, and dependency injection. C# 8+ allows default implementations.

Default Interface Methods.exp: C# 8+ default interface methods allow adding members to interfaces without breaking existing implementations. Implementations can override the default. Useful for API evolution and trait-like patterns. Not available in .NET Framework 4.8.

Generic Constraints.exp: Constraints restrict type parameters: `where T : class` (reference), `struct` (value), `notnull` (non-nullable), `new()` (parameterless constructor), base class, interface, or `unmanaged` (blittable). Multiple constraints are stacked.

Covariance & Contravariance.exp: Covariance (`out`) allows using a more derived type in output positions (e.g., `IEnumerable<Dog>` as `IEnumerable<Animal>`). Contravariance (`in`) allows less derived input (e.g., `IComparer<Animal>` as `IComparer<Dog>`). Only applies to interfaces/delegates with reference types.

Generic Methods.exp: Type parameters can be defined on methods (not just classes). The compiler infers types from arguments. Generic methods enable type-safe algorithms without boxing. Combine with constraints for additional capabilities.

IDisposable & IAsyncDisposable.exp: IDisposable defines a deterministic cleanup pattern. The `using` statement ensures Dispose() is called even on exceptions. `IAsyncDisposable` (C# 8+) enables async cleanup with `await using`. Implement the dispose pattern properly for classes holding unmanaged resources.

Arrays.exp: Fixed-size, zero-indexed collections of elements of the same type. Arrays are reference types with a fixed length set at creation. Supports multi-dimensional (rectangular) and jagged (array-of-arrays) forms.

List<T>.exp: List<T> is a generic dynamic array that grows as needed. Provides O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove at arbitrary positions. Use for ordered collections where size changes. Implements IList<T>, ICollection<T>, IEnumerable<T>.

Dictionary<TKey, TValue>.exp: Dictionary provides O(1) key-value lookups via hash table. Keys must be unique and properly implement GetHashCode/Equals. Use TryGetValue for safe access. Use ConcurrentDictionary for thread-safe scenarios.

HashSet<T> & SortedSet<T>.exp: HashSet<T> is an unordered set with O(1) add/remove/lookup. SortedSet<T> maintains sorted order (O(log n)). Both implement ISet<T> with set operations: UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, SymmetricExceptWith.

Queue<T> & Stack<T>.exp: Queue<T> is FIFO (Enqueue/Dequeue/Peek). Stack<T> is LIFO (Push/Pop/Peek). Both use arrays internally with O(1) amortized operations. Use for breadth-first vs depth-first processing patterns.

LINQ Basics.exp: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) enables querying any IEnumerable<T> with SQL-like syntax. Query syntax (`from x in xs where ...`) or method syntax (`.Where().Select()`) produce the same IL. Deferred execution until enumeration.

LINQ Methods Deep.exp: LINQ provides projection (Select, SelectMany), filtering (Where, OfType), ordering (OrderBy, ThenBy, Reverse), grouping (GroupBy, ToLookup), joins (Join, GroupJoin), aggregation (Sum, Average, Min, Max, Count, Aggregate), set ops (Distinct, Union, Intersect, Except), partitioning (Skip, Take, SkipWhile, TakeWhile), and element ops (First, Last, Single, ElementAt, DefaultIfEmpty).

LINQ GroupBy & Joins.exp: GroupBy partitions sequences into groups with a key. Join performs inner joins on matching keys. GroupJoin creates a hierarchical result (left outer join). Zip combines two sequences element-by-element. All support custom equality comparers.

Concurrent Collections.exp: System.Collections.Concurrent provides thread-safe collections: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,T> (lock-free ops), ConcurrentQueue<T> (FIFO), ConcurrentStack<T> (LIFO), ConcurrentBag<T> (unordered), BlockingCollection<T> (bounded producer/consumer).

PLINQ (Parallel LINQ).exp: PLINQ automatically parallelizes LINQ queries via `AsParallel()`. Uses partitioning and thread pooling. Control parallelism with `WithDegreeOfParallelism`, `WithExecutionMode`, `WithCancellation`. Results can be unordered (`AsUnordered`) for better performance.

try / catch / finally.exp: Structured exception handling: `try` guards code, `catch` handles exceptions (specific or general), `finally` always executes (cleanup). Exceptions bubble up the call stack until caught. Unhandled exceptions crash the process.

Exception Filters (when).exp: C# 6 exception filters using `when` keyword catch exceptions only when a condition is true. Unlike catching and re-throwing, filters don't unwind the stack. Useful for conditional handling based on exception data.

Custom Exceptions.exp: Create custom exceptions by inheriting from Exception. Follow best practices: end class name with `Exception`, implement the three standard constructors, use serialization if needed, provide additional properties for rich error data.

Guard Clauses & Argument Validation.exp: Validate arguments early using guard clauses. Use `ArgumentException`, `ArgumentNullException`, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. C# 11 lets you specify the nameof parameter. Consider using `ThrowHelper` patterns or a library like Ardalis.GuardClauses to reduce inlining.

Throw Helpers.exp: Throw helpers are `static` local/member methods that throw exceptions. The JIT sees `throw` as a cold path and doesn't inline the helper, reducing method size and improving performance. Use for validation-heavy APIs.

Result Pattern (Functional Error Handlin.exp: Instead of exceptions for expected failures, use a Result type to return success/failure explicitly. Common in domain-driven design. Integrates with `switch` expressions for exhaustive handling. Libraries like FluentResults or OneOf formalize this pattern.

async / await Basics.exp: async/await enables non-blocking asynchronous code. async methods return Task, Task<T>, or ValueTask<T>. Await suspends the method without blocking the thread. Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code to avoid capturing SynchronizationContext.

Task & Task<T>.exp: Task represents an async operation. Task<T> produces a value. Tasks can be awaited, combined (WhenAll, WhenAny), or continued (ContinueWith, but prefer await). Status tracks lifecycle: Created, WaitingForActivation, RanToCompletion, Faulted, Canceled.

Cancellation.exp: CancellationToken from CancellationTokenSource enables cooperative cancellation. Pass to async methods. Throw OperationCanceledException when cancelled. Use Register for callbacks. Linked tokens combine multiple sources.

ValueTask & ValueTask<T>.exp: ValueTask<T> (C# 7+) is a struct that can wrap a synchronous result or a Task<T>. Avoids allocation when the result is already available. Use only for hot paths where sync completion is common. Can only be awaited once (use AsTask() for multiple).

Async Streams (IAsyncEnumerable).exp: C# 8+ async streams enable async iteration with `await foreach`. Methods return `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` using `yield return` with `await`. Supports CancellationToken, ConfigureAwait, and LINQ via System.Linq.Async.

Channel<T>.exp: System.Threading.Channels provides thread-safe producer/consumer queues. Bounded channels (backpressure) limit capacity; unbounded grow indefinitely. ChannelReader exposes ReadAllAsync() for async streams. Perfect for pub/sub and pipeline patterns.

Task Parallel Library (Dataflow).exp: System.Threading.Tasks.Dataflow provides actor-like message passing blocks: BufferBlock<T>, ActionBlock<T>, TransformBlock<TInput,TOutput>, BatchBlock<T>, JoinBlock<T1,T2>. Link blocks into pipelines with completion propagation. Fine-grained parallelism control.

Thread Synchronization.exp: Use `lock` for mutual exclusion (Monitor syntactic sugar). For finer control: Monitor (Wait/Pulse), Mutex (cross-process), Semaphore/SemaphoreSlim (counting), ReaderWriterLockSlim (read-heavy), Barrier (phased), CountdownEvent, ManualResetEvent. Prefer higher-level primitives.

Parallel.For / Parallel.ForEach.exp: System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel provides parallel loops: Parallel.For (indexed), Parallel.ForEach (enumerable), Parallel.Invoke (multiple actions). Controls degree of parallelism and supports thread-local state (overloads). Use for CPU-bound parallel work.

File & Directory Operations.exp: System.IO provides File (static methods), FileInfo (instance), Directory, DirectoryInfo, and Path. Read/write text, bytes, or lines. Use async methods for I/O-bound work. Guard against path traversal and IO exceptions.

StreamReader / StreamWriter.exp: StreamReader/StreamWriter provide text-level access over streams. Support different encodings, buffer sizes, and async operations. Use `using` for proper disposal. FileStream provides raw byte-level access.

System.Text.Json.exp: System.Text.Json (high-performance, UTF-8) serializes/deserializes JSON. Supports source generators (AOT-friendly), custom converters, ignore/modify serialization via attributes, JsonDocument (DOM), and JsonSerializerOptions for configuration.

System.Text.Json Source Generators.exp: C# 9+ source generators for System.Text.Json eliminate runtime reflection. Declare partial classes with [JsonSerializerSerializable] (or [JsonSourceGenerationOptions]) for compile-time serialization. Enables native AOT, reduces startup, avoids reflection.

XML Serialization.exp: XmlSerializer serializes to/from XML. Control output with attributes ([XmlElement], [XmlAttribute], [XmlIgnore], [XmlArray]). Supports complex object graphs. XDocument/Linq to Xml provides LINQ-friendly XML manipulation.

Binary Serialization (obsolete).exp: BinaryFormatter (now obsolete/unsafe) serializes object graphs including private members. .NET 8+ throws PlatformNotSupportedException. Use JSON, Protobuf, or MessagePack instead. Never use BinaryFormatter in new code due to security risks (deserialization vulnerabilities).

Protocol Buffers (Protobuf).exp: Google.Protobuf provides compact, cross-language serialization via .proto definitions. Much smaller/faster than JSON. Use with gRPC. Generate C# classes from .proto files. Ideal for high-performance internal services and wire protocols.

Span<T> & ReadOnlySpan<T>.exp: Span<T> is a stack-allocated ref struct providing safe, allocation-free views over contiguous memory (arrays, strings, native memory). No heap allocation. Ideal for high-performance string parsing, buffer manipulation, and slicing operations.

Memory<T> & ReadOnlyMemory<T>.exp: Memory<T> is the heap-friendly counterpart to Span<T>. Can be stored in fields, async methods, and lambdas. Use Span<T> for synchronous processing, Memory<T> when the buffer needs to survive on the heap or cross async boundaries.

ref struct & readonly ref struct.exp: ref struct types are stack-only (cannot be boxed, used as generic type args, stored in heap, or be a field of a class). Used by Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>. `readonly ref struct` ensures all fields are readonly. Enables safe stack-only memory handling.

stackalloc.exp: stackalloc allocates memory on the stack (fast, no GC pressure). Use with Span<T> for safe access. Available in unsafe and safe contexts (via Span). Be mindful of stack space (~1 MB per thread). Best for small temporary buffers.

Unsafe Code & Pointers.exp: C# supports pointer operations in `unsafe` blocks. Enables direct memory access, pointer arithmetic, and fixed memory. Use for interop and performance-critical code. Requires `/unsafe` compiler option. Prefer Span<T> over raw pointers when possible.

Ref Returns & Ref Locals.exp: ref returns allow methods to return references (avoiding copying). ref locals alias existing variables. `ref readonly` returns read-only references. Useful for performance in large struct manipulation and array-like data structures.

Memory Pool & ArrayPool.exp: ArrayPool<T> reuses arrays to reduce allocation and GC pressure. MemoryPool<T> wraps ArrayPool for Memory<T>. Rent and return buffers. Critical in high-throughput server applications (ASP.NET Core, Dataflow). Always return rented buffers.

P/Invoke (Platform Invoke).exp: P/Invoke calls native functions from DLLs using DllImport. Specify CharSet, CallingConvention, EntryPoint. Marshal data between managed and unmanaged memory. Use LibraryImport (source-generated) in .NET 7+ for better performance.

COM Interop.exp: COM interop enables calling COM components from .NET (and .NET components from COM). Use COM import attributes, RCW (Runtime Callable Wrapper). .NET 5+ improved COM activation. Common for Office automation, Windows shell extensions, and legacy COM libraries.

Fixed Size Buffers.exp: Fixed-size buffers (fixed keyword) define inline arrays in structs for interop scenarios. Used in unsafe context. The buffer is embedded in the struct layout, matching native memory layouts. Commonly used with P/Invoke and binary protocol parsing.

Marshal Class.exp: System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal provides methods for allocating/freeing unmanaged memory, converting between managed/unmanaged types, structure layout, COM interop, and size computations. Essential for low-level interop scenarios.

xUnit.net Basics.exp: xUnit is .NET's most popular test framework. Use [Fact] for parameterless tests, [Theory] with [InlineData], [ClassData], or [MemberData] for parameterized tests. Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is the standard structure. Use IClassFixture for shared context.

NUnit Basics.exp: NUnit uses [Test], [TestCase], [SetUp], [TearDown], [OneTimeSetUp]. Supports assertions with Assert.That (constraint model), categories, retries, parallel execution. Classic assertions (AreEqual) also work but constraint model is preferred.

Moq (Mocking).exp: Moq creates mock objects for interfaces and classes. Setup method behavior, verify invocations, use Callback for side effects. Supports strict vs loose mocking (default: loose). Combine with It.Is<T>() for argument matching.

FluentAssertions.exp: FluentAssertions provides readable, self-documenting assertions. Supports chaining, object graph comparison, collections, strings, timespans, exceptions, and more. Integrates with xUnit, NUnit, MSTest. Produces detailed failure messages.

TDD with C#.exp: Test-Driven Development cycle: Red (write failing test), Green (write minimal code to pass), Refactor (improve code while tests pass). Tests drive API design. Use parameterized tests for edge cases. Keep tests fast, isolated, and deterministic.

NuGet Package Manager.exp: NuGet is the package manager for .NET. `dotnet add package` installs packages. `dotnet restore` resolves dependencies. PackageReference in .csproj stores versions. nuget.config controls sources. Use Central Package Management for multi-project solutions.
NuGet Package Manager.code:
# Add packages
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer --version 8.0.0

# Restore
dotnet restore

# List packages
dotnet list package

dotnet list package --vulnerable  # Check for vulnerabilities

# Pack and publish
# dotnet pack -o ./nupkg
# dotnet nuget push ./nupkg/*.nupkg --api-key <key> --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json

// .csproj snippet
// <PackageReference Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.28" />

ASP.NET Core Minimal API.exp: ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs provide a concise way to build HTTP APIs with minimal ceremony. Use top-level statements, route handlers with dependency injection, and middleware. Perfect for microservices and simple endpoints.

Entity Framework Core.exp: EF Core is an object-relational mapper (ORM). Models map to database tables via DbContext. Supports migrations, LINQ queries, change tracking, eager/lazy/explicit loading, and providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, etc.

Blazor Basics.exp: Blazor builds interactive web UIs using C# instead of JavaScript. Blazor Server runs logic on the server via SignalR. Blazor WebAssembly runs compiled .NET in the browser. Blazor Hybrid embeds in native apps (MAUI, WPF). Components are .razor files.

Dependency Injection.exp: ASP.NET Core has built-in DI with three lifetimes: Singleton (one instance), Scoped (per request), Transient (new each time). Register services in Program.cs. The framework auto-injects into constructors of controllers, minimal APIs, and middleware.

Configuration & Options.exp: .NET supports configuration from JSON, environment variables, CLI args, and more via IConfiguration. Options pattern with IOptions<T> (reloadable), IOptionsSnapshot<T> (scoped, reloads per request), IOptionsMonitor<T> (singleton, observes changes). Strongly-typed settings with validation.

Source Generators.exp: C# 9+ source generators run at compile-time to emit C# source files. Create an IncrementalGenerator implementing IIncrementalGenerator. Access syntax trees, semantic models, and attributes. Used by System.Text.Json, Regex, and MediatR for compile-time code gen.

Compile-Time Code Generation with Roslyn.exp: Roslyn (the C# compiler platform) provides APIs for syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation, and compilation. Use CSharpSyntaxTree, SemanticModel, Compilation, and SyntaxGenerator to build or analyze code programmatically.

Native AOT Compilation.exp: Native AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compiles .NET directly to native code (no JIT/IL). Enables fast startup, small self-contained binaries, no runtime compilation. Limited to compatible APIs (no reflection by default). Enable with `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>` in .csproj.
Native AOT Compilation.code:
<!-- .csproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
    <StripSymbols>true</StripSymbols>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

// AOT-compatible code
static void Main(string[] args)
{
    // Avoid reflection-heavy patterns
    // Use source generators (System.Text.Json)
    // Avoid dynamic, BinaryFormatter, expressions

    Console.WriteLine("Native AOT app");

    // Trimming-friendly
    var result = JsonSerializer.Serialize(
        new Person("Alice", 30),
        SourceGenContext.Default.Person);
    Console.WriteLine(result);
}

[JsonSerializable(typeof(Person))]
public partial class SourceGenContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

public record Person(string Name, int Age);

// Publish command:
// dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained

Function Pointers (delegate*).exp: C# 9 function pointers (`delegate*<T>`) enable efficient native-like function pointer calls without delegate allocation. Used in unsafe contexts for interop and high-performance callbacks. More efficient than delegates (no object allocation).

Regex Source Generators.exp: C# 11+ Regex source generators ([GeneratedRegex]) compile regular expressions at build time. Eliminates runtime compilation (!), provides IntelliSense, and is AOT-compatible. RegexOptions regex options can be passed declaratively.

Raw String Literals.exp: C# 11 raw string literals use triple quotes `"""..."""` for multi-line strings. No escaping needed for quotes, backslashes. Indentation is determined by the closing `"""` position. Perfect for JSON, XML, SQL, regex embedded in code.

Interceptors (Experimental).exp: Interceptors (C# 12 experimental) allow a source generator to replace a method call with a different implementation at compile time. Used for advanced AOP scenarios. Requires `[InterceptsLocation]` attribute. Still experimental, could change.

List Patterns.exp: C# 11 list patterns enable matching on arrays and lists in switch expressions. Supports slice patterns (`..`), discard (`_`), nested patterns. Useful for parsing, validation, and sequence matching without manual indexing.

Collection Expressions.exp: C# 12 collection expressions use `[x, y, z]` syntax to create lists, arrays, spans, and other collection types. The compiler infers the type from the target. Supports spread operator `..` to inline other collections.

Default Lambda Parameters.exp: C# 12 allows default parameter values in lambdas. Works with both lambda expressions and method group conversions. The default applies when the argument is omitted at the call site.

ref readonly Parameters.exp: C# 12 `ref readonly` parameters combine ref (pass by reference, avoid copy) with readonly (guarantee caller's value is not modified). Best for large readonly structs. The caller provides data without defensive copies.

Alias Any Type.exp: C# 12 global/using aliases can refer to any type, not just named types. Tuple types, array types, pointer types, nullable types — all can be aliased. Improves readability for complex type signatures.

params Collections.exp: C# 12 extends `params` to work with `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `IEnumerable<T>` beyond just arrays. The compiler creates the collection efficiently with no allocation when using span overloads.

Small Methods (Fits in Your Head).exp: Mark Seemann's core heuristic: methods should fit in your head — at most ~10–15 lines. Small methods reduce cognitive load, simplify testing, and force good naming. Extract until you can't extract anymore; each method does one thing at one level of abstraction.

Command-Query Separation.exp: CQS (from Bertrand Meyer, popularized by Seemann) says: a method should be a command (mutates state, returns void/Task) OR a query (returns a value, no side effects), never both. This makes code predictable, testable, and safe to compose.

Pure Functions & Determinism.exp: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects (no I/O, no mutation). Pure functions are trivial to test, cache, parallelize, and reason about. Push side effects to the edges of your architecture.

Cyclomatic Complexity & Guard Clauses.exp: Cyclomatic complexity measures independent paths through code. Keep each method's complexity ≤ 4 (1 + number of decisions). Use guard clauses (early return) to flatten nesting. Extract conditional logic into well-named methods.

API Surface & Information Hiding.exp: Minimize the public API surface of each type. Mark everything `private` by default, then promote only what external consumers need. Fewer public members = less coupling, easier refactoring, simpler testing. Apply the Interface Segregation Principle.

Property-Based Testing.exp: Property-Based Testing (from FsCheck for .NET) tests general properties/ invariants instead of specific examples. The framework generates random inputs to find edge cases. Properties like: roundtrip, idempotence, commutativity, and invariant preservation.

SUT & Test Data Builders.exp: Test Data Builder pattern (from Growing Object-Oriented Software) constructs test objects with sensible defaults and explicit overrides. Avoids repetitive Arrange code, makes tests readable, and isolates test changes when constructors change.

Postel's Law & Defensive Coding.exp: Postel's Law: "Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept." Accept flexible inputs (handle edge cases gracefully) but produce strict, predictable outputs. Use null checks, validation, and normalization at boundaries.

Dependency Inversion & Composition Root.exp: Depend on abstractions, not concretions. Build a Composition Root (the entry point of the application) where all dependencies are wired together. This enables unit testing with mocks, delayed decisions about implementations, and parallel development.

Parameter Objects & Immutability.exp: Replace long parameter lists (3+ parameters) with a parameter object. Using `record` types gives you immutability, value equality, and deconstruction for free. Parameter objects make call sites self-documenting and simplify method evolution.

Install.exp: Cypress is an open-source end-to-end testing framework installed via npm. It includes its own test runner, assertion library, and browser control with automatic waiting.
Install.code: npm install cypress --save-dev && npx cypress open

Test Structure.exp: Cypress tests use Mocha-style describe/it blocks. Tests run in a real browser with automatic waiting, DOM snapshotting, and time-travel debugging.

Assertions.exp: Cypress bundles Chai assertions with should and expect syntax. Assertions automatically retry until the element meets the condition or times out.

Config & Plugins.exp: Cypress is configured via cypress.config.js. The config file controls browsers, timeouts, baseUrl, video recording, and plugins for extending functionality.

get.exp: cy.get selects elements by CSS selectors, returning a jQuery-wrapped element. It supports chaining and built-in retry-ability.

find.exp: cy.find scopes the selection to descendants of a previously yielded element. It is ideal for navigating within a specific container.

contains.exp: cy.contains selects elements by their text content, which is more resilient to DOM structure changes than CSS selectors.

Best Practices.exp: Use data-* attributes like data-cy for robust selectors that resist CSS and text changes. Avoid brittle selectors tied to implementation details.

click.exp: cy.click simulates a mouse click on a DOM element. It supports options like multiple clicks, position offsets, and force-clicking hidden elements.

type.exp: cy.type simulates keyboard input into form fields character by character. It supports special keys via curly braces like {enter}.

select.exp: cy.select picks an option from a <select> element by value, text, or index. It supports multiple selection when the multiple attribute is present.

hover.exp: cy.trigger simulates hover events since Cypress lacks a native hover command. It shows hidden menus and tooltips.

Intercept.exp: cy.intercept spies on and modifies HTTP requests at the network level. It can stub responses, wait for requests, and assert on request details.

Mock.exp: Request stubbing returns static data instead of hitting the real server, making tests fast, deterministic, and independent of backend availability.

Wait.exp: cy.wait pauses test execution until a specific aliased network request completes. It can also wait for a specified amount of time.

Stub.exp: Stubbing replaces server responses entirely, useful for testing edge cases, loading states, and error handling without a real server.

API Testing.exp: Test API endpoints directly with cy.request. It bypasses the UI and allows testing backend logic, authentication, and data shapes.

Fixtures.exp: Fixtures are external data files (JSON, images, etc.) stored in cypress/fixtures. They provide realistic test data that can be reused across tests.

Custom Commands.exp: Custom commands wrap reusable logic into chainable Cypress commands via Cypress.Commands.add, improving test readability and reducing duplication.

Custom Commands with TypeScript.exp: Custom commands can be strongly typed using TypeScript. Augment the Cypress namespace for autocomplete and type safety.

Test Data.exp: Test data factories generate consistent, repeatable data for tests. Using beforeEach hooks ensures a clean state before each test run.

Screenshots.exp: Cypress automatically captures screenshots on test failure. Manual screenshots can be taken with cy.screenshot for visual documentation.

Videos.exp: Cypress records video of the entire test run. Videos are stored in cypress/videos and can be configured or disabled in cypress.config.js.

CI Integration.exp: Cypress runs headlessly in CI with cypress run. The Cypress GitHub Action or Docker image provides browsers and dependencies.

Accessibility Testing.exp: Use cypress-axe for automated accessibility checks. It scans the DOM for WCAG violations and integrates directly into your test assertions.

Mount.exp: Component testing mounts individual components in isolation using cy.mount. It requires the @cypress/react or @cypress/vue adapter.

Props.exp: Props are passed directly to the mounted component to test different states and configurations without needing the full application.

Events.exp: Event callbacks can be verified using Cypress spies. cy.spy wraps a function and tracks whether it was called with expected arguments.

Page Objects.exp: Page Objects encapsulate page-specific selectors and actions into reusable classes, reducing test duplication and insulating tests from UI changes.

Real World.exp: Real-world E2E tests simulate complete user journeys like signup, purchase, or search. They test critical business flows from start to finish.

Multi-Origin.exp: cy.origin enables testing across multiple domains, useful for OAuth flows, payment gateways, and third-party integrations.

Debugging.exp: Cypress debugging tools include cy.pause to halt execution, cy.debug to log the current subject, and browser DevTools for interactive inspection.

Cypress Dashboard.exp: Cypress Dashboard records test runs, provides parallelization, flaky test detection, and video/screenshot history. Connect via project ID.

Parallelization.exp: Split test files across multiple CI machines to reduce test suite duration. Requires Cypress Dashboard for orchestration.
Parallelization.code:
# CI config (GitHub Actions example)
npx cypress run --record --parallel --group 'E2E'

Flaky Test Detection].exp: Cypress Cloud automatically detects flaky tests by analyzing test history. It provides flakiness scores and auto-retries for unreliable tests.

What is Django.exp: Django is a high-level Python web framework that encourages rapid development with a clean, pragmatic design. It follows the 'batteries-included' philosophy, providing ORM, admin panel, authentication, forms, templates, and more out of the box. Django uses the MTV (Model-Template-View) architectural pattern, which is similar to MVC but with different naming. It emphasizes DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and security by default.
What is Django.code:
# Install Django
pip install django

# Create a project
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite

# Run development server
python manage.py runserver

# Create an app
python manage.py startapp blog

# Project structure:
# mysite/
#   manage.py
#   mysite/
#     settings.py
#     urls.py
#     wsgi.py
#   blog/
#     models.py
#     views.py
#     urls.py

Project Structure.exp: A Django project consists of a project directory and one or more apps. The project contains settings, root URL configuration, and WSGI/ASGI configuration. Apps are reusable modules that contain models, views, templates, and static files. The manage.py script is a command-line utility for administrative tasks. key files: settings.py (configuration), urls.py (URL routing), wsgi.py (deployment entry), asgi.py (async deployment entry). Each app has its own migrations, admin, tests, and apps configuration.
Project Structure.code:
mysite/
├── manage.py
├── mysite/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py   # Database, apps, middleware, templates
│   ├── urls.py       # Root URL configuration
│   ├── asgi.py       # Async server entry
│   └── wsgi.py       # WSGI server entry
└── blog/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── admin.py      # Model registration for admin
    ├── apps.py       # App configuration
    ├── models.py     # Database models
    ├── views.py      # Request handlers
    ├── urls.py       # App URL patterns
    ├── templates/    # HTML templates
    ├── migrations/   # Database migrations
    └── tests.py      # Unit tests

Settings & Configuration.exp: Django settings control every aspect of the framework. Key settings: INSTALLED_APPS (list of enabled apps), MIDDLEWARE (request/response processing pipeline), DATABASES (database configuration), TEMPLATES (template engine config), STATIC_URL/STATIC_ROOT (static files), MEDIA_URL/MEDIA_ROOT (user uploads). Use python-decouple or django-environ for environment variables. SECRET_KEY must be kept secret. DEBUG=False in production. ALLOWED_HOSTS restricts domain names.
Settings & Configuration.code:
# settings.py — key configurations
from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent

SECRET_KEY = 'django-insecure-...'  # CHANGE in production
DEBUG = True  # Set to False in production
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['localhost', '.example.com']

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'blog',  # Your app
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
]

ROOT_URLCONF = 'mysite.urls'

DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3',
        'NAME': BASE_DIR / 'db.sqlite3',
    }
}

LANGUAGE_CODE = 'en-us'
TIME_ZONE = 'UTC'
STATIC_URL = 'static/'

Defining Models.exp: Models are Python classes that define the structure of your database tables. Each model maps to a single database table, and each attribute maps to a database column. Django automatically creates the table schema, manages relationships (ForeignKey, ManyToManyField, OneToOneField), and provides a powerful QuerySet API. Common field types: CharField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, DateTimeField, TextField, EmailField, URLField, FileField, ImageField. Field options: null, blank, default, unique, choices, verbose_name, help_text.
Defining Models.code:
from django.db import models
from django.utils import timezone

class Category(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    description = models.TextField(blank=True)

    class Meta:
        verbose_name_plural = 'categories'
        ordering = ['name']

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    author = models.ForeignKey(
        'auth.User', on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='blog_posts'
    )
    category = models.ForeignKey(
        Category, on_delete=models.SET_NULL,
        null=True, related_name='posts'
    )
    tags = models.ManyToManyField('Tag', blank=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

Migrations.exp: Migrations are Django's way of propagating model changes to the database schema. They're Python files that describe database operations. Key commands: makemigrations (creates migration files), migrate (applies migrations), sqlmigrate (shows SQL), showmigrations (lists migrations). Migrations track dependencies and can be merged. Always create migrations after changing models. Use --name for custom migration names. For data migrations, create empty migration and use RunPython.
Migrations.code:
# Terminal commands
python manage.py makemigrations          # Create migrations
python manage.py migrate                  # Apply migrations
python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0001     # View SQL
python manage.py showmigrations           # List all migrations

# After changing a model, always run:
# python manage.py makemigrations <app_name>
# python manage.py migrate

# Data migration example:
# python manage.py makemigrations <app> --empty

# Generated file: blog/migrations/0002_populate_slugs.py
from django.db import migrations

def populate_slugs(apps, schema_editor):
    Post = apps.get_model('blog', 'Post')
    for post in Post.objects.all():
        post.slug = post.title.lower().replace(' ', '-')
        post.save()

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [
        ('blog', '0001_initial'),
    ]
    operations = [
        migrations.RunPython(populate_slugs),
    ]

QuerySet API.exp: QuerySets are lazy database lookups that allow chaining filters. They are evaluated only when iterated, sliced, or converted to list. Key methods: all(), filter(), exclude(), get(), create(), update(), delete(), order_by(), values(), values_list(), select_related(), prefetch_related(), annotate(), aggregate(), distinct(), count(), exists(), first(), last(), latest(), earliest(). Field lookups: exact, iexact, contains, icontains, in, gt, gte, lt, lte, startswith, endswith, range, date, year, month, day, isnull, regex, iregex.
QuerySet API.code:
from django.db.models import Count, Q
from blog.models import Post

# Basic queries
posts = Post.objects.all()
posts = Post.objects.filter(published=True)
posts = Post.objects.exclude(category=None)

# Chaining
posts = Post.objects.filter(
    published=True
).select_related('author').order_by('-created')

# Complex filters with Q
posts = Post.objects.filter(
    Q(title__icontains='django') |
    Q(body__icontains='django')
)

# Aggregation
from django.db.models import Count, Avg
stats = Post.objects.aggregate(
    total=Count('id'),
    avg_comments=Avg('comment_count')
)

# Annotation
categories = Category.objects.annotate(
    post_count=Count('posts')
).filter(post_count__gt=0)

# Related objects
post = Post.objects.get(id=1)
comments = post.comment_set.all()  # reverse relation

# Update
Post.objects.filter(published=False).update(published=True)

# Defer / Only (performance)
Post.objects.defer('body').all()
Post.objects.only('title', 'created')

Relationships.exp: Django supports three relationship types: ForeignKey (many-to-one), ManyToManyField (many-to-many), and OneToOneField (one-to-one). ForeignKey requires on_delete option (CASCADE, PROTECT, SET_NULL, SET_DEFAULT, SET(), DO_NOTHING, RESTRICT). related_name defines reverse relation name (default: modelname_set). ManyToManyField can use through for intermediary models with extra fields. OneToOneField extends another model (like inheritance). Generic Foreign Keys allow relations to any model.
Relationships.code:
from django.db import models
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

# One-to-Many (ForeignKey)
class Comment(models.Model):
    post = models.ForeignKey(
        'Post', on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='comments'
    )
    author = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    body = models.TextField()
    created = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

# Many-to-Many with through table
class Membership(models.Model):
    person = models.ForeignKey('Person', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    group = models.ForeignKey('Group', on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    date_joined = models.DateField(auto_now_add=True)
    invite_reason = models.CharField(max_length=64)

class Group(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=128)
    members = models.ManyToManyField(
        'Person', through='Membership'
    )

# One-to-One
class Profile(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(
        User, on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='profile'
    )
    bio = models.TextField(blank=True)
    avatar = models.ImageField(upload_to='avatars/')

# Usage
user = User.objects.get(id=1)
user.profile.bio  # OneToOne reverse
user.blog_posts.all()  # ForeignKey reverse
post.comments.all()  # ForeignKey reverse (related_name)

Function-Based Views.exp: Function-based views (FBVs) are simple Python functions that take an HttpRequest and return an HttpResponse. They are the most straightforward way to handle requests. The function receives the request object and optional URL parameters. Returns HttpResponse, render(), redirect(), or JsonResponse. Can be decorated with @login_required, @require_http_methods, @csrf_exempt, etc. Simple and explicit but can become repetitive for CRUD operations.

Class-Based Views.exp: Class-based views (CBVs) organize view logic into reusable classes. Django provides generic CBVs: ListView, DetailView, CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView, FormView, TemplateView, RedirectView. CBVs use attributes and methods for configuration: model, template_name, context_object_name, form_class, success_url, paginate_by. Override methods: get_queryset(), get_context_data(), form_valid(), get_success_url(). Mixins allow combining reusable behavior. CBVs reduce boilerplate for CRUD but have a steeper learning curve.

URL Configuration.exp: URL configuration maps URL patterns to views using django.urls.path() and re_path(). Each URL pattern has a route, view, optional kwargs, and a unique name. Include() allows nesting app URL configs. path converters: str, int, slug, uuid, path. Custom path converters can be defined. Use namespacing with app_name and include with namespace. The {% url %} template tag reverses URL names. For complex patterns, use re_path() with regex. Always name your URLs for maintainability.
URL Configuration.code:
# mysite/urls.py (root)
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include
from django.conf import settings
from django.conf.urls.static import static

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('blog.urls')),
    path('api/', include('api.urls')),
]

# Serve media files in development
if settings.DEBUG:
    urlpatterns += static(
        settings.MEDIA_URL,
        document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT
    )


# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

app_name = 'blog'

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.PostListView.as_view(), name='post_list'),
    path('<slug:slug>/', views.PostDetailView.as_view(), name='post_detail'),
    path('create/', views.PostCreateView.as_view(), name='post_create'),
    path('<slug:slug>/update/', views.PostUpdateView.as_view(), name='post_update'),
    path('<slug:slug>/delete/', views.PostDeleteView.as_view(), name='post_delete'),
]

Template Language.exp: Django template language uses {{ variables }} and {% tags %}. Variables can be attributes, dictionary keys, or list indices. Filters transform variables: date, default, length, upper, lower, title, pluralize, slugify, truncatechars, safe, escape, join. Tags control logic: {% if %}, {% for %}, {% block %}, {% extends %}, {% include %}, {% url %}, {% load %}, {% static %}. Template inheritance with {% extends %} and {% block %} is the most powerful feature. Context processors make variables available in all templates.
Template Language.code:
My Blog

{% if user.is_authenticated %}

Welcome, {{ user.username }}!

Logout {% else %} Login {% endif %}
{% block content %} {% endblock %}
{% extends 'base.html' %} {% block title %}All Posts{% endblock %} {% block content %} {% for post in posts %}

{{ post.title }}

By {{ post.author }} | {{ post.created|date:"F j, Y" }}

{{ post.body|truncatechars:200 }}

{% empty %}

No posts yet.

{% endfor %} {% if is_paginated %}
{% if page_obj.has_previous %} Previous {% endif %} Page {{ page_obj.number }} of {{ page_obj.paginator.num_pages }} {% if page_obj.has_next %} Next {% endif %}
{% endif %} {% endblock %}

Static Files.exp: Static files (CSS, JS, images) are managed via django.contrib.staticfiles. In development, use runserver. In production, use collectstatic to gather files. Configure STATIC_URL, STATICFILES_DIRS (additional directories), STATIC_ROOT (production destination). Use {% load static %} and {% static 'path' %} in templates. For user uploads, use MEDIA_URL and MEDIA_ROOT with ImageField/FileField. Whitenoise is a popular package for serving static files in production.
Static Files.code: # settings.py — static & media files import os STATIC_URL = '/static/' STATICFILES_DIRS = [ BASE_DIR / 'static', BASE_DIR / 'blog' / 'static', ] STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'staticfiles' MEDIA_URL = '/media/' MEDIA_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'media' {% load static %} # Production deployment # python manage.py collectstatic # This gathers all static files into STATIC_ROOT # With Whitenoise (production): MIDDLEWARE.insert(1, 'whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware') STORAGES = { 'staticfiles': { 'BACKEND': 'whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage', }, }

Django Forms.exp: Django forms handle HTML form generation, validation, and processing. Form classes define fields with validation rules. Forms can be bound (with data) or unbound. Common fields: CharField, EmailField, IntegerField, BooleanField, DateField, ChoiceField, MultipleChoiceField, FileField, ImageField. Validators: built-in (required, min_length, max_length, min_value, max_value), regex, custom. Widgets control HTML rendering: TextInput, Textarea, Select, CheckboxInput, RadioSelect, FileInput. Form rendering: form.as_p, form.as_table, form.as_ul, or manual field-by-field.

Form Processing.exp: Form processing follows a pattern: GET renders empty form, POST validates and processes. Check request.method, instantiate form with request.POST (and request.FILES for uploads), call form.is_valid(), access cleaned_data, redirect on success or re-render with errors. ModelForm.save() creates or updates a model instance. Use commit=False for pre-save processing. FormSets manage multiple forms of the same type. Inline form sets handle related model forms.

User Authentication.exp: Django's built-in authentication system handles users, groups, permissions, and sessions. The User model provides username, password, email, first_name, last_name. Extend via OneToOneField (Profile model) or AbstractUser (custom user model). Key views: LoginView, LogoutView, PasswordChangeView, PasswordResetView. Decorators: @login_required, @permission_required, @user_passes_test. Mixins: LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin. django.contrib.auth.urls provides all auth URL patterns.
User Authentication.code:
# settings.py LOGIN_URL = '/accounts/login/' LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/' LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = '/' # mysite/urls.py urlpatterns += [ path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')), ] # Provides these URLs automatically: # accounts/login/ [name='login'] # accounts/logout/ [name='logout'] # accounts/password_change/ [name='password_change'] # accounts/password_reset/ [name='password_reset'] # In views from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin @login_required def profile_view(request): return render(request, 'profile.html', { 'user': request.user }) # Class-based class ProfileView(LoginRequiredMixin, TemplateView): template_name = 'profile.html' # In templates {% if user.is_authenticated %}

Welcome, {{ user.username }}

{% csrf_token %}
{% else %} Login {% endif %}

Permissions & Groups.exp: Django's permission system assigns permissions to users and groups. Each model gets three default permissions: add_, change_, delete_, and optionally view_. Groups bundle permissions for role-based access. Check permissions with user.has_perm(), @permission_required, or PermissionRequiredMixin. Custom permissions can be defined in model Meta. The admin interface provides group and permission management. Object-level permissions require third-party packages like django-guardian.
Permissions & Groups.code: from django.db import models from django.contrib.auth.models import User from django.contrib.auth.decorators import permission_required # Custom permission in model Meta class Article(models.Model): title = models.CharField(max_length=200) content = models.TextField() status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=[ ('draft', 'Draft'), ('published', 'Published'), ]) class Meta: permissions = [ ('can_publish', 'Can publish articles'), ('can_archive', 'Can archive articles'), ] # Checking permissions @permission_required('blog.can_publish') def publish_article(request, pk): article = Article.objects.get(pk=pk) article.status = 'published' article.save() return redirect('article_detail', pk=pk) # In templates {% if perms.blog.can_publish %} Publish {% endif %} # Programmatic user.has_perm('blog.can_publish') user.has_perms(['blog.add_article', 'blog.change_article']) # Groups from django.contrib.auth.models import Group, Permission editor_group, created = Group.objects.get_or_create(name='Editors') perm = Permission.objects.get(codename='can_publish') editor_group.permissions.add(perm) user.groups.add(editor_group)

Admin Customization.exp: Django's admin interface provides automatic CRUD for models. Register models with admin.site.register() or use @admin.register() decorator. Customize with ModelAdmin options: list_display, list_filter, search_fields, list_editable, list_per_page, ordering, date_hierarchy, readonly_fields, fieldsets, exclude, inlines. Enhance with actions, custom templates, and widget overrides. Admin has built-in authentication, permissions, and history tracking.

DRF Basics.exp: Django REST Framework (DRF) is a powerful toolkit for building Web APIs. Install with pip install djangorestframework. Core concepts: Serializers (convert complex types to/from JSON), Views (APIView, ViewSets), Routers (auto-generate URL patterns), Authentication & Permissions. DRF provides browsable API, content negotiation, throttling, filtering, and versioning. Use ModelSerializer for model-based serializers, ReadOnlyModelViewSet for read-only endpoints.

ViewSets & Routers.exp: ViewSets combine logic for multiple actions (list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update, destroy) into a single class. ModelViewSet provides all CRUD operations. Routers automatically generate URL patterns from ViewSets. DefaultRouter creates API root view. Custom actions with @action decorator. Filter backends: DjangoFilterBackend, SearchFilter, OrderingFilter. Override get_queryset, perform_create, get_serializer_class for customization.
ViewSets & Routers.code:
# views.py
from rest_framework import viewsets, filters, status
from rest_framework.decorators import action
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from django_filters.rest_framework import DjangoFilterBackend
from .models import Post, Comment
from .serializers import PostSerializer, CommentSerializer

class PostViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Post.objects.filter(published=True)
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
    lookup_field = 'slug'

    filter_backends = [
        DjangoFilterBackend,
        filters.SearchFilter,
        filters.OrderingFilter,
    ]
    filterset_fields = ['category__slug', 'author']
    search_fields = ['title', 'body']
    ordering_fields = ['created', 'title']

    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(author=self.request.user)

    @action(detail=True, methods=['post'],
            permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated])
    def comment(self, request, slug=None):
        post = self.get_object()
        serializer = CommentSerializer(data=request.data)
        if serializer.is_valid():
            serializer.save(post=post, author=request.user)
            return Response(serializer.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
        return Response(serializer.errors, status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)

    @action(detail=False)
    def recent(self, request):
        recent_posts = self.get_queryset()[:5]
        serializer = self.get_serializer(recent_posts, many=True)
        return Response(serializer.data)


# urls.py
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from .views import PostViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register(r'posts', PostViewSet, basename='post')

urlpatterns = router.urls

Testing in Django.exp: Django's test framework extends Python's unittest. Use TestCase for database-backed tests. Client simulates browser requests. Factory Boy creates test data. pytest-django is a popular alternative. Key assertions: assertEqual, assertContains, assertTemplateUsed, assertRedirects, assertQuerysetEqual. Tests live in tests.py per app or a tests/ directory. Run with python manage.py test. Use --keepdb to preserve test database between runs.

Production Deployment.exp: Django deployment requires a production-ready web server (Gunicorn, uWSGI), reverse proxy (Nginx, Apache), and database (PostgreSQL). Environment variables for secrets. Use django-environ or python-decouple. Disable DEBUG, configure ALLOWED_HOSTS, use secure cookies, enable HTTPS. Static files served via Whitenoise or CDN. Media files served via Nginx or cloud storage (S3, GCS). Database connection pooling with pgbouncer. Caching with Redis/Memcached. Celery for async tasks. Sentry for error tracking.
Production Deployment.code:
# requirements.txt
gunicorn
psycopg2-binary
python-decouple
whitenoise[brotli]
dj-database-url
redis
celery
sentry-sdk

# settings.py — production settings
import os
from decouple import config, Csv

DEBUG = config('DEBUG', default=False, cast=bool)
SECRET_KEY = config('SECRET_KEY')
ALLOWED_HOSTS = config('ALLOWED_HOSTS', cast=Csv())

# Database
import dj_database_url
DATABASES = {
    'default': dj_database_url.config(
        default=config('DATABASE_URL')
    )
}

# Static files (Whitenoise)
MIDDLEWARE.insert(1, 'whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware')
STORAGES = {
    'staticfiles': {
        'BACKEND': 'whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage',
    },
}

# Security
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD = True

# Caching
CACHES = {
    'default': {
        'BACKEND': 'django.core.cache.backends.redis.RedisCache',
        'LOCATION': config('REDIS_URL'),
    }
}

# Celery
CELERY_BROKER_URL = config('REDIS_URL')

# Gunicorn: gunicorn mysite.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 4

# Nginx config snippet:
# location /static/ { alias /path/to/staticfiles/; }
# location /media/ { alias /path/to/media/; }
# location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000; }

What is Docker.exp: Containerization platform that packages applications with their complete dependencies into isolated units called containers.

Containers vs Images.exp: Images are read-only blueprints; containers are runnable, isolated instances created from those blueprints.

Docker Architecture.exp: Docker uses a client-server architecture with a CLI communicating via REST API to a daemon (dockerd) that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes.
Docker Architecture.code:
# Components:
# Client (docker CLI) -> REST API -> Dockerd (daemon) -> containerd -> runc
# dockerd: high-level management
# containerd: container lifecycle
# runc: OCI runtime (spawns containers)

Docker Desktop.exp: Desktop application for macOS, Windows, and Linux that includes Docker Engine, Docker CLI, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and a GUI management dashboard.
Docker Desktop.code:
# Docker Desktop includes:
# - Docker Engine + CLI
# - Docker Compose
# - Built-in Kubernetes
# - Extensions marketplace
# - Dev Environments
# - Resource management UI

WSL2 Backend.exp: On Windows, Docker Desktop can run the Linux kernel inside a lightweight WSL2 VM for native Linux container performance without Hyper-V.
WSL2 Backend.code:
# Enable WSL2 backend in Docker Desktop Settings > Resources > WSL Integration
# Then run:
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash

Daemon Configuration.exp: Dockerd behavior is configured via daemon.json, controlling storage driver, log driver, registry mirrors, insecure registries, and resource limits.

docker info.exp: Display system-wide information about the Docker installation, including OS, storage driver, CPUs, memory, and running container counts.

Lifecycle Management.exp: Create, launch, stop, and clean up container runtimes explicitly through Docker commands.
Lifecycle Management.code:
docker run -d --name app nginx
docker stop app
docker rm app

Listing & Inspecting.exp: List running containers with docker ps, all containers with -a, and view detailed metadata with docker inspect.
Listing & Inspecting.code:
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker inspect app

Dockerfile Basics.exp: Instruction set for creating container images. Each instruction creates a layer in the final image.
Dockerfile Basics.code:
FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache nodejs
COPY app.js .
CMD ["node", "app.js"]

FROM Variants.exp: Choose base images wisely: alpine (5MB), slim (Debian minimal), distroless (language runtime only), or scratch (empty) for different size and security trade-offs.
FROM Variants.code:
FROM alpine:3.19          # 5MB, musl libc
FROM node:20-slim         # Debian minimal
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20   # 120MB, no shell
FROM scratch              # truly empty

RUN Layers.exp: Each RUN instruction creates a new layer. Chain commands with && and clean up in the same layer to reduce image size.
RUN Layers.code:
# BAD: three layers
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# GOOD: single layer
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y curl && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY vs ADD.exp: COPY copies files from context into the image. ADD does the same plus supports remote URLs and auto-extracting tar archives. Prefer COPY unless you need ADD's extras.
COPY vs ADD.code:
COPY ./app /app              # simple, preferred
COPY --chown=node:node . /app
ADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /tmp/   # ADD supports URLs
ADD archive.tar.gz /tmp/                    # ADD auto-extracts

ARG vs ENV.exp: ARG defines build-time variables (not in final image unless persisted). ENV defines runtime environment variables that persist in the final image.
ARG vs ENV.code:
ARG NODE_VERSION=20
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}
ARG BUILD_ENV              # build only: --build-arg BUILD_ENV=prod
ENV NODE_ENV=production    # persists in image

WORKDIR.exp: Sets the working directory for all subsequent Dockerfile instructions (RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD). Creates the directory if it does not exist.
WORKDIR.code:
FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app               # all subsequent commands run here
COPY package.json .        # copies to /app/package.json
RUN npm install

USER.exp: Switch to a non-root user for better security. Always create a dedicated user; never run containers as root unless absolutely necessary.
USER.code:
FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN chown -R app:app /app
USER app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

EXPOSE.exp: Documents which ports the container listens on at runtime. It is documentation only — does not publish the port. Use -p or -P at runtime to publish.
EXPOSE.code:
FROM nginx
EXPOSE 80                   # documents port 80
EXPOSE 443/tcp              # can specify protocol
# docker run -p 8080:80 nginx to actually publish

LABEL.exp: Add metadata as key-value pairs to the image. Used for versioning, maintainer info, and organization. Use with --filter for image queries.
LABEL.code:
FROM alpine
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="myapp"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="1.0.0"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.vendor="Acme Corp"
# Query: docker images --filter label=org.opencontainers.image.vendor=Acme

SHELL.exp: Override the default shell (Linux: /bin/sh, Windows: cmd) used by RUN instructions. Useful for Windows containers or custom shells.
SHELL.code:
FROM alpine
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]    # default is /bin/sh
RUN echo "using bash now"

# Windows example:
# SHELL ["powershell", "-Command"]

HEALTHCHECK.exp: Tells Docker how to test if the container is working. Docker checks the command periodically; exits with 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy.

Multi-Stage Build.exp: Use multiple FROM statements to chain build environments. Copy only required artifacts to the final stage, drastically reducing image size.
Multi-Stage Build.code:
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app/server

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
CMD ["/server"]

BuildKit.exp: Modern Docker build backend (enabled by default in newer versions) with parallel builds, secrets mounting, SSH mounts, and better caching.
BuildKit.code:
# Enable BuildKit (default in Docker 23+)
export DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1

# Build with secrets (no secret in image layers)
# docker build --secret id=mysecret,src=./secret.txt .
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mysecret cat /run/secrets/mysecret

Buildx.exp: Extended build capabilities built on BuildKit. Enables multi-architecture builds, simultaneous builds for linux/amd64, linux/arm64, etc.
Buildx.code:
docker buildx create --name mybuilder --use
docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

# Build for multiple architectures
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  -t myapp:latest --push .

Cache Mounts.exp: Persist package manager caches across builds using BuildKit cache mounts, speeding up repeated RUN instructions significantly.
Cache Mounts.code:
FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app

# Cache npm packages across builds
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

# Cache apt packages
# RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt \
#     apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3

.dockerignore.exp: Prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the Docker daemon during builds, reducing context size and improving build speed.

docker run deep.exp: The primary command to create and start containers. Supports --name, --rm (auto-remove on exit), --restart, -d (detach), --network, and many more flags.

Interactive Mode.exp: Run containers interactively with -it (--interactive + --tty) for shell access, debugging, or one-off commands.
Interactive Mode.code:
docker run -it --rm alpine /bin/sh
# Inside container:
# / # apk add curl
# / # exit

Detachment.exp: Run containers in the background with -d flag. Re-attach with docker attach, or follow logs with docker logs -f.
Detachment.code:
docker run -d --name redis redis:alpine
docker attach redis          # attaches to STDOUT/STDERR
Ctrl+P Ctrl+Q               # detach without stopping

Resource Limits.exp: Constrain container CPU, memory, and disk I/O using --memory, --cpus, --memory-swap, and --blkio-weight flags.

Logging Drivers.exp: Configure how containers send logs. Drivers: json-file (default), syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, gcplogs, and local (efficient).
Logging Drivers.code:
docker run --log-driver=local --log-opt max-size=10m nginx
docker run --log-driver=syslog --log-opt syslog-address=udp://192.168.1.1:514 nginx
# daemon.json default: "log-driver": "json-file"

Restart Policies.exp: Control automatic container restarts: no (never), always, on-failure[:max-retries], unless-stopped (also restarts after daemon restart).
Restart Policies.code:
docker run --restart no              # never restart (default)
docker run --restart always           # always restart
docker run --restart on-failure:5     # restart on error, max 5 times
docker run --restart unless-stopped   # restart unless manually stopped

stop vs kill.exp: docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, 10s timeout), then SIGKILL. docker kill sends any signal (default SIGKILL) immediately.
stop vs kill.code:
docker stop --time=30 app      # SIGTERM + 30s timeout
docker kill app                  # immediate SIGKILL
docker kill -s HUP app           # send SIGHUP (reload config)

update.exp: Dynamically update container resource constraints, restart policy, and other configuration on a running container without recreating it.
update.code:
docker update --memory=1g --cpus=2 app
docker update --restart=always app

rename.exp: Rename a running or stopped container without affecting its internal state, IP, or volumes.
rename.code:
docker run -d --name oldname nginx
docker rename oldname newname

wait.exp: Block the shell until a container stops, then return its exit code. Useful for scripting and CI pipelines.
wait.code:
docker run -d --name job busybox sh -c "exit 42"
docker wait job
# Output: 42

Port Mapping Deep.exp: Map container ports to the host with -p (specific) or -P (random ephemeral ports). Supports IPv4/IPv6, multiple protocols, and ranges.
Port Mapping Deep.code:
docker run -p 8080:80/tcp nginx              # TCP only
docker run -p 192.168.1.1:8080:80 nginx      # bind to specific IP
docker run -p 80:80 -p 443:443 nginx         # multiple ports
docker run -P nginx                          # random ports

Environment Variables.exp: Pass configuration via -e flags, --env-file, or ENV instructions in Dockerfile. Variables are isolated per container.
Environment Variables.code:
docker run -e DB_HOST=localhost -e DB_PORT=5432 app
docker run --env-file .env app
# Inside: echo $DB_HOST

Port Forwarding.exp: Map isolated internal container ports onto host interfaces, enabling external access to containerized services.

DNS Resolution.exp: Containers on user-defined bridges resolve each other by container name or network alias. Docker embeds a DNS server at 127.0.0.11.
DNS Resolution.code:
docker network create mynet
