docker run --network mynet --name web nginx
docker run --network mynet alpine ping web   # resolves by name

Network Drivers Deep.exp: bridge (default, NAT), host (no isolation), overlay (multi-host), macvlan (MAC per container), ipvlan (IP per container), none (isolated).
Network Drivers Deep.code:
# bridge: default, NAT'd, containers communicate via IP/name
# host: shares host network stack, no port mapping needed
# none: loopback only, fully isolated
# overlay: swarm multi-host, requires key-value store
# macvlan: assign real MAC from physical network

User-Defined Bridge.exp: Create custom bridge networks for automatic DNS resolution, network isolation between groups, and attach/detach containers dynamically.
User-Defined Bridge.code:
docker network create --driver bridge --subnet 172.20.0.0/16 mynet
docker network connect mynet container1
docker network disconnect mynet container1
docker network inspect mynet

Host Network.exp: Remove network isolation to run directly on the host's network stack. No port mapping needed; container sees host interfaces.
Host Network.code:
docker run -d --network host nginx
# Access at http://localhost:80 directly
# No -p flag needed

Macvlan.exp: Assign a real MAC address to each container, making them appear as physical devices on the network. Useful for legacy apps that require direct network access.
Macvlan.code:
docker network create -d macvlan \
  --subnet=192.168.1.0/24 \
  --gateway=192.168.1.1 \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  my-macvlan

docker run --network my-macvlan --ip=192.168.1.100 nginx

Ipvlan.exp: Assign IP addresses to containers sharing the host's MAC address. L2 mode (same subnet) and L3 mode (routing between subnets) supported.
Ipvlan.code:
docker network create -d ipvlan \
  --subnet=10.0.0.0/24 \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  -o ipvlan_mode=l2 \
  my-ipvlan

Network Aliases.exp: Give a container multiple DNS names within a network. Useful for running multiple variants of the same service.
Network Aliases.code:
docker run --network mynet --network-alias api-v1 --network-alias api-v2 nginx
# Both api-v1 and api-v2 resolve to this container on mynet

Container Networking Model.exp: Docker's CNM defines Sandbox (namespace), Endpoint (veth pair), and Network (bridge/overlay) as core primitives for container networking.
Container Networking Model.code:
# Sandbox: network namespace (isolated stack)
# Endpoint: veth pair connecting sandbox to network
# Network: group of endpoints (bridge, overlay, etc.)
# libnetwork implements CNM

Overlay Networks.exp: Multi-host networks that span across Docker swarm nodes, enabling container communication across different hosts securely over VXLAN.
Overlay Networks.code:
docker network create --driver overlay --attachable my-overlay
docker service create --network my-overlay --name web --replicas 3 nginx

Named Volumes.exp: Persistent data directories managed by Docker, isolated from container lifecycle. Survive container removal and can be shared across containers.
Named Volumes.code:
docker volume create mydata
docker run -v mydata:/data alpine echo "stored"
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect mydata
docker volume rm mydata

Bind Mounts.exp: Mount a host file or directory into a container at a specific path. Changes are reflected instantly on both sides.
Bind Mounts.code:
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path nginx
# Short form: -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src
# Long form: --mount type=bind,source=$(pwd)/src,target=/app/src

tmpfs Mounts.exp: Mount a temporary filesystem stored in memory (RAM), not on disk. Data is lost when the container stops. Ideal for secrets or cache.

Storage Drivers.exp: Manage image layers and container writable layers. overlay2 (default, modern), aufs (legacy), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfs.
Storage Drivers.code:
# overlay2 (default, recommended)
# - Union mount of layers
# - Copy-on-write
# - Best performance, lowest overhead
# Check: docker info | grep "Storage Driver"

Volume Drivers.exp: Plugins that extend Docker volumes to remote storage systems: NFS, SSHFS, S3, Azure File, Google Cloud, REX-Ray, Portworx.
Volume Drivers.code:
docker volume create --driver vieux/sshfs \
  -o sshcmd=user@host:/remote/path \
  -o password=secret \
  sshvolume

docker run -v sshvolume:/data alpine

Backup & Restore Volumes.exp: Back up volume data using a temporary container that mounts the volume and creates a tar archive.
Backup & Restore Volumes.code:
# Backup
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data

Bind Mount Deep.exp: Bind mounts can be read-only, create missing host paths automatically, and support SELinux relabeling with :Z or :z suffixes.
Bind Mount Deep.code:
docker run -v $(pwd):/app:ro nginx               # read-only
docker run -v $(pwd):/app:z nginx                # shared SELinux
docker run -v $(pwd):/app:Z nginx                # private SELinux
# Long form:
docker run --mount type=bind,source=$(pwd),target=/app,readonly nginx

Permissions.exp: Container processes run as root by default, creating files owned by root on bind-mounted directories. Use --user or USER to match host UID/GID.
Permissions.code:
# Run with host user's UID/GID
docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v $(pwd):/app alpine touch /app/test.txt

# Or set ownership in Dockerfile
COPY --chown=node:node . /app

Compose File Structure.exp: YAML file defining services, networks, and volumes for multi-container applications. Version 3 targets Swarm; version 2 targets single-engine.
Compose File Structure.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    networks:
      - frontend
  api:
    build: ./api
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
networks:
  frontend: {}
  backend: {}
volumes:
  data: {}

Profiles.exp: Selectively start services with --profile. Services only start when their profile is activated, enabling different environments (dev, test, staging).
Profiles.code:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: ["tools"]       # only with --profile tools
  mailhog:
    image: mailhog/mailhog
    profiles: ["debug", "tools"]

# docker compose --profile tools up

Extends.exp: Inherit and override service definitions from another Compose file or within the same file, reducing duplication across environments.
Extends.code:
# base.yml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    ports: ["80:80"]

# override.yml (extends merges configs)
services:
  web:
    extends:
      file: base.yml
      service: web
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production

depends_on Deep.exp: Control startup order between services. Supports condition: service_started, service_healthy (requires healthcheck), or service_completed_successfully.
depends_on Deep.code:
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      migrations:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]
  migrations:
    build: ./migrations

Healthcheck in Compose.exp: Define container health checks in Compose. Automatically used by depends_on condition: service_healthy and by Swarm for rolling updates.
Healthcheck in Compose.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s

env_file.exp: Load environment variables from one or more files. Supports multiple env_file entries; values are available to the container at runtime.
env_file.code:
services:
  app:
    image: node:20
    env_file:
      - ./common.env
      - ./secrets.env    # keep out of version control
    # Or inline:
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production

Secrets in Compose.exp: Manage sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates) using Docker secrets. Mounted as files at /run/secrets/ inside the container.
Secrets in Compose.code:
services:
  app:
    image: myapp
    secrets:
      - db_password
      - tls_cert

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./db_password.txt
  tls_cert:
    external: true    # pre-created with docker secret create

Configs in Compose.exp: Manage non-sensitive configuration files (config files, nginx conf, etc.) similar to secrets. Mounted at the specified target path.
Configs in Compose.code:
services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    configs:
      - source: nginx_conf
        target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
      - source: ssl_cert
        target: /etc/nginx/ssl/cert.pem

configs:
  nginx_conf:
    file: ./nginx/default.conf
  ssl_cert:
    external: true

Deploy Section.exp: Swarm-only deployment configuration: replicas, update config, rollback config, restart_policy, placement constraints, resources, and endpoint mode.
Deploy Section.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    deploy:
      replicas: 5
      update_config:
        parallelism: 2
        delay: 10s
        order: start-first
      rollback_config:
        parallelism: 1
        order: stop-first
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
        max_attempts: 3
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.5"
          memory: 256M
      placement:
        constraints: [node.role == worker]

Compose Watch.exp: Automatically update running containers when source files change (Compose 2.22+). Supports sync, rebuild, and restart actions.
Compose Watch.code:
services:
  app:
    image: node:20
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package.json

# docker compose up --watch

Swarm Init.exp: Initialize a Docker Swarm cluster, transforming the host into a manager node. Swarm manages services across multiple hosts.
Swarm Init.code:
docker swarm init --advertise-addr 192.168.1.10
# Outputs join tokens for workers and managers

Node Types.exp: Managers run the control plane and Raft consensus (odd count recommended). Workers run only tasks. Nodes can be promoted or demoted.
Node Types.code:
# Add worker: docker swarm join --token WORKER_TOKEN
docker node ls
docker node promote node2
docker node demote node1
docker node update --availability drain node3

Raft Consensus.exp: Swarm uses the Raft algorithm to maintain a consistent cluster state across manager nodes. Requires at least 3 managers for high availability.
Raft Consensus.code:
# Best practice: 3 or 5 managers
# Raft tolerates (n-1)/2 failures
# 3 managers -> tolerate 1 failure
# 5 managers -> tolerate 2 failures
# docker swarm init --force-new-cluster (recover)

Service Replication.exp: Deploy replicated services across Swarm nodes with --replicas. Docker schedules tasks evenly across available nodes.
Service Replication.code:
docker service create --replicas 3 --name web -p 80:80 nginx
docker service scale web=5
docker service ps web

Rolling Updates.exp: Update services incrementally with controlled parallelism and delay. Supports automatic rollback on failure and health check gate.
Rolling Updates.code:
docker service update --image nginx:1.25 --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 30s web
# Or in Compose deploy.update_config

Secrets Deep.exp: Encrypted secrets stored in the Swarm Raft store. Only granted services can access them. Mounted as tmpfs files at /run/secrets/.
Secrets Deep.code:
echo "mypassword" | docker secret create db_pass -
docker service create --secret db_pass --name db postgres
# Inside container: cat /run/secrets/db_pass
# Secrets are encrypted at rest and in transit

Configs in Swarm.exp: Similar to secrets but for non-sensitive config files. Configs are stored in the Swarm Raft store and mounted into containers.
Configs in Swarm.code:
docker config create nginx_conf ./default.conf
docker service create --config src=nginx_conf,target=/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf --name web nginx

docker stack.exp: Deploy a complete Compose application to Swarm as a stack. Stack name prefixes all service names for isolation.
docker stack.code:
docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yml myapp
docker stack ls
docker stack services myapp
docker stack ps myapp
docker stack rm myapp

Swarm Mode Networking.exp: Swarm uses ingress overlay network for routing mesh, and can attach services to custom overlay networks for multi-host communication.
Swarm Mode Networking.code:
# Ingress network: routes published ports to any node
docker network create --driver overlay --subnet 10.0.10.0/24 my-overlay
docker service create --network my-overlay --name api nginx

Routing Mesh.exp: Swarm's routing mesh allows any node in the cluster to accept traffic on published ports and route it to a container on any other node.
Routing Mesh.code:
# Publish port 80 on all Swarm nodes
# Traffic to any node:80 -> routed to a healthy container
docker service create --name web --publish published=80,target=80 --replicas 5 nginx
# curl http://any-swarm-node:80

Seccomp Profiles.exp: Linux syscall filter (Secure Computing Mode) that restricts which system calls a container can make. Docker ships a default seccomp profile allowing ~300 of ~450 syscalls.
Seccomp Profiles.code:
docker run --security-opt seccomp=default.json nginx
# Custom profile: allow specific syscalls only
docker run --security-opt seccomp=custom-profile.json nginx
# Disable seccomp (not recommended):
# docker run --security-opt seccomp=unconfined nginx

AppArmor.exp: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) system that confines programs to a limited set of resources. Docker generates and loads an AppArmor profile for containers by default.
AppArmor.code:
docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-default nginx
# Load custom profile:
# apparmor_parser -r custom-profile
# docker run --security-opt apparmor=custom-profile nginx

Linux Capabilities.exp: Fine-grained privileges for container processes. Drop all capabilities with --cap-drop=all, then add only required ones. Avoid --privileged.
Linux Capabilities.code:
docker run --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE nginx
# Common capabilities to add:
# NET_BIND_SERVICE: bind to privileged ports (<1024)
# CHOWN, SETUID, SETGID, DAC_OVERRIDE: file operations
# SYS_PTRACE: strace/ltrace
# Never use --privileged (gives all capabilities)

Read-Only Root.exp: Mount the container's root filesystem as read-only. Writable paths use tmpfs or volume mounts. Prevents attackers from modifying the filesystem.
Read-Only Root.code:
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /var/run nginx
# --read-only makes / read-only
# Explicit --tmpfs for paths that need writes
# Volumes are still writable

User Namespaces.exp: Map container root (UID 0) to a non-privileged host UID, so root inside the container has no special privileges on the host. Enabled via daemon.json.

Content Trust.exp: Verify image publisher identity and image integrity using digital signatures (Docker Notary). Only signed images can be pulled or run.
Content Trust.code:
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
docker pull alpine:latest   # only pulls if signed
docker push myapp:latest    # signs and pushes
# Keys: root key, repository key, timestamp key, snapshot key

Image Scanning.exp: Scan container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in OS packages and application dependencies. Use docker scout or third-party tools.
Image Scanning.code:
docker scout quickview alpine:latest
docker scout cves alpine:latest
docker scout recommendations alpine:latest
# Third-party: Trivy, Snyk, Grype, Clair
# trivy image alpine:latest

Secrets Management.exp: Never bake secrets into images. Use Docker secrets (Swarm), --secret (BuildKit build), --env-file, or dedicated tools like Vault.
Secrets Management.code:
# Bad: secret in image layers
# ENV DB_PASSWORD=supersecret

# Good: runtime secret
docker run -e DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_pass myapp

# Better: docker secret (Swarm only)
echo "supersecret" | docker secret create db_pass -

gVisor.exp: Container sandbox runtime (runsc) that adds a kernel between the container and the host OS, intercepting syscalls for stronger isolation.

Security Best Practices.exp: Defense-in-depth: run non-root, read-only root, drop capabilities, enable content trust, scan images, use secrets, and avoid --privileged.
Security Best Practices.code:
FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
USER app
COPY --chown=app:app . .

# Run command:
docker run \
  --read-only \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  myapp

docker events.exp: Stream real-time events from the Docker daemon: container start/stop/destroy, image pull, volume mount, network connect, etc.
docker events.code:
docker events              # all events
docker events --filter 'type=container'
docker events --filter 'event=die' --filter 'image=nginx'
# Output: 2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z container start abc123 (image=nginx)

Prometheus Metrics.exp: Docker daemon exposes native Prometheus metrics at /metrics endpoint. Configure in daemon.json for cluster-level monitoring with Prometheus + Grafana.

ELK Stack with Docker.exp: Centralized logging with Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana. Containers send logs via the gelf log driver to Logstash or directly to Elasticsearch.
ELK Stack with Docker.code:
docker run --log-driver gelf --log-opt gelf-address=udp://logstash:12201 nginx

# docker-compose.yml for ELK
services:
  elasticsearch:
    image: docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.x
  logstash:
    image: docker.elastic.co/logstash/logstash:8.x
    ports: ["12201:12201/udp"]
  kibana:
    image: docker.elastic.co/kibana/kibana:8.x
    ports: ["5601:5601"]

cAdvisor.exp: Google's cAdvisor (container advisor) exposes real-time resource usage and performance metrics per container. Often paired with Prometheus.

Resource Monitoring Deep.exp: docker stats shows live CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O per container. Pair with --no-stream for a single snapshot.
Resource Monitoring Deep.code:
docker stats                  # live stream
docker stats --no-stream      # single snapshot
docker stats app1 app2         # specific containers
docker stats --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}"

Logging Drivers.exp: Containers can use different log drivers: json-file (default), local (efficient compression), none (no logs), syslog, journald, fluentd, awslogs, gelf, gcplogs.

Telemetry Logs.exp: View container STDOUT/STDERR output with docker logs. Supports tailing, timestamps, since/until filtering, and following.
Telemetry Logs.code:
docker logs app
docker logs -f app           # follow
docker logs --tail 100 app   # last 100 lines
docker logs --since 5m app   # last 5 minutes
docker logs -t app           # with timestamps

Docker in Docker.exp: Run Docker inside a Docker container (dinD) for CI pipelines that need to build and push images. Use --privileged or mount /var/run/docker.sock.
Docker in Docker.code:
# Mount host's Docker socket (preferred):
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker:24-cli build -t myapp .

# True dinD (requires --privileged):
docker run --privileged -d --name dind docker:24-dind

Caching Strategies.exp: Speed up CI builds by caching layers. Use --cache-from to pull a previously built image and use its layers as cache. Combine with BuildKit.
Caching Strategies.code:
# Pull cache image, then use it
# docker pull myapp:latest || true
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache \
  --cache-to=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache,mode=max \
  -t myapp:latest .

Multi-Arch Builds.exp: Build images for multiple architectures (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) simultaneously using docker buildx. Use --platform flag and push manifest lists.
Multi-Arch Builds.code:
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  -t myuser/myapp:latest \
  --push .
# Creates a single manifest list referencing all architectures

GitHub Actions with Docker.exp: Build and push Docker images in GitHub Actions workflows. Use docker/login-action, docker/setup-buildx-action, and docker/build-push-action.
GitHub Actions with Docker.code:
# .github/workflows/docker.yml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

Docker Layer Caching.exp: Preserve Docker image layers across CI runs. Use GitHub Actions cache or registry cache mounts to avoid rebuilding unchanged layers.
Docker Layer Caching.code:
# GitHub Actions cache (via build-push-action)
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
  with:
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

# Or inline cache in registry:
# --cache-from=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache
# --cache-to=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache,mode=max

Build Cache Optimization.exp: Structure Dockerfiles for maximum cache reuse: install dependencies before copying source, use cache mounts for package managers.
Build Cache Optimization.code:
# Cache-optimized Dockerfile
FROM node:20 AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Kubernetes Integration.exp: Docker Desktop includes a single-node Kubernetes cluster. Enable in Settings > Kubernetes. Use kubectl directly or via the Docker Desktop UI.
Kubernetes Integration.code:
# Enable Kubernetes in Docker Desktop Settings
kubectl config use-context docker-desktop
kubectl get nodes
kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --type=LoadBalancer

Dev Environments.exp: Create reproducible development environments from Git repositories. Docker Desktop clones, builds, and runs the project without installing tools locally.
Dev Environments.code:
# From Docker Desktop Dashboard:
# Dev Environments > Create > Paste Git URL
# Or CLI:
docker dev environments create https://github.com/user/project

Extensions.exp: Extend Docker Desktop functionality with marketplace extensions: disk usage analyzers, secret managers, database GUIs, Prometheus/Grafana, and more.
Extensions.code:
# Browse marketplace at: https://hub.docker.com/extensions
# Install via CLI:
docker extension install docker/disk-usage-extension
# List installed:
docker extension ls

Resource Settings.exp: Configure CPU, memory, swap, and disk image size for Docker Desktop's VM. Adjust based on workload needs (default: 2 CPUs, 8GB RAM, 64GB disk).
Resource Settings.code:
# Settings > Resources > Advanced
# CPUs: 4
# Memory: 8 GB (16 GB for heavy workloads)
# Swap: 2 GB
# Disk image size: 128 GB
# Apply & Restart to take effect

Image Size Optimization.exp: Minimize image size: use alpine or distroless, multi-stage builds, chain RUN commands, clean package manager caches, and omit debug tools.
Image Size Optimization.code:
FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .build-deps build-base \
    && pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt \
    && apk del .build-deps
# Also consider:
# - Combine RUN layers
# - COPY --from=builder (multi-stage)
# - .dockerignore to exclude files

Security Scanning.exp: Regularly scan images for vulnerabilities. Integrate scanning into CI/CD. Use docker scout, Trivy, Grype, or Snyk to detect and fix CVEs.
Security Scanning.code:
# Docker Scout
docker scout quickview alpine

# Trivy (recommended: fast, offline-capable)
trivy image alpine:latest
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH myapp:latest

# Fix by updating base images and packages

Dockerfile Linter (Hadolint).exp: Static analysis for Dockerfiles. Checks for best practice violations, security issues, and common mistakes. Integrates with IDEs and CI.
Dockerfile Linter (Hadolint).code:
hadolint Dockerfile
# Example violations:
# - DL3008: Pin package versions (apk add curl=8.5.0)
# - DL3006: Always tag FROM (FROM alpine:3.19)
# - DL3018: Use --no-cache with apk
# - DL3042: Use COPY instead of ADD unless needed

.dockerignore Deep.exp: Exclude unnecessary files from build context to speed builds, reduce image size, and avoid cache invalidation from irrelevant file changes.
.dockerignore Deep.code:
# Essential entries
node_modules
.git
.gitignore
*.md
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
.env
.env.*
*.log
dist
coverage
.tests
.gitlab-ci.yml
.github
.idea
.vscode
*.swp

Tagging Strategy.exp: Use semantic versioning tags (1.2.3, 1.2, 1) plus descriptive tags (stable, latest, nightly). Avoid mutable tags in production; use digest pinning for immutable deployments.
Tagging Strategy.code:
# Good:
# myapp:1.2.3        specific version
# myapp:1.2           minor version (mutable)
# myapp:sha-a1b2c3d  git commit SHA
# myapp@sha256:...    pin by digest (immutable)

# Bad:
# myapp:latest        ambiguous, mutable

Non-Root User.exp: Always run containers as a non-root user. Create a dedicated user in Dockerfile and use USER directive. This limits damage from container breaches.
Non-Root User.code:
FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . .
USER app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# At runtime also:
# docker run --user 1000:1000 ...

Read-Only Filesystem.exp: Mount root filesystem as read-only to prevent attackers from modifying binaries or configuration. Use tmpfs for writable paths like /tmp.

Graceful Shutdown.exp: Handle SIGTERM properly in your application so docker stop can gracefully shut down. Use dumb-init or tini for proper signal handling.

Namespaces.exp: Linux namespaces isolate containers: pid (process tree), net (network stack), mnt (mount points), uts (hostname), ipc (SysV IPC), user (UID mapping). Docker creates one namespace set per container.

Cgroups.exp: Control groups (cgroups) limit and account resource usage per container: CPU shares/quota, memory limit/soft limit, block I/O throttling, and PID count. Managed by containerd via cgroup v2.

OCI Spec & containerd.exp: Docker uses containerd (high-level container runtime) which uses runc (low-level OCI runtime) to spawn containers. The OCI spec standardizes image format and runtime configuration for interoperability.

Overlay2 Storage Deep.exp: Overlay2 layers filesystem changes using Copy-on-Write. Image layers are read-only; the container adds a writable upperdir. Reads check upperdir first, then fall through to lowerdir(s).

Veth Pairs & Bridge Forwarding.exp: Each container gets one end of a veth pair; the other end connects to the Docker bridge (docker0). The bridge forwards traffic between containers and to the host via iptables NAT/masquerade.

iptables & NAT.exp: Docker manages iptables rules for container networking: MASQUERADE (outbound NAT to host IP), DNAT (port publishing), FORWARD policy, and inter-container traffic isolation.

Troubleshooting Exec.exp: Debug running containers with docker exec for shell access, process inspection, network diagnostics, and file system exploration without stopping the container.
Troubleshooting Exec.code:
docker exec -it web sh                     # interactive shell
docker exec web cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf  # read file
docker exec web ps aux                      # list processes
docker exec web netstat -tlnp               # check listening ports
docker exec web wget -qO- http://localhost/health  # test internal endpoint

// Debug container with a sidecar image (nicolaka/netshoot):
docker run -it --network container:web nicolaka/netshoot
# Now you have curl, tcpdump, nmap, iperf, dig, etc.

Dockerfile Optimization.exp: Optimize Dockerfiles by: ordering layers from least to most frequently changing, using cache mounts, pinning base image digests, and removing build-time dependencies.
Dockerfile Optimization.code:
# Step 1: Pin base image by digest (immutable, no surprises):
FROM node:20-slim@sha256:<hash>

# Step 2: Install system deps before app deps:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Step 3: Copy dependency manifests first (cache layer):
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

# Step 4: Copy source code last (changes most often):
COPY . .

# Step 5: Remove build deps in final layer:
RUN npm cache clean --force

Multi-Stage Build Patterns.exp: Advanced multi-stage patterns: build-target selection with --target, copying from external images, using build arguments for environment, and distroless final stages for minimal attack surface.
Multi-Stage Build Patterns.code:
# build-stage produces the artifact
FROM golang:1.22 AS build-stage
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app/server

# test-stage runs unit tests (can run in CI: docker build --target test-stage)
FROM build-stage AS test-stage
RUN go test ./...

# security-stage scans for vulnerabilities
FROM aquasec/trivy:latest AS security-stage
COPY --from=build-stage /app/server /server
RUN trivy filesystem --severity CRITICAL,HIGH /server

# final: minimal distroless image
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build-stage /app/server /server
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

# Build only the test stage:
# docker build --target test-stage -t myapp:test .

Compose Development Workflow.exp: Use Docker Compose for local development with hot reload: mount source code as volumes, use profiles for dev services, and leverage Compose Watch for auto-restart.
Compose Development Workflow.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src          # live code reload (nodemon/hot reloader)
      - ./package.json:/app/package.json
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=development
      - DB_HOST=db
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package.json

  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]

  # Dev-only tools behind a profile:
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    profiles: ["dev-tools"]

volumes:
  pgdata:

# Start: docker compose --profile dev-tools up
# Watch mode (Compose 2.22+): docker compose up --watch

Docker Build Secrets.exp: Inject secrets at build time without baking them into image layers using BuildKit's --secret flag. Mounted as temp files only during the build step, never persisted.
Docker Build Secrets.code:
# Build with a secret:
# echo "ghp_abc123" > ~/.npm-token
# docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t myapp .

# Dockerfile:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# Mount secret only during this RUN step (not in final image):
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci --only=production

# SSH mount for private git dependencies:
# docker build --ssh default .
# RUN --mount=type=ssh pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/org/private-repo

Structured Logging.exp: Write JSON-structured logs to STDOUT/STDERR so Docker's logging drivers can forward them to centralized systems (Elasticsearch, Loki, CloudWatch). Avoid writing logs to files inside the container.

CI/CD Pipeline Patterns.exp: Production-grade Docker CI/CD: multi-arch builds, SBOM generation, vulnerability scanning, image signing, and atomic rollouts with health check gating.
CI/CD Pipeline Patterns.code:
# GitHub Actions production pipeline
jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push multi-arch image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
          sbom: true           # generate SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)
          provenance: true     # generate SLSA provenance

      - name: Scan image for CVEs
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH

      - name: Sign image with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --key env://COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY \
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

Production Monitoring Stack.exp: Monitor Docker hosts and containers in production with Prometheus + Grafana + cAdvisor + Node Exporter. Set up alerting for container restarts, OOM kills, and resource exhaustion.
Production Monitoring Stack.code:
services:
  cadvisor:
    image: gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:latest
    volumes:
      - /:/rootfs:ro
      - /var/run:/var/run:ro
      - /sys:/sys:ro
      - /var/lib/docker:/var/lib/docker:ro
    ports: ["8080:8080"]

  node-exporter:
    image: prom/node-exporter:latest
    volumes:
      - /proc:/host/proc:ro
      - /sys:/host/sys:ro
      - /:/rootfs:ro
    command:
      - '--path.procfs=/host/proc'
      - '--path.sysfs=/host/sys'
      - '--path.rootfs=/rootfs'
    ports: ["9100:9100"]

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'
      - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus'

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    environment:
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme

volumes:
  prometheus-data:
  grafana-data:

# Alert on: container_oom_killed_total > 0, container_restarts > N, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes < threshold

Backup & Disaster Recovery.exp: Backup strategy for production Docker hosts: volume backups using temporary containers, Swarm state backup (Raft logs), image registry mirroring, and automated recovery procedures.
Backup & Disaster Recovery.code:
# 1. Backup named volumes:
docker run --rm -v myapp_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/myapp_data-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# 2. Backup Swarm Raft state (all manager state):
# Stop Docker, backup the Raft directory:
sudo systemctl stop docker
sudo tar czf /backup/swarm-raft-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /var/lib/docker/swarm
sudo systemctl start docker

# 3. Periodic backup cron (host system):
# 0 2 * * * docker run --rm -v app_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
#   tar czf /backup/app_data-$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# 4. Restore a volume backup:
docker run --rm -v myapp_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/myapp_data-20250101.tar.gz -C /data

# 5. Mirror registry for offline/disaster recovery:
# docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --restart always --name registry registry:2
# docker pull myapp:latest && docker tag myapp:latest localhost:5000/myapp:latest && docker push localhost:5000/myapp:latest

Routing.exp: Routing defines how an application responds to client requests at specific endpoints (URIs) and HTTP methods. Express provides intuitive methods like app.get(), app.post(), and app.all() for route definition.
Routing.code: const express = require('express'); const app = express(); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Home')); app.post('/api/users', (req, res) => res.status(201).json({ id: 1 }));

Middleware.exp: Middleware functions execute in sequence during the request-response cycle, with access to the request and response objects. They can modify objects, end the cycle, or call the next middleware via next().
Middleware.code: const logger = (req, res, next) => { console.log(req.method, req.url); next(); }; app.use(logger); app.use(express.json());

App Setup.exp: Setting up an Express app involves creating the app instance, configuring middleware, defining routes, and starting the server with app.listen(). Includes error handling middleware defined last.
App Setup.code: const express = require('express'); const app = express(); const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; app.use(express.json()); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.json({ status: 'OK' })); app.listen(PORT);

Built-in.exp: Express includes built-in middleware: express.json() for JSON body parsing, express.urlencoded() for form data, express.static() for static files, and express.Router() for modular routing.
Built-in.code: app.use(express.json({ limit: '10mb' })); app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false })); app.use(express.static('public', { maxAge: '1d' }));

Third-party.exp: Third-party middleware adds cookie-parsing (cookie-parser), logging (morgan), compression (compression), CORS (cors), and session management (express-session).
Third-party.code: const cors = require('cors'); const morgan = require('morgan'); app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://example.com' })); app.use(morgan('combined'));

Custom.exp: Custom middleware encapsulates reusable logic for auth, validation, logging, or request transformation. A middleware function takes req, res, and next parameters.
Custom.code: const validateUser = (req, res, next) => { const { email, password } = req.body; if (!email || !password) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Required' }); req.validated = { email, password }; next(); }; app.post('/login', validateUser, loginHandler);

Error Handling.exp: Error-handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next) and catches errors from preceding middleware and routes. Define it last in the middleware stack.
Error Handling.code: app.use((err, req, res, next) => { const status = err.status || 500; const message = err.message || 'Error'; console.error(err.stack); res.status(status).json({ error: message }); });

Router.exp: Express Router enables modular, mountable route handlers. Routers act as mini-applications with their own middleware and routes, keeping code organized by feature.
Router.code: const router = express.Router(); router.use(authMiddleware); router.get('/', (req, res) => res.json([{ id: 1 }])); router.post('/', (req, res) => res.status(201).json(req.body)); module.exports = router; app.use('/api/users', userRouter);

Route Params.exp: Route parameters capture values from the URL path. They are defined with a colon prefix and accessed via req.params. Params can be optional or use regex patterns.
Route Params.code: app.get('/users/:userId', (req, res) => { const id = req.params.userId; res.json({ userId: id }); }); app.get('/files/:filename(\\.png)', handler);

Query Strings.exp: Query strings pass key-value pairs after the ? in the URL. Express parses them and makes them available via req.query. Useful for filtering, pagination, and search parameters.
Query Strings.code: app.get('/api/users', (req, res) => { const { page = 1, limit = 10, sort } = req.query; const skip = (page - 1) * limit; res.json({ page, limit, sort }); });

Headers.exp: Request headers are accessed via req.headers. Response headers are set with res.set() or res.header(). CORS headers, content negotiation, and caching are common use cases.
Headers.code: app.use((req, res, next) => { res.header('X-Powered-By', 'Express'); res.header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*'); next(); }); const userAgent = req.headers['user-agent'];

Body Parsing.exp: Express can parse various request body formats: JSON (express.json()), URL-encoded form data (express.urlencoded()), raw text, and multipart file uploads (multer).
Body Parsing.code: app.use(express.json()); app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true })); const multer = require('multer'); const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' }); app.post('/upload', upload.single('file'), (req, res) => res.json(req.file));

File Upload.exp: File uploads in Express use the multer middleware. Multer handles multipart/form-data and provides file metadata including original name, size, mimetype, and temp file path.
File Upload.code: const storage = multer.diskStorage({ destination: './uploads', filename: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, Date.now() + '-' + file.originalname) }); const upload = multer({ storage, limits: { fileSize: 5e6 } }); app.post('/profile', upload.single('avatar'), handler);

Pug.exp: Pug (formerly Jade) is a template engine for Express with terse syntax using indentation instead of tags. It supports variables, conditionals, iteration, mixins, and layout inheritance.
Pug.code: app.set('view engine', 'pug'); app.set('views', './views'); // views/index.pug: doctype html html head title= title body h1 Welcome #{name}

EJS.exp: EJS (Embedded JavaScript) uses plain HTML with <% %> tags for logic and <%= %> for output. It includes partials, layouts via express-ejs-layouts, and supports async rendering.
EJS.code:
app.set('view engine', 'ejs'); app.set('views', './views'); // views/index.ejs:

Welcome <%= name %>

<% if (user) { %>

Logged in

<% } %>

Handlebars.exp: Handlebars is a logic-less template engine with {{mustache}} syntax. It enforces strict separation of logic from presentation using helpers and partials instead of inline code.
Handlebars.code:
const exphbs = require('express-handlebars'); app.engine('handlebars', exphbs()); app.set('view engine', 'handlebars'); // views/index.handlebars:

Welcome {{name}}

MongoDB.exp: Integrating MongoDB with Express uses Mongoose ODM for schemas, models, and validation. Mongoose provides a schema-based solution for modeling application data.
MongoDB.code: const mongoose = require('mongoose'); mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URI); const User = mongoose.model('User', { name: String, email: String }); app.get('/users', async (req, res) => res.json(await User.find()));

SQL/Prisma.exp: Prisma ORM integrates with Express for type-safe database access. It supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and SQL Server with auto-generated query client.
SQL/Prisma.code: const { PrismaClient } = require('@prisma/client'); const prisma = new PrismaClient(); app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => { const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: Number(req.params.id) }, include: { posts: true } }); res.json(user); });

Redis.exp: Redis with Express is used for caching, session storage, and rate limiting. Connect-redis stores Express sessions in Redis for fast, persistent session management.
Redis.code: const session = require('express-session'); const RedisStore = require('connect-redis')(session); const redis = require('redis'); const client = redis.createClient(); app.use(session({ store: new RedisStore({ client }), secret: 'secret', resave: false, saveUninitialized: false }));

JWT.exp: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide stateless authentication. After login, a signed token containing user claims is sent to the client, which includes it in the Authorization header for protected routes.
JWT.code: const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken'); const token = jwt.sign({ userId: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '24h' }); const verifyToken = (req, res, next) => { const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1]; try { req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET); next(); } catch (e) { res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid token' }); } };

Sessions.exp: Express-session creates server-side sessions stored in memory or external stores like Redis. A signed cookie identifies the session, keeping user data on the server for security.
Sessions.code: const session = require('express-session'); app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false, saveUninitialized: true, cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, maxAge: 86400000 } })); app.get('/login', (req, res) => { req.session.userId = user.id; res.redirect('/'); });

Passport.exp: Passport.js provides strategy-based authentication supporting local, OAuth (Google, GitHub, Facebook), JWT, and many other providers. serializeUser/deserializeUser manage session persistence.
Passport.code: const passport = require('passport'); const LocalStrategy = require('passport-local'); passport.use(new LocalStrategy(async (username, password, done) => { const user = await User.findOne({ username }); if (!user || !user.verifyPassword(password)) return done(null, false); return done(null, user); })); app.post('/login', passport.authenticate('local', { successRedirect: '/', failureRedirect: '/login' }));

Best Practices.exp: REST API best practices include proper HTTP methods and status codes, consistent naming (plural nouns), versioning, pagination, filtering, sorting, and comprehensive error responses.
Best Practices.code: const sendSuccess = (res, data, status = 200) => res.status(status).json({ success: true, data }); const sendError = (res, message, status = 400) => res.status(status).json({ success: false, error: message });

Versioning.exp: API versioning prevents breaking changes from affecting existing clients. Common strategies include URL-based (/api/v1/), header-based (Accept-Version), and query-parameter versioning.
Versioning.code: const v1 = express.Router(); const v2 = express.Router(); v1.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json({ version: 'v1' })); v2.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json({ version: 'v2' })); app.use('/api/v1', v1); app.use('/api/v2', v2);

Documentation.exp: API documentation with Swagger/OpenAPI defines endpoints, schemas, and auth. Swagger UI provides interactive documentation. JSDoc comments auto-generate OpenAPI specs.
Documentation.code: const swaggerJsdoc = require('swagger-jsdoc'); const swaggerUi = require('swagger-ui-express'); const specs = swaggerJsdoc({ definition: { openapi: '3.0.0', info: { title: 'My API', version: '1.0.0' } }, apis: ['./routes/*.js'] }); app.use('/api-docs', swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(specs));

Socket.io Integration.exp: Socket.io enables real-time bidirectional communication between the server and clients. Express apps integrate Socket.io by wrapping the HTTP server and attaching socket handlers with namespace support.
Socket.io Integration.code: const http = require('http'); const { Server } = require('socket.io'); const server = http.createServer(app); const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: '*' } }); io.on('connection', (socket) => { console.log('User connected'); socket.on('message', (data) => io.emit('message', data)); socket.on('disconnect', () => console.log('Disconnected')); }); server.listen(3000);

ws Library.exp: The ws library is a lightweight WebSocket implementation for Express. It attaches to the HTTP server and provides a simple event-based API with support for rooms and binary data.
ws Library.code: const { WebSocketServer } = require('ws'); const server = app.listen(3000); const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server }); wss.on('connection', (ws) => { ws.on('message', (data) => wss.clients.forEach(client => client.send(data))); ws.send('Connected'); });

Broadcasting.exp: Socket.io rooms and namespaces organize connections into logical groups for targeted broadcasting. The broadcast flag sends to all clients except the sender, and rooms isolate groups.
Broadcasting.code: io.on('connection', (socket) => { socket.join('room-' + userId); socket.broadcast.to('room-' + userId).emit('user-online', userId); io.to('room-' + userId).emit('notification', { text: 'New message' }); });

Helmet.exp: Helmet secures Express apps by setting various HTTP headers including Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection, Strict-Transport-Security, and X-Content-Type-Options.
Helmet.code: const helmet = require('helmet'); app.use(helmet()); app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({ directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"], scriptSrc: ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"] } }));

Rate Limiting.exp: express-rate-limit protects against brute-force attacks by limiting repeated requests from the same IP. Rate limits are configurable per window with custom messages and headers.
Rate Limiting.code: const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit'); const limiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, max: 100, standardHeaders: true, legacyHeaders: false, message: { error: 'Too many requests' } }); app.use('/api/', limiter);

Compression.exp: compression middleware reduces response size using gzip/deflate. It automatically compresses JSON, text, and other compressible responses, improving bandwidth usage and load times.
Compression.code: const compression = require('compression'); app.use(compression({ threshold: 0, level: 6 })); // Skip compression for small SSE or already-compressed responses

Input Validation.exp: Input validation libraries like Joi, express-validator, or Zod prevent injection attacks and malformed data. Validation middleware sanitizes and validates request bodies, params, and queries.
Input Validation.code: const { body, validationResult } = require('express-validator'); app.post('/user', [ body('email').isEmail().normalizeEmail(), body('age').isInt({ min: 0 }) ], (req, res) => { const errors = validationResult(req); if (!errors.isEmpty()) return res.status(400).json({ errors: errors.array() }); });

What is FastAPI.exp: FastAPI is a modern, fast (high-performance) Python web framework for building APIs with Python 3.8+ based on standard Python type hints. It automatically generates OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation and is built on Starlette for async support. Key features: automatic request validation via Pydantic models, automatic API docs at /docs and /redoc, async/await support, dependency injection system, WebSocket support, OAuth2 with JWT out of the box. FastAPI is one of the fastest Python frameworks, on par with Node.js and Go.

Project Structure.exp: FastAPI projects can be structured by domain or by layer. A typical structure separates routes, models, schemas, services, and database. Use APIRouter for modular route organization. Config via Pydantic Settings. Alembic for database migrations. Dependency injection keeps views clean. Testing with TestClient from Starlette. Environment variables managed with pydantic-settings.
Project Structure.code:
myapi/
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── main.py              # FastAPI app creation
│   ├── config.py             # Settings via Pydantic
│   ├── database.py           # DB connection
│   ├── dependencies.py       # Shared dependencies
│   ├── models/
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── user.py           # SQLAlchemy models
│   ├── schemas/
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── user.py           # Pydantic schemas
│   ├── routers/
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   ├── users.py          # User endpoints
│   │   └── items.py          # Item endpoints
│   └── services/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── user_service.py   # Business logic
├── alembic/                  # DB migrations
├── tests/
├── requirements.txt
└── .env

# app/main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from app.routers import users, items

def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI(title='My API', version='1.0.0')
    app.include_router(users.router, prefix='/users', tags=['users'])
    app.include_router(items.router, prefix='/items', tags=['items'])
    return app

app = create_app()

Configuration.exp: Pydantic Settings handles configuration via environment variables with validation and type coercion. Inherit from BaseSettings, define fields with types and defaults. Load from .env file easily. Auto-completion in IDEs. SecretStr for sensitive values (hides in repr). Settings can be used as a dependency via Depends(). Configuration is validated at startup, catching misconfigurations early.
Configuration.code:
# app/config.py
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
from pydantic import PostgresDsn, SecretStr
from typing import Optional

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    # App
    app_name: str = 'FastAPI App'
    debug: bool = False
    version: str = '1.0.0'

    # Database
    database_url: PostgresDsn = 'postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/db'

    # Auth
    secret_key: SecretStr = SecretStr('change-me')
    jwt_algorithm: str = 'HS256'
    access_token_expire_minutes: int = 30

    # Redis
    redis_url: Optional[str] = None

    # CORS
    allowed_origins: list[str] = ['*']

    class Config:
        env_file = '.env'
        env_file_encoding = 'utf-8'

settings = Settings()


# .env file
# DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb
# SECRET_KEY=super-secret-key-12345
# DEBUG=true


# Using settings in app
from app.config import settings

app = FastAPI(title=settings.app_name, debug=settings.debug)

Path Parameters.exp: Path parameters declare dynamic URL segments with type hints. FastAPI automatically validates types, extracts values, and generates OpenAPI docs. Use Path() from fastapi for additional validation: ge, le, gt, lt, min_length, max_length, regex, deprecated, description, alias, title. Order matters — fixed paths before parameterized ones. Enum parameters for restricted choices. Path parameters are always strings in URLs but converted to declared type.

Query Parameters.exp: Query parameters come from URL ?key=value after the ?. Declare as function parameters not in the path. Default values make them optional. Optional with Optional[type] = None. Use Query() for validation: min_length, max_length, regex, ge, le, multiple values with list, aliases, deprecated, description. Required query params have no default. Boolean conversion accepts true/false/1/0/on/off. Query parameter lists: q: list[str] = Query(default=None).

Multiple Parameters.exp: FastAPI can mix path, query, and body parameters. It figures out parameter sources automatically: path params from URL path, query params from URL query string, and body params from Pydantic models. Use singular values in the function signature for path/query params, and Pydantic models for request bodies. FastAPI handles nested models, unions, and optional fields.

Pydantic Models.exp: Pydantic models define the structure, type, and validation of request/response data. Define with BaseModel and type-annotated fields. Automatic validation, serialization, and JSON Schema generation. Field() for advanced configuration: default, alias, title, description, ge, le, min_length, max_length, regex, examples. Nested models for complex structures. Union types for polymorphic data. Optional fields with Optional[type] or default. Config class for model-wide settings (orm_mode, extra, frozen).
Pydantic Models.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr
from typing import Optional, List
from datetime import datetime

# Basic model
class ItemBase(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=100)
    description: Optional[str] = Field(None, max_length=500)
    price: float = Field(..., ge=0, description='Price must be non-negative')
    tax: Optional[float] = None
    tags: List[str] = []

class ItemCreate(ItemBase):
    pass

class Item(ItemBase):
    id: int
    created_at: datetime
    owner_id: int

    class Config:
        from_attributes = True  # ORM mode

# Nested models
class Image(BaseModel):
    url: str
    name: str

class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: Optional[str] = None
    images: List[Image] = []

# Union types
from typing import Union

class Cat(BaseModel):
    pet_type: str = 'cat'
    meow_count: int

class Dog(BaseModel):
    pet_type: str = 'dog'
    bark_volume: float

class Pet(BaseModel):
    pet: Union[Cat, Dog]

# Email validation
class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    username: str = Field(..., min_length=3, pattern='^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$')
    password: str = Field(..., min_length=8)

Field Validation.exp: FastAPI + Pydantic provide rich validation. Field() constraints: ge, le, gt, lt, min_length, max_length, pattern (regex), multiple_of. Custom validators with @field_validator (Pydantic v2) for cross-field or complex validation. @model_validator for whole-model validation. Validation occurs automatically on request body parsing. Error responses include detailed validation messages.

Response & Status Codes.exp: FastAPI automatically validates and serializes responses using response_model parameter. Benefits: documentation generation, response filtering (exclude fields not in model), type validation. Use response_model_exclude_unset, response_model_exclude_none, response_model_exclude, response_model_include for granular control. Set status_code with status codes from fastapi.status. Return Pydantic models, dicts, or lists. Custom response classes: JSONResponse, HTMLResponse, PlainTextResponse, FileResponse, StreamingResponse, RedirectResponse.

Schema Inheritance.exp: Use Pydantic model inheritance to avoid duplication between create/update/read schemas. Create base models with common fields, then extend for specific use cases. exclude_unset for partial updates (PATCH). private attributes with PrivateAttr. Computed fields with @computed_field (Pydantic v2). Generic models with TypeVar for reusable patterns. Config inheritance through class hierarchy.
Schema Inheritance.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime

# Base schema — shared fields
class UserBase(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    bio: Optional[str] = None

# Create — all required
class UserCreate(UserBase):
    password: str = Field(..., min_length=8)

# Update — all optional (for PATCH)
class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    username: Optional[str] = None
    email: Optional[str] = None
    bio: Optional[str] = None
    password: Optional[str] = None

# Response — includes server-generated fields
class User(UserBase):
    id: int
    is_active: bool = True
    created_at: datetime

    class Config:
        from_attributes = True

# List response
class UsersList(BaseModel):
    users: list[User]
    total: int
    page: int
    per_page: int

# Usage
@app.get('/users/', response_model=UsersList)
def list_users(page: int = 1, per_page: int = 20):
    users, total = get_users(page, per_page)
    return UsersList(users=users, total=total, page=page, per_page=per_page)

@app.patch('/users/{user_id}', response_model=User)
def update_user(user_id: int, user: UserUpdate):
    # Only update fields that were sent
    update_data = user.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    updated = update_user_in_db(user_id, update_data)
    return updated

Dependencies.exp: FastAPI's dependency injection system elegantly handles shared logic. Dependencies are callables (functions, classes, generators) declared as function parameters with Depends(). They can return values, perform checks, manage resources. Dependencies can themselves have dependencies. Use for: database sessions, authentication, permissions, configuration, request preprocessing. BackgroundTasks for post-response operations.

Security Dependencies.exp: FastAPI provides built-in tools for security schemes: OAuth2 with JWT tokens, HTTP Basic, API keys in headers/query/cookies. fastapi.security provides Security() and dependency classes: OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer, HTTPBearer, HTTPBasic, HTTPDigest, APIKeyHeader, APIKeyQuery, APIKeyCookie. Combine with python-jose for JWT and passlib for password hashing.

SQLAlchemy with FastAPI.exp: SQLAlchemy is the most common ORM with FastAPI. Configure engine, session local, and Base declarative model. Use dependency injection to get DB sessions per request. Session per request pattern ensures proper cleanup. Alembic for migrations. Async SQLAlchemy with asyncpg for async database operations. Pydantic models with from_attributes=True convert ORM objects to schemas.
SQLAlchemy with FastAPI.code:
# app/database.py
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL = 'postgresql://user:pass@localhost/db'

engine = create_engine(SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(autocommit=False, autoflush=False, bind=engine)
Base = declarative_base()

# Dependency
from app.database import SessionLocal

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()


# app/models.py
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, Boolean, ForeignKey, Text, DateTime
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from app.database import Base

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'users'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    username = Column(String, unique=True, index=True)
    email = Column(String, unique=True, index=True)
    hashed_password = Column(String)
    is_active = Column(Boolean, default=True)
    created_at = Column(DateTime, default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    items = relationship('Item', back_populates='owner')

class Item(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'items'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    title = Column(String, index=True)
    description = Column(Text)
    owner_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('users.id'))
    owner = relationship('User', back_populates='items')

Async Database.exp: FastAPI supports async database operations natively. Use async SQLAlchemy with asyncpg driver. Create async engine and session. Endpoints become async def. Use await on async database calls. Async sessions use async with context manager. Computations still run synchronously; use run_in_executor for blocking operations or use proper async libraries. SQLAlchemy 1.4+ has native async support.
Async Database.code:
# app/database.py (async)
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

DATABASE_URL = 'postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost/db'

engine = create_async_engine(DATABASE_URL)
async_session = async_sessionmaker(
    engine, class_=AsyncSession, expire_on_commit=False
)
Base = declarative_base()

async def get_db():
    async with async_session() as session:
        yield session


# app/models.py (async) — same column definitions


# app/routers/users.py (async endpoints)
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy import select
from app import schemas, models
from app.database import get_db

router = APIRouter()

@router.get('/users/', response_model=list[schemas.User])
async def list_users(
    skip: int = 0,
    limit: int = 100,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)
):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(models.User).offset(skip).limit(limit)
    )
    users = result.scalars().all()
    return users

@router.get('/users/{user_id}', response_model=schemas.User)
async def get_user(user_id: int, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(models.User).where(models.User.id == user_id)
    )
    user = result.scalar_one_or_none()
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='User not found')
    return user

@router.post('/users/', response_model=schemas.User, status_code=201)
async def create_user(
    user: schemas.UserCreate,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)
):
    hashed_password = get_password_hash(user.password)
    db_user = models.User(
        username=user.username,
        email=user.email,
        hashed_password=hashed_password
    )
    db.add(db_user)
    await db.commit()
    await db.refresh(db_user)
    return db_user

OAuth2 & JWT.exp: FastAPI has first-class support for OAuth2. Common patterns: OAuth2 with password flow and JWT tokens. python-jose for JWT encoding/decoding, passlib for password hashing with bcrypt. Token endpoints return access_token and token_type. Protected routes use Depends(get_current_user) which validates the Bearer token. Refresh tokens for longer sessions. Scopes for fine-grained permissions.

WebSockets.exp: FastAPI supports WebSockets natively via Starlette. Use @app.websocket() for WebSocket endpoints. Accept and close connections manually. Receive JSON/text/bytes messages. Send JSON/text/bytes messages. WebSocket disconnect handling. Dependencies can be used with WebSockets using Depends(). For production, use WebSocket managers for broadcasting to multiple clients. FastAPI's WebSocket support is asynchronous and efficient.

Testing.exp: FastAPI provides TestClient based on Starlette's test client (uses httpx under the hood). TestClient can be used as a context manager for async endpoints. Override dependencies with app.dependency_overrides. Test database setup/teardown with pytest fixtures. Test WebSocket endpoints with TestClient's websocket_connect. Test status codes, response models, headers. Use pytest with httpx for advanced HTTP testing.
Testing.code:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app
import pytest

client = TestClient(app)

# Basic test
def test_read_main():
    response = client.get('/')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {'message': 'Hello World'}

# Test with query params
def test_read_item():
    response = client.get('/items/42?q=test')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {'item_id': 42, 'q': 'test'}

# Test POST with body
def test_create_item():
    response = client.post(
        '/items/',
        json={'name': 'Foo', 'price': 10.0}
    )
    assert response.status_code == 201
    data = response.json()
    assert data['name'] == 'Foo'
    assert data['price'] == 10.0
    assert 'id' in data

# Test authentication
def test_auth():
    response = client.post(
        '/token',
        data={'username': 'alice', 'password': 'secret'}
    )
    assert response.status_code == 200
    token = response.json()['access_token']

    response = client.get(
        '/users/me',
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'}
    )
    assert response.status_code == 200

# Override dependencies
def override_get_db():
    test_db = create_test_database()
    yield test_db
    test_db.close()

app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = override_get_db

# Async tests require pytest-asyncio
@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_async_endpoint():
    async with AsyncClient(app=app, base_url='http://test') as ac:
        response = await ac.get('/')
    assert response.status_code == 200

What is Firebase.exp: Firebase is a comprehensive app development platform by Google. Provides backend services: authentication, real-time database, Firestore, storage, hosting, functions, analytics, and more. Serverless — no infrastructure management. Acquired by Google in 2014.
What is Firebase.code:
# Firebase services overview
# Firestore: NoSQL document database
# Auth: user authentication
# Storage: file uploads
# Hosting: web hosting
# Functions: serverless backend
# Analytics: app tracking
# Messaging: push notifications

Firebase Console & Setup.exp: Start at console.firebase.google.com. Create a project, register your app (iOS/Android/Web), and add the Firebase SDK. Firebase CLI for local development: emulators, deployment, and cloud functions.
Firebase Console & Setup.code:
# Install Firebase CLI
npm install -g firebase-tools

# Login
firebase login

# Init a project
firebase init
# Select: Firestore, Functions, Hosting, etc.

# Start emulators (local dev)
firebase emulators:start

# Deploy to production
firebase deploy

Firebase vs Firestore.exp: Firebase has two database options: Realtime Database (JSON tree, real-time sync, low latency) and Firestore (document/collection model, richer queries, multi-region, better scaling). Firestore is recommended for new projects.

Firebase SDKs.exp: Multiple SDKs: Web (JS/TS), iOS (Swift), Android (Kotlin/Java), Flutter, Unity, C++, Admin SDK (server-side, Node.js/Python/Go/Java). The Web SDK comes in modular (v9+) and namespaced (v8) flavors.

Firebase Emulators.exp: Local emulators for Firestore, Auth, Functions, Storage, Hosting, and PubSub. Enables offline development without touching production. Data persisted between sessions or cleared on restart.

Email & Password Auth.exp: Built-in email/password authentication. createUserWithEmailAndPassword() for signup, signInWithEmailAndPassword() for login. Additional: email verification, password reset, profile management.

Google Sign-In.exp: One-tap Google sign-in using Firebase Auth + Google provider. Configure OAuth consent screen and enable Google in Firebase Console Auth -> Sign-in method.

Anonymous Auth.exp: Create temporary anonymous accounts. Convert to permanent by linking credentials. Useful for cart/activity before user signs up. signInAnonymously() creates a transient user.

Security Rules (Auth).exp: Firestore Security Rules control who can read/write data. Built on Firebase Auth UID. Regular + recursive wildcards. Rules are evaluated on every request — keep them strict.

Documents & Collections.exp: Firestore is a NoSQL document database. Data organized as documents (in collections). Documents contain key-value pairs. Subcollections for nested data. Documents have a max size of 1 MiB.

CRUD Operations.exp: addDoc creates auto-ID. setDoc sets with known ID (or merges with merge:true). updateDoc updates specific fields. deleteDoc removes doc. Firestore does not support server-side UPDATE or DELETE with filters.

Queries & Filters.exp: Firestore supports compound queries with where(), orderBy(), limit(), startAt/startAfter/endAt/endBefore. Composite indexes required for certain queries. No 'OR' queries — use multiple queries or in() for up to 10 values.

Real-time Listeners.exp: onSnapshot() registers a real-time listener. Fires immediately with current data and again on every change. Returns an unsubscribe function. Use with a cleanup in component lifecycle.

Batched Writes & Transactions.exp: batchedWrite executes multiple writes atomically (up to 500). runTransaction performs a read-then-write with automatic retry. Use transactions for counters, balances, and reservations.

Cloud Storage.exp: Firebase Storage for user-generated content (images, videos, files). Uses GCS underneath. Security Rules based on auth. Upload with put() / putString(), download with getDownloadURL().

Firebase Hosting.exp: Host web apps, microservices, or static content. Supports custom domains, SSL, CDN (via Fastly). Deploy with firebase deploy --only hosting. Dynamic content via Cloud Functions or Cloud Run rewrites.

Storage Security Rules.exp: Storage Security Rules control file access. Validate file size, content type, and auth status. Path pattern matching with {wildcards}.

HTTP Functions.exp: Cloud Functions runs serverless backend code (Node.js, Python, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby, .NET). Triggers: HTTP, Firestore changes, Auth events, Storage events, PubSub, Scheduled. Request/response with Express-like API.

Firestore Triggers.exp: Trigger functions on Firestore document events: onCreate, onUpdate, onDelete, onWrite. Access to snap (new) and context (event info). Useful for denormalization, notifications, aggregation.

Auth & Scheduled Triggers.exp: Auth triggers on user creation/deletion. Scheduled functions with cron syntax. Use for cleanup, reports, data sync. Functions time out at 60s (HTTP) or 540s (background).

Admin SDK.exp: Firebase Admin SDK runs in privileged environments (server, Cloud Functions). Can bypass security rules. Supports: Firestore, Auth, Storage, FCM (messaging), Machine Learning. Initialize with service account JSON.

Firestore Data Modeling.exp: NoSQL design for Firestore: denormalize, avoid joins, use subcollections for hierarchical data. Patterns: root collections for top-level entities, subcollections for related data, references for many-to-many.

Security Rules Deep.exp: Security rules can validate data on write (request.resource), check existing data (resource), enforce types, sizes, and complex conditions. Rules are evaluated every request — test thoroughly.

Performance & Costs.exp: Firestore costs: reads, writes, deletes, and stored data. Avoid unindexed queries (full scan). Use collection group indexes for subcollection queries. Limit with listener count. Use offline persistence.

Firebase Cloud Messaging.exp: FCM sends push notifications and data messages to client apps. Topics for pub/sub (any client subscribed can receive). Device groups for multi-device. Admin SDK for server-side sending.

Analytics & Crashlytics.exp: Firebase Analytics tracks user events automatically (screen views, user properties) and custom events. Crashlytics reports app crashes with stack traces, logs, and non-fatal errors.

What is Flask.exp: Flask is a lightweight Python web microframework that gives you just the essentials to build web applications. It's minimal, flexible, and unopinionated — you choose your tools (ORM, template engine, etc.). Flask is built on Werkzeug (WSGI toolkit) and Jinja2 (template engine). It's ideal for small to medium projects, APIs, microservices, and prototypes. The 'micro' in microframework means Flask keeps the core simple but is extensible via extensions.
What is Flask.code:
# Install Flask pip install flask # app.py — minimal Flask app from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route('/') def hello(): return '

Hello, Flask!

' if __name__ == '__main__': app.run(debug=True) # Run: python app.py # Visit: http://127.0.0.1:5000 # Or with flask CLI: # export FLASK_APP=app.py # export FLASK_ENV=development # flask run

Application Structure.exp: Flask applications can be structured as a single file or as packages. For larger apps, use the Application Factory pattern with Blueprints. A typical Flask project has: app/ directory (__init__.py factory, models.py, routes/, templates/, static/), config.py, requirements.txt, run.py. Blueprints organize routes into modular components. The app factory pattern allows multiple app instances and better testability. Always keep configuration separate from code.
Application Structure.code:
myflaskapp/
├── run.py              # Entry point
├── config.py            # Configuration classes
├── requirements.txt     # Dependencies
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py      # App factory
│   ├── models.py        # Database models
│   ├── forms.py         # WTForms
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   ├── main.py      # Main blueprint
│   │   └── auth.py      # Auth blueprint
│   ├── templates/
│   │   ├── base.html
│   │   └── index.html
│   └── static/
│       ├── css/
│       └── js/

# run.py
from app import create_app

app = create_app()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(debug=True)


# app/__init__.py
from flask import Flask
from config import Config

def create_app(config_class=Config):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_class)

    # Register blueprints
    from app.routes.main import bp as main_bp
    app.register_blueprint(main_bp)

    from app.routes.auth import bp as auth_bp
    app.register_blueprint(auth_bp, url_prefix='/auth')

    return app

Configuration.exp: Flask configuration is managed via app.config dictionary. Load from object, file, or environment variables. Flask has built-in configs: DEBUG, TESTING, SECRET_KEY, SERVER_NAME. Common extensions add their own config keys. Use python-decouple or python-dotenv for environment variables. Config classes organize settings by environment (Development, Testing, Production). SECRET_KEY is required for sessions and CSRF protection — always keep it secret in production.
Configuration.code:
# config.py
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

basedir = os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname(__file__))

class Config:
    SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY') or 'dev-key-change-in-production'
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL') or \
        'sqlite:///' + os.path.join(basedir, 'app.db')
    SQLALCHEMY_TRACK_MODIFICATIONS = False
    MAIL_SERVER = os.environ.get('MAIL_SERVER', 'smtp.gmail.com')
    MAIL_PORT = int(os.environ.get('MAIL_PORT', 587))
    MAIL_USE_TLS = True
    MAIL_USERNAME = os.environ.get('MAIL_USERNAME')
    MAIL_PASSWORD = os.environ.get('MAIL_PASSWORD')

class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = True

class ProductionConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = False
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')

class TestingConfig(Config):
    TESTING = True
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = 'sqlite:///:memory:'


# Usage in factory:
app.config.from_object(config_class)

# .env file (never commit to git):
# SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key
# DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost/db
# MAIL_USERNAME=user@example.com

Route Decorators.exp: Flask uses the @app.route() decorator to bind URLs to view functions. URL parts can be dynamic with <variable_name> or <converter:variable_name>. Converters: string (default), int, float, path (accepts slashes), uuid. HTTP methods via methods parameter. url_for() generates URLs from endpoint names. The request object contains all incoming data (args, form, json, headers, cookies, files). abort() returns HTTP errors. redirect() redirects to another URL.

Request & Response.exp: The request object provides access to all incoming data. request.args (query strings), request.form (form data), request.json (JSON body), request.files (uploads), request.headers, request.cookies, request.method. The response object can be customized: make_response(), set headers, set cookies, set status codes. JSON responses with jsonify(). File uploads handled via request.files with secure_filename for sanitization.

Blueprints.exp: Blueprints organize related routes, templates, and static files into reusable modules. They're like mini-applications within the main app. Create a Blueprint object, define routes with @bp.route(), register with app.register_blueprint(). Blueprints support url_prefix for namespacing, subdomain for multi-subdomain apps, and template_folder/static_folder. Use current_app and url_for with endpoint_name.view_name pattern across blueprints.

Jinja2 Templates.exp: Flask uses Jinja2 as its default template engine. Templates go in the templates/ folder. Use {{ }} for expressions, {% %} for control flow, {# #} for comments. Template inheritance with {% extends %} and {% block %}. Include partials with {% include %}. Special variables: config, request, session, g, url_for, get_flashed_messages. Autoescaping is enabled for .html templates. Filters: safe, capitalize, lower, upper, title, trim, striptags, escape, default, length, join, round, format, truncate.
Jinja2 Templates.code:
Home About {% if current_user.is_authenticated %} Logout {% else %} Login {% endif %}
{% with messages = get_flashed_messages(with_categories=true) %} {% if messages %} {% for category, message in messages %}
{{ message }}
{% endfor %} {% endif %} {% endwith %}
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
{% extends 'base.html' %} {% block title %}Home{% endblock %} {% block content %}

Welcome to Flask!

{% if current_user.is_authenticated %}

Hello, {{ current_user.username }}!

{% endif %} {% endblock %}

Static Files.exp: Static files (CSS, JS, images) are served from the static/ folder. Use url_for('static', filename='...') to generate URLs. Flask automatically serves static files in development.
