In production, use a web server (Nginx) or CDN. Flask-Assets or webpack can bundle and minify assets. Custom static URL path via app's static_url_path. Multiple static folders possible with Blueprint static_folder or via send_from_directory.
Static Files.code: {# CSS Example: static/css/style.css #} /* body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; line-height: 1.6; } nav { background: #333; padding: 1rem; } nav a { color: #fff; margin-right: 1rem; } .alert { padding: 1rem; margin: 1rem 0; border-radius: 4px; } .alert-success { background: #d4edda; color: #155724; } .alert-error { background: #f8d7da; color: #721c24; } */

Flask-SQLAlchemy.exp: Flask-SQLAlchemy integrates SQLAlchemy ORM into Flask. Install: pip install flask-sqlalchemy. Configure database URI in app.config. Define models as classes inheriting from db.Model. Column types: Integer, String, Text, Boolean, DateTime, Float, ForeignKey. Relationships: db.relationship() for backrefs. Create tables with db.create_all(). Session management is automatic. Flask-Migrate (Alembic) handles schema migrations.
Flask-SQLAlchemy.code:
# app/__init__.py — initialization
from flask import Flask
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
from flask_migrate import Migrate

db = SQLAlchemy()
migrate = Migrate()

def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = 'sqlite:///app.db'
    app.config['SQLALCHEMY_TRACK_MODIFICATIONS'] = False

    db.init_app(app)
    migrate.init_app(app, db)

    from app.routes import main, auth
    app.register_blueprint(main.bp)
    app.register_blueprint(auth.bp)

    return app


# app/models.py
from app import db
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class User(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    username = db.Column(db.String(80), unique=True, nullable=False)
    email = db.Column(db.String(120), unique=True, nullable=False)
    password_hash = db.Column(db.String(128))
    created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime, default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    posts = db.relationship('Post', backref='author', lazy='dynamic')

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'<User {self.username}>'

class Post(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = db.Column(db.String(200), nullable=False)
    body = db.Column(db.Text, nullable=False)
    created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime, default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    user_id = db.Column(db.Integer, db.ForeignKey('user.id'), nullable=False)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'<Post {self.title}>'

CRUD Operations.exp: SQLAlchemy CRUD follows a session-based pattern. Create: db.session.add(obj). Read: Model.query.all(), Model.query.get(id), Model.query.filter_by(). Update: modify object attributes and commit. Delete: db.session.delete(obj). Always call db.session.commit() to persist changes. Query filters: filter(), filter_by(), order_by(), limit(), offset(), first(), first_or_404(), get_or_404(), paginate(). Aggregations with db.func.count(), db.func.sum(). Relationships: user.posts, post.author.
CRUD Operations.code:
# CRUD operations
from app import db
from app.models import User, Post

# CREATE
user = User(username='alice', email='alice@example.com')
db.session.add(user)
db.session.commit()

post = Post(title='Hello World', body='First post!', author=user)
db.session.add(post)
db.session.commit()

# READ
all_users = User.query.all()
user = User.query.get(1)
user = User.query.filter_by(username='alice').first()
user = User.query.filter(User.email.endswith('@example.com')).all()

# Pagination
page = User.query.paginate(page=1, per_page=20, error_out=False)
page.items  # items on this page
page.total  # total items
page.pages  # total pages
page.has_prev, page.has_next, page.prev_num, page.next_num

# UPDATE
user = User.query.get(1)
user.email = 'alice@newdomain.com'
db.session.commit()

# DELETE
db.session.delete(user)
db.session.commit()

# Relationships
user = User.query.get(1)
user.posts.all()  # all posts by user
post = Post.query.get(1)
post.author.username  # author relationship

# Complex queries
from sqlalchemy import func

# Count posts per user
users_with_counts = db.session.query(
    User.username,
    func.count(Post.id).label('post_count')

Migrations (Flask-Migrate).exp: Flask-Migrate wraps Alembic for database migrations. Initialize with flask db init. Auto-detect model changes with flask db migrate -m 'message'. Apply with flask db upgrade. Rollback with flask db downgrade. View history with flask db history. Check current revision with flask db current. Merge conflicts by editing migration files manually. Always review auto-generated migrations before applying.
Migrations (Flask-Migrate).code:
# Terminal commands
flask db init                  # Initialize migrations (creates migrations/ folder)
flask db migrate -m 'Add User and Post models'  # Create migration
flask db upgrade               # Apply migration
flask db downgrade             # Rollback last migration
flask db history               # View migration history
flask db current               # Current revision

# Migration file example:
# migrations/versions/abc123_add_user_and_post_models.py
"""Add User and Post models

Revision ID: abc123
Revises:
Create Date: 2024-01-15 10:30:00
"""
from alembic import op
import sqlalchemy as sa

revision = 'abc123'
down_revision = None

def upgrade():
    op.create_table('user',
        sa.Column('id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('username', sa.String(length=80), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('email', sa.String(length=120), nullable=False),
        sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint('id'),
        sa.UniqueConstraint('username'),
        sa.UniqueConstraint('email')
    )
    op.create_table('post',
        sa.Column('id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('title', sa.String(length=200), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('body', sa.Text(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('user_id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.ForeignKeyConstraint(['user_id'], ['user.id']),
        sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint('id')
    )

def downgrade():
    op.drop_table('post')
    op.drop_table('user')

WTForms.exp: Flask-WTF integrates WTForms for form handling and CSRF protection. Define form classes with fields and validators. Common fields: StringField, PasswordField, BooleanField, SelectField, TextAreaField, FileField, DateField, IntegerField, FloatField, RadioField, SelectMultipleField, HiddenField, SubmitField. Validators: DataRequired, Email, Length, EqualTo, NumberRange, URL, Regexp, AnyOf, Optional. CSRF protection is enabled by default. Render forms manually or with macros.
WTForms.code:
# app/forms.py
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import StringField, PasswordField, BooleanField, \
    TextAreaField, SelectField, SubmitField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, Email, Length, EqualTo

class RegistrationForm(FlaskForm):
    username = StringField('Username',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(min=3, max=80)])
    email = StringField('Email',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Email()])
    password = PasswordField('Password',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(min=8)])
    confirm_password = PasswordField('Confirm Password',
        validators=[DataRequired(), EqualTo('password')])
    accept_tos = BooleanField('Accept Terms',
        validators=[DataRequired()])

        ('user', 'User'), ('editor', 'Editor'), ('admin', 'Admin')
    ])

class PostForm(FlaskForm):

        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(max=200)])
    body = TextAreaField('Content',
        validators=[DataRequired()])
    category = SelectField('Category', coerce=int)
    submit = SubmitField('Publish')

Flask-Login.exp: Flask-Login manages user sessions. Install: pip install flask-login. User model must implement is_authenticated, is_active, is_anonymous, get_id(). Use login_required decorator to protect views. login_user() logs in a user, logout_user() logs out. current_user proxy provides access to logged-in user. Remember me with remember=True. User loader callback reloads user from session ID. Requires SECRET_KEY for session signing. Flask-Bcrypt for password hashing.

Flask RESTful.exp: Flask-RESTful simplifies API building with Resource classes. Install: pip install flask-restful. Define resources as classes with methods for HTTP verbs (get, post, put, delete, patch). Request parsing with reqparse for validation. Fields marshaling with marshal_with for consistent responses. Alternatively, use Flask's built-in jsonify() and request.get_json() for simpler APIs. Flask-RESTx adds Swagger documentation.
Flask RESTful.code:
# app/api.py — Flask-RESTful
from flask import Blueprint
from flask_restful import Api, Resource, reqparse, fields, marshal_with
from app.models import Post
from app import db

api_bp = Blueprint('api', __name__, url_prefix='/api/v1')
api = Api(api_bp)

# Request parser
post_parser = reqparse.RequestParser()
post_parser.add_argument('title', type=str, required=True, help='Title is required')
post_parser.add_argument('body', type=str, required=True)
post_parser.add_argument('user_id', type=int, required=True)

# Response fields
post_fields = {
    'id': fields.Integer,
    'title': fields.String,
    'body': fields.String,
    'created_at': fields.DateTime(dt_format='iso8601'),
    'author': fields.String(attribute=lambda x: x.author.username),
}

class PostResource(Resource):
    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def get(self, post_id=None):
        if post_id:
            return Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        return Post.query.all()

    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def post(self):
        args = post_parser.parse_args()
        post = Post(title=args['title'], body=args['body'], user_id=args['user_id'])
        db.session.add(post)
        db.session.commit()
        return post, 201

    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def put(self, post_id):
        post = Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        args = post_parser.parse_args()
        post.title = args['title']
        post.body = args['body']
        db.session.commit()
        return post

    def delete(self, post_id):
        post = Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        db.session.delete(post)
        db.session.commit()
        return '', 204

api.add_resource(PostResource, '/posts', '/posts/<int:post_id>')


# Simpler JSON API without Flask-RESTful
@bp.route('/api/posts', methods=['GET'])
def get_posts():
    posts = Post.query.all()
    return jsonify([{
        'id': p.id,
        'title': p.title,
        'body': p.body,
        'created_at': p.created_at.isoformat(),
        'author': p.author.username
    } for p in posts])

Dart Basics.exp: Dart is a client-optimized language with sound null safety, type inference, and async/await. It compiles either ahead-of-time (AOT) for production or just-in-time (JIT) for hot reload.

Widgets.exp: Everything in Flutter is a widget. StatelessWidget builds immutable UI, while StatefulWidget manages mutable state that can trigger rebuilds via setState.

MaterialApp.exp: MaterialApp wraps your app with Material Design conventions, including theming, navigation, and localization. It provides Scaffold and other Material widgets.

Hot Reload.exp: Flutter's hot reload injects source code changes into the running Dart VM in under a second. It preserves app state so you can iterate on UI without restarting.
Hot Reload.code:
# Press r in the terminal or click the lightning bolt in IDE
# State is preserved on hot reload (not hot restart)
# Only modified widgets are rebuilt

Row.exp: Row arranges child widgets horizontally. It uses MainAxisAlignment for horizontal alignment and CrossAxisAlignment for vertical alignment.

Column.exp: Column arranges child widgets vertically with support for scrolling via Expanded and Flexible widgets for proportional sizing.

Stack.exp: Stack overlays children on top of each other, positioning them with Positioned widget relative to the stack edges.

Container.exp: Container combines painting, positioning, and sizing widgets. It supports padding, margins, borders, background color, and constraints.
Container.code:
Container(
  padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
  color: Colors.white,
  child: Text('Content')
)

Expanded & Flexible.exp: Expanded forces a child to fill available space in a Row or Column. Flexible allows the child to be smaller than available space if needed.
Expanded & Flexible.code:
Row(children: [
  Expanded(flex: 2, child: Container(color: Colors.red)),
  Expanded(flex: 1, child: Container(color: Colors.blue)),
])

AnimatedContainer.exp: AnimatedContainer automatically animates changes to its properties like color, size, padding, and border radius over a specified duration.
AnimatedContainer.code:
AnimatedContainer(
  duration: Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  color: isActive ? Colors.blue : Colors.grey,
  width: isActive ? 200 : 100,
  child: Text('Animate'),
)

TweenAnimationBuilder.exp: TweenAnimationBuilder animates a value from a start to end point using a curve. It rebuilds the widget tree on each frame during the animation.
TweenAnimationBuilder.code:
TweenAnimationBuilder<double>(
  tween: Tween(begin: 0, end: 1),
  duration: Duration(seconds: 2),
  builder: (context, value, child) => Opacity(opacity: value, child: child),
  child: Text('Fade in'),
)

Hero.exp: Hero animates a widget from one screen to another during navigation. Both screens must have a Hero widget with the same tag for the shared transition.

CustomPainter.exp: CustomPainter lets you draw custom graphics using a Canvas API with Paint objects. It's essential for charts, signatures, and complex visual effects.

setState.exp: setState is the simplest state management approach, notifying the framework to rebuild the widget tree when state changes inside StatefulWidget.

Provider.exp: Provider exposes values down the widget tree via InheritedWidget. It is the recommended simple state management solution for Flutter apps.

Riverpod.exp: Riverpod improves on Provider with compile-time safety, no BuildContext dependency, and support for async providers and code generation.

Bloc.exp: Bloc separates business logic from UI using streams of events and states. It enforces unidirectional data flow and testability.

Isolates.exp: Isolates are independent workers that run Dart code in parallel with their own memory heap. Use compute() for simple parallel tasks or Isolate.spawn for complex ones.

Futures & Streams.exp: Futures represent single async values, while Streams represent sequences of async events. Both are core to Flutter's async programming model.

Routes.exp: Named routes map string identifiers to widget builders. Navigator.push and Navigator.pop handle stack-based navigation.

Navigator 2.0.exp: Navigator 2.0 provides declarative routing with pages list, allowing deep linking and full control over the navigation stack.

GoRouter.exp: GoRouter provides declarative, URL-based routing with support for deep linking, redirects, and nested navigation using ShellRoute.

Form.exp: Form widget groups form fields for validation and saving. It uses a GlobalKey to access form state and validate all fields at once.

TextFormField.exp: TextFormField is a Material Design text input with built-in validation, error display, and controller access for programmatic manipulation.

Validation.exp: Form validation uses validator callbacks that return error strings or null. AutovalidateMode controls when validation triggers automatically.
Validation.code:
TextFormField(
  autovalidateMode: AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction,
  validator: (v) => v!.length < 3 ? 'Too short' : null
)

http.exp: The http package provides a simple, stream-based HTTP client for making REST API calls. It returns Response objects with status codes and bodies.

dio.exp: Dio is a powerful HTTP client with interceptors, request cancellation, timeout handling, and file download/upload progress tracking.

REST API.exp: REST APIs are consumed by mapping JSON responses to Dart models using fromJson/toJson methods. jsonDecode parses raw JSON strings.
REST API.code:
final json = jsonDecode(response.body);
final user = User.fromJson(json);

GraphQL.exp: GraphQL queries request specific fields from the server, reducing over-fetching. The graphql_flutter package integrates with the widget tree.
GraphQL.code: final result = await client.query(QueryOptions(document: gql('{ users { name email } }')));

SharedPreferences.exp: SharedPreferences stores simple key-value pairs persistently. It is platform-native, backed by NSUserDefaults on iOS and SharedPreferences on Android.

SQLite.exp: SQLite provides relational local storage via the sqflite package. Tables are created with SQL and queried using raw or helper methods.
SQLite.code: final db = await openDatabase('mydb.db', version: 1, onCreate: (db, v) => db.execute('CREATE TABLE items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)'));

Hive.exp: Hive is a lightweight, NoSQL key-value database written in Dart. It is fast and supports type adapters for complex objects without native dependencies.

Platform Channels.exp: Platform channels enable bidirectional communication between Dart and native Kotlin/Swift code via MethodChannel for platform-specific features.

iOS/Android Specific.exp: Platform-specific code uses dart:io Platform checks or conditional imports to handle OS differences in UI, permissions, and behavior.
iOS/Android Specific.code: if (Platform.isIOS) { /* iOS code */ } else if (Platform.isAndroid) { /* Android code */ }

Material 3.exp: Material 3 (Material You) is the latest Material Design iteration with dynamic color theming based on wallpaper colors. Enable via useMaterial3 flag.
Material 3.code:
MaterialApp(
  theme: ThemeData(
    useMaterial3: true,
    colorSchemeSeed: Colors.blue,
    brightness: Brightness.light
  )
)

Web.exp: Flutter Web compiles Dart to JavaScript and renders via CanvasKit or HTML renderers. Responsive layouts use LayoutBuilder and MediaQuery for breakpoints.

Widget Testing.exp: Widget tests verify individual widget behavior using the flutter_test package. They run in a simulated environment without a real device.

Unit Testing.exp: Unit tests test individual functions and classes in isolation. Use the test package with expect, group, and setUp for organized tests.

Integration Testing.exp: Integration tests run on a real device or emulator, testing the full app flow from user interactions to UI changes.

Flutter DevTools.exp: Flutter DevTools is a suite of debugging and profiling tools: widget inspector, timeline view, memory/CPU profiler, network logging, and app size analysis.
Flutter DevTools.code:
flutter pub global activate devtools
flutter run --observatory-port=9200
# Then run: devtools

# Key DevTools features:
# - Widget Inspector: see widget tree and properties
# - Timeline: frame-by-frame performance analysis
# - Memory: track allocations and leaks
# - Network: monitor HTTP traffic in real-time

Performance Profile.exp: Use Flutter's performance overlay and profile mode to identify jank, rebuild causes, and layout inefficiencies during development.

Firebase Auth.exp: Firebase Authentication provides backend services for email/password, phone, OAuth (Google, Facebook, Apple), and anonymous auth in Flutter.

Firestore.exp: Cloud Firestore is a flexible, scalable NoSQL database for Flutter apps. It provides real-time listeners, offline support, and automatic data synchronization.

Cloud Messaging.exp: Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) sends push notifications to Flutter apps. Supports notification messages, data messages, and topic-based subscriptions.

Game Loops & Architecture.exp: The game loop is the heart of every game: input, update, render. Fixed timestep decouples simulation from framerate. Use accumulator pattern for fixed-update with variable rendering.

ECS (Entity-Component-System).exp: ECS decouples data (components) from behavior (systems), iterated over entities (IDs). Cache-friendly, data-oriented design. Favors composition over inheritance.

Design Patterns in Games.exp: Common patterns: Singleton (GameManager), Observer (events), Command (input buffering), Object Pool (bullets), State (AI), Flyweight (shared data). Use wisely—patterns solve problems, don't force them.

Game Feel & Juice.exp: Juice is the extra polish: screen shake, particle bursts, tweening, sound cues, hit-stop, flash effects. These positive feedback loops make gameplay satisfying and responsive.

Feedback Loops.exp: Positive loops amplify (snowballing—winner gets stronger), negative loops stabilize (rubber-banding—last place gets boost). Both used carefully to balance engagement and fairness.

Difficulty Curves.exp: Difficulty should ramp gradually with optional plateaus. Player-skill vs challenge must stay in flow channel—too easy bores, too hard frustrates. Adaptive difficulty adjusts in real-time.

Game Economy & Balancing.exp: Virtual economies manage resources (gold, XP, mana). Balance via tuning loops: playtest, gather data, adjust. Watch for inflation, grinding, and dominant strategies in multiplayer.

State Machines for Game Logic.exp: Finite state machines model entity behavior. Each state has Enter/Update/Exit. Transitions triggered by events or conditions. Hierarchical FSM nests states for complexity.

Collision Detection \u2014 AABB & Circle.exp: AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) is the fastest overlap test. Circle-circle uses distance vs radius sum. Broad-phase uses simple checks before narrow-phase.

Collision Detection \u2014 SAT & GJK.exp: SAT (Separating Axis Theorem) checks all potential separating axes. GJK (Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi) iteratively finds closest distance between convex shapes. EPA expands GJK for collision info.

Physics Integration (Euler, Verlet, RK4).exp: Euler: simple but unstable. Verlet: excellent for springs/cloth (stores position, not velocity). RK4: 4th-order Runge-Kutta, most accurate for forces, used in scientific simulations.

Friction & Restitution.exp: Friction opposes sliding (Coulomb model: static vs kinetic). Restitution (bounciness, 0–1) controls energy retained after collision. Combined via coefficient of restitution formula.

Joints & Constraints.exp: Joints connect rigid bodies: revolute (hinge), prismatic (slider), distance (rod), spring, fixed. Constraints restrict degrees of freedom. Solved via iterative impulse solvers (PBD, sequential impulses).

Raycasting.exp: Raycasting fires a ray and returns first intersected object. Used for shooting, line-of-sight, mouse picking. Möller–Trumbore algorithm for triangle intersection.

Spatial Partitioning.exp: Partition space to avoid O(n²) checks. Grid: simple, good for uniform分布. Quadtree/Octree: recursive subdivision, adapts to density. BVH: bounding volume hierarchy for dynamic objects.

Physics Engine Architecture.exp: Engines loop: broadphase (detect pairs), narrowphase (generate contacts), solve constraints, integrate. Common engines: Box2D, Bullet, PhysX, Jolt. Determinism matters for multiplayer.

Rendering Pipeline.exp: The graphics pipeline transforms 3D data to pixels. Stages: vertex shader → tessellation → geometry → rasterization → fragment shader → output merger. Modern GPUs are massively parallel.

Shaders \u2014 Vertex & Fragment.exp: Vertex shaders transform vertices and pass data. Fragment (pixel) shaders compute final color. GLSL/HLSL syntax. Input: attributes (per-vertex), uniforms (per-draw), varyings (interpolated).

Lighting Models.exp: Lambertian diffuse: max(N·L, 0). Blinn-Phong adds specular: pow(N·H, shininess). PBR uses microfacet models (Cook-Torrance BRDF) with roughness/metalness for physically-based results.

Shadows.exp: Shadow mapping: render depth from light's view, then sample during main pass. PCF (percentage-closer filtering) softens edges. Cascaded shadow maps split depth for large scenes.

Post-Processing.exp: Full-screen passes applied after rendering: bloom (bright-pass + blur), tone-mapping (HDR to LDR), color grading, SSR (screen-space reflections), SSAO (ambient occlusion), motion blur.

GPU Instancing & Batching.exp: Instancing renders many copies with one draw call—each instance has per-instance data (transform, color). Static batching merges static objects. Dynamic batching groups small meshes.

LODs (Level of Detail).exp: Switch mesh complexity based on distance or screen-size. LOD 0 (full detail) near camera, LOD 1-3 further. Cross-fading or popping. Impostors (billboard textures) for extreme distance.

Culling (Frustum, Occlusion).exp: Frustum culling: discard objects outside camera view frustum using plane tests. Occlusion culling: skip objects behind occluders. Hierarchical Z-buffer (Hi-Z) for GPU occlusion.

Audio Engines & Middleware.exp: Audio engines manage playback, mixing, effects. Options: OpenAL (open-source), FMOD (popular in AAA), Wwise (full pipeline), Web Audio API (browser). Middleware handles platform differences.

3D Audio (Positional Audio).exp: Position audio sources in 3D space using attenuation curves (linear, inverse, logarithmic). Listener has position/orientation. HRTF (head-related transfer function) for realistic spatialization.

DSP Effects.exp: Digital Signal Processing: reverb (convolution or feedback delay), EQ (low/high/band-pass filters), chorus, flange, distortion, compressor. Graph of AudioNodes in Web Audio / audio middleware.

Sound Pooling.exp: Pre-allocate audio instances to avoid garbage-collection hits. Pool returns a free source; if all in use, steal oldest or skip. Crucial for frequent sounds (footsteps, gunshots).

Music Systems.exp: Dynamic music adapts to gameplay. Techniques: horizontal resequencing (swap sections), vertical layering (add/subtract layers), stingers (transition cues). MIDI vs audio stems.

FMOD / Wwise Basics.exp: FMOD Studio: event-driven audio, parametric controls, real-time mixing. Wwise: full sound design pipeline with SoundBanks, RTPCs (real-time parameter controls), States, and Switches.

Adaptive Audio.exp: Audio reacts to game state: combat intensity, health, speed, environment. Blend snapshots, adjust reverb zones, trigger stingers. Prevents audio fatigue and heightens immersion.

Vectors.exp: Vectors represent positions, directions, velocities. Operations: add, subtract, scale, dot product (angle), cross product (perpendicular in 3D), normalize (unit length). Foundation of game math.

Matrices & Transforms.exp: 4×4 matrices encode translation, rotation, scale. Matrix multiplication composes transforms. Model→World→View→Projection pipeline. Inverse matrix undoes transformation.

Quaternions.exp: Quaternions represent rotation without gimbal lock. q = (cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2) * axis). Unit quaternion for rotation. Slerp for smooth interpolation. Multiply to compose rotations.

Interpolation (Lerp, Slerp, Easing).exp: Lerp: linear interpolation (a + t*(b-a)). Slerp: spherical for quaternions. Easing functions: ease-in (quadratic), ease-out, ease-in-out, elastic, bounce. Used in animations and transitions.

Noise Functions.exp: Perlin noise: smooth, gradient-based, lattice noise. Simplex noise: faster, fewer artifacts, scales to N-dimensions. Used for terrain, textures, procedural generation. Fractal Brownian Motion layers octaves.

Curves & Splines.exp: Catmull-Rom: interpolates through control points (used for camera paths). Bézier: uses control points (Cubic: 4 points). Hermite: specifies tangents. NURBS: rational curves for CAD.

Trigonometry for Games.exp: Sine/cosine for oscillating motion, circular movement, wave effects. Atan2 for angle between points. Used in aiming, field-of-view checks, projectile trajectories, Lissajous patterns.

Coordinate Spaces.exp: Local (object) → World → View (camera) → Clip → Screen. Normalized device coordinates (NDC): [-1,1]. UV/texel coordinates: [0,1] for textures. Proper transforms prevent visual glitches.

Finite State Machines.exp: FSM: entity is in exactly one state at a time. Transitions defined by events/conditions. Simple, predictable AI. HFSM (Hierarchical) nests states for reuse. Drawback: becomes unwieldy with many states.

Behavior Trees.exp: Tree of tasks: Sequence (all succeed), Selector (first success), Condition, Action, Decorator (invert, repeat, cooldown). Blackboard stores shared data. More modular than FSM.

GOAP (Goal-Oriented Action Planning).exp: AI picks actions based on goals and world state. Planner searches for cheapest action sequence achieving the goal. Used in F.E.A.R. Actions have preconditions and effects.

Utility AI.exp: Each action gets a score based on context (distance, health, ammo). Highest-scoring action executes. Scores computed via response curves (linear, logistic, exponential). Smooth, tunable, realistic.

A* Pathfinding.exp: A* finds shortest path using g(n) (cost from start) + h(n) (heuristic to goal). Guarantees optimal path with admissible heuristic. Open set (priority queue), closed set (visited).

Dijkstra & JPS Pathfinding.exp: Dijkstra: A* with h(n)=0, finds shortest to all nodes. JPS (Jump Point Search): speeds up A* on uniform-cost grids by jumping over empty areas. Symmetry reduction for open spaces.

Navmesh.exp: Navigation mesh: walkable surface represented as convex polygons. A* on navmesh graph, then funnel algorithm for path straightening. Handles any-angle movement, dynamic obstacles.

Flocking & Steering Behaviors.exp: Boids model: separation (avoid neighbors), alignment (match velocity), cohesion (move to center). Steering behaviors: seek, flee, pursue, evade, wander, obstacle avoidance. Combined via weighted blending.

Skeletal Animation.exp: Mesh bound to a bone hierarchy (skeleton). Each vertex weighted to 1-4 bones (skinning). Animation stores per-bone transforms at keyframes. Interpolated and applied as matrix palette.

Blend Trees.exp: Blend between multiple animations based on parameters. 1D blend: idle→walk→run by speed. 2D blend: direction + speed. Freeform Cartesian for complex spaces. Additive blends for layers.

Inverse Kinematics (IK).exp: IK computes joint angles to reach a target position. CCD (Cyclic Coordinate Descent): iterative joint rotation. FABRIK: forward-and-backward reaching. Two-bone IK: analytic solution for arms/legs.

Blend Shapes (Morph Targets).exp: Store multiple vertex positions for the same mesh. Interpolate between shapes for facial animation, morphing. Basis shape + delta arrays. Weighted combination for complex expressions.

Animation State Machines.exp: Graph of animation states with transitions, blend times, and conditions. Parameters drive transitions (bool, float, int, trigger). Cross-fade between animations prevents popping.

Animation Rigging.exp: Constraint-based system layered on top of animation: aim constraints (look-at), parent constraints, chain IK, twist correction. Used for procedural adjustments without modifying original clips.

Motion Matching.exp: Match live pose + trajectory to database of animations. Search for nearest neighbor by feature vector (root velocity, foot positions). Blend at transitions. Used in The Last of Us, Assassin's Creed.

Input Abstraction.exp: Abstract input layer decouples game logic from hardware. Query actions (Jump, Shoot) instead of keys. Allows swapping keyboard/gamepad/touch without game changes.

Input Rebinding.exp: Allow players to reassign keys/buttons at runtime. Store bindings in config file. Detect conflicts, validate (ensure at least one binding per action). Present UI with waiting-for-input prompt.

Action Mapping.exp: Map abstract actions to concrete inputs. Digital (button press) vs Analog (stick, trigger). Value: 0/1 for digital, -1..1 for axis. Dead zones, inversion, sensitivity curves per action.

Gamepad Input.exp: Gamepad API provides sticks, buttons, triggers (pressure-sensitive), and rumble. Standard mapping: left stick move, right stick look, A/B/X/Y, shoulder buttons. XInput (Windows) / GameController (macOS/Linux).

Touch & Gesture Input.exp: Touch events: touchstart, touchmove, touchend. Multi-touch tracking via identifier. Gestures: tap, double-tap, swipe, pinch (zoom), rotate, long-press. Gesture recognizers abstract raw touch.

Gyroscope & Motion Sensors.exp: DeviceOrientation/Motion APIs provide alpha (compass), beta (tilt front-back), gamma (tilt left-right). Acceleration with/without gravity. Used for tilt controls, VR head tracking, step counting.

Haptics & Accessibility.exp: Haptic feedback: gamepad rumble (continuous/impulse), phone vibration. Accessibility: color-blind modes, subtitle sizing, remappable controls, auto-aim, slow-motion assists, single-switch input.

Perlin & Simplex Noise.exp: Perlin noise: lattice-based gradient noise (Ken Perlin, 1985). Simplex noise: faster, better isotropy, scales to any dimension. Fractal noise (FBM) layers octaves for natural-looking terrain.

Cellular Automata.exp: Grid of cells with states evolving by rules. Conway's Game of Life: birth on 3 neighbors, death on <2 or >3. Used for cave generation (cave-like automata with B678/S345678 rules).

Wave Function Collapse.exp: WFC generates tile-based patterns matching input examples. Start with maximum entropy (superposition), observe (collapse) lowest-entropy cell, propagate constraints. Used for infinite worlds, architecture, puzzles.

L-Systems.exp: Lindenmayer systems: recursive string rewriting for plants, fractals. Axiom + production rules. Each symbol is a turtle graphics command (F=forward, +=turn left, -=turn right, [=push, ]=pop).

Dungeon Generation.exp: BSP (Binary Space Partition): recursively split rooms. Random walk: drunkard's walk for cave-like tunnels. Prefab-based: stitch hand-designed rooms. Delaunay + MST for connecting rooms with corridors.

Terrain Generation.exp: Heightmap generation via FBM noise. Erosion simulation (hydraulic, thermal) adds realism. Biomes determined by temperature + humidity noise. GPU tessellation for dynamic detail.

Procedural Textures.exp: Generate textures mathematically: Voronoi (cellular), checkerboard, marble (sine + noise), wood (concentric rings), brick (tiling patterns). No external assets needed—infinite resolution.

Client-Server Architecture.exp: The server is authoritative: validates actions, simulates world state. Clients send input, receive updates. Thin client vs thick client. Tick rate, bandwidth, and latency tradeoffs.

Peer-to-Peer & Relay.exp: P2P: players connect directly—low latency, complex NAT traversal (STUN/TURN/ICE). Relay: server forwards traffic—simpler NAT handling, adds latency. Rollback netcode for fighting games.

Netcode & State Synchronization.exp: Authoritative server sends world state deltas. Client-side prediction hides latency. Entity interpolation smooths other players. Snapshot compression (bitpacking, delta encoding).

Lag Compensation & Prediction.exp: Client predicts own movement immediately (no input lag). Server rewinds time for hit detection (lag compensation). Extrapolation estimates positions of others. Reconciliation corrects prediction errors.

Rollback Netcode.exp: Fighting game technique: simulate future frames, roll back when server disagrees. Saves snapshots for rollback. Input delay + prediction for responsive feel. GGPO-style implementation.

Matchmaking & Lobbies.exp: Matchmaking: skill-based (ELO, TrueSkill), ping-based, party support. Lobbies: pre-game rooms with player slots, ready states, chat. Steamworks / Epic Online Services for cross-platform.

WebSocket & REST for Games.exp: WebSocket: persistent full-duplex connection for real-time game data. REST: HTTP for authentication, leaderboards, store. gRPC / MessagePack for efficient binary protocols.

NAT Punchthrough & Relay Servers.exp: NAT (Network Address Translation) blocks direct P2P connections. STUN: discover public IP/port. TURN: relay traffic when P2P fails. ICE: combine STUN/TURN candidates. Server relay for fallback.

CPU Profiling.exp: Instrument your game to find hot spots. Frame time budget: 16ms (60fps). Tools: Chrome DevTools (web), Tracy (native), Unreal Insights, Unity Profiler. Identify dominant systems (physics, AI, rendering).

GPU Profiling & Optimization.exp: RenderDoc, NVIDIA Nsight, AMD Radeon GPU Profiler. Analyze draw calls, shader complexity, bandwidth. Bottlenecks: vertex-bound, pixel-bound, bandwidth-bound. Reduce overdraw, optimize shaders.

Memory Management.exp: Avoid GC spikes: object pooling, structs (value types), pre-allocate arrays. Memory fragmentation. Asset lifetime management. Leak detection. Addressable assets for streaming.

Draw Call Optimization.exp: Each draw call has CPU overhead. Batching: static (combine meshes), dynamic (GPU instancing). Reduce material changes (sort by shader/texture). Texture atlasing. SRP Batcher (Unity).

Asset Streaming & Bundling.exp: Stream assets in background while game runs. Priority loading (nearby first). Texture mipmap streaming. Asset bundles for DLC/patches. Compression: ASTC (mobile), BC7 (desktop), Oodle.

Threading & Job Systems.exp: Main thread handles rendering, game logic offloaded to worker threads. Job system: small, independent work units scheduled across cores. Task graph for dependencies. Fiber-based scheduling.

Level-of-Detail Strategies.exp: Geometric LOD: swap mesh complexity by distance. Shader LOD: simpler shaders for distant objects. Texture LOD: mipmaps. Animation LOD: lower update rate for distant characters. Impostor billboards.

Binary vs JSON vs XML.exp: JSON: human-readable, flexible, larger size. Binary: compact, fast to parse, fixed schema. Protocol Buffers / MessagePack: cross-language, version-tolerant. XML: verbose, used in legacy formats.

Save Game Data Design.exp: Save format: versioned for forward compatibility. Separate player data from world state. Auto-save on checkpoints. Manifest file for save listing. Corruption prevention: atomic writes, CRC checksums.

Cloud Saves & Sync.exp: Steam Cloud, Epic Cloud Save, Google Play Cloud, iCloud. Sync on close, download on launch. Conflict resolution: last-write-wins, merge strategies. Offline queue with deferred upload.

Compression for Game Data.exp: Deflate/gzip: general purpose, good compression. LZ4: extremely fast decompression. Oodle Kraken (used in AAA). Texture compression: BCn, ASTC, ETC2. Mesh compression: Draco, meshoptimizer.

Config Files & Settings.exp: Separate game settings (video, audio, controls) from save data. INI, JSON, TOML, or binary config. Detect GPU/display on first launch. Cloud sync settings across devices.

Auto-Save & Checkpoints.exp: Save at safe points: level transitions, after major events, on pause menu. Auto-save timer (every 5-10 min). Rotating slots (3 auto-saves). Prevent save during combat. Async save to avoid frame spikes.

CI/CD for Games.exp: Automated build pipeline: trigger on commit, build for all platforms, run tests, upload artifacts. Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI. Perforce/Git LFS for large binary assets.
CI/CD for Games.code:
# GitHub Actions game build workflow
name: Build & Deploy
on: push to main
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: lfs: true
      - name: Build
        run: |
          if runner.os == 'Windows'; then
            .\build.bat -platform=Win64
          else
            ./build.sh -platform=${{ runner.os == 'macOS' ? 'Mac' : 'Linux' }}
          fi
      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: game-${{ runner.os }}
          path: build/

Platform-Specific Builds.exp: Windows: MSVC, DirectX, Steamworks. macOS: Metal, App Bundle, notarization. Linux: Vulkan/OpenGL, AppImage/Flatpak. Console: Xbox GDK, PS5 SDK, Switch NX. Mobile: Android AAB, iOS IPA.

Asset Building & Cooking.exp: Cook assets: convert source (PNG, FBX, WAV) to runtime format (DDS, mesh, Ogg). Deterministic builds. Dependency graph for incremental building. Asset bundles for patching.

Content Patching & DLC.exp: Binary patching: bsdiff, Courgette for executables. Asset bundles for new content. Patch size minimization: chunk-based downloads. Steamworks UGC (User-Generated Content). Modding support.

Steam & Console Integration.exp: Steamworks SDK: achievements, leaderboards, friends, cloud saves, matchmaking, DRM. Console SDKs: Xbox Live, PSN, Nintendo Switch Online. Cross-platform accounts and progression.

Crash Reporting & Telemetry.exp: Crash reporters: Crashpad (Chrome), Google Breakpad, Unity Cloud Diagnostics. Symbolication for native crashes. Telemetry: frame rate, memory usage, heat maps. GDPR compliance for player data.

Color Blindness Modes.exp: 8% of males have color vision deficiency. Modes: Protanopia (red-blind), Deuteranopia (green-blind), Tritanopia (blue-blind). Use patterns/shapes/icons in addition to color. Simulate in dev tools.

Subtitle Systems.exp: Dialogue subtitles, sound effect captions, directional indicators (who is speaking). Timed text with character-by-character reveal. Closed captions for cutscenes. Accessibility: font size, background opacity.

Text Localization (i18n).exp: Separate text from code. Locale files (JSON, YAML, PO). Placeholders for dynamic values. Pluralization rules (gettext ICU). RTL languages: Arabic, Hebrew. Font fallback for CJK characters.

Font Rendering & Text Layout.exp: Bitmap fonts (sprite sheets) vs Signed Distance Field (SDF). SDF: resolution-independent, glow/shadow effects. TrueType/OpenType rendering: FreeType, HarfBuzz for complex scripts. Kerning, ligatures.

Input Remapping & Accessibility.exp: Full control remapping UI. Hold/toggle options. Slow mode (game speed reduction). Auto-aim assistance. Single-switch input for motor disabilities. Speech-to-text for voice commands.

Difficulty Options & Assist Modes.exp: Granular difficulty sliders: enemy damage, health, speed, AI reaction time. Invulnerability mode. Infinite ammo. Skip puzzle option. Checkpoint frequency. Celeste-style assist mode inspires inclusion.

GDScript Deep.exp: Godot's primary scripting language. Dynamically typed with optional typing. Signals as first-class citizens. Features: match statements, @onready, @export, static typing, lambda functions.

C# in Godot.exp: Godot supports C# via .NET. Full access to engine API, async/await, LINQ, third-party libraries. Scene scripts in C#. Slightly slower iteration than GDScript but better tooling and performance.

Scene Tree & Nodes.exp: Every Godot project is a tree of nodes. Scenes are reusable node subtrees. Access via $ notation (get_node). Node lifecycle: _enter_tree, _ready, _process, _exit_tree. Groups and signals enable decoupling.

Signals & Groups.exp: Signals are Godot's event system: type-safe, built-in or custom. Connect via editor or code with bind/flags. Groups tag nodes for bulk operations. Alternative to tight coupling.
Signals & Groups.code:
extends Node

signal health_changed(old_value: int, new_value: int)
signal died()

func take_damage(amount: int) -> void:
    var old = health
    health -= amount
    if health <= 0:
        health = 0
        died.emit()
    health_changed.emit(old, health)

func _ready():
    # Connect with one-shot
    health_changed.connect(_on_health_changed, CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)
    # Groups
    add_to_group("enemies")
    # Call on all group members
    get_tree().call_group("enemies", "pause")
    # Get all group nodes
    var enemies = get_tree().get_nodes_in_group("enemies")

Tilemaps & TileSets.exp: TileMapLayer node for grid-based levels. TileSet resource defines tiles with physics, navigation, terrain (auto-tiling). Custom data layers per tile. Animated and random tiles.
Tilemaps & TileSets.code:
extends TileMapLayer

func _ready():
    # Create tileset programmatically
    var tileset = TileSet.new()
    var source = TileSetAtlasSource.new()
    source.texture = preload("res://tileset.png")
    source.texture_region_size = Vector2i(16, 16)
    tileset.add_source(source)
    
    # Set tile at coordinates
    set_cell(Vector2i(5, 3), 0, Vector2i(0, 0))
    
    # Terrain (auto-tiling)
    # Set terrain bits per corner for automatic connections
    set_cells_terrain_connect(get_used_cells(), 0, 0)

Animation Player & AnimationTree.exp: AnimationPlayer: keyframe animation for any node property. AnimationTree: state machine blending with parameters. Blend spaces (1D/2D). Root motion for animation-driven movement.

Particles & Shaders.exp: GPUParticles2D/3D for high-performance particle systems. Particle shaders control emission, velocity, color over lifetime. CanvasItem shaders for 2D, Spatial for 3D. VisualShaders for node-based editing.

Multiplayer & Export.exp: Godot's high-level multiplayer API: scene replication, RPCs (remote procedure calls), authority modes. Export presets for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, Web. Autoloads for persistent singletons.

Input Map & Actions.exp: Godot's Input Map defines named actions (move_left, jump) bound to keys/buttons. Access via Input singleton. Action strength for analog input. Input events vs polling. Input processing order.

Resources & Resource System.exp: Resources are reusable data containers (.tres, .res). Built-in vs external resources. Custom resources for game data (items, stats, dialogue). Resource cache and preloading.

Editor Plugins & @tool Scripts.exp: @tool scripts run in the editor for live preview, custom gizmos, inspector plugins. EditorPlugin for adding docks, buttons, menus. Build custom importers, exporters, and level editors.
Editor Plugins & @tool Scripts.code:
tool
 extends EditorPlugin

const MainDock = preload("res://addons/my_tool/dock.tscn")
var dock_instance: Control

func _enter_tree() -> void:
    # Add custom button to toolbar
    add_tool_menu_item("Generate Level", Callable(self, "_generate_level"))
    
    # Add dock to editor
    dock_instance = MainDock.instantiate()
    add_control_to_dock(DOCK_SLOT_LEFT_UR, dock_instance)
    
    # Custom inspector plugin
    var inspector_plugin = preload("res://addons/my_tool/item_inspector_plugin.gd").new()
    add_inspector_plugin(inspector_plugin)

func _exit_tree() -> void:
    remove_tool_menu_item("Generate Level")
    remove_control_from_docks(dock_instance)
    dock_instance.queue_free()

GDExtension & C++ Bindings.exp: GDExtension (Godot 4): dynamically link C++ libraries without recompiling engine. Full performance for compute-heavy systems. Bind classes, expose to GDScript. Replace GDNative from Godot 3.

Godot XR Tools.exp: Godot XR: OpenXR integration for VR/AR. XROrigin3D, XRCamera3D, XRController3D nodes. Hand tracking, passthrough AR. Optimized for standalone headsets (Quest, Pico). XR-specific shaders and performance.

Godot 4 Render Modes.exp: Godot 4 offers 3 renderers: Forward+ (desktop, many lights, SSAO, glow), Mobile (faster, no SSAO, simpler), Compatibility (OpenGL 3.3 / GLES 3.0 fallback). Switch per-platform in Project Settings.
Godot 4 Render Modes.code:
# Project Settings → Rendering → Renderer
# Options: forward_plus, mobile, gl_compatibility

# RenderingDevice singleton for advanced GPU operations
func setup_forward_plus():
    # Full glow & SSAO
    get_viewport().use_taa = true
    get_viewport().scaling_3d_scale = 0.75  # FSR upscaling

func setup_mobile():
    # Limit lights for performance
    RenderingServer.directional_soft_shadow_filter_set_quality(
        RenderingServer.SHADOW_QUALITY_HARD)
    RenderingServer.positional_soft_shadow_filter_set_quality(
        RenderingServer.SHADOW_QUALITY_HARD)

# Query current renderer
func get_renderer_name() -> String:
    match RenderingServer.get_rendering_device().get_device_name():
        var name: return "Forward+ (" + name + ")"
        _: return "Compatibility"

Blueprint vs C++ Deep.exp: Blueprint: visual scripting, fast iteration, ideal for designers, slower at runtime (noding overhead). C++: performance-critical systems, engine extensions, complex algorithms. Best practice: C++ for base classes, Blueprint for gameplay.

Gameplay Ability System.exp: GAS: robust ability framework for skills, buffs, cooldowns. Core: UAbilitySystemComponent, UGameplayAbility, UGameplayEffect, UAttributeSet. Supports stacking, tags, replication. Used in AAA shooters and RPGs.

Enhanced Input.exp: UE5's Enhanced Input system replaces Action/Axis mappings. UInputAction with modifiers (deadzone, chorded) and triggers (pressed, held, double-tap). UInputMappingContext for context-sensitive bindings.

UMG Deep.exp: Unreal Motion Graphics (UMG) for HUD and menus. Widget Blueprint: Canvas Panel, Horizontal/Vertical Box, Overlay. BindWidget for C++ access. Animations (widget animations). Retainer Box for render caching.

Niagara VFX.exp: Niagara is UE's next-gen VFX system. Emitters with particle spawn/update/render stages. Modules for forces, noise, collisions. GPU particles for massive counts. Data interfaces for external data.

Chaos Physics.exp: UE5's Chaos Physics replaces PhysX. Destructible meshes with fracture modes (Voronoi, clustered). Cloth simulation. Vehicle dynamics with modular suspension/engine/transmission. Custom constraints.

Control Rig & IK.exp: Control Rig: procedural animation system within UE. Full-body IK with FABRIK solver. Aim constraints, multi-priority IK. Sequencer integration for cinematic rigging. Python scripting for automation.

GameplayTags & GameFeatures.exp: GameplayTags: hierarchical tag system (Aura.Fire.Major). Fast, editor-managed. Used for state, interaction rules, ability blocking. GameFeatures: modular content plugins enabling/disabling entire systems.

World Partition & OFPA.exp: UE5's World Partition system replaces level streaming. One File Per Actor (OFPA): each actor in its own package. World partition grid with streaming cells. Runtime loading/unloading based on player proximity. HLOD for distant meshes.

MetaSounds.exp: UE5's high-performance audio system. Node-based graph: oscillators, envelopes, filters, delays, convolution reverb. Parameter control via Blueprint/C++ at audio rate. Real-time synthesis replacing legacy Sound Cues.

Animation Blueprint & State Machines.exp: AnimBP: per-bone animation blending, state machines, blend spaces, aim offsets, layered blending. Cached pose for performance. Sub-anim instances for weapon/ability-specific animations. Root motion extraction.

Smart Objects & State Tree.exp: Smart Objects: interactive world objects with behavior definitions (sit, lean, open). State Tree: hierarchical behavior tree with state transitions, conditions, and tasks. Lightweight, data-driven AI for smart interactions.

PCG Framework.exp: Procedural Content Generation framework in UE5. Graph-based node system: terrain spawning, scatter, noise filtering, density mapping. Runtime and editor generation. Integration with World Partition and Landscape.

Mass Entity System & AI.exp: UE5's Mass framework: data-oriented ECS for thousands of AI agents. Fragments (data), processors (logic), archetypes (composition). LOD system (full simulation → LOD → off-screen). Crowd avoidance, movement, AI sensory.

DOTS/ECS Deep.exp: Data-Oriented Tech Stack: Entities (archetypes), Components (structs only), Systems (run on main thread or jobs). Burst-compiled. No garbage collection. Massive performance for thousands of entities.

URP & HDRP.exp: Universal Render Pipeline: cross-platform, performant, single-pass forward rendering. High-Definition RP: PC/console AAA quality, deferred rendering, ray tracing, volumetric lighting.

Addressables.exp: Unity's asset management system for loading/unloading assets at runtime. Async loading with async/await or callbacks. Remote content delivery (asset bundles from cloud). Dependency management and reference counting.

Input System.exp: Unity's new Input System: action-based, device-agnostic. InputActionAssets for visual editing. C# events or generated wrapper code. Callbacks, value processors, interactions (hold, tap, multi-tap).

UI Toolkit.exp: UI Toolkit (UIE): web-style UI with USS (CSS-like styling) and UXML (XML-based layout). Runtime UI for games, Editor UI for tools. Data binding, event system, dynamic list views.
UI Toolkit.code:
<ui:UXML xmlns:ui="UnityEngine.UIElements">
  <ui:VisualElement class="hud-container">
    <ui:Label text="Score: 0" name="ScoreLabel" class="score-text" />
    <ui:ProgressBar name="HealthBar" low-value="0" high-value="100" value="100" />
    <ui:Button text="Pause" name="PauseButton" />
  </ui:VisualElement>
</ui:UXML>

public class HUDController {
    private Label scoreLabel;
    public HUDController(VisualElement root) {
        scoreLabel = root.Q<Label>("ScoreLabel");
        root.Q<Button>("PauseButton").clicked += () => Time.timeScale = 0;
    }

}

Cinemachine & Timeline.exp: Cinemachine: intelligent camera system—virtual cameras, blends, noise (shaking), dolly tracks, 3rd-person follow, aiming dead zones. Timeline: cinematic sequence editor for cutscenes, camera cuts, animation tracks.

Burst Compiler & Jobs System.exp: Burst: high-performance LLVM-based compiler that translates C# to highly optimized native code. Unity Jobs System: safe multithreading with JobHandle and dependency management. ParallelFor jobs.

Profiling & Optimization.exp: Profiler window: CPU/GPU/Rendering/Memory usage. Deep Profiler traces every call. Memory Profiler for leak detection. Frame Debugger shows draw calls. Optimization: reduce draw calls, LODs, occlusion culling, object pooling.

Scriptable Objects Deep.exp: ScriptableObjects as data containers: avoid MonoBehaviour overhead, enable asset-based architecture. Use for game events, item definitions, dialogue trees, level configs. Create asset at runtime with CreateInstance. Custom editors for inspector polish.

Unity Gaming Services.exp: UGS: Unity's cloud platform—Authentication, Cloud Save, Cloud Code, Lobby, Relay (P2P), Economy, Analytics. Unity Gaming Services SDK. Cross-platform player identity and persistence without custom backend.

Scene Management & Multi-Scene.exp: LoadSceneMode.Additive for multi-scene workflows (persistent managers, UI layer, gameplay levels). SceneManager events (sceneLoaded, activeSceneChanged). Addressables scene loading. DontDestroyOnLoad pattern. Editor tooling for multi-scene editing.

Custom Editor Tools.exp: Unity Editor extending: CustomEditor, PropertyDrawer, EditorWindow, ScriptableWizard, Gizmos, MenuItem. IMGUI vs UI Toolkit for editor UI. SerializedObject/SerializedProperty introspection. Scene GUI for in-world editing handles.

NavMesh & AI Navigation.exp: Unity AI Navigation: NavMesh baking, NavMeshAgent pathfinding, OffMeshLinks for gaps/jumps, NavMeshObstacle for dynamic obstacles. Agent avoidance (RVOS). NavMeshSurface, NavMeshLink, NavMeshModifier components.

VFX Graph.exp: Unity Visual Effect Graph: GPU-accelerated particle systems, node-based graph editor. Event system, exposed properties for runtime control. Capacities (particle limits). Integration with Shader Graph for custom blocks and outputs.

GCP Account & Projects.exp: Create a GCP account at console.cloud.google.com. Free tier: $300 credit for 90 days + 20+ always-free services (Cloud Run 2M req/mo, Firestore 1GB, BigQuery 1TB/mo, Cloud Functions 2M invocations/mo). Projects organize all GCP resources — every resource belongs to one project. Project ID (globally unique, immutable), Project Name (human-readable), Project Number (auto-assigned). Folders group projects hierarchically under an Organization node. Resource Manager manages IAM at project/folder/org level. Cloud Shell is browser-based terminal with gcloud, kubectl, and docker pre-installed.
GCP Account & Projects.code:

# curl https://sdk.cloud.google.com | bash

gcloud init

# List projects
gcloud projects list

# Create project
gcloud projects create my-project-123 --name="My Project"

# Set project
gcloud config set project my-project-123

# List regions
gcloud compute regions list

# Cloud Shell: always free, 5GB home dir
# gcloud, kubectl, docker, python, node, java pre-installed
# Opens via console.cloud.google.com or `gcloud cloud-shell ssh`

GCP Regions & Zones.exp: GCP has 40+ regions, 120+ zones worldwide. Zones are isolated within regions (one zone failure doesn't affect others). Multi-region: us, eu, asia (for Spanner, Cloud Storage). Region picker: choose nearest to users + cheapest. Some regions are lower CO2 (carbon-neutral since 2007, 100% renewable energy matching since 2017). Premium Tier routes traffic over Google's network (high performance, low latency). Standard Tier routes over public internet (lower cost).

gcloud compute zones list --filter=region:us-central1

# Check which services are available in a region

# us-east1: South Carolina

GCP IAM Deep.exp: IAM on GCP: Who (principal) can do What (role) on Which (resource). Principals: Google Account, Service Account, Google Group, Workspace Domain, Cloud Identity domain. Roles: Basic (Owner/Editor/Viewer — too broad), Predefined (fine-grained, e.g., roles/storage.objectViewer), Custom (your own). Service Accounts are identities for VMs, Cloud Functions, GKE pods (no passwords). Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads (AWS/Azure/on-prem) impersonate service accounts. Policy bindings at any level: organization, folder, project, resource. IAM Conditions add context (resource tags, access time, IP range).
GCP IAM Deep.code:
# List IAM policies
gcloud projects get-iam-policy my-project

# Add IAM binding
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project \
  --member user:alice@example.com \
  --role roles/storage.objectViewer

# Create service account
gcloud iam service-accounts create my-sa --display-name "My Service Account"

# Create and download key
gcloud iam service-accounts keys create my-sa-key.json \
  --iam-account my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Workload Identity Federation (AWS)
# gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create my-pool
# gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws my-provider ...

Compute Engine (GCE).exp: Compute Engine is GCP's IaaS VMs. Machine families: General-purpose (E2, N2, N2D, C3), Compute-optimized (C2, C2D, C3), Memory-optimized (M1, M2, M3), Accelerator (A2, G2, with GPUs). Sole-tenant nodes for dedicated hardware. Preemptible VMs (up to 91% off, max 24h, no SLA) and Spot VMs (no max runtime, preempted when needed). Committed use discounts (1yr/3yr, up to 57% off). Instance templates for creating identical VMs. Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) autoscale, autoheal, and rolling update. Shielded VMs (secure boot, vTPM, integrity monitoring) for security.
Compute Engine (GCE).code:
# Create VM
gcloud compute instances create my-vm \
  --zone us-central1-a \

Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).exp: GKE is managed Kubernetes. Modes: Standard (pay for nodes) and Autopilot (pay per pod, no node management). Features: automatic upgrades and repair, cluster autoscaler, workload identity (GCP IAM for pods), Config Connector (Kubernetes CRDs for GCP resources), Cloud Service Mesh (Istio), GKE Sandbox (gVisor), multi-cluster ingress, Binary Authorization, Artifact Registry. Cloud Run.exp: Cloud Run is serverless containers: deploy any container, auto-scale to zero, pay per request + CPU/memory during request. Request-based scaling (KPA, Knative). Concurrency: one container handles multiple requests in parallel (up to 250). CPU allocation: only during request (default, cheaper) or always (background work). Ingress controls traffic sources. Cloud Run for Anthos runs on GKE for hybrid. Revision-based with traffic splitting (canary deployments). Max request timeout: 60 min (3600s). Max container instance: 60 concurrent requests. Mount Cloud Storage via FUSE. VPC connectors for private networking.
Cloud Run.code:
# Deploy container to Cloud Run

  --image gcr.io/my-project/my-image:latest \
  --region us-central1 \
  --platform managed \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --memory 512Mi \
  --cpu 1 \
  --min-instances 0 \
  --max-instances 10 \
  --concurrency 80 \
  --timeout 300 \
  --set-env-vars "NODE_ENV=production,DB_URL=postgresql://..."

# Traffic split (canary)
gcloud run services update-traffic my-service \
  --to-revisions my-service-00001=90,my-service-00002=10

# Deploy from source (buildpacks, no Dockerfile)
gcloud run deploy my-service --source . --region us-central1

Languages: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, PHP. Eventarc allows filtering by attribute. Cloud Functions (2nd gen) supports longer timeouts, more memory, and concurrency. App Engine.exp: App Engine is PaaS: just write code, GCP handles everything. Standard environment: sandboxed (faster, cheaper). Flexible environment: Docker-based, supports any runtime. Services: can have multiple services (default, api, worker). Versions: deploy multiple versions, traffic splitting. Cron jobs via cron.yaml. Task queues for async processing. Search, Memcache, Mail APIs. No VPC in Standard — use Serverless VPC Access. Ideal for web apps and REST APIs with variable traffic.

Object versioning keeps history. Object Lifecycle Management transitions/deletes objects. Retention policies (WORM) via Bucket Lock. Signed URLs for temporary access (no authentication required). Signed Policy Documents for uploads. Pub/Sub notifications on object changes. Requester Pays shifts cost to requestor. gsutil CLI for full management. Transfer Service imports from S3, Azure, HTTP, or on-prem.

BigQuery.exp: BigQuery is serverless data warehouse (petabyte-scale). Columnar storage, separation of compute and storage. SQL standard (no need to learn new query language). Slot-based pricing: on-demand ($5/TB processed) or flat-rate (slots). Clustering orders data within partitions. Partitioning divides table by date/range. BI Engine for sub-second queries on dashboards. BigQuery ML trains models using SQL (linear regression, XGBoost, deep learning). Authorized views share specific data. External tables query data in Cloud Storage, Sheets, Bigtable. Max query size: unlimited. Streaming insert with real-time analytics.

Cloud SQL.exp: Cloud SQL is managed PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server. Automated backups, point-in-time recovery, failover (regional HA), read replicas (including cross-region). Cloud SQL Proxy for secure IAM-based auth. Up to 30TB storage, 96 vCPUs, 624GB RAM. Flags configure DB parameters. Private IP via VPC. Maintenance windows for updates. Database Migration Service for migrations from on-prem or other clouds. Cloud SQL Insights provides query performance analytics. Integration with Vertex AI enables in-database ML predictions.

Cloud Spanner.exp: Spanner is globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database. SQL + ACID transactions at global scale. Horizontal scaling via splits (auto-sharding). Interleaved tables for parent-child row locality. TrueTime globally synchronizes clocks. Commit timestamps for MVCC. Multi-region configurations (e.g., nam3: US, 3 regions, 5 replicas). Compute capacity measured in nodes (2-2000+ nodes) or processing units (100-1000s PUs). Key features: strongly consistent global reads, secondary indexes, foreign keys, array types, generated columns. Best for globally scaled financial apps, games, supply chain.
Cloud Spanner.code:
# Create Spanner instance
gcloud spanner instances create my-instance \
  --config regional-us-central1 \
  --description "Production instance" \
  --processing-units 100

# Create database
gcloud spanner databases create my-db --instance my-instance

# DDL
gcloud spanner databases ddl update my-db --instance my-instance --ddl='
  CREATE TABLE Users (
    UserId INT64 NOT NULL,
    Name STRING(100) NOT NULL,
    Email STRING(255) NOT NULL,
    CreatedAt TIMESTAMP NOT NULL OPTIONS (allow_commit_timestamp=true),
  ) PRIMARY KEY (UserId);

  CREATE TABLE Orders (
    OrderId INT64 NOT NULL,
    UserId INT64 NOT NULL,
    Total NUMERIC NOT NULL,
    CreatedAt TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (UserId) REFERENCES Users(UserId)
  ) PRIMARY KEY (OrderId),
    INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Users ON DELETE CASCADE;
'

# Query
gcloud spanner databases execute-sql my-db --instance my-instance \
  --sql='SELECT u.Name, COUNT(o.OrderId) as OrderCount
    FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Orders o ON u.UserId = o.UserId
    GROUP BY u.UserId, u.Name'

Firestore & Bigtable.exp: Firestore is NoSQL document DB for mobile/web apps. Real-time listeners, offline support (IndexedDB cache), strong consistency. Collections contain documents (1MB max). Subcollections for nested data. Composite indexes for complex queries. Security Rules control access. Multi-region replication. Bigtable is wide-column NoSQL for large-scale analytics and HBase workloads. Sub-10ms latency, millions of ops/sec. Node-based clusters (SSD or HDD). Native HBase compatibility. Ideal for time-series, ad-tech, IoT, ML feature stores. Column families for access locality.

VPC & Networking.exp: GCP VPC is global (spans regions). Subnets are regional, can span zones. Firewall rules (allow/deny, ingress/egress, target tags). Cloud NAT for private instances to reach internet. Cloud Router dynamically routes between VPC and on-prem via BGP. VPC Peering and Shared VPC for multi-project networking. Private Google Access lets VMs access Google APIs via internal IP. Packet Mirroring sends traffic to security appliances. Network Service Tiers: Premium vs Standard. Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer for private traffic. Cloud Armor for WAF and DDoS protection.

Cloud Load Balancing.exp: GCP Load Balancing is globally distributed, single anycast IP. Types: Global HTTP(S) LB (L7, cross-region), Global SSL Proxy (non-HTTP HTTPS, L4), Global TCP Proxy (TCP, L4), Regional Internal LB (ILB, L4), Regional External (L4, for specific region). Backend services route to instance groups, serverless NEGs (Cloud Run, Functions), or zonal NEGs. Health checks: HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, SSL. Cloud CDN caches responses at edge. Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) controls access based on identity and context. Cloud Armor rules block or throttle traffic.

Organization Policy Service: constraints on resources at org/folder/project level (e.g., disable public IPs, restrict regions). Cloud KMS: key management, HSM option, key rotation, CMEK for customer-managed encryption keys. Secret Manager: store API keys, passwords, certificates. Binary Authorization: enforce signed container images. VPC Service Controls: define security perimeters around Google-managed services. Cloud Armor & DDoS Protection.exp: Google Cloud Armor provides WAF and DDoS protection. WAF rules: pre-configured rules (SQLi, XSS, LFI, RFI, RCE, scanners, protocol attacks), rate limiting, IP blacklist/whitelist, geo-based access control, custom expressions (CEL — Common Expression Language). Cloud Armor Managed Protection Plus adds L7 DDoS, bill protection, and DDoS response team. Cloud IDS (intrusion detection) monitors east-west traffic. Cloud Pub/Sub.exp: Pub/Sub is fully managed async messaging. Topics (channels) and Subscriptions (pull, push, or BigQuery). At-least-once delivery. Message retention up to 7 days. Cloud Composer & Workflows.exp: Cloud Composer is managed Apache Airflow. DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) define workflows as Python files. Operators for GCP services (BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, Kubernetes). Airflow Web UI for monitoring, triggers, logs. Scheduled triggers (cron) and event-based (Pub/Sub sensors). Works with any Airflow operator via KubernetesPodOperator. Workflows is serverless workflow orchestration (low-code YAML, parallel branches, subworkflows, HTTP calls, service account auth, 1yr execution timeout, event arc triggers). Cheaper and simpler than Composer for linear workflows.

# Workflows YAML
main:
  params: [event]
  steps:
  - validate:
      call: sys.log
      args:
        severity: INFO
        text: ${event}
  - classify:
      call: http.post
      args:
        url: https://ml-service-xxx-uc.a.run.app/classify
        body: ${event.body}
      result: category
  - switch:
      switch:
        - condition: ${category.prediction == 'fraud'}
          next: sendAlert
      next: processOrder
  - processOrder:
      call: googleapis.bigquery.query
      args:
        projectId: my-project
        sql: "INSERT INTO orders (data) VALUES (@data)"
        parameters:
          data: ${event.body}
  - sendAlert:
      call: http.post
      args:
        url: https://hooks.slack.com/...
        body: { text: "Alert: ${event.body}" }
    next: processOrder

# Deploy

Cloud Build & CI/CD.exp: Cloud Build is a fully managed CI/CD platform. Build triggers auto-start builds on git push (Cloud Source Repos, GitHub, Bitbucket). cloudbuild.yaml defines build steps as containers. Steps run sequentially in isolated Docker containers. Substitutions: built-in ($PROJECT_ID, $BUILD_ID, $BRANCH_NAME, $SHORT_SHA) and custom. Artifacts can be pushed to Artifact Registry or Cloud Storage. Cloud Build supports Kaniko caching for faster Docker builds. Approvals for production deployments. Common mistake: running all steps sequentially instead of parallelizing independent tasks. Use step timeouts to prevent hung builds.

  entrypoint: gcloud
  args: ['run', 'deploy', 'my-service', '--image', 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/my-repo/my-app:$SHORT_SHA', '--region', 'us-central1']

  machineType: 'E2_HIGHCPU_8'
  logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY

timeout: '1800s'
substitutions:

# Build trigger creation
gcloud builds triggers create github \
  --name my-trigger \
  --repo-name my-repo --repo-owner my-org --branch-pattern ^main$ \
  --build-config cloudbuild.yaml \
  --substitutions _ENV=production

Pub/Sub.exp: Pub/Sub is GCP's fully managed async messaging. Topics are named channels. Subscriptions: pull (consumer pulls messages), push (Pub/Sub sends to HTTP endpoint), BigQuery (direct to table), Cloud Storage (object writes). At-least-once delivery — consumers must handle duplicates. Exactly-once processing available via subscriber-side deduplication (message ID tracking). Dead-letter topics capture poison messages after maxDeliveryAttempts. Filtering by message attributes reduces irrelevant deliveries. Ordering keys maintain message order within a partition. Schema registry validates message structure. Seek to timestamp replays messages. Common mistake: not setting ackDeadline high enough for processing time. Use flow control to limit outstanding messages.
Pub/Sub.code:
# Create topic
gcloud pubsub topics create my-topic

# Create pull subscription with dead-letter
gcloud pubsub subscriptions create my-sub --topic my-topic \
  --ack-deadline 60 \
  --message-retention-duration 7d \
  --max-delivery-attempts 5 \
  --dead-letter-topic my-dlq

# Create push subscription (to Cloud Run)
gcloud pubsub subscriptions create my-push-sub --topic my-topic \
  --push-endpoint https://my-service-xxx-uc.a.run.app/webhook \
  --push-auth-service-account my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --min-retry-delay 10s --max-retry-delay 600s

# Create BigQuery subscription (direct to table)
gcloud pubsub subscriptions create my-bq-sub --topic my-topic \
  --bigquery-table my-project:my_dataset.my_table

# Publish with ordering key
gcloud pubsub topics publish my-topic --message "Order 123" --ordering-key "user-456"

# Python subscriber with flow control
# from google.cloud import pubsub_v1
# subscriber = pubsub_v1.SubscriberClient()
# subscription_path = subscriber.subscription_path('my-project', 'my-sub')
# flow_control = pubsub_v1.types.FlowControl(max_messages=100)
# future = subscriber.subscribe(subscription_path, callback=callback, flow_control=flow_control)

# Seek to timestamp (replay messages)
# gcloud pubsub subscriptions seek my-sub --time "2026-01-15T00:00:00Z"

Cloud Run Deep Dive.exp: Cloud Run is serverless containers with auto-scaling to zero. Revisions track deployments — each deploy creates a new revision. Traffic splitting: send % of traffic to specific revision (canary deployments, rollbacks). Min instances (0-~1000): 0 means scale to zero (cost-effective), >0 means keep instances warm (reduces cold starts). Max instances (default 100) caps concurrent instance count. Concurrency: how many requests one container handles simultaneously (default 80, max 250). VPC connector enables access to private VPC resources (Cloud SQL, Memorystore) without public IP. CPU allocation: only during request (default, cheaper) or always (needed for background threads). Cloud Run jobs for batch workloads. Common mistake: setting min instances too high for variable traffic wastes money. Use CPU always for apps with background processing.
Cloud Run Deep Dive.code:
# Deploy with advanced config
gcloud run deploy my-service --source . --region us-central1 \
  --platform managed \
  --memory 1Gi \
  --cpu 2 \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --max-instances 25 \
  --concurrency 80 \
  --timeout 300 \
  --cpu-boost \
  --set-env-vars "DB_URL=postgresql://..." \
  --set-secrets "API_KEY=my-secret:latest" \
  --service-account my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --vpc-connector my-vpc-connector \
  --egress-settings all \
  --allow-unauthenticated

# Traffic splitting (canary: 10% to new revision)
gcloud run services update-traffic my-service \
  --to-revisions my-service-00001=90,my-service-00002=10

# Rollback to previous revision
gcloud run services update-traffic my-service --to-revisions my-service-00001=100

# Create VPC connector for private networking
# gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors create my-vpc-connector \
#   --region us-central1 --network my-vpc --range 10.8.0.0/28

# Scheduled Cloud Run job
gcloud run jobs create my-job --image my-image --region us-central1 --task-count 10 --max-retries 3
# gcloud scheduler jobs create http my-schedule --schedule "0 * * * *" --uri https://us-central1-run.googleapis.com/... \
#   --oauth-service-account-email my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Dockerfile optimization
# FROM node:20-alpine
# WORKDIR /app
# COPY package*.json ./
# RUN npm ci --only=production
# COPY . .
# CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Secret Manager.exp: Secret Manager stores API keys, passwords, certificates, and other sensitive data. Secrets contain versions — each version stores the secret value. Access via IAM roles: Secret Manager Admin, Secret Manager Viewer, Secret Manager Secret Accessor. Automatic rotation: use Eventarc + Cloud Functions or Pub/Sub + Cloud Run. Replication: automatic (synced to multiple regions) or user-managed (choose regions). Common mistake: not enabling automatic replication for multi-region apps — secrets may not be available in all regions. Use CMEK (customer-managed encryption keys) for compliance. Version aliases: latest always points to the newest version. Integration with Cloud Run, GKE, Compute Engine, Cloud Functions.
Secret Manager.code:
# Create secret
printf "my-password" | gcloud secrets create my-secret --data-file=- \
  --replication-policy automatic \
  --labels env=production,team=backend

# Add new version
printf "new-password" | gcloud secrets versions add my-secret --data-file=-

# Access secret
# gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret my-secret

# Access specific version
gcloud secrets versions access 2 --secret my-secret

# Grant access to service account
gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding my-secret \
  --member serviceAccount:my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor

# Disable/destroy version
gcloud secrets versions disable 1 --secret my-secret
gcloud secrets versions destroy 1 --secret my-secret

# Set up rotation with Cloud Functions (Eventarc trigger)
# gcloud functions deploy rotate-secret --gen2 --runtime nodejs20 \
#   --trigger-event google.cloud.secretmanager.secret.v1.rotate \
#   --trigger-resource projects/my-project/secrets/my-secret

# IAM: only grant Secret Accessor at secret level, not project level
# Prefer user-managed replication for compliance:
# gcloud secrets create my-secret --data-file=- \
#   --replication-policy user-managed \
#   --locations us-east1,us-west1

Cloud Deploy.exp: Cloud Deploy automates delivery to Cloud Run, GKE, and Anthos. Delivery pipelines define the deployment process. Targets represent environments (dev, staging, prod). Promotion strategies: automatic (promote to next target on success) or manual (require approval). Rollbacks can be automatic on failure or manual. Skaffold is the underlying engine — skaffold.yaml defines the app, manifests, and deployment strategy. Canary deployment: incremental traffic shifting (e.g., 25%, 50%, 100%). Verification phases test the deployment (e.g., Cloud Build CI, custom checks). Common mistake: not testing canary deployments with real traffic. Use Cloud Deploy's built-in verification capabilities.
Cloud Deploy.code:
# clouddeploy.yaml
deliveryPipeline:
  serialPipeline:
    stages:
    - targetId: dev
    - targetId: staging
    - targetId: prod

targets:
- id: dev
  description: Development environment
  run:
    location: projects/my-project/locations/us-central1
- id: staging
  description: Staging environment
  run:
    location: projects/my-project/locations/us-central1
- id: prod
  description: Production environment
  requireApproval: true
  run:
    location: projects/my-project/locations/us-central1

# skaffold.yaml
apiVersion: skaffold/v4beta6
kind: Config
build:
  artifacts:
  - image: my-app
    docker:
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
manifests:
  rawYaml:
  - kubernetes/*.yaml
deploy:
  cloudrun:
    projectId: my-project
    region: us-central1

# Create delivery pipeline
gcloud deploy apply --file clouddeploy.yaml --region us-central1 --project my-project

# Create release
gcloud deploy releases create my-release --delivery-pipeline my-pipeline \
  --region us-central1 --build-artifacts ./build.json \
  --images my-app=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/my-repo/my-app:abc123

# Promote to next target (manual approval for prod)
# gcloud deploy targets update prod --description "Production" --require-approval
# gcloud deploy rollouts create my-rollout --release my-release --delivery-pipeline my-pipeline \
#   --region us-central1 --target-id prod

What is Git.exp: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code, enabling collaboration and history management. GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting Git repositories.
What is Git.code:
git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

git init & clone.exp: Create a new local repository with git init, or copy an existing remote repository using git clone with HTTPS or SSH URLs.
git init & clone.code:
git init my-project
cd my-project
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git

git add & commit.exp: Stage changes with git add and record them in history with git commit. The staging area lets you craft precise commits with meaningful messages.
git add & commit.code:
git add file.txt
git add .
git commit -m "Add initial setup"
git commit -am "Update readme"

git status & log.exp: git status shows the current state of working directory and staging area. git log displays commit history with various formatting options.
git status & log.code:
git status
git log
git log --oneline --graph --all
git log --oneline -5

git diff.exp: Compare changes between working directory, staging area, and commits. Use diff to review changes before staging or committing.
git diff.code:
git diff
git diff --staged
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
git diff branch1..branch2

Config levels.exp: Git config has three levels: system (all users), global (your account), local (per-repo). Each level overrides the one above. Use --list to view all settings.
Config levels.code:
git config --system --list
git config --global --list
git config --local --list
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
