Git Aliases.exp: Create shortcuts for frequent commands using git config alias. Aliases can chain commands and accept arguments for powerful shorthand.
Git Aliases.code:
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"
git config --global alias.unstage "reset HEAD --"
git lg  # uses alias

gitignore deep.exp: The .gitignore file uses glob patterns to exclude files. Negate patterns with !, ignore directories with trailing /, and use ** for nested patterns. Global gitignore applies to all repos.
gitignore deep.code:
# .gitignore examples
node_modules/
*.log
!important.log  # override negation
build/**/*.o
# Global gitignore:
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global

gitattributes.exp: The .gitattributes file controls how Git handles files per-path: line endings (CRLF vs LF), diff drivers, merge strategies, and language detection. Essential for cross-platform teams.
gitattributes.code:
# .gitattributes
*.js text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
*.pbxproj merge=union
*.txt linguist-language=Text

Hook basics.exp: Git hooks are scripts in .git/hooks/ that trigger on actions like commit, push, or merge. Client hooks (pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg) and server hooks (pre-receive, post-receive) enforce policies.
Hook basics.code:
# .git/hooks/pre-commit (make executable)
#!/bin/sh
npm run lint || exit 1

# Skip hooks temporarily:
git commit --no-verify
git push --no-verify

git worktree.exp: Worktrees let you check out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories. Share the same repository but maintain independent working directories and index files.
git worktree.code:
git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch
git worktree add -b feature/new ../feature-new main
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix

git branch.exp:
Branches are lightweight pointers to commits. List, create, rename, and delete branches to isolate work on features or fixes.

Visual:
main  ●──●──●──●
            \
feature      ●──●──●
Each branch is just a pointer. Creating a branch doesn't copy files — it just creates a new label.
git branch.code:
git branch
git branch feature-login
git branch -d old-branch
git branch -m old-name new-name

git checkout & switch.exp: Switch between branches using checkout or the newer switch command. checkout can also restore files from history.
git checkout & switch.code:
git checkout main
git switch feature-login
git checkout -b new-branch
git switch -c new-branch

git merge.exp:
Integrate changes from one branch into another. Fast-forward merges apply commits directly; three-way merges create a merge commit.

Merge vs Rebase:
MERGE (preserves history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
         \    /
feature   ●──●

REBASE (linear history)
main  ●──●──●──●──●
               /
feature       ●──●
Merge keeps ancestor relationships; rebase rewrites history for a clean line.
git merge.code:
git switch main
git merge feature-login
git merge --no-ff feature-login

Merge conflicts.exp: When parallel changes conflict, Git marks the file. Manually edit to resolve, then stage and commit the resolution.
Merge conflicts.code:
# Edit file to resolve <<<<<<< markers
git add resolved-file.txt
git merge --continue
git merge --abort

Merge strategies.exp: Git supports multiple merge strategies: recursive (default for two branches), octopus (multiple branches), ours (keep current), subtree. Pass -s to select strategy and -X for options.
Merge strategies.code:
git merge -s recursive -X theirs feature
git merge -s ours feature
git merge -s octopus branch1 branch2 branch3
git merge -X patience feature

Squash merge.exp: Squash merging combines all commits from a feature branch into a single new commit on the target branch. Cleaner history but loses granular commit details.
Squash merge.code:
# On GitHub: select "Squash and merge"
# Locally:
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "feat: add complete feature"

merge --squash vs squash merge.exp: merge --squash stages all changes without committing (you commit manually). GitHub's squash merge auto-commits. Both flatten history; use when granular commits lack individual value.
merge --squash vs squash merge.code:
# merge --squash (manual commit required):
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature
git commit -m "Add everything"

# What it does: apply all diffs, none of the commits

git merge-tree.exp: merge-tree computes the three-way merge result without touching the index or working tree. Useful for previewing merge outcomes or scripting merge logic.
git merge-tree.code:
git merge-tree main feature
git merge-tree --write-tree main feature
git merge-tree -z main feature | xargs -0

Orphan branches.exp: Orphan branches share no commit history with the current branch. Useful for things like gh-pages, documentation, or starting a project in a subdirectory with separate history.
Orphan branches.code:
git checkout --orphan gh-pages
git rm -rf .
git commit --allow-empty -m "Initial orphan commit"
git push origin gh-pages

git rebase.exp:
Reapply commits from one branch onto another tip for a linear history. Use interactive rebase to squash, reorder, or edit commits.

Visual:
BEFORE:
main    A──B──C
         \
feature  D──E

AFTER rebase:
main    A──B──C
               \
feature        D'──E'
D' and E' are NEW commits (different hashes). The original D/E still exist until garbage collected. Rebase rewrites history — never rebase shared/pushed branches.
git rebase.code:
git rebase main
git rebase -i HEAD~3
git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort

Interactive rebase (fixup, reword, drop,.exp: Interactive rebase opens an editor where you choose actions per commit: pick (keep), reword (edit message), edit (amend content), squash (combine with previous), fixup (squash discarding message), drop (delete), exec (run command).
Interactive rebase (fixup, reword, drop,.code:
git rebase -i HEAD~5
# Commands:
# pick abc123 Add feature
# fixup def456 WIP
# reword 789ghi Fix typo
# exec npm test  # run between commits
# drop 012jkl Broken commit
# squash 345mno Combine with previous

Rebase strategies.exp: Rebase offers strategies like --rebase-merges (preserve merge commits), --strategy recursive, --strategy-option theirs for conflict resolution, and --ignore-date to reset timestamps.
Rebase strategies.code:
git rebase --rebase-merges main
git rebase -s recursive -X theirs main
git rebase --ignore-date main
git rebase --committer-date-is-author-date main

rebase --onto.exp: rebase --onto replays commits onto a different base than upstream. Extract a feature branch from the wrong parent, or move a sub-branch to start from a different point.
rebase --onto.code:
# Move feature (based on wrong-branch) to main:
git rebase --onto main wrong-branch feature

# Cherry-pick a range onto a new base:
git rebase --onto main old-base feature

Autosquash.exp: Autosquash automatically arranges fixup! and squash! commits during interactive rebase. Combined with git commit --fixup/--squash, it streamlines fixup workflows.
Autosquash.code:
git commit --fixup abc123  # creates "fixup! original msg"
git commit --squash def456  # creates "squash! original msg"
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5

# One-liner fixup:
git commit --fixup abc123 && git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3

When NOT to rebase.exp: Never rebase commits that exist on a shared/public branch. Rebase rewrites history — anyone who pulled your old branch will have divergent history. The bane of rebasing is the force push that breaks collaborators.
When NOT to rebase.code:
# GOLDEN RULE:
# If others have pulled your branch, DO NOT rebase it.
# Instead: merge or revert.

# If you MUST rebase a pushed branch (solo dev):
git push --force-with-lease origin feature

# Safer alternative:
git merge main

git stash.exp: Temporarily save uncommitted changes to clean your working directory. Apply, drop, or list stashes to manage WIP context switches.
git stash.code:
git stash
git stash push -m "WIP login form"
git stash list
git stash pop
git stash drop stash@{0}

Stash deep.exp: Stashes are stored as commits on the reflog of refs/stash. --include-untracked or --all captures untracked/ignored files. Stash show inspects contents without applying.

Partial stash.exp: Stash only specific files or hunks with --patch for interactive selection. You can also stash individual pathspecs using git stash push -- <path> since Git 2.13.
Partial stash.code:
git stash push -m "Only src changes" -- src/
git stash push --patch -m "Selective hunks"
git stash push -m "Modules only" -- "*.py"
git stash --  # deprecated form

Stash across branches.exp: Stash is not branch-specific — you can stash on one branch and pop on another. Git auto-merges if changes apply cleanly; conflicts are handled manually.
Stash across branches.code:
git switch feature
git stash push -m "WIP on feature"
git switch main
git stash pop  # applies feature's WIP to main

# Check stash origin branch:
git stash list --format="%gd %gs (%an)"

Create branch from stash.exp: Turn a stash into a proper branch with git stash branch. This creates a new branch starting at the commit where the stash was originally created.
Create branch from stash.code:
git stash branch new-feature-branch stash@{0}

# Without specifying stash, uses the latest:
git stash branch new-feature-branch

# Equivalent to:
# git checkout -b new-feature-branch <stash-origin-commit>
# git stash pop

git reset & revert.exp: Reset moves branch pointers (soft, mixed, hard). Revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit, safe for shared history.
git reset & revert.code:
git reset HEAD~1
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git revert HEAD
git revert abc123

Reset modes deep (--soft, --mixed, --har.exp: --soft: moves HEAD only (changes stay staged). --mixed (default): moves HEAD and unstages changes (working tree unchanged). --hard: moves HEAD, unstages, and discards working tree changes. --hard is DESTRUCTIVE.
Reset modes deep (--soft, --mixed, --har.code:
# Starting with staged + unstaged changes:
git reset --soft HEAD~1  # commits undone, changes STAY staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1 # commits undone, changes UNSTAGED
git reset --hard HEAD~1  # commits gone, changes DISCARDED

# Safety: use --hard only if you're sure

git restore.exp: Restore is the modern alternative to checkout for restoring files. Restore working tree from index (default) or a specific commit. --staged un stages, --source <tree> picks from a commit.
git restore.code:
git restore file.txt          # discard working tree changes
git restore --staged file.txt  # unstage
git restore --source HEAD~2 file.txt  # restore from old version
git restore -SW .  # unstage AND discard all changes

git switch.exp: Switch is the modern alternative to checkout for branch operations. Cleaner semantics: switch branches, detach with --detach, create with -c, and return to previous with @{-1}.
git switch.code:
git switch main
git switch -c new-feature
git switch --detach HEAD~3
git switch -  # previous branch
git switch -c bug-fix @{-1}

Reflog deep.exp: The reflog is Git's safety net — it records every HEAD movement including resets, rebases, and merges. Entries expire in 90 days (30 for unreachable). Use it to recover from almost any mistake.
Reflog deep.code:
git reflog                         # view history
git reflog show main               # branch-specific reflog
git reflog --date=iso              # with timestamps
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}          # go back to earlier state
git checkout main@{one.week.ago}   # time travel

# Expiry config:
git config gc.reflogExpire 180.days

Orphan commits.exp: Orphan commits have no parent (root commits). The first commit in a repo is always an orphan. Create new root commits for independent history lines like gh-pages or separate documentation.
Orphan commits.code:
# First commit = orphan by definition
git log --all --max-parents=0 HEAD  # find root commits

# Create an orphan branch:
git checkout --orphan docs
git rm -rf .
git commit --allow-empty -m "root"

# Preserve orphan with git replace:
git replace --graft <orphan-hash> <parent-hash>

filter-branch vs filter-repo.exp: git filter-branch rewrites history en masse but is slow and dangerous. git filter-repo is the recommended replacement — faster, safer, and designed for large-scale history rewrites like purging secrets or splitting repos.
filter-branch vs filter-repo.code:
# OLD (filter-branch - deprecated):
git filter-branch --force --index-filter \
  'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch secrets.txt' \
  --prune-empty -- --all

# NEW (filter-repo - recommended):
git filter-repo --path secrets.txt --invert-paths
git filter-repo --path src/ --path tests/
git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M

# After filter-repo, push with:
git remote add origin <url>
git push --force --all

git remote.exp: Remotes are references to remote repository URLs. Manage connections to push, pull, and fetch from collaboration sources.
git remote.code:
git remote -v
git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote remove origin

git push & pull.exp:
Push local commits to a remote branch and pull (fetch + merge) remote changes into your current branch. Set upstream for convenience.

Push vs Pull vs Fetch:
LOCAL                     REMOTE
●──●──●  push ——————→  ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←————— pull   ●──●──●
●──●──●  ←—— fetch ——  ●──●──●
        (no merge)

PUSH  = upload + merge to remote
PULL  = fetch + merge (may conflict)
FETCH = download only (review first)
Always pull before push to avoid rejection. Use `git pull --rebase` for cleaner history.
git push & pull.code:
git push origin main
git push -u origin feature
git pull
git pull --rebase

git fetch.exp:
Download commits, files, and references from a remote without merging. Use fetch to review changes before integrating.

Fetch vs Pull:
FETCH: origin/main updated, main stays
main     ●──●──●──●
             \
origin/main  ●──●──●──●

PULL: origin/main updated AND merged
main     ●──●──●──●──●──●
                       (merge commit)
Fetch is safe — it never changes your working tree. Always fetch before push to check for remote changes.
git fetch.code:
git fetch origin
git fetch --all
git log origin/main
git diff main origin/main

Pull Requests.exp: PRs propose changes from a fork or branch for review before merging. Include descriptions, reviewers, and link to issues for context.
Pull Requests.code:
# Create a branch, push, then open PR on GitHub
git switch -b fix-bug
git push -u origin fix-bug
# Then open PR at github.com/user/repo/pulls

Pull request workflow.exp:
The full PR lifecycle: fork/clone → branch → commit → push → open PR → request reviewers → address feedback → update branch → merge. Draft PRs signal work-in-progress.

PR Lifecycle:
Fork → Clone → Branch → Commit → Push → PR (Draft) → 
  ↓
Request Review → Address Feedback → Update Branch →
  ↓
Approve → Merge (Squash/Rebase/Merge) → Delete Branch
Use draft PRs for early feedback. Update the branch with more commits or rebase — avoid force pushes on shared PR branches.
Pull request workflow.code:
# Full PR workflow:
git switch -c feat/new-button
git commit -m "Add new button"
git push -u origin feat/new-button
# Open PR via:
gh pr create --title "feat: add new button" --body "Closes #42"

# Update PR:
git push origin feat/new-button  # adds commits automatically

Code review.exp: Code review is the process of examining code changes before merging. Focus on correctness, style, design, and test coverage. Use inline comments, suggestion blocks, and review approval flows.
Code review.code:
# CLI review flow:
gh pr checkout 42
git diff main...HEAD

# Suggested changes:
# ```suggestion
# const newValue = 42;
# ```

# Approve:
gh pr review --approve --body "LGTM!"
gh pr review --request-changes --body "Fix edge case"

Merge queue.exp: Merge queues group PRs and test them together before merging to main. Prevents semver conflicts where individual PRs pass CI but fail when combined. Available on GitHub with merge queues beta.
Merge queue.code:
# .github/merge-queue.yml
merge_strategy:
  method: squash
  required_checks:
    - 'Tests (ubuntu-latest)'
    - 'Lint'

# PR comment to add to queue:
/queue

PR & Issue templates.exp: Templates standardize PR and issue creation with YAML frontmatter or Markdown forms. Use checkboxes, dropdowns, and text areas to gather consistent information.
PR & Issue templates.code:
# .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
---
name: Bug fix
about: Fix a bug
---

## Description
<!-- What does this PR fix? -->

## Testing
- [ ] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Manual QA

## Closes
Fixes #42

# .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml
name: Bug Report
description: File a bug report
body:
  - type: textarea
    attributes:
      label: Steps to reproduce

GH CLI deep.exp: The gh CLI provides full GitHub workflow from the terminal: create PRs, manage issues, run workflows, review code, and manage releases. Use gh extension for custom functionality.
GH CLI deep.code:
gh auth login
github repo create my-app --public --clone
github pr create --title "Feature" --body "Closes #12" --assignee @me
github pr review 42 --approve
github run list --workflow=test.yml
github release create v1.0.0 --notes "First release"
github issue list --label bug
github extension install gh-metrics

git cherry-pick.exp: Apply specific commits from one branch onto another. Useful for selective porting of changes without merging entire branches.
git cherry-pick.code:
git cherry-pick abc123
git cherry-pick abc123..def456
git cherry-pick --continue
git cherry-pick --abort

Sparse checkout.exp: Sparse checkout lets you work with only a subset of files in the working tree. Ideal for monorepos where you only need specific directories. Combined with cone mode for performance.
Sparse checkout.code:
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/user/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set apps/web packages/shared
git sparse-checkout add docs

# Without clone:
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set src/

Shallow & deep clone.exp: Shallow clones (--depth 1) fetch only the latest commits — fast for CI. Deep clones fetch full history. --depth=N fetches N commits. --shallow-since filters by date.
Shallow & deep clone.code:
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> fastest clone, no history

git clone --depth 5 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> last 5 commits

git clone --shallow-since="2024-01-01" https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> commits since date

# Unshallow later:
git fetch --unshallow

Partial clone.exp: Partial clones defer downloading blob data until needed. --filter=blob:none skips all blobs at clone time — files are fetched on checkout. --filter=tree:0 skips trees too. Dramatically reduces clone time.
Partial clone.code:
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> fast clone, 90% less data
# -> files downloaded on git checkout/restore

git clone --filter=tree:0 https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> even lighter: trees fetched on dir access

git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/user/repo.git
# -> metadata only

git bundle.exp: Bundle packs commits and refs into a single file for offline transport. Transfer via USB, email, or air-gapped networks. The receiver can pull or fetch from the bundle as if it were a remote.
git bundle.code:
# Create bundle:
git bundle create repo.bundle HEAD main
git bundle create update.bundle --since=2.weeks main

# Receive:
git clone repo.bundle dest-dir
git fetch update.bundle main

# Verify:
git bundle verify update.bundle
git bundle list-heads update.bundle

git archive.exp: Export a snapshot of the repository as a tar or zip archive without the .git directory. Perfect for distribution, deployments, or sharing code without history.
git archive.code:
git archive --format=zip HEAD > project.zip
git archive --format=tar HEAD | gzip > project.tar.gz
git archive --format=zip -o latest.zip main
git archive --prefix=project-v1.0/ HEAD | gzip > v1.0.tar.gz

git bisect run.exp: Bisect run automates git bisect by passing a script that exits 0 (good) or non-zero (bad). Git will binary-search the range and find the first bad commit automatically.
git bisect run.code:
# Manual:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0.0
git bisect run npm test

# Script approach:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0.0 --
git bisect run ./test-bug.sh

# test-bug.sh:
# #!/bin/bash
# npm run build && npm test

# Result: first commit where test fails

git blame & annotations.exp: git blame annotates each line with the commit, author, and date that last modified it. Useful for tracking when/why a change was made. -L limits to line range; -w ignores whitespace.
git blame & annotations.code:
git blame file.txt
git blame -L 10,30 file.txt
git blame -w -C -C file.txt  # detect moved lines
git log -p -S "search-term" -- file.txt  # search commit content

# Annotations via blame ignore revs:
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

git grep.exp: git grep searches files in any revision, not just working tree. Faster than system grep by limiting to tracked files. Supports regex, line numbers, file names, and context.
git grep.code:
git grep "TODO"
git grep -n "function" -- *.js
git grep -c "class" HEAD~5  # count matches at old revision
git grep --cached "TODO"     # search staged
git grep -e "import" --and -e "from"  # multi-pattern

Blob objects.exp: Blobs store file content identified by SHA-1 hash. The blob hash is deterministic — same content always produces the same hash (content-addressable). Blobs don't store filenames — that's the tree's job.
Blob objects.code:
echo "hello" | git hash-object --stdin -w
git hash-object -w file.txt
git cat-file -p <blob-hash>
git cat-file -t <blob-hash>  # prints "blob"

Tree objects.exp: Trees represent directory snapshots. A tree maps filenames → blob hashes (files) or sub-tree hashes (directories), plus permissions. Trees are also content-addressed by hash.
Tree objects.code:
git cat-file -p main^{tree}
git cat-file -p HEAD:src/
git ls-tree HEAD
git ls-tree -r HEAD  # recursive

# Create a tree manually:
git write-tree  # creates tree from current index

Commit objects.exp: A commit is a snapshot pointer containing: tree hash (root directory), parent commit hash(es), author/committer info, timestamp, and message. The commit hash is what you see in git log.
Commit objects.code:
git cat-file -p HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD  # prints "commit"

# Inspect commit structure:
# tree <root-tree-hash>
# parent <parent-commit-hash>
# author Name <email> timestamp
# committer Name <email> timestamp
#
# Commit message

git log --format=raw HEAD

Packfiles.exp: Git stores objects in two forms: loose (individual files in .git/objects/) and packed (efficient deltas in .git/objects/pack/). Packfiles compress objects using delta encoding — storing only differences between versions.
Packfiles.code:
git gc  # pack loose objects
git count-objects -v  # see loose vs packed
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/*.idx | head -30
git repack -ad  # repack everything
git prune  # remove unreachable loose objects

git gc.exp: Garbage collection packs loose objects into packfiles and prunes unreachable objects. Auto-runs on threshold (6700 loose objects). Manual gc optimizes repository size and performance.
git gc.code:
git gc  # auto mode
git gc --aggressive  # slower, better compression
git gc --prune=now   # remove all unreachable
git gc --auto        # only if needed

# Config:
git config gc.auto 5000
git config gc.aggressiveWindow 250

git fsck.exp: Filesystem check verifies repository integrity by scanning all objects and references. Detects dangling blobs, missing objects, and corruption. Run after hardware failures or suspicious behavior.
git fsck.code:
git fsck
git fsck --full     # check all objects
git fsck --lost-found  # recover dangling objects

git fsck --unreachable  # show unreachable

# Repair dangling objects:
git fsck --lost-found  # results in .git/lost-found/

git rev-parse.exp: rev-parse resolves any Git revision specifier to a SHA-1 hash. Parse branch names, tags, relative refs (HEAD~3), dates (@{yesterday}), or ranges. Essential for scripting and plumbing.
git rev-parse.code:
git rev-parse HEAD
git rev-parse main
git rev-parse HEAD~3
git rev-parse @{yesterday}
git rev-parse HEAD:src/index.js

git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD  # branch name
git rev-parse --show-toplevel    # repo root

git cat-file.exp: cat-file is the primary plumbing command to inspect Git objects. Pass type flag (-t), size (-s), pretty-print (-p), or check existence (-e). View any object by hash or revision.
git cat-file.code:
git cat-file -p HEAD       # pretty-print commit
git cat-file -p abc123     # print any object
git cat-file -t abc123     # blob | tree | commit
git cat-file -s abc123     # object size in bytes

git cat-file --batch-check < hashes.txt  # batch mode
git cat-file --batch-all-objects --unordered | head

Actions (CI/CD).exp: GitHub Actions automates workflows (test, build, deploy) triggered by events like push, PR, or schedule. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/.
Actions (CI/CD).code:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm install && npm test

Workflow syntax.exp: Workflow YAML defines triggers (on), jobs (parallel by default), steps (sequential), actions (reusable units), and expressions (${{ }}). Use if: conditionals, concurrency groups, and environment targets.
Workflow syntax.code:
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/**']
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      env:
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]

jobs:
  build:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    concurrency: ci-${{ github.ref }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Event: ${{ github.event_name }}"

Matrix builds.exp: Matrix strategies run the same job across multiple configurations (OS, version, environment). Use include to add variants, exclude to remove, and fail-fast to cancel all on failure.
Matrix builds.code:
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [18, 20, 22]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node: 20
            coverage: true
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node: 22
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm test
      - if: matrix.coverage
        run: npm run coverage

Reusable workflows.exp: Call a workflow from another workflow using the uses keyword with secrets and inputs. Reusable workflows reduce duplication across repos. They must be in a public repo or same org.
Reusable workflows.code:
# Caller workflow:
jobs:
  call-lint:
    uses: org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/lint.yml@v1
    with:
      node-version: 20
    secrets:
      token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

# Reusable workflow (lint.yml):
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        type: string
        required: true
    secrets:
      token:
        required: true
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run lint

Environment protection.exp: GitHub Environments add protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers, and deployment branch restrictions. Combined with secrets per-environment for secure deployments.
Environment protection.code:
# Create environment via UI: Settings > Environments

# Workflow using environments:
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://app.example.com
    steps:
      - run: deploy.sh
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PRODUCTION_API_KEY }}

# Protected: requires approval before deploy

Self-hosted runners.exp: Self-hosted runners run Actions on your own infrastructure. Register at repo/org/enterprise level. Use labels for routing. Ideal for custom hardware, internal networks, or cost savings at scale.
Self-hosted runners.code:
# Register a runner:
# Settings > Actions > Runners > Add runner
./config.sh --url https://github.com/user/repo --token ABC123
./run.sh

# Workflow targeting self-hosted:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]
    steps:
      - run: nvidia-smi

# Scale sets: use actions/actions-runner-controller on Kubernetes

OIDC.exp: OpenID Connect (OIDC) lets workflows authenticate to cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, HashiCorp) without storing long-lived secrets. Exchange a JWT token for temporary cloud credentials.
OIDC.code:
# AWS example:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456:role/GitHubActions
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-bucket

# Azure:
# - uses: Azure/login@v1
#   with:
#     client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
#     tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
#     allow-no-subscriptions: true

Issues & Projects.exp: GitHub Issues track bugs, features, and tasks. Projects organize issues into boards with columns for planning and tracking work.
Issues & Projects.code:
# Create via GitHub UI
github issue create --title "Bug" --body "Description"
github issue list
github issue view 42

GitHub Pages.exp: Host static websites directly from a repository. Configure source branch and folder in Settings, then access at username.github.io/repo.
GitHub Pages.code:
# Enable in Settings > Pages
# Build and deploy action:
# - uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
#   with:
#     github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
#     publish_dir: ./dist

Forks & Upstream.exp:
Fork a repository to contribute without direct write access. Sync your fork by adding the original repo as an upstream remote.

Fork + Upstream Flow:
UPSTREAM (original/repo)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ fork (copy on GitHub)
ORIGIN (your/repo on GitHub)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ clone
LOCAL (your machine)
  ●──●──●
    ↑ add upstream remote
  ●──●──●──●  (sync from upstream)
Use `origin` for your fork, `upstream` for the original. Send PRs from your fork back to upstream.
Forks & Upstream.code:
# Fork via GitHub UI, then:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/repo.git
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main
git push

Projects (Beta).exp: GitHub Projects provides spreadsheet-style project tracking with custom fields, views (table, board, roadmap), and automation. Link issues/PRs across repos in a single org-level project.
Projects (Beta).code:
# Create via UI: Projects > New project
# Or via GraphQL API:
gh project create owner --title "Sprint Q2" --template "Team planning"
gh project item-add owner 42 --repo owner/repo --issue 123

# Fields: Iteration, Single Select, Text, Number, Date, Tracks
# Automation: Status = "In Progress" when PR opened

Discussions.exp: GitHub Discussions provide a forum-style space for Q&A, ideas, and announcements — separate from the issue tracker. Useful for community engagement, RFCs, and collective decision-making.
Discussions.code:
# Create via GitHub UI: Discussions tab

# Categorize:
# - Q&A (mark accepted answer)
# - Ideas (convert to issue)
# - Announcements (locked)
# - General

# Link discussion in PR:
gh pr create --title "RFC: new API" --discussion 42

Codespaces.exp: GitHub Codespaces provides cloud-hosted development environments configured by a devcontainer.json file. Start, stop, and customize VSCode environments from any browser or VS Code.

Dependabot.exp: Dependabot automates dependency updates by scanning manifest files and opening PRs for out-of-date packages. Configure version strategies, schedule, and reviewers in dependabot.yml.
Dependabot.code:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
      day: "monday"
    versioning-strategy: increase
    open-pull-requests-limit: 10
    reviewers:
      - "team-maintainers"
    labels:
      - "dependencies"
  - package-ecosystem: "docker"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "monthly"

Secret scanning & code scanning.exp: Secret scanning detects exposed credentials (keys, tokens) in repos. Code scanning (CodeQL) finds vulnerabilities via static analysis. Both integrate into PR checks to prevent merging insecure code.
Secret scanning & code scanning.code:
# Enable: Settings > Security > Code security

# CodeQL workflow:
# .github/workflows/codeql.yml
name: CodeQL
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  analyze:
    uses: github/codeql-action/.github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml@v3

# Secret scanning is automatic on public repos.
# Custom patterns for private repos:
# Settings > Security > Secret scanning > Custom patterns

Branch protection rules.exp: Branch protection rules enforce workflows: require PRs, status checks, up-to-date branches, signed commits, or specific reviewers. Essential for main branch security and compliance.
Branch protection rules.code:
# Configure: Settings > Branches > Add rule
# Branch name pattern: main, release/*
# Protect matching branches:
#  ☑ Require a pull request before merging
#    ☑ Require approvals (1-6)
#  ☑ Require status checks
#    ☑ Require branches up-to-date
#  ☑ Require conversation resolution
#  ☑ Require signed commits
#  ☑ Require linear history
#  ☑ Allow force pushes (with restrictions)
#  ☑ Allow deletions

# Via API:
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection \
  --method PUT --input protection.json

GitLab CI.exp: GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, jobs, and runners. Supports Kubernetes integration, auto DevOps, and built-in container registry. Jobs run in isolated environments.
GitLab CI.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

test:
  stage: test
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm install
    - npm test
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml

build:
  stage: build
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
  script:
    - npm run build

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  environment: production
  script:
    - kubectl apply -f deploy/

BitBucket Pipelines.exp: BitBucket Pipelines uses bitbucket-pipelines.yml for CI/CD with built-in Docker support and deployment environments. Integrates with Jira for traceable deployments.
BitBucket Pipelines.code:
# bitbucket-pipelines.yml
image: node:20

pipelines:
  default:
    - step:
        name: Test
        caches:
          - node
        script:
          - npm install
          - npm test
  branches:
    main:
      - step:
          name: Deploy
          deployment: production
          script:
            - npm run build
            - pipe: atlassian/aws-s3-deploy:1.1.0
              variables:
                AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: $AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
                AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: $AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

Gerrit.exp: Gerrit is a code review system for Git that uses a push-to-review workflow. Changes are pushed to refs/for/<branch> and must be reviewed and +2'ed before submission. Common in large-scale enterprise projects.
Gerrit.code:
# Clone:
git clone ssh://user@gerrit:29418/project && scp -p gerrit:hooks/commit-msg .git/hooks/

# Push for review:
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main

# Patch sets (amend existing change):
git commit --amend
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main

# Review scores:
# -1/0/+1: Looks good (any reviewer)
# -2/+2: Approve (maintainer only)
# Submit: merge after approval

Git LFS.exp: Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces large files (binaries, assets, models) with text pointers in the repo while storing content on a remote server. Essential for game dev, ML, and design assets.
Git LFS.code:
git lfs track "*.psd"
git lfs track "*.zip"
git add .gitattributes  # stores LFS patterns
git lfs migrate import --include="*.psd" --everything

# Clone with LFS:
git lfs clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

# Check LFS:
git lfs ls-files
git lfs status

Git submodules.exp: Embed one repository inside another as a submodule. Pins a specific commit so the parent repo tracks exact dependency versions.
Git submodules.code:
git submodule add https://github.com/user/lib.git lib
git submodule update --init --recursive
git submodule foreach git pull
git submodule status

Submodules vs subtrees.exp: Submodules reference external repos as pointers; subtrees merge external code directly into your repo. Subtrees give you full control (no external dependency), submodules keep history separate. Choose subtrees for stability, submodules for active external development.
Submodules vs subtrees.code:
# Subtree add:
git subtree add --prefix lib/vendor https://github.com/user/lib.git main --squash

# Subtree pull:
git subtree pull --prefix lib/vendor https://github.com/user/lib.git main --squash

# Subtree push:
git subtree push --prefix lib/vendor origin vendor-branch

# Key difference:
# - Submodule: .gitmodules, commit pointer, needs --recursive clone
# - Subtree: files in your repo, no special clone needed

Monorepo strategies.exp: Monorepos store multiple projects in a single repository. Strategies: Nx/Turborepo for JS, Bazel for polyglot, Gradle for JVM, and Pants for Python. Tooling handles selective builds and tests.
Monorepo strategies.code:
# Directory structure:
# apps/
#   web/
#   mobile/
#   admin/
# packages/
#   shared-ui/
#   utils/
#   types/
# tools/
#   ci/
#   scripts/

# Nx affected builds:
nx affected:test --base=main

# GitHub Actions path filtering:
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'apps/web/**'
      - 'packages/shared-ui/**'

Gitignore.exp: The .gitignore file specifies intentionally untracked files (build artifacts, dependencies, env files) that Git should ignore.

Commit Messages.exp: Write clear, conventional commit messages. Use imperative mood, capitalize first word, and include scope/tag for automatic changelogs.
Commit Messages.code:
# Conventional Commits
feat: add user login page
fix: resolve null pointer on profile load
chore: update dependencies
docs: improve API documentation

Branch Strategies.exp: Common branching models: Git Flow (develop/release/hotfix), GitHub Flow (feature branches -> main), and trunk-based development for CI/CD.
Branch Strategies.code:
# GitHub Flow:
# main (production-ready)
# feature/* (short-lived feature branches)
# Fix/merge via PR

# Git Flow:
# main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*

Signing Commits.exp: Sign commits with GPG or SSH keys to verify authorship. GitHub marks signed commits as Verified for trust and authenticity.
Signing Commits.code:
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global user.signingkey KEY_ID
git commit -S -m "Signed commit"
git log --show-signature

Squashing Commits.exp: Combine multiple commits into one for cleaner history. Use squash during merge on GitHub or interactive rebase locally.
Squashing Commits.code:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
# Change 'pick' to 'squash' for commits to merge
git merge --squash feature-branch
git commit -m "Add complete feature"

Conventional commits.exp: Conventional Commits specification standardizes commit messages: type(scope): description. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert. Enables automatic versioning and changelog generation.
Conventional commits.code:
# Types:
# feat:     new feature (minor release)
# fix:      bug fix (patch release)
# BREAKING CHANGE: major release!
# chore:    maintenance
# docs:     documentation only
# refactor: code change without fix/feat
# perf:     performance improvement
# test:     adding/fixing tests
# ci:       CI/CD changes

feat(api): add user authentication endpoint
fix(ui): resolve button alignment on mobile

BREAKING CHANGE: removed deprecated v1 endpoints

# Tools: commitlint, standard-version, semantic-release

Semantic versioning with tags.exp: Semantic versioning (semver): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR = breaking changes, MINOR = features, PATCH = fixes. Tag releases with annotated tags and push them to trigger deployment workflows.
Semantic versioning with tags.code:
# Version bump examples:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"
git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Add user profiles (feature)"
git tag -a v1.1.1 -m "Fix login redirect (patch)"
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Rewrite API (breaking)"

# Push tags:
git push origin --tags

# Auto-tag with CI:
# GITHUB_REF will be refs/tags/v1.0.0
# Use semantic-release or similar for automation

Trivial merges.exp: Trivial merges (fast-forward only) keep linear history without merge commits. Use when feature branches have a single commit or no divergent history. Configure branch settings to require linear history.
Trivial merges.code:
# Fast-forward only:
git merge --ff-only feature-branch
# -> Fails if branch has diverged

# PR settings (GitHub):
# Require linear history = "Rebase and merge" only

# Config:
git config --global merge.ff only

# Team convention:
# - Single-commit branch: rebase + fast-forward
# - Multi-commit branch: squash merge

Clean history.exp: A clean Git history is readable, searchable, and bisectable. Guidelines: one logical change per commit, write descriptive messages, squash WIP/fixup commits, rebase before merging, avoid merge commits in feature branches.
Clean history.code:
# Before pushing, clean up:
git rebase -i HEAD~5
# - squash fixup! and WIP entries
# - reword unclear messages
# - drop broken commits

# Check bisect safety:
git bisect start HEAD v1.0
# Each commit should compile and pass tests

# .git-blame-ignore-revs for formatting commits:
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
# Add formatting commit hashes there

Code review checklist.exp: A systematic code review checklist covers: correctness (edge cases, error handling), security (input validation, auth), performance (N+1 queries, memory), style (project conventions), testing (coverage, meaningful tests), and documentation (API, README).
Code review checklist.code:
# Review checklist:
# [ ] Does the code work? (correctness)
# [ ] Are edge cases handled? (null, empty, errors)
# [ ] Is it secure? (injection, auth, secrets)
# [ ] Is it performant? (complexity, DB queries)
# [ ] Follows project conventions? (lint, style)
# [ ] Tests included and meaningful?
# [ ] Documentation updated? (README, API docs)
# [ ] No debugging code? (console.log, TODO)

# PR template checklist:
- [ ] I have added tests
- [ ] I have updated documentation
- [ ] My code follows project style

CI gates.exp: CI gates are automated checks that block merging if they fail. Common gates: lint, type check, unit tests, integration tests, build, security scan, coverage threshold. Combine with branch protection to enforce.
CI gates.code:
# .github/workflows/ci-gates.yml
name: CI Gates
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run lint
  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run typecheck
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run test -- --coverage
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm run build

What is Go.exp: Go is a compiled, statically-typed language designed for simplicity, concurrency, and fast execution. Built by Google for systems programming and microservices. Common mistake: assuming Go is like Java/C# — Go has no classes, no inheritance, no exceptions, and no generics (pre-1.18). Best practice: embrace Go's simplicity — prefer composition over inheritance, use explicit error returns instead of exceptions, and leverage goroutines for concurrency.

Go Syntax.exp: Go syntax emphasizes clarity and brevity. Uses curly braces for blocks and semicolons are optional. Comments use // or /* */. Common mistake: placing the opening brace on a new line — Go requires the opening brace on the same line as the declaration (enforced by gofmt). Best practice: run gofmt or go fmt on all code to enforce canonical formatting; use meaningful names even for short variables.

Your First Program.exp: Every Go program starts with a package declaration and a main() function for executables. The package must be 'main' for a runnable binary. Common mistake: using 'print' or 'println' for serious output — prefer fmt.Println for formatted output to stdout. Best practice: structure all real programs with package main, a main() function, and use imports for standard library packages rather than built-in print.

Go Playground.exp: The Go Playground (go.dev/play) lets you write, run, and share Go code in your browser. Great for experimentation and sharing bug repros.

go run vs go build.exp: go run compiles and runs a program without producing a binary. go build produces a standalone executable in the current directory.
go run vs go build.code:
# Run directly (no binary)
go run main.go

# Build an executable
# Produces ./program (or .exe on Windows)
go build -o program main.go

GOPATH & Module Basics.exp: GOPATH was the original workspace location. Modern Go uses modules (go mod) instead. GOPATH is still used for global binary installs via go install.
GOPATH & Module Basics.code:
export GOPATH=$HOME/go
# Install a tool globally
go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@latest
# Installed binaries go to $GOPATH/bin

Variable Declaration.exp: Declare variables using var, const, or short declaration (:=). Types can be explicit or inferred. Common mistake: using := outside a function — it only works inside function bodies; package-level declarations require var or const. Best practice: use := for local variables with clear initialization; use var for zero-value declarations (var x int); use const for compile-time constants. Scope and shadowing: inner scopes can redeclare a name from an outer scope — the inner declaration shadows the outer one. Always check that you haven't accidentally shadowed a package-level variable inside a function using :=.

Primitive Types.exp: Go includes bool, string, int, uint, float32, float64, complex64, and more. Integer types have fixed sizes (int8, int16, int32, int64). Rune is an alias for int32 representing a Unicode code point. Complex numbers (complex64, complex128) are first-class with real+imag syntax. String literals come in two forms: raw (backtick-quoted, no escapes) and interpreted (double-quoted, supports \n, \t, etc.). Common mistake: confusing int and int64 — int is platform-dependent (32 or 64 bit); int64 is always 64 bit. Use int unless you need a specific size.
Primitive Types.code:
var active bool = true
var score int64 = 1000
var ratio float32 = 2.5
var c complex128 = 1 + 2i

// Rune — Unicode code point
type rune = int32
var r rune = '\u0041' // 'A'
var han rune = '世'    // Chinese character

// Raw vs interpreted strings
raw := `hello\nworld`   // literal backslash-n
interp := "hello\nworld" // actual newline

Type Conversion.exp: Explicitly convert between compatible types using T(value) syntax. Go does NOT do implicit type conversion.

Constants.exp: Constants are immutable values that must be known at compile time. Use const keyword with iota for enumerated constants. iota resets to 0 in each const block and increments by 1 for each line. Common mistake: thinking constants can be computed at runtime — they must be determinable at compile time, so function calls or runtime expressions don't work. Best practice: use iota for sequential numeric enums; use typed constants (const X type = val) for type safety; use untyped constants for flexibility in expressions.

Zero Values.exp: Variables declared without an explicit initial value are assigned a zero value: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for strings, nil for pointers/slices/maps/channels/interfaces.
Zero Values.code:
var i int     // 0
var f float64 // 0
var b bool    // false
var s string  // ""
var p *int    // nil
fmt.Println(i, f, b, s, p)

Short Declaration (:=).exp: Use := inside functions for type-inferred variable declaration and assignment. Cannot use at package level. At least one variable on left must be new.
Short Declaration (:=).code:
name := "Alice"
age := 30
// Re-declaration with new variable
age, year := 31, 2026 // age reassigned, year new

Type Inference.exp: Go infers types from the right-hand side of := or var declarations. Untyped numeric constants get default types (int, float64, complex128) when needed.
Type Inference.code:
x := 42       // int
pi := 3.14    // float64
c := 1 + 2i   // complex128

var y float64 = 3
z := y         // z is float64 (inferred from y)

Arithmetic Operators.exp: Standard math: +, -, *, /, %. Go supports ++ and -- but only as statements, not expressions.
Arithmetic Operators.code:
x := 10 + 5
y := 20 - 3
z := 4 * 5
q := 20 / 4
r := 17 % 5
x++ // statement, OK
// y = x++ // compile error

Comparison Operators.exp: Compare values using ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Return boolean results. Valid for comparable types.

Logical Operators.exp: Combine booleans with &&, ||, and !. Short-circuit evaluation is supported: && stops on first false, || stops on first true.

Bitwise Operators.exp: Manipulate bits using &, |, ^, <<, >>, and &^ (AND NOT, a.k.a. bit clear).

Increment/Decrement Statements.exp: ++ and -- are statements, not expressions. They cannot be used in assignments or comparisons. Only postfix notation is allowed.

Operator Precedence.exp: Go operator precedence from highest to lowest: *, /, %, <<, >>, &, &^; then +, -, |, ^; then ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=; then &&; then ||. Use parentheses to clarify.

If & Else.exp: Standard conditional branching. Parentheses are optional; braces are required. If can include a short statement before the condition.

Switch Statement.exp: Multi-way branching on a single expression. Cases don't fall through by default. Use fallthrough keyword explicitly when needed.
Switch Statement.code:
switch day {
case "Monday":
	fmt.Println("Work day")
case "Saturday", "Sunday":
	fmt.Println("Weekend")
default:
	fmt.Println("Other day")
}

For Loop.exp: Go has only one loop construct. Use for with init, condition, and post, or as while/infinite loop.

Break & Continue.exp: Exit loops early with break or skip to next iteration with continue. Labels let you break/continue outer loops.

Label Statements.exp: Labels mark a position in code for break, continue, or goto. Use them to exit or continue outer loops from nested inner loops.

Type Switch.exp: A switch that asserts the dynamic type of an interface value. Each case specifies a type. Useful with interface{} or any.
Type Switch.code:
var v any = 42
switch t := v.(type) {
case int:
	fmt.Printf("int: %d\n", t)
case string:
	fmt.Printf("string: %s\n", t)
default:
	fmt.Printf("unknown: %T\n", t)
}

Defer.exp: Defer postpones a function call until the surrounding function returns. Deferred calls are executed in LIFO order. Arguments are evaluated immediately.

Goto.exp: Goto jumps to a labeled statement within the same function. Cannot jump over variable declarations or into blocks. Use sparingly — goto is widely discouraged in idiomatic Go. Prefer structured control flow (for, if/else, switch) over goto. The only acceptable uses are breaking out of deeply nested loops or error cleanup in generated code.
Goto.code:
i := 0
loop:
if i < 3 {
	fmt.Println(i)
	i++
	goto loop
}

Function Declaration.exp: Define functions with func keyword. Specify parameter types and return types explicitly.

Multiple Return Values.exp: Functions can return multiple values. Commonly used for (result, error) pattern.

Named Return Values.exp: Name return values for cleaner code. They act as variables initialized to zero values. A bare return returns the current values of named returns.

Variadic Functions.exp: Accept variable number of arguments using ... syntax. Creates a slice of the arguments. Only the last parameter can be variadic.

Anonymous Functions & Closures.exp: Functions without a name assigned to variables or passed directly. Closures capture surrounding variables by reference, not by value.

init Functions.exp: init() runs automatically when a package is initialized, before main(). Multiple init() calls in a file run in order; across files they run in lexical order. No parameters or return values.

Function Values.exp: Functions are first-class values in Go. They can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions (higher-order functions).

Arrays.exp: Fixed-size sequences with homogeneous elements. Size is part of the type ([3]int != [4]int). Passed by value (copied) when assigned or passed to functions.

Slices.exp: Dynamic-length views backed by an underlying array. Slice expression [low:high] creates a view into an existing array or slice without copying data.
Slices.code:
nums := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
part := nums[1:4]  // [2, 3, 4]
nums = append(nums, 6) // may allocate new backing array
fmt.Println(len(nums), cap(nums))

Slice Internals.exp: A slice is a descriptor: pointer to underlying array, length, capacity. Append grows by doubling the capacity up to 1024, then ~25% growth. Slicing beyond len but within cap reuses the backing array.
Slice Internals.code:
s := make([]int, 3, 5) // len=3, cap=5
s2 := s[:5]            // extends view to cap
s[0] = 10
fmt.Println(s2[0])      // 10 (same backing array)

copy(s2, []int{1,2,3,4,5}) // copy elements

Maps.exp: Unordered key-value collections built on hash tables. Keys must be comparable types (== works). Maps are reference types; zero value is nil.

Range Loops.exp: Iterate with range over slices, maps, strings, channels. For slices: returns index, value. For maps: returns key, value. For strings: returns byte index, rune.

make vs new.exp: make(T, args) creates slices, maps, and channels (initialized, ready to use). new(T) allocates zero value and returns *T. make returns T (not *T).
make vs new.code:
s := make([]int, 5)    // slice ready to use
m := make(map[int]string) // map ready for insertion

p := new(int)    // *int pointing to 0
*p = 42
fmt.Println(*p)

// new for struct
u := new(User)   // *User with zero fields

Pointer Basics.exp: Pointers hold memory addresses. Use & to get a variable's address and * to dereference (read or write through the pointer). Zero value is nil. Go has automatic memory management with garbage collection — allocated memory is freed when no references remain. Unlike C/C++, you don't manually free memory. The GC runs concurrently with a short STW pause. Escape analysis determines whether values live on the stack or heap: if a pointer escapes the function scope, the value is heap-allocated.
Pointer Basics.code:
x := 42
p := &x         // p points to x, type *int
fmt.Println(*p) // 42 (dereference)
*p = 100        // changes x to 100
fmt.Println(x)  // 100

Pointers to Structs.exp: Access struct fields through pointers using dot notation. Go automatically dereferences struct pointers for field access.

Pointers as Parameters.exp: Go is pass-by-value. Use pointers to allow a function to modify its caller's data, or to avoid copying large structs.

new() Function.exp: new(T) allocates zero-value storage for T and returns *T. It never returns nil. Equivalent to &T{} for structs. Use when you need a pointer to a zero-valued instance.

Pointer vs Value Receiver.exp: Use pointer receiver (*T) when the method modifies the receiver, or when the struct is large. Use value receiver (T) for small, immutable types. Pointer receiver avoids copying on each call.

Struct Definition.exp: Group related fields into a struct type. Exported fields start with uppercase letter for visibility across packages.

Struct Tags.exp: Struct tags are metadata strings attached to fields, commonly used by encoding/json, validation libraries, and ORMs. Tags appear after the field type in backticks.

Anonymous (Embedded) Fields.exp: Embed types without a field name. Their methods and fields are promoted to the embedding struct. Not inheritance, but composition.

Struct Methods.exp: Attach methods to types using receiver syntax. Methods are functions with a receiver parameter between func and method name.

Pointer Receivers.exp: Pointer receiver allows modification of the struct. Value receiver works on a copy. Consistency: if any method has pointer receiver, all should.

Struct Comparison.exp: Structs with only comparable fields (no slices, maps, or functions) can be compared with == and used as map keys.

Constructor Functions.exp: Go has no constructors. Use factory functions (NewXxx or New) that return a pointer to a struct, optionally performing validation or initialization.

Interface Definition.exp: Define interfaces as a set of method signatures. Any type implementing all methods implicitly satisfies the interface. Interfaces are satisfied implicitly. Methods vs functions: a method is a function with a receiver parameter (func (t Type) MethodName()). Methods can only be defined on types within the same package. Functions are standalone (func Name()). Use methods when behavior depends on receiver state; use functions for stateless operations. Prefer methods for types that model domain concepts.

Implicit Implementation.exp: Go uses structural typing. A type satisfies an interface simply by implementing its methods. No explicit declaration like 'implements' is needed.

Type Assertions.exp: Extract the concrete value from an interface using value.(Type). The two-value form prevents panics: val, ok := x.(Type).

Empty Interface (any).exp: interface{} (or 'any' in Go 1.18+) accepts values of any type. Used before generics for containers. Now used when truly any type is needed.

Interface Composition.exp: Combine interfaces by embedding them in a new interface. A type must implement all embedded interfaces' methods to satisfy the composed interface.

Interface Values & Nil.exp: An interface value is a (type, value) pair. An interface is nil only when both the type and value are nil. A nil pointer inside a non-nil interface is not nil!

Best Practices (Accept interfaces, retur.exp: Accept interfaces to allow flexibility from callers; return concrete types so callers can access fields and methods without type assertions.

Error Interface.exp: Errors are values implementing the built-in error interface: Error() string. Functions return nil to indicate success.

Error Checking.exp: Idiomatic Go checks errors immediately. Use guard clauses for early returns. Handle errors once — don't ignore or handle them multiple times. For debugging, use stack traces: when a panic occurs, Go prints the full goroutine stack. Use debug.PrintStack() or runtime/debug.Stack() to capture stacks without panicking. The errors package can also include stack information with libraries like pkg/errors or fmt.Errorf+%w for error chains.

Custom Error Types.exp: Create custom error types by implementing the Error() string method. Custom types carry additional context for callers to inspect.

Sentinel Errors.exp: Sentinel errors are predefined error variables (convention: names start with Err) used as sentinel values for specific failure conditions. Compare with == or use errors.Is.

Error Wrapping.exp: Use fmt.Errorf with %w to wrap errors, preserving the original error for errors.Is and errors.As. %W (uppercase) is NOT valid; use lowercase %w.

errors.Is and errors.As.exp: errors.Is(err, target) checks if any error in the chain matches target. errors.As(err, targetType) finds the first error of a given type. Both work through wrapping layers.

Panic & Recover.exp: Panic stops normal execution and unwinds the stack. Recover catches a panic inside a deferred function. Only use panics for truly exceptional, unrecoverable situations.

Goroutines.exp: Lightweight concurrent execution managed by the Go runtime (not OS threads). Launch with go keyword. Goroutines share the same address space; use channels or sync primitives for coordination.

Channels.exp: Typed conduits for goroutine communication. Use ch := make(chan T) to create. Send: ch <- v. Receive: v := <-ch. Block until both ends are ready.
Channels.code:
ch := make(chan int)
go func() { ch <- 42 }()
value := <-ch // blocks until value sent
fmt.Println(value) // 42

Buffered Channels.exp: Channels with capacity: make(chan T, cap). Send blocks only when buffer is full; receive blocks only when buffer is empty. Reduces synchronization points.
Buffered Channels.code:
ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 1
ch <- 2
// Non-blocking sends until buffer full
fmt.Println(<-ch) // 1
fmt.Println(<-ch) // 2

Range & Close.exp: Sender closes a channel with close(ch). Receiver can range over the channel, receiving values until the channel is closed. Detect closed channels with v, ok := <-ch.

Select Statement.exp: Wait on multiple channel operations simultaneously. Select blocks until one case is ready. Use default for non-blocking operations. Use nil channels to disable cases.
Select Statement.code:
select {
case msg := <-ch1:
	fmt.Println(msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
	fmt.Println(msg)
case <-time.After(1 * time.Second):
	fmt.Println("timeout")
default:
	fmt.Println("no message ready")
}

WaitGroup.exp: sync.WaitGroup blocks until all goroutines finish. Add(n) increments the counter, Done() decrements, Wait() blocks until counter reaches 0. Typically Add is called before starting goroutines.

sync.Once.exp: sync.Once ensures a function is executed exactly once, even across multiple goroutines. Used for lazy initialization, singleton setup, and one-time configuration.

Mutex & RWMutex.exp: sync.Mutex provides mutual exclusion. Lock/Unlock protects critical sections. sync.RWMutex allows multiple readers or one writer. RLock/RUnlock for read-only access.

Worker Pools.exp: Fixed number of goroutines processing jobs from a channel. Controls concurrency, limits resource usage. Use a buffered channel for jobs and close it to signal completion.

Fan-in / Fan-out.exp: Fan-out: multiple goroutines read from one channel (distributes work). Fan-in: multiple goroutines write to one channel (multiplexing results). Use a merge function with sync.WaitGroup.

Package Declaration.exp: Every Go file belongs to a package. Executables use 'package main', libraries use any descriptive name. One directory = one package.

Importing Packages.exp: Use import for dependencies. Standard library packages have short paths; remote packages use full module paths. go mod tidy manages required versions. Key tooling commands: go doc shows documentation for any package/symbol (go doc fmt.Println), go clean removes built artifacts (go clean -cache), go version prints the Go version. Use go doc for quick reference without leaving the terminal.

Exported Names.exp: Capitalized names are exported (public), lowercase are unexported (package-private). Exported names are accessible across packages; unexported only within the same package.
Exported Names.code:
type User struct{}      // Exported
type user struct{}      // Unexported
func Public() {}          // Exported
func private() {}         // Unexported
const MaxValue = 100      // Exported
const minValue = 1        // Unexported

Package Initialization (init).exp: init() runs when a package is imported. Multiple init()s across a package run in file name order. init() functions cannot be called directly. They run before main().

Internal Packages.exp: Packages under an 'internal/' directory are only importable by code rooted at the internal's parent. Enforces encapsulation boundaries within a module.
Internal Packages.code:
project/
└── internal/
    └── auth/
        └── token.go  // only importable by project/...

package internal/auth
// This can ONLY be imported by code inside project/

Blank Imports.exp: Import a package solely for its side effects (init() execution) using _. The dot alias '.' imports all exported names into the current namespace.

Import Cycles.exp: Go does not allow import cycles. A cannot import B if B imports A (directly or indirectly). Break cycles by extracting shared types into a third package, or using interfaces.

Reading Files (os.ReadFile).exp: os.ReadFile (Go 1.16+) reads a file into memory. Replaces deprecated ioutil.ReadFile. Use for small files. For large files, use bufio.Scanner or io.Copy with limited buffer.

Writing Files (os.WriteFile).exp: os.WriteFile writes data to a file, creating or truncating it. The third argument is file permissions (Unix mode). Replaces deprecated ioutil.WriteFile.

Buffered I/O (bufio).exp: bufio provides buffered reading and writing for efficiency. bufio.Scanner reads line-by-line (default) or via SplitFunc. bufio.Writer buffers writes to reduce syscalls.

io.ReadAll.exp: io.ReadAll reads from an io.Reader until EOF, returning the full byte slice. Replaces ioutil.ReadAll. Works with any reader: files, HTTP bodies, strings, etc.

io.Copy.exp: io.Copy copies from an io.Reader to an io.Writer until EOF. Efficiently streams data without loading everything into memory. Returns bytes copied and any error.
io.Copy.code:
src, _ := os.Open("source.txt")
defer src.Close()
dst, _ := os.Create("dest.txt")
defer dst.Close()

written, err := io.Copy(dst, src)
fmt.Printf("copied %d bytes\n", written)

File Permissions & ioutil Deprecation.exp: ioutil is deprecated since Go 1.16. Replace ioutil.ReadFile with os.ReadFile, ioutil.WriteFile with os.WriteFile, ioutil.ReadAll with io.ReadAll, ioutil.TempFile with os.CreateTemp.

Directory Operations.exp: Read directories with os.ReadDir (returns sorted []os.DirEntry). Walk directory trees with filepath.Walk or filepath.WalkDir. Create dirs with os.MkdirAll.

Test Functions.exp: Write tests in *_test.go files. Test functions follow func TestXxx(t *testing.T). Use t.Error/t.Fatal for failures. Run with go test.

Table-Driven Tests.exp: Define test cases as a slice of structs. Iterate over them for clean, DRY tests that cover many inputs. Each case can include a name for clear failure output.

Subtests.exp: Run subtests with t.Run(name, fn) for hierarchical test organization. Subtests share setup/teardown and can be run selectively with go test -run pattern.

Test Helpers.exp: Helper functions in tests reduce boilerplate. Call t.Helper() to mark a function as a test helper so failure line numbers point to the caller, not the helper.

Test Coverage.exp: Go has built-in coverage. Run go test -cover to see percentage. go test -coverprofile=coverage.out generates a profile. Use go tool cover -html=coverage.out for visual report.
Test Coverage.code:
# Run with coverage
$ go test -cover ./...
# Output: ok  myapp/mypkg  0.002s  coverage: 85.2% of statements

# Generate HTML report
go test -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
go tool cover -html=coverage.out -o coverage.html

Fuzzing.exp: Go 1.18+ fuzzing randomly generates inputs to find bugs. Fuzz test: func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). Seed with f.Add(), then f.Fuzz(targetFn).

Benchmarks.exp: Measure performance with BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B). b.N is adjusted by the framework for stable timing. Use b.ResetTimer() and b.ReportAllocs() for accurate measurements.

fmt Package.exp: Formatted I/O with Print, Printf, Println, Sprintf, Fprintf. Verbs: %v (value), %+v (with fields), %T (type), %d (int), %s (string), %#v (Go-syntax).
fmt Package.code:
fmt.Println("Hello")
fmt.Printf("Value: %d, Type: %T\n", 42, 42)
s := fmt.Sprintf("hex: %x", 255) // "ff"
fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)

strings & strconv Packages.exp: strings: Contains, Split, Join, ToUpper, ToLower, Trim, Replace, Builder (efficient string building). strconv: Atoi, Itoa, ParseBool, FormatFloat, ParseInt.
strings & strconv Packages.code:
s := "hello world"
fmt.Println(strings.ToUpper(s))
parts := strings.Split(s, " ")

n, _ := strconv.Atoi("42")
s2 := strconv.Itoa(42)

var b strings.Builder
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
	b.WriteString("a")
}
fmt.Println(b.String())

io Package.exp: Core I/O interfaces: io.Reader, io.Writer, io.Closer, io.Seeker. Utility functions: io.Copy, io.ReadAll, io.MultiReader, io.TeeReader, io.LimitReader.
io Package.code:
var w io.Writer = os.Stdout
fmt.Fprint(w, "output")

// MultiReader chains readers
r := io.MultiReader(strings.NewReader("a"), strings.NewReader("b"))

// TeeReader mirrors reads to a writer
pr, pw := io.Pipe()
io.Copy(os.Stdout, pr) // reads from pr

encoding/json Package.exp: Marshal/Unmarshal Go values to/from JSON. Struct tags control field names, omitempty skips zero values. Use json.NewDecoder for streaming JSON (files, HTTP).

flag Package.exp: Parse command-line flags with flag package. Supports -flag, -flag=x, --flag (double dash works). Types: String, Int, Bool, Duration, Float64, or custom flag.Value.

log Package.exp: Simple logging to stderr with timestamps. log.Printf, log.Fatalf (calls os.Exit(1)), log.Panicf (calls panic). Use log.New for custom output, flags, and prefix.

os/exec Package.exp: Run external commands. exec.Command(name, args...). cmd.Output() returns stdout, cmd.CombinedOutput() returns both. Pipe stdin/stdout/stderr for interactive commands.
os/exec Package.code:
cmd := exec.Command("ls", "-la")
out, err := cmd.Output()
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(string(out))

// With pipes
cmd.Stdin = strings.NewReader("input data")
cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout
cmd.Stderr = os.Stderr
cmd.Run()

time Package.exp: Time and duration with nanosecond precision. Parse (reference time: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006 = 1 2 3 4 5 6 -7). Timer/Ticker for events. Sleep for pauses.

context Package.exp: Context propagates deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values. Create with context.Background() or context.TODO(). Derive with WithCancel, WithTimeout, WithDeadline, WithValue.

sync Package.exp: Synchronization primitives: Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, Pool, Map (concurrent-safe map). sync.Map is optimized for read-heavy or append-only patterns.
sync Package.code:
var mu sync.Mutex
var counter int

var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		mu.Lock()
		counter++
		mu.Unlock()
	}()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println("Counter:", counter)

Go Modules.exp: Go modules define a project's dependencies and versioning. go.mod declares the module path and requirements. go.sum contains checksums for reproducibility. Cross-compilation is built-in: set GOOS and GOARCH env vars to target different platforms (GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build). Common targets: linux/amd64, darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, windows/amd64. Use go tool dist list to see all supported targets. Cross-compilation doesn't require additional toolchains — Go includes all targets in the standard distribution.

Workspace Mode.exp: Go 1.18+ workspace mode (go.work) lets you work on multiple modules simultaneously. Useful for local development across interdependent modules. go work init creates the file.
Workspace Mode.code:
go.work file:
go 1.22

use (
	./myapp
	./sharedlib
	./tools
)

# Commands
$ go work init ./myapp ./sharedlib
$ go work use ./newmod
$ go work sync

Build Tags.exp: Build tags (or build constraints) conditionally compile files. Placed at top of file: //go:build tag. Multiple tags combine with &&, ||, and !. Use for platform-specific code or feature flags.

go generate.exp: go generate scans //go:generate directives to run tools automatically. Commonly used for code generation: protobufs, stringers, mocks, and embed. Run with go generate ./....

go tooling (vet, fmt, fix).exp: go vet detects suspicious constructs (e.g., unreachable code, wrong Printf verbs). go fmt automatically formats code to canonical style. go fix updates old API usage to newer versions.
go tooling (vet, fmt, fix).code:
go vet ./...      # static analysis
# Detects: unreachable code, wrong Printf args, etc.

go fmt ./...      # formats all files
# Equivalent to: gofmt -l -w .

go fix ./...      # migrate deprecated APIs
go tool pprof     # CPU/memory profiling
go tool trace     # execution trace

Dependency Management (go get).exp: go get manages module dependencies. Latest compatible version: go get pkg@latest. Specific version: go get pkg@v1.2.3. Upgrade minor: go get -u ./.... Remove unused: go mod tidy.
Dependency Management (go get).code:
go get github.com/gorilla/mux@latest
# upgrades to latest tagged version

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@v1.8.0
# specific version

go get -u ./...
# upgrade all direct/indirect deps

go mod tidy
# removes unused deps, adds missing

Generics.exp: Go 1.18+ supports type parameters for functions and types. Use constraints (interface with type sets) to restrict acceptable types. 'any' is a shortcut for interface{}. Comparable constraint for ==.

HTTP Server (net/http).exp: Build HTTP servers with http.HandleFunc or http.Handler interface. http.ListenAndServe starts the server. Default mux is http.DefaultServeMux.

HTTP Client.exp: http.Client with Get, Post, Do methods. Respect context cancellation, always close response body, set timeouts to avoid hanging connections.

Routing & ServeMux (Go 1.22+).exp: Go 1.22 enhanced the default mux with method-based routing and path parameters using {param} and {param...} patterns.

Middleware Pattern.exp: Middleware wraps http.Handler to add cross-cutting concerns: logging, auth, recovery, rate limiting, CORS. Use a function that takes and returns http.Handler.

Templates (html/template).exp: html/template generates safe HTML output with automatic context-aware escaping. Use template.ParseFiles or template.New(). Execute with a data struct and func map.

TLS & HTTPS.exp: Use http.ListenAndServeTLS to serve HTTPS. Generate self-signed certs with crypto/tls or use Let's Encrypt via autocert. Always serve HTTPS in production.

TCP & UDP Sockets.exp: Low-level networking with net.Dial (TCP/UDP) and net.Listen. Build custom protocols. Use bufio for line-based protocols. Always set deadlines.

database/sql Interface.exp: database/sql provides a generic SQL interface. Open a database with sql.Open (driver name + DSN). Use sql.DB for connection pooling. Run queries with Query, QueryRow, Exec.

Querying (Query & QueryRow).exp: Query returns *sql.Rows (cursor). Iterate with rows.Next() and rows.Scan(). QueryRow returns at most one row, returns sql.ErrNoRows if none. Always close rows.

Prepared Statements.exp: Prepare statements with db.Prepare for repeated execution. Prevents SQL injection and improves performance. Use $1, $2 (PostgreSQL) or ? (MySQL/SQLite) placeholders.

Transactions.exp: Use db.Begin() to start a transaction. tx.Exec, tx.Query within the transaction. Commit or Rollback. Ensures atomicity — all operations succeed or none do.

Connection Pooling.exp: sql.DB manages a connection pool. Configure with SetMaxOpenConns (max concurrent), SetMaxIdleConns (idle pool), SetConnMaxLifetime (connection age), SetConnMaxIdleTime.
Connection Pooling.code:
db, _ := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)

// Tune the pool
db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)   // max simultaneous connections
db.SetMaxIdleConns(5)    // keep 5 idle
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5 * time.Minute)  // recycle connections
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(1 * time.Minute)   // close idle connections

// Ping checks a connection from the pool
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
db.PingContext(ctx)

Migrations (golang-migrate).exp: Manage schema changes with migration tools like golang-migrate/migrate. Migration files: 001_create_users.up.sql and 001_create_users.down.sql. Run up/down programmatically via CLI.

Database Drivers.exp: Register database drivers via blank imports. Common drivers: lib/pq (PostgreSQL), go-sql-driver/mysql (MySQL), mattn/go-sqlite3 (SQLite), mongo-driver (MongoDB).

Go Design Philosophy.exp: Learning Go emphasizes simplicity: no inheritance, no generics (until 1.18), no exceptions. Go favors composition over inheritance, explicit error handling, and readability over cleverness. Bodner calls this 'the boring language that gets things done'. The key insight: Go is designed for large teams maintaining code over years.

nil & Zero Values Mental Model.exp: Know Go teaches the nil mental model: nil is a value, not an error. Nil slices have len=0 and can append to. Nil maps return zero values but panic on write. Nil interfaces have dynamic type nil (not just value nil). A nil pointer inside an interface makes it non-nil! Book insight: always think about what zero value means for your types.

slog Structured Logging (Go 1.21+).exp: slog provides structured, leveled logging with key-value pairs. Levels: Debug, Info, Warn, Error. Use slog.New with JSONHandler or TextHandler. slog.Group for nested keys. slog.Attr for reusable attributes. The book recommendation: always use structured logging for production.

errors.Join & Error Handling (Go 1.20+).exp: errors.Join combines multiple errors into one. Useful for batch validation and deferred cleanup. Know Go emphasizes thinking of errors as values that can be combined. Also new: fmt.Errorf with multiple %w (Go 1.20+ can wrap multiple errors).

maps & slices Packages (Go 1.21+).exp: Standard library packages for generic operations on maps and slices. No more hand-rolling Contains, DeleteFunc, Filter, etc. These are type-safe and efficient.

Range over Iterators & func (Go 1.23+).exp: Go 1.23 adds range-over-iterator support. Any function with func(yield func(K, V) bool) can be ranged. The iter package provides Seq and Seq2 types. Libraries can expose iterators instead of requiring callbacks.

Embedding (//go:embed).exp: go:embed embeds files into the binary at compile time. Supports files, directories, and globs. Embed as []byte, string, or embed.FS. Know Go recommends embed for static assets over reading files at runtime.

Race Detector & Data Races.exp: The Go race detector catches concurrent unsafe access. Run with -race flag. Learning Go: if two goroutines access the same variable without synchronization, it's a race. Know Go says 'always run tests with -race before shipping'. The detector has ~false negative rate but no false positives.

Profiling & pprof.exp: Go's built-in profiler: CPU, memory, goroutine, mutex, block profiles. Learning Go: always profile before optimizing. Use net/http/pprof for web apps, runtime/pprof for CLIs. The book's advice: 'measure, don't guess'.

sync/atomic (Go 1.19+ Typed API).exp: Go 1.19+ added typed atomic values: atomic.Int64, atomic.Value, etc. Learning Go recommends them over sync.Mutex for simple counters and flags. The zero value is ready to use, no initialization needed.

CLI Applications (Cobra).exp: Build powerful CLI applications with Cobra (spf13/cobra), the framework behind kubectl, gh, and hugo. Cobra handles commands, flags, subcommands, and help generation. Commands are structured as a tree with Run functions. Use PersistentFlags for flags shared across subcommands and LocalFlags for command-specific ones. Best practice: organize commands in a cmd/ directory; use Viper (spf13/viper) with Cobra for config file support.

Web Frameworks (Gin, Echo).exp: While net/http suffices for many cases, frameworks like Gin (gin-gonic/gin) and Echo (labstack/echo) add routing with parameters, middleware chaining, request binding/validation, and grouped routes. Gin uses a radix tree router for high performance. Echo has built-in middleware for CORS, logging, recovery, and CSRF. Common mistake: adding a framework when the standard library would suffice — start with net/http and add a framework only when you need advanced routing or middleware. Best practice: use Gin for REST APIs with JSON; use Echo if you prefer a more minimalist API.

gRPC & Protocol Buffers.exp: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for serialization. Define services in .proto files, generate Go code with protoc.
