Defaults can be expressions or even function calls — they're evaluated at call time, not definition time. Common mistake: thinking defaults trigger on null — they only trigger on undefined. Best practice: put default parameters after required ones so calling code can skip them; avoid complex default expressions that hide bugs.

Rest Parameters.exp: Rest parameters (...) collect remaining arguments into a real array (unlike the array-like arguments object). Must be the last parameter. Common mistake: confusing rest with the arguments object — arguments is array-like (no .map/.filter) and includes ALL parameters, not just the extras. Best practice: prefer rest over arguments for clarity; use rest in destructuring to capture remaining items.

Closures.exp: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned. This is JavaScript’s most powerful pattern — it enables data privacy (module pattern), function factories, event handlers with state, and memoization. Common mistake: closures capture variables by reference, not by value — loop closures all see the final value unless you use let or an IIFE. Best practice: use closures for encapsulation (hide implementation details); be mindful of memory if the closure retains large objects.

Objects.exp: Objects are the foundation of JavaScript — almost everything is an object or can behave like one. Crockford calls objects 'containers of properties, where each property has a name and a value'. Objects are passed by reference, making them efficient but also dangerous when mutated in place. Eloquent JavaScript describes objects as 'octopuses with any number of tentacles' — they can hold any type. The Good Parts recommends object literals as the simplest and safest way to create objects, avoiding new Object() and similar verbose forms.

This Keyword.exp: this is one of JavaScript's most misunderstood features. Crockford calls this 'a source of enormous confusion'. Its value depends entirely on HOW a function is called: method call → the object, plain call → undefined (strict) or global (sloppy), constructor call (new) → the new instance, call/apply/bind → explicitly set. Eloquent JavaScript calls this 'the function's context'. Arrow functions avoid the confusion by inheriting this from the enclosing scope — Crockford recommends using them for callbacks. The Good Parts says: 'this is always bound to the global object in inner functions' — capture it with a variable (that = this) or use arrow functions.

Prototypes.exp: Prototypal inheritance is JavaScript's native inheritance model. Crockford explains: 'a prototype is an object from which other objects inherit properties'. Unlike classical inheritance (classes inherit from classes), objects inherit directly from objects. Object.create() creates a new object with a specified prototype. The Good Parts advocates for prototypal over classical inheritance — it's simpler and more flexible. Eloquent JavaScript describes the prototype chain as 'a series of objects linked together' ending at Object.prototype. When you access a property, JavaScript walks the chain until found. Favor composition over inheritance in large systems.

Classes.exp: Class syntax (ES2015) is sugar over prototypes: class defines a constructor, methods go on the prototype, and static methods go on the constructor itself. Supports extends for inheritance and super for parent calls. Common mistake: thinking classes are a new inheritance model — they're still prototypal underneath. Best practice: use class syntax over manual prototype manipulation for readability; prefer composition over deep inheritance chains.

Inheritance.exp: extends creates a subclass that inherits from a parent class. super() calls the parent constructor; super.method() calls a parent method. Subclasses can override methods and access parent implementations. Common mistake: forgetting to call super() in the subclass constructor — causes ReferenceError. Best practice: keep inheritance shallow (1-2 levels max); prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for code reuse.

Getters & Setters.exp: Getters (get) and setters (set) let you define properties that call functions when accessed or assigned. They look like normal property access but can run validation, computation, or logging. Common mistake: getters should not have side effects (callers expect property-like behavior). Best practice: use getters for computed properties and setters for validation; avoid expensive operations in getters since callers don't expect function-call overhead.

Arrays.exp: Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Arrays are objects — typeof [] returns 'object'. The length property is auto-updated but can be set manually (truncates or creates empty slots). Common mistake: using for...in on arrays (iterates keys as strings and includes inherited properties). Best practice: use array literal [] over new Array(); use for...of, forEach, or array methods (map/filter) for iteration.
Arrays.code:
const fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];
console.log(fruits[0]);        // 'apple' — zero-indexed
console.log(fruits.length);    // 3

const arr = new Array(3);      // [empty × 3] — creates sparse array!
console.log(arr.length);       // 3
console.log(arr[0]);           // undefined (empty slot)

// Methods that mutate
fruits.push('date');           // add to end
fruits.pop();                  // remove from end
fruits.unshift('apricot');     // add to start
fruits.shift();                // remove from start

// Checking arrays
console.log(Array.isArray(fruits)); // true — use this, not typeof

Array Methods.exp: Eloquent JavaScript calls array methods like map, filter, and reduce 'higher-order functions' — functions that operate on other functions. They enable a declarative style: you describe WHAT you want, not HOW. This is more readable and less error-prone than manual for loops. map transforms each element, filter selects elements, reduce combines elements into a single value, find locates the first match, some checks if any element matches, every checks if all match. The Good Parts cautions against mutating arrays while iterating — use map/filter to create new arrays instead.

Destructuring.exp: Unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables. Supports nested destructuring, default values, and rest patterns. Common mistake: trying to destructure null or undefined — throws TypeError. Best practice: provide defaults for safe destructuring; use renaming (object: { oldName: newName }) to avoid naming conflicts.

Map & Set.exp: Map stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type (objects, functions, primitives) — unlike objects which only accept strings/symbols. Map preserves insertion order and has O(1) lookup. Set stores unique values of any type. Common mistake: using objects as maps — object keys are always strings; Map keys preserve type (number key 1 !== string key '1'). Best practice: use Map over plain objects for dynamic key collections; use Set for deduplication and fast membership checks.

WeakMap & WeakSet.exp: WeakMap holds 'weak' references to object keys — if no other reference to the key exists, the entry is garbage collected. WeakSet similarly holds weak references to objects. Not iterable and no .size property because the contents could change anytime due to GC. Common mistake: expecting WeakMap/WeakSet to be iterable or have .size — they don't by design. Best practice: use WeakMap for private data (closure alternative), caching associated with DOM elements, or preventing memory leaks from long-lived references.

Iterators & Generators.exp: Iterators are objects with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Any object with [Symbol.iterator] is iterable (works with for...of, spread, destructuring). Generators (function*) simplify iterator creation — they pause at each yield and resume on the next call. Common mistake: generators are single-use iterables — you can't restart them; create a new generator each time. Best practice: use generators for lazy sequences, infinite streams, and async iteration (async function*).

DOM Manipulation.exp: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's API for HTML. Select elements with querySelector (single) or querySelectorAll (NodeList). Modify content via textContent, innerHTML, or classList. Common mistake: using innerHTML when textContent is safer (innerHTML parses HTML and can introduce XSS). Best practice: cache DOM references in variables (querying the DOM is slow); use classList.add/remove/toggle instead of className string manipulation; prefer textContent over innerHTML for text-only changes.

Events.exp: Events signal user interaction (click, keydown, submit, scroll). addEventListener(type, handler) attaches a handler. Events flow through three phases: capture (outer to inner), target, and bubble (inner to outer). Common mistake: using inline event handlers (onclick=) — they create global functions and only allow one handler per event. Best practice: use addEventListener over onclick; use event delegation (listen on parent) for dynamic child elements; call removeEventListener to prevent memory leaks.

Forms & Validation.exp: Handle form submission, read input values, and validate before sending. The submit event fires on the form element (not the button). Access fields via the elements collection or by id. Use e.preventDefault() to stop submission and validate first. Common mistake: listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form — the form can also be submitted via Enter key. Best practice: validate on submit (not on every keystroke for performance); use the Constraint Validation API (required, minlength, pattern attributes) for basic checks.

Fetch API.exp: fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object. The Response must be parsed (.json(), .text()) before data is available. fetch only rejects on network errors — HTTP errors (404, 500) still resolve. Common mistake: forgetting that fetch doesn't reject on HTTP error status — check response.ok. Best practice: always handle network errors with .catch(); use AbortController to cancel in-flight requests; set appropriate Content-Type headers for POST/PUT.

Local Storage.exp: localStorage persists data across browser sessions (no expiration). sessionStorage persists only for the current tab session — cleared when the tab closes. Both store strings only — objects must be serialized with JSON.stringify/parse. Storage limit is ~5-10MB per origin. Common mistake: storing objects directly — they become '[object Object]'; always use JSON.stringify. Best practice: wrap localStorage access in try/catch (private browsing may throw); use JSON for structured data; clear unused keys to stay under quota.

Timers.exp: setTimeout runs a function once after a delay; setInterval runs repeatedly at the interval. Both return an ID passed to clearTimeout/clearInterval to cancel. Common mistake: assuming setInterval runs at exact intervals — if the callback takes longer than the interval, calls stack up. Best practice: use recursive setTimeout instead of setInterval for precise timing; always clear timers in cleanup code to prevent memory leaks; use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations (more efficient than setTimeout).

Promises.exp: A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never. States: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved), or rejected (error). .then() handles fulfillment, .catch() handles rejection, .finally() runs regardless. Promises are microtasks — they resolve before macrotasks like setTimeout. Common mistake: not returning the promise from .then() breaks the chain — the next .then() receives undefined. Best practice: always return promises from chains; handle rejection at the end of the chain (not per-link); use Promise.all for parallel work.

Async/Await.exp: async functions always return a Promise. await pauses execution until the awaited promise settles — but only within the async function (the caller continues). Common mistake: calling async functions without awaiting them — they still run but you lose the return value and error handling. Best practice: wrap await calls in try/catch for error handling; use Promise.all for independent parallel async operations (sequential await is slower); top-level await works in ES modules.

Fetch & HTTP.exp: fetch() makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise<Response>. Always check response.ok — fetch only rejects on network errors, not HTTP errors. GET is default; POST/PUT/PATCH require method and body. Common mistake: not checking response.ok — a 404 resolves successfully. Best practice: always check .ok and throw for non-2xx; use AbortController for timeout/cancellation; set Content-Type for requests with body.

Event Loop.exp: The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model — single-threaded but non-blocking. Eloquent JavaScript explains: 'when a program needs to wait, it schedules a callback and continues running other code'. The call stack runs synchronously; async callbacks go to the task queue. Promises and async/await use the microtask queue (higher priority than macrotasks like setTimeout). This means promise callbacks run BEFORE timer callbacks, even zero-delay timers. Crockford says: 'understanding the event loop is essential — everything in JavaScript happens in a single thread, and if you block it, the whole page freezes'.

Web Workers.exp: Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread — they can't access the DOM, window, or parent scope. Communicate with the main thread via postMessage() and onmessage. Workers are great for CPU-intensive tasks (image processing, data parsing, encryption). Common mistake: trying to access DOM or window inside a worker — not available. Best practice: use workers for expensive computations that would block the UI; use structuredClone or Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer) for efficient data passing; terminate workers when done to free resources.

Async Iteration.exp: Async iteration (for await...of) consumes async iterables with [Symbol.asyncIterator] that returns promises from next(). async function* defines an async generator. Useful for streaming data (paginated APIs, WebSocket messages, file chunks). Common mistake: using for...of instead of for await...of on async iterables — for...of doesn't await promises. Best practice: use async generators for streaming scenarios; handle errors inside the loop with try/catch.

ES Modules.exp: Share code with import/export syntax, and run modules in modern browsers or bundlers.
ES Modules.code:
export function hello() { return 'hi'; }  // named export
import { hello } from './module.js';        // named import from module

Spread Syntax.exp: Expand iterable values into arrays or function calls, and merge object properties effortlessly.
Spread Syntax.code:
const copy = [...[1, 2]];         // spread: expand iterable into array
const merged = { ...{ a: 1 }, b: 2 }; // spread: merge object properties

Optional Chaining.exp: Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits to undefined if the value before ?. is null or undefined — without throwing. Works with property access (?.), method calls (?.()), and dynamic access (?.[]). Common mistake: thinking ?. prevents 'undefined is not a function' for methods that don't exist — it does, but only when the object itself is null/undefined. Best practice: combine ?. with ?? for safe deep access chains; don't overuse — if a value should always exist, let it throw (fail fast).

Nullish Coalescing.exp: ?? returns the right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined. Unlike || which returns the right operand for ANY falsy value (0, '', false). Common mistake: using || for defaults when 0 or '' are valid values — || treats them as absent. Best practice: use ?? for default values when the left side could be a valid falsy value (empty string, zero, false); use || for truly absent values (when undefined/null and falsy should both get the default).

Dynamic Import.exp: import() is a function-like expression that dynamically loads a module at runtime. It returns a Promise resolving to the module namespace object. Enables code splitting (load only what's needed), lazy loading (load on user interaction), and conditional imports (platform detection). Common mistake: dynamic imports are NOT hoisted — they execute when reached. Best practice: use dynamic imports for large libraries not needed on initial load (charts, editors, heavy utilities); combine with top-level await in module scripts.

Promise Combinators.exp: Promise.all waits for ALL promises — rejects fast if ANY rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for ALL to settle (resolve or reject) — never rejects, returns results with status. Promise.race returns the first settled promise. Promise.any returns the first fulfilled promise — rejects only if ALL reject. Common mistake: using Promise.all when one failure shouldn't fail the whole batch — use allSettled. Best practice: use all for dependent parallel work (must all succeed), allSettled for independent results, race for timeouts, any for fastest success.

React.exp: React is a component-based UI library. Components return JSX (JavaScript XML) describing what to render. Props pass data from parent to child; state manages component-local data that triggers re-renders. Common mistake: mutating state directly (this.state.x = 5) instead of using setState or the state setter. Best practice: prefer functional components with hooks (useState, useEffect) over class components; keep components small and focused; lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.

Vue.exp: Vue is a progressive framework with reactive templates and a component system. Options API uses data(), methods, computed, and watch. Composition API (setup) provides better code organization. Common mistake: using normal variables in data() instead of reactive ref() or reactive() — Vue can only track reactive objects. Best practice: prefer the Composition API for complex logic reuse; use computed for derived state instead of methods in templates; use v-bind:key in v-for for efficient re-rendering.

Express.exp: Express is a minimalist Node.js web framework. Define routes with app.get/post/put/delete. Middleware functions (app.use) process requests in order — they can modify req/res, end the request, or call next(). Common mistake: forgetting to call next() in middleware — the request hangs. Best practice: structure routes with express.Router() for modularity; use error-handling middleware (4 args) for centralized errors; parse bodies with express.json() middleware.

Next.js.exp: Next.js is a React framework for production with file-based routing (pages/ or app/), SSR/SSG, and API routes. Pages/ directory: each file becomes a route. App Router (app/) uses layouts, loading states, and server components. Common mistake: fetching data in client components when server components would be more efficient. Best practice: use server components for initial data fetching (rendered on server, smaller JS bundle); use getStaticProps (Pages Router) for SSG; leverage Suspense boundaries for streaming.

NestJS.exp: NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework built with TypeScript that uses decorators for controllers, providers, modules, and middleware. It supports Express or Fastify under the hood. Common mistake: forgetting to register providers in module decorators — unregistered providers cause runtime injection errors. Best practice: use modules to organize features; keep controllers thin (delegate logic to services); leverage dependency injection for testability.

Vite.exp: Vite is a fast build tool that uses native ES modules for dev (instant HMR) and Rollup for production builds. Supports JS, TS, JSX, CSS, and assets out of the box. Common mistake: thinking Vite only works for frontend frameworks — it works with vanilla JS and library development too. Best practice: use vite.config.js for custom configuration (aliases, plugins, proxy); leverage HMR for fast iteration.

JSON.exp: JSON.parse converts JSON strings to objects; JSON.stringify serializes objects to JSON strings. Essential for data exchange and API communication. Common mistake: JSON.parse throws on invalid JSON — always wrap in try/catch or use a safe parser. Best practice: use JSON.stringify's replacer and space arguments for controlled serialization; avoid storing undefined, BigInt, or circular references — they're silently dropped or throw.

Math & Number.exp: Math provides constants and methods for math operations: random, floor, round, ceil, max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, sin, cos, PI, E. Number offers parseInt, parseFloat, isNaN, isFinite, isInteger, and EPSILON. Common mistake: using Math.floor for rounding — use Math.round for standard rounding and Math.trunc for integer truncation. Best practice: use Number.isNaN over global isNaN (global coerces, Number.isNaN doesn't); use Math.max/Math.min with spread for arrays; avoid floating-point equality checks — use epsilon comparison.
Math & Number.code:
console.log(Math.PI);                 // 3.14159...
console.log(Math.random());             // random float 0–1
console.log(Math.floor(3.9));           // 3 (round down)
console.log(Math.round(3.5));           // 4 (standard rounding)
console.log(Math.trunc(-3.9));          // -3 (remove decimal, no rounding)
console.log(Math.max(1, 5, 3));        // 5
console.log(Math.max(...[1, 5, 3]));   // 5 (spread array)
console.log(Number.parseInt('42px'));   // 42 (parses until non-digit)
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN));         // true (no coercion)
console.log(Number.isFinite(Infinity)); // false
console.log(Number.isInteger(3.0));     // true
console.log(Number.EPSILON);            // ~2.2e-16 (for float comparison)

Date & Time.exp: Date handles date/time operations: creation, formatting, arithmetic, and timezone handling. Months are zero-indexed (0 = January). Date objects are mutable — all set methods mutate in place. Common mistake: date parsing with strings is unreliable across browsers — use Date.parse cautiously or a date library. Best practice: use toISOString() for storage/serialization; use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localized display; use timestamps (Date.now()) for calculations to avoid month-index confusion.

String Methods.exp: Strings have built-in methods for manipulation: slice, substring, split, replace/replaceAll, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, trim, includes, startsWith, endsWith, repeat, padStart/padEnd, match, matchAll, and charAt. Strings are immutable — all methods return a new string. Common mistake: confusing slice (accepts negative indices) with substring (treats negative as 0). Best practice: use replaceAll (ES2021) over replace with global regex for simpler replacement; use template literals for concatenation; use includes over indexOf for readability.

Proxy & Reflect.exp: Proxy wraps an object to intercept operations (get, set, delete, etc.) via traps. Reflect provides methods that mirror the default proxy behavior for forwarding.

Intl API.exp: Intl provides locale-aware formatting for dates, numbers, currencies, and collation. Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, and ListFormat are the most common.
Intl API.code:
const date = new Date();                           // current date
const df = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('de-DE', { dateStyle: 'full' }); // German locale
console.log(df.format(date));                      // localized date string

const nf = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
console.log(nf.format(1234.56));                   // '$1,234.56'

TypedArrays (ArrayBuffer).exp: TypedArrays provide views over raw binary data in an ArrayBuffer. Types include Int8Array, Uint8Array, Float64Array, and more for performance-critical work.
TypedArrays (ArrayBuffer).code:
const buf = new ArrayBuffer(16);   // allocate 16 bytes of memory
const view = new Float64Array(buf);   // 64-bit float view over buffer
view[0] = 3.14159;                    // write float at index 0
console.log(view[0]);                 // read back: 3.14159
// Also useful for WebSocket/WebRTC binary protocols

structuredClone & Deep Copy.exp: structuredClone creates a deep copy of an object, handling circular references and types like Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and Blob.
structuredClone & Deep Copy.code:
const original = { name: 'Doge', tags: ['cool', 'fun'], meta: { created: new Date() } };
const clone = structuredClone(original);             // deep copy everything
clone.tags.push('smart');                             // modify clone only
console.log(original.tags);                           // ['cool', 'fun']
console.log(clone.tags);                              // ['cool', 'fun', 'smart']

Hoisting Explained.exp: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution. var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined — accessing them before declaration returns undefined, not ReferenceError. let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized — they exist in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block start until declaration, so accessing them throws ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted entirely (body included), so they can be called before their definition. Function expressions are NOT hoisted — use them only after the assignment line.

Global Scope.exp: The global scope is the outermost scope. In browsers, window is the global object; in Node.js, it's global. Variables declared with var at the top level become properties of the global object. let, const, and class at the top level do NOT become global object properties — they exist in the global scope but are not properties of window/global. Relying on global variables is considered bad practice — they create naming conflicts and make code hard to reason about. The Good Parts: minimize global scope by using IIFEs or modules.

Lexical Scoping.exp: Lexical (static) scoping means a variable's scope is determined by its position in the source code, not by how functions are called at runtime. Inner functions can access variables from outer scopes, but not vice versa. This is the foundation of closures — a function remembers the scope in which it was defined. JavaScript has no dynamic scoping — this is not scope, it's context (determined by call pattern). Understanding lexical scope helps predict which variables are accessible at any point in the code.

Object.is.exp: Object.is (ES6) compares two values for equality. It behaves like === except for two edge cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true (NaN === NaN is false), and Object.is(0, -0) returns false (0 === -0 is true). Use Object.is when you need NaN equivalence or need to distinguish signed zeros. For most cases, === is sufficient and more readable. Object.is does NOT perform deep object comparison — references must match. It's available on all modern platforms and polyfillable for older ones.

SameValueZero.exp: SameValueZero is an equality algorithm used by Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes. It behaves like Object.is but treats -0 and 0 as equal. This means NaN is considered equal to itself (unlike ===) but -0 equals 0 (unlike Object.is). It's not directly callable in user code but is used internally by Set.has(), Map.has(), and includes(). Understanding it helps explain why Set.has(NaN) returns true but indexOf(NaN) returns -1.

The Event Loop.exp: The event loop is JavaScript's concurrency model: single-threaded, non-blocking, and asynchronous by necessity. The call stack runs synchronous code. When an async operation completes, its callback is queued. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) go to the task queue. Microtasks (Promise.then, async/await, queueMicrotask) go to the microtask queue. After each macrotask, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue before processing the next macrotask. This means promise callbacks run before setTimeout callbacks, even zero-delay ones. Blocking the call stack with long synchronous work freezes the page.

Microtasks vs Macrotasks.exp: Microtasks include Promise.then/catch/finally, MutationObserver, and queueMicrotask. Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, and UI rendering (browser). After every macrotask, the event loop processes all pending microtasks before the next macrotask or render. This is why Promise-based code runs before timer callbacks. queueMicrotask() explicitly schedules a microtask. Microtasks can starve the event loop if they continuously enqueue more microtasks — causing the page to become unresponsive despite no single long task.

Callbacks.exp: A callback is a function passed to another function for later execution. They are the foundation of async JavaScript — used in setTimeout, event handlers, fs.readFile, and fetch. Callback-based code suffers from 'callback hell' (pyramid of doom) when nested. Modern alternatives: Promises and async/await. The error-first callback pattern (Node.js convention) passes error as the first argument: callback(err, result). Always handle errors in callbacks — unhandled errors silently disappear.

ES Modules (ESM).exp: ES Modules (ES6) use import and export statements. Each module has its own scope — no global leakage. Named exports export multiple values with specific names. Default export exports a single main value per module. Dynamic import() (ES2020) loads modules on demand (returns a Promise). ESM is static — imports are hoisted and resolved before execution, enabling tree-shaking. Modules are strict by default. Use type='module' on script tags in browsers, or 'type': 'module' in package.json for Node.js.

CommonJS (CJS).exp: CommonJS is Node.js's original module system using require() and module.exports. require() loads modules synchronously — fine for servers but not browsers. module.exports can be any value. exports is a shorthand reference to module.exports — reassigning exports breaks the reference. Node.js supports both CJS (file.js or .cjs) and ESM (.mjs or type='module' package.json). Use require() for dynamic conditional imports. CJS modules are not tree-shakeable because exports are determined at runtime.

Memory Lifecycle.exp: JavaScript manages memory automatically via garbage collection. The lifecycle: (1) Allocate — memory is reserved when you create values (objects, arrays, closures, DOM nodes); (2) Use — references point to the allocated memory as your code runs; (3) Release — when a value is no longer reachable, its memory becomes eligible for garbage collection. Reachability means the value can be accessed from a root (global object, current call stack, active closures). Values can become unreachable when all references go out of scope, are reassigned, or set to null.

Garbage Collection.exp: Modern JavaScript engines use generational garbage collection. Young generation: new objects are allocated here — collected frequently (minor GC) since most objects die young. Old generation: objects that survive multiple GC cycles are promoted here — collected less often (major GC). The mark-and-sweep algorithm: starting from roots (global object, stack, DOM), the GC marks all reachable objects, then sweeps (frees) unmarked objects. Common memory leaks: detached DOM elements (referenced in JS but removed from DOM), forgotten timers holding references, global variable accumulation, and closures retaining large unnecessary data.

Console Debugging.exp: Browser DevTools console is essential for debugging. console.log() prints values. console.error() and console.warn() print with severity icons and stack traces. console.table() renders arrays/objects as sortable tables. console.time()/timeEnd() measures execution. console.group()/groupEnd() nests logs. console.count() counts calls. console.trace() prints the call stack. Using debugger; statement pauses execution. For real debugging, use Sources panel breakpoints — they're more precise than console.log scatterguns.

Performance Debugging.exp: Performance debugging identifies slow code. Use the Performance panel to record activity: look for long tasks (>50ms block main thread), forced reflow (reading layout properties after DOM mutations), and layout thrash (alternating reads/writes in loops). Lighthouse audits performance. Use performance.now() for precise timing. The Network panel shows request timing and waterfall. Avoid: forcing layout with offsetWidth/Height in loops, heavy synchronous work on the main thread, and excessive DOM manipulations without batching.

Debugging Memory Leaks.exp: Memory leaks cause page slowdown and crashes. Use the Memory panel to take heap snapshots — compare 'before' and 'after' to see retained objects. Common patterns: detached DOM nodes (elements referenced in JS but removed from DOM), closures holding large data, global caches without cleanup, forgotten timers/intervals, and event listeners not removed. Look for 'Detached HTML elements' in heap snapshots. The Performance panel's memory timeline shows heap growth over time — steady growth indicates a leak.

Architecture.exp: Kubernetes clusters consist of a control plane managing worker nodes. The control plane runs the API server, scheduler, controller manager, and etcd as core components.

Pods.exp: Pods are the smallest deployable units, containing one or more containers with shared storage and network. Each pod gets a unique cluster IP.
Pods.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest

kubectl Basics.exp: kubectl is the CLI for controlling Kubernetes clusters. Common commands manage resources, view logs, exec into containers, and port-forward.
kubectl Basics.code:
kubectl create deployment myapp --image=nginx
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl logs pod-name
kubectl exec -it pod-name -- /bin/sh

Namespaces.exp: Namespaces provide virtual cluster isolation for multi-tenant environments. Resources in one namespace are invisible to other namespaces by default.
Namespaces.code:
kubectl create namespace staging
kubectl get pods --namespace=staging
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging

Deployments.exp: Deployments manage ReplicaSets and provide declarative updates with rolling updates, rollbacks, and scaling capabilities.
Deployments.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.21

StatefulSets.exp: StatefulSets manage stateful applications with stable network identities, ordered deployment, and persistent storage per pod.
StatefulSets.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
spec:
  serviceName: "db"
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:13
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data

DaemonSets.exp: DaemonSets ensure all or selected nodes run a copy of a pod, ideal for logging, monitoring, and networking agents that run on every node.
DaemonSets.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fluentd
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: fluentd
        image: fluent/fluentd:v1.16

Jobs & CronJobs.exp: Jobs run a pod to completion, useful for batch processing and migrations. CronJobs run jobs on a recurring schedule using cron syntax.
Jobs & CronJobs.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: myapp:latest
        command: ["node", "migrate.js"]
      restartPolicy: Never
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: cleanup
            image: alpine
            command: ["sh", "-c", "find /data -delete"]

ClusterIP.exp: ClusterIP exposes a service on an internal cluster IP accessible only within the cluster. It is the default Service type for internal communication.
ClusterIP.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80

NodePort.exp: NodePort exposes a service on each node's IP at a static port, making it accessible externally via nodeIP:nodePort.
NodePort.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
  - port: 80
    nodePort: 30080

LoadBalancer.exp: LoadBalancer provisions an external load balancer from cloud providers and assigns a public IP for internet-facing services.
LoadBalancer.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Ingress.exp: Ingress exposes HTTP/S routes to services with host/path-based routing, TLS termination, and virtual hosting.
Ingress.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - host: myapp.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: myapp
            port:
              number: 80

Network Policies.exp: Network Policies control traffic flow between pods using label selectors and port rules. By default all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed.
Network Policies.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - port: 8080

ConfigMaps.exp: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs or files that pods consume as environment variables or volumes.
ConfigMaps.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_ENV: production
  APP_DEBUG: "false"

Secrets.exp: Secrets store sensitive data like passwords and API keys base64-encoded. They are injected into pods as environment variables or mounted volumes.
Secrets.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
type: Opaque
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=

kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=password123

Environment Variables.exp: Environment variables in pods reference ConfigMaps and Secrets directly or via configMapKeyRef and secretKeyRef selectors.
Environment Variables.code:
containers:
- name: app
  env:
  - name: APP_ENV
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: APP_ENV
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: db-secret
        key: password

ResourceQuotas.exp: ResourceQuotas limit total resource consumption per namespace, preventing any single team or app from exhausting cluster resources.
ResourceQuotas.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "50"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"

LimitRanges.exp: LimitRanges set minimum and maximum resource constraints per pod or container within a namespace, preventing runaway resource usage.
LimitRanges.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
spec:
  limits:
  - max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: 2Gi
    min:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: 256Mi
    type: Container

Volumes.exp: Container volumes provide temporary or persistent storage attached to pods. Volume types include emptyDir, hostPath, and cloud disks.
Volumes.code:
volumes:
- name: data
  emptyDir: {}
containers:
- name: app
  volumeMounts:
  - mountPath: /data
    name: data

PersistentVolumes.exp: PersistentVolumes are cluster-wide storage resources provisioned by administrators or dynamically via StorageClass.
PersistentVolumes.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data

PVCs.exp: PersistentVolumeClaims request storage resources from a PersistentVolume, binding to matching volumes based on capacity and access modes.
PVCs.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi

StorageClass.exp: StorageClass provisions PersistentVolumes dynamically based on cloud provider storage types like SSD, HDD, or custom parameters.
StorageClass.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd

HPA.exp: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically scales pod replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics from Prometheus.
HPA.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Pods
    pods:
      metric:
        name: requests_per_second
      target:
        type: AverageValue
        averageValue: 1000

VPA.exp: Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts CPU and memory requests for pods based on actual usage, improving resource efficiency.
VPA.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: app
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: Auto
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
    - containerName: '*'
      minAllowed:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 256Mi
      maxAllowed:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 8Gi

Cluster Autoscaler.exp: Cluster Autoscaler automatically adds or removes nodes in a cloud provider's node group based on pending pod resource requests.
Cluster Autoscaler.code:
# Cluster Autoscaler scales the node group when pods can't be scheduled
# AWS: deploy to EKS with IAM role
# GCP: enable node auto-provisioning
# Azure: enable cluster autoscaler in AKS

kubectl get nodes # Check current nodes

Helm Basics.exp: Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. Charts package YAML templates into reusable, configurable releases with versioning.
Helm Basics.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm install my-release bitnami/nginx
helm list
helm uninstall my-release

Chart Structure.exp: Helm charts follow a standard directory structure. Values.yaml provides defaults, and templates use Go templating for dynamic resource generation.
Chart Structure.code:
mychart/
  Chart.yaml          # Metadata: name, version, description
  values.yaml         # Default configuration values
  templates/          # Go template YAML files
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    _helpers.tpl       # Named templates (partials)
  charts/             # Subchart dependencies
  crds/               # Custom Resource Definitions

Values & Templates.exp: Helm templates use Go template syntax with Sprig functions. Values are injected from values.yaml or --set CLI flags.
Values & Templates.code:
# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        resources:
          {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 10 }}

Helm Hooks.exp: Hooks run actions at specific points in a release lifecycle: pre/post install, upgrade, delete. Useful for database migrations and validation.
Helm Hooks.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  annotations:
    helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade
    helm.sh/hook-weight: "-5"
    helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: myapp:latest
        command: ["node", "migrate.js"]

CRDs.exp: Custom Resource Definitions extend the Kubernetes API with custom resources that behave like built-in objects.
CRDs.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Database
    plural: databases
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              engine:
                type: string
              version:
                type: string

Operators.exp: Operators automate application management by extending Kubernetes with custom controllers. They watch CRD resources and reconcile desired state.

Service Mesh.exp: Service meshes like Istio provide traffic management, security, and observability for microservices. They use sidecar proxies to intercept network traffic.
Service Mesh.code:
# Istio features:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
spec:
  hosts:
  - myapp
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /v2
    route:
    - destination:
        host: myapp-v2
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: myapp-v1

# Traffic splitting (canary)
kind: DestinationRule
spec:
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2

RBAC.exp: Role-Based Access Control restricts API access via Roles (namespace-scoped) and ClusterRoles (cluster-scoped) bound to users or ServiceAccounts.
RBAC.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

ServiceAccounts.exp: ServiceAccounts provide identities for pods to authenticate with the Kubernetes API, used with RBAC for fine-grained permissions.
ServiceAccounts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: my-app-sa
---
# Pod using the SA
spec:
  serviceAccountName: my-app-sa

Pod Security.exp: Pod Security Standards (restricted, baseline, privileged) enforce security contexts at the namespace level, preventing privileged containers.
Pod Security.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: baseline

Metrics Server.exp: Metrics Server collects resource utilization data from kubelet and exposes it via the Metrics API, enabling kubectl top and HPA.

Prometheus.exp: Prometheus monitors Kubernetes with time-series metrics collection, alerting, and Grafana dashboards for visualization.
Prometheus.code:
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack

Logging.exp: Logging in Kubernetes uses fluentd or Loki to collect container logs and forward them to Elasticsearch, Loki, or cloud logging services.
Logging.code:
# View logs
kubectl logs -l app=myapp --tail=100
kubectl logs pod-name --previous

# Structured logging
# Use JSON log format in applications
# Deploy fluent-bit DaemonSet to collect logs
# Send to Elasticsearch or Loki

What is Kotlin.exp: Kotlin is a modern, statically-typed language that runs on the JVM, JS, and Native targets. It's concise, safe, and fully interoperable with Java.

Kotlin Syntax.exp: Kotlin omits semicolons and uses `fun` for functions, `val` for read-only references, and `var` for mutable ones. Types come after colons.
Kotlin Syntax.code:
val name: String = "Doge"
var age = 5
fun greet() = "Hello"
println("$name is $age")

Variables & Types.exp: Kotlin infers types. `val` (immutable like final) and `var` (mutable). Basic types: String, Int, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Char, Byte, Short.
Variables & Types.code:
val pi = 3.14159
var counter = 0
val visible: Boolean = true
val items = listOf(1, 2, 3)
println(pi::class.simpleName)

Null Safety.exp: Kotlin eliminates null pointer exceptions with nullable types (`?`), safe calls (`?.`), Elvis operator (`?:`), and the not-null assertion (`!!`).
Null Safety.code:
var name: String? = null
println(name?.length)
println(name ?: "Default")
name = "Doge"
println(name!!.length)

Kotlin Playground.exp: The Kotlin Playground is an online IDE to experiment with Kotlin code. It supports multiplatform targets, embedded snippets, and sharing via URLs.

Multiplatform Overview.exp: Kotlin Multiplatform shares business logic across JVM, JS, iOS, Android, and Native. Write once in shared modules; platform code in target modules.

Project Structure.exp: Standard Kotlin projects use Gradle with `src/main/kotlin` and `src/test/kotlin`. Multiplatform adds `commonMain`, `jvmMain`, `iosMain` source sets.
Project Structure.code:
Project/
 ├── build.gradle.kts
 ├── settings.gradle.kts
 └── src/
    ├── main/kotlin/
    │   └── Main.kt
    └── test/kotlin/
        └── MainTest.kt

If & When expressions.exp: `if` and `when` are expressions that return values. `when` replaces Java's switch and supports smart casts, ranges, and arbitrary conditions.
If & When expressions.code:
val score = 85
val grade = when {
    score >= 90 -> 'A'
    score >= 80 -> 'B'
    else -> 'F'
}
val max = if (a > b) a else b
println(grade)

for & while Loops.exp: `for` iterates over ranges, collections, or anything with an iterator. `while` and `do..while` work as expected. Ranges use `..`, `until`, `downTo`, `step`.

Range & Progression.exp: Ranges (`1..10`) define intervals. Progressions control step direction. Use `in` to check membership, `until` for exclusive end.
Range & Progression.code:
val closed = 1..5
val half = 1 until 5
val descending = 5 downTo 1
val step = 0..10 step 2
println(3 in closed)
println(3 in half)

Equality Checks.exp: `==` calls `equals()` (structural equality). `===` checks referential identity. `!=` and `!==` are the negated forms.
Equality Checks.code:
val a = listOf(1, 2)
val b = listOf(1, 2)
val c = a
println(a == b)   // true — structural
println(a === b)  // false — different references
println(a === c)  // true — same reference

Exception Handling.exp: Use `try-catch-finally`. Kotlin has no checked exceptions. `catch` blocks can filter by exception type, and `finally` always executes.

try as Expression.exp: `try` is an expression in Kotlin. It returns the last expression in the `try` block or the matching `catch` block. Use `finally` for side effects.

Function Declaration.exp: Functions use `fun` with explicit return types. Expression bodies omit braces. Single-expression functions infer the return type automatically.

Default & Named Args.exp: Parameters can have default values. Named arguments allow skipping or reordering parameters, improving readability for functions with many parameters.
Default & Named Args.code:
fun createUser(name: String, age: Int = 18, active: Boolean = true) {}
createUser("Alice")
createUser("Bob", active = false)
createUser(age = 25, name = "Charlie")

Lambda & Higher-Order.exp: Lambdas are function literals. Higher-order functions take or return functions. Trailing lambda syntax removes parentheses for clean DSL-like code.

Extension Functions.exp: Add new functions to existing classes without inheritance. Extensions are resolved statically — they don't actually modify the class.
Extension Functions.code:
fun String.isEmail() = this.contains('@') && this.contains('.')
fun List<Int>.product() = fold(1) { acc, i -> acc * i }

println("test@example.com".isEmail())
println(listOf(2, 3, 4).product())

Infix Functions.exp: Infix functions are called without dot or parens. Single-parameter member or extension functions marked with `infix`. Common in DSLs.
Infix Functions.code:
infix fun Int.times(str: String) = str.repeat(this)
println(3 times "Ha ")  // Ha Ha Ha

// Built-in: to
val map = mapOf(1 to "one", 2 to "two")

Operator Overloading.exp: Kotlin allows overloading operators like `+`, `-`, `*`, `[]`, `()` via functions named `plus`, `minus`, `times`, `get`, `invoke`.
Operator Overloading.code:
data class Vector(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    operator fun plus(other: Vector) = Vector(x + other.x, y + other.y)
    operator fun get(index: Int) = if (index == 0) x else y
}
val v1 = Vector(1, 2)
val v2 = Vector(3, 4)
println(v1 + v2)  // Vector(x=4, y=6)

tailrec.exp: `tailrec` optimises recursive functions into iterative loops when the recursive call is in tail position. No stack overflow risk.

Inline Functions.exp: `inline` inlines the function body at call sites, avoiding lambda object allocation. Use for higher-order functions with lambda parameters.

Lists & Arrays.exp: `listOf` creates read-only lists, `mutableListOf` for mutable. `arrayOf` for arrays. Lists are covariant; arrays are invariant.
Lists & Arrays.code:
val readOnly = listOf("a", "b", "c")
val mutable = mutableListOf("a", "b")
mutable.add("d")
val arr = arrayOf(1, 2, 3)
println(readOnly[1])
println(mutable)

Maps & Sets.exp: `mapOf`/`mutableMapOf` for key-value pairs. `setOf`/`mutableSetOf` for unique elements. Immutable by default.
Maps & Sets.code:
val map = mapOf("key1" to 1, "key2" to 2)
val set = setOf(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
val mutableMap = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
mutableMap["Doge"] = 5
println(map["key1"])
println(set)

Sequences.exp: Sequences provide lazy evaluation for collection chains. Use `asSequence()` for large datasets to avoid intermediate list allocations.

Functional Operations.exp: Kotlin provides rich functional APIs: map, filter, reduce, fold, flatMap, sortedBy, distinct, zip, unzip, associate, and more.
Functional Operations.code:
val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
println(nums.map { it * 2 })
println(nums.filter { it % 2 == 0 })
println(nums.fold(0) { acc, i -> acc + i })
println(nums.flatMap { listOf(it, -it) })
println(nums.associateWith { it * it })

Grouping & Partitioning.exp: `groupBy` groups elements by a key selector. `partition` splits into two lists based on a predicate. `groupingBy` for eager grouping.

Windowed & Chunked.exp: `chunked(size)` splits collection into fixed-size lists. `windowed(size)` creates sliding windows. Both support partial windows and steps.

Element Operations.code:
val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
println(nums.first { it > 1 })    // 2
println(nums.singleOrNull { it > 5 }) // null
println(nums.take(2))             // [1, 2]
println(nums.drop(2))             // [3, 2, 1]
println(nums.distinct())          // [1, 2, 3]

Class Basics.exp: Classes use `class` with a primary constructor in the header. Properties declared in the constructor are automatically generated with getters/setters.
Class Basics.code:
class Person(val name: String, var age: Int)
val p = Person("Alice", 30)
println(p.name)
p.age = 31

Inheritance & Interfaces.exp: Classes are final by default — use `open` to allow inheritance. Override methods with `override`. Interfaces can have abstract and default implementations.

Data Classes.exp: `data class` automatically generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions. Perfect for DTOs and value objects.
Data Classes.code:
data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)
val u1 = User(1, "Alice")
val u2 = u1.copy(name = "Bob")
println(u1)
println(u1 == User(1, "Alice"))
val (id, name) = u1  // destructuring

Sealed Classes & Interfaces.exp: Sealed types restrict hierarchies to a fixed set of subclasses defined in the same file. Perfect for representing states or algebraic data types.

Object & Companion.exp: `object` declares a singleton. `companion object` defines static-like members inside a class. Objects can also implement interfaces as anonymous instances.

Value & Inline Classes.exp: `value class` wraps a single value without heap allocation overhead. Use `@JvmInline` for JVM interop. Prevents primitive boxing in many cases.

Type Aliases.exp: Type aliases provide alternative names for existing types, improving readability without introducing new types. Useful for function types and complex generics.
Type Aliases.code:
typealias UserMap = Map<Int, User>
typealias Predicate<T> = (T) -> Boolean
typealias Callback = (Result) -> Unit

val users: UserMap = mapOf(1 to User(1, "Alice"))
val isAdult: Predicate<Int> = { it >= 18 }

Delegation.exp: `by` delegates interface implementation to another object. `by lazy` for lazy initialization. Delegated properties via `observable`, `vetoable`, or custom delegates.

Abstract Classes & Nested.exp: Abstract classes can have constructors, state, and both abstract and concrete methods. Nested/inner classes differ by whether they hold an outer reference.

Generic Functions & Classes.exp: Generics enable type-safe code with type parameters. Functions and classes can be parameterised with one or more type parameters.
Generic Functions & Classes.code:
class Box<T>(val value: T)
fun <T> List<T>.secondOrNull(): T? = if (size >= 2) this[1] else null

val intBox = Box(42)
val strBox = Box("Hello")
println(listOf(1, 2, 3).secondOrNull())

Variance \u2014 out & in.exp: `out T` makes a type covariant (producer). `in T` makes it contravariant (consumer). Declaration-site variance avoids wildcards.

Reified Type Parameters.exp: `reified` in inline functions preserves the type at runtime, enabling `is` checks, T::class, and `createInstance()` without passing Class<T>.
Reified Type Parameters.code:
inline fun <reified T> isA(value: Any) = value is T
inline fun <reified T> className() = T::class.simpleName

println(isA<String>("hello"))  // true
println(className<Int>())       // "Int"

Star Projections.exp: `*` for unknown type arguments. `MutableList<*>` is a mutable list of unknown type — safe to read as `Any?`, but not to write.

Type Bounds & Where.exp: `T : UpperBound` constrains type parameters. Multiple bounds use `where` clause. Use `Nothing` for impossible values.
Type Bounds & Where.code:
fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf(a: T, b: T) = if (a > b) a else b

interface Serializable
fun <T> copy(value: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Serializable
    = value

println(maxOf(3, 7))

Launch & Async.exp: `launch` fires a fire-and-forget coroutine. `async` starts a coroutine that returns a `Deferred` result via `await()`. Both are non-blocking.

Dispatchers.exp: Dispatchers determine thread pools: Default for CPU, IO for I/O, Main for UI, Unconfined for testing. `withContext` switches dispatchers.

Structured Concurrency.exp: Coroutines lifetime ties to parent scope. Cancellation propagates downward; errors bubble up. `coroutineScope` waits for all children to complete.

supervisorScope.exp: supervisorScope isolates child failures: one child's exception doesn't cancel siblings or parent. Use for parallel independent work.

Coroutine Context & Scope.exp: CoroutineContext combines Dispatcher, Job, and elements. `CoroutineScope` manages lifecycle. `Job` tracks lifecycle of a coroutine.

Cancellation & Timeouts.exp: Cancellation is cooperative — check `isActive` or use `yield()`. `withTimeout` throws TimeoutCancellationException. `withTimeoutOrNull` returns null.

Exception Handling.exp: Uncaught exceptions cancel parent. Use `try-catch` inside coroutine, or `CoroutineExceptionHandler` for top-level exceptions.

coroutineScope vs runBlocking.exp: `coroutineScope` suspends without blocking a thread. `runBlocking` blocks the current thread for bridge mode. Use coroutineScope in suspend functions.

Flow Basics.exp: Flow is a cold async stream. Use `flow { }` builder with `emit()`, collect with `collect()`. Cold means nothing happens until collected.

Flow Builders.exp: Additional builders: `flowOf` for fixed values, `asFlow` on collections/ranges, `channelFlow` for concurrent emission, `callbackFlow` for callback APIs.

Flow Operators.exp: Intermediate operators: map, filter, transform, take, drop, debounce, sample, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest.

StateFlow.exp: StateFlow holds observable state. Hot flow — always has a value. Emits only distinct values. Ideal for ViewModels and UI state.

SharedFlow.exp: SharedFlow emits events to multiple collectors. Hot flow with replay cache. Use `MutableSharedFlow` for one-shot events like toasts.

CallbackFlow.exp: callbackFlow bridges callback-based APIs into Flows. Use `send()` inside, `awaitClose()` to clean up. Context preserving.

Combining Flows.exp: `zip` pairs elements one-to-one. `combine` merges latest values. `merge` interleaves multiple flows into one.

Context Receivers.exp: Context receivers declare dependency on context types without inheritance. Functions can receive multiple contexts for modular APIs.

Contracts.exp: Contracts tell the compiler about function behavior. Use `callsInPlace`, `returnsNotNull`, `implies` for smarter analysis and fewer warnings.

@JvmInline & JvmAnnotations.exp: `@JvmInline` marks inline classes on JVM. `@JvmStatic`, `@JvmOverloads`, `@JvmField`, `@Throws` control Kotlin-to-Java interop.

Type Erasure & Reified.exp: JVM erases generic types at runtime. `inline` + `reified` preserves them. `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")` for manual casts.

Reflection.exp: Kotlin reflection (`::class`, `::memberProperty`) inspects types at runtime. Use `memberProperties`, `functions`, `annotations` for meta-programming.
Reflection.code:
data class Person(val name: String, val age: Int)

val kClass = Person::class
println(kClass.simpleName)  // Person
println(kClass.memberProperties)

val prop = Person::name
val person = Person("Alice", 30)
println(prop.get(person))  // Alice

Annotations.exp: Kotlin annotations: `@Target`, `@Retention`, custom annotation classes. Apply to classes, functions, properties, or expressions with `@file:`, `@get:` etc.

Destructuring Declarations.exp: Destructuring decomposes objects into variables with `componentN()` functions. Data classes auto-generate them; custom classes can implement operator fun componentN().

KMP Overview.exp: Kotlin Multiplatform shares logic across platforms. Business logic, data models, and networking in commonMain; platform UIs in platform-specific source sets.

expect/actual.exp: `expect` declares platform-agnostic API in common code. `actual` provides platform-specific implementations. Compiler ensures all expects have actuals.

Common Code.exp: CommonMain uses Kotlin stdlib-common, kotlinx.coroutines, kotlinx.serialization. Shared data models, repository logic, and ViewModels live here.

Platform-Specific Code.exp: Platform source sets (jvmMain, iosMain, jsMain) provide actual implementations. Access platform APIs and libraries from each target.

KMP Libraries & Frameworks.exp: KMP has a growing ecosystem: Ktor for networking, SQLDelight for databases, Koin for DI, kotlinx.serialization, and Compose Multiplatform for UI.

kotlin.test Basics.exp: `kotlin.test` provides `@Test`, `assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertNull`, `assertThrows`. Annotations work with JUnit 4/5, and multiplatform testing.

Kotest.exp: Kotest is a multiplatform test framework with behavior specs, property-based testing, matchers, and data-driven tests.

MockK.exp: MockK is a Kotlin-first mocking library. Supports coroutines, spies, relaxed mocks, capturing, and verification with expressive DSL.

Property-Based Testing.exp: Property testing verifies invariants across many random inputs. Kotest and kotlin-check use generators (`Arb`) and properties (`forAll`).

Coroutine Testing.exp: `kotlinx-coroutines-test` provides `runTest`, `TestScope`, and virtual time. `advanceTimeBy`, `advanceUntilIdle` skip delays instantly.

JUnit 5 Integration.exp: Kotlin works seamlessly with JUnit 5. Use `@ParameterizedTest`, `@MethodSource`, `@ValueSource` with Kotlin collections and lambdas.

Gradle Kotlin DSL.exp: Gradle Kotlin DSL provides type-safe build scripts with autocomplete and refactoring. Use `build.gradle.kts` with `plugins { }` and `dependencies { }`.

Version Catalogs.exp: Version catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` centralise dependency versions. Access via `libs.some.dependency` in build scripts.

buildSrc & Convention Plugins.exp: buildSrc stores shared build logic as Kotlin sources. Convention plugins apply common configurations across modules — DRY for multi-module projects.

KSP & K2 Compiler.exp: KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) is a compiler plugin for annotation processing. K2 compiler (1.9+) offers faster compilation and improved type inference.

Dokka & Tooling.exp: Dokka generates Kotlin documentation (KDoc). Supports multiplatform projects, HTML/MD/JavaDoc outputs. Often used with Gradle's `dokka` plugin.

Scope Functions Deep.exp: Kotlin's five scope functions differ by receiver (this vs it) and return value (context vs lambda result). `let` for transformations, `apply` for configuration, `run` for computations, `with` for grouping calls, `also` for side effects.

Lambda with Receiver.exp: Lambda with receiver allows calling methods on an implicit `this` inside the lambda. The `receiver` type is the context. Used by `apply`, `run`, `with`, `buildString`, and custom DSLs. From Kotlin in Action.

Type-Safe Builders & @DslMarker.exp: Type-safe builders (from Kotlin in Action) use nested lambdas with receivers. `@DslMarker` restricts implicit receivers to the nearest enclosing scope, preventing ambiguous `this` in nested builders.

SAM Conversion.exp: Single Abstract Method (SAM) conversion lets you pass a lambda where a Java functional interface is expected. Kotlin has built-in function types, so SAM conversion mainly applies to Java interop. From Head First Kotlin.

Java Interop.exp: Kotlin is 100% interoperable with Java. Key annotations: `@JvmStatic` for static methods, `@JvmOverloads` for overloaded methods, `@JvmField` for fields, `@Throws` for checked exceptions, `@JvmName` to resolve signature clashes.

Kotlin Idioms.exp: Common Kotlin idioms from Head First Kotlin and Kotlin in Action: default arguments for builders, `require`/`check` for preconditions, `use` for Closeable, `takeIf`/`takeUnless` for conditional returns, `TODO()` for stubs, `runCatching` for try-catch expressions.

Jetpack Compose Basics.exp: Jetpack Compose is a declarative UI toolkit. State-driven, composable functions with `@Composable`, `remember`, `mutableStateOf`, and modifiers.

ViewModel & State.exp: ViewModel survives configuration changes. Use `viewModel()` in Compose, expose `StateFlow`, and collect as Compose state with `collectAsState()`.

LiveData & StateFlow.exp: LiveData is lifecycle-aware. StateFlow is the coroutines-native alternative. Use `asLiveData()` to bridge StateFlow to LiveData for legacy code.

Room Database.exp: Room is a SQLite ORM. Use `@Entity`, `@Dao`, `@Database`. Coroutines support via suspend functions and Flow return types in DAOs.

Retrofit & Networking.exp: Retrofit type-safe HTTP client used with Kotlin coroutines. Define `suspend` functions in API interfaces. Use kotlinx.serialization or Moshi for JSON.

Navigation Compose.exp: Navigation Compose provides type-safe navigation in Compose. Define routes with `NavHost`, navigate with `navController.navigate()`, pass safe args.

Mobile Game Landscape.exp: Mobile gaming is the largest segment of the games industry. Phones and tablets offer unique constraints: touch input, limited battery, thermal throttling, fragmented hardware, and interrupt-driven usage (calls, notifications). Success requires designing for short sessions, efficient resource use, and broad device compatibility. The major engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot) all support mobile export with platform-specific optimizations.

Choosing a Mobile Engine.exp: Unity dominates mobile with 60%+ market share — excellent cross-platform support, massive asset store, and C# scripting. Unreal Engine targets high-end mobile with stunning visuals but heavier APK sizes and higher device requirements. Godot is lightweight, open-source, and exports to Android/iOS with minimal overhead but a smaller mobile community. For 2D mobile games, Godot or Unity 2D are great choices. For 3D, Unity balances quality and performance; Unreal excels on flagship devices.

Mobile Build Pipeline.exp: Building for mobile involves multiple steps: code compilation, asset compression, texture format conversion (ETC2 for Android, PVRTC/ASTC for iOS), architecture-specific binaries (ARM64, ARMv7), and final packaging. Unity uses the Build Settings window or command-line builds. Android produces APK or AAB (Android App Bundle). iOS produces IPA via Xcode. Each platform requires specific SDKs, NDKs, and provisioning profiles.
Mobile Build Pipeline.code:
# Android build (Unity CLI)
/Applications/Unity/Unity.app/Contents/MacOS/Unity \
  -batchmode -quit \
  -projectPath /path/to/project \
  -executeMethod BuildScript.AndroidBuild \
  -buildTarget Android \
  -logFile build.log

# iOS build (xcodebuild)
xcodebuild \
  -project MyGame.xcodeproj \
  -scheme MyGame \
  -configuration Release \
  -archivePath MyGame.xcarchive \
  archive

Touch Events & Multi-Touch.exp: Mobile input is fundamentally different from mouse/keyboard. Touch events provide position, phase (began/moved/ended/cancelled), and a unique finger ID for multi-touch. The screen is a direct manipulation surface — what you touch is what you interact with. Input latency on mobile typically ranges from 40-100ms. Always handle the cancelled phase (system interrupts like calls). Maximum simultaneous touches varies from 5-10 depending on device.

Gesture Recognition.exp: Common mobile gestures: tap, double-tap, long-press, swipe, pinch-to-zoom, rotate, drag, flick. Implement gesture recognizers that track touch state over time. A tap is a brief touch/release within a distance threshold (usually < 10px) and time threshold (< 300ms). A swipe requires minimum velocity and distance. Pinch tracks two touch points' distance changes. Use dead zones (small ignored movements) to prevent jitter from noisy touch input.

Virtual Joysticks & Buttons.exp: Virtual controls overlay the screen with touch zones mapped to game actions. Joysticks track a touch point within a radius — the normalized offset from center becomes the input vector. Buttons trigger on touch began within their rect. Place controls in the lower screen thirds (thumb zones) and avoid the notch/camera cutout area. Consider configurable layouts for accessibility. Scale controls relative to screen resolution and aspect ratio.

Haptic Feedback.exp: Haptic feedback improves immersion and confirms actions. Android uses VibrationEffect with amplitude control. iOS uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, UINotificationFeedbackGenerator, and UISelectionFeedbackGenerator for different haptic patterns. Unity's Handheld.Vibrate() provides basic support; plugins like Lofelt provide advanced haptic design. Use haptics sparingly — overuse drains battery and annoys players. Respect system-level haptic settings.

Battery & Thermal Optimization.exp: Mobile devices throttle performance when overheating. CPU/GPU intensive tasks, background networking, and inefficient rendering drain battery. Profile thermal impact: measure temperature rise per operation. Key strategies: reduce CPU frame time (< 16ms for 60fps), minimize GPU overdraw, batch draw calls (< 100), use efficient physics (fewer colliders, simpler shapes), and reduce WiFi/cellular polling. iOS reports thermal state via ProcessInfo.thermalState. Android monitors via PowerManager.

Memory Management.exp: Mobile has limited RAM (2-8GB shared with OS). Texture memory is the biggest consumer: a 2048x2048 RGBA texture = 16MB. Android's onTrimMemory() warns of impending kill. iOS issues memory warnings via didReceiveMemoryWarning. Load assets progressively, unload unused scenes, use mipmaps (saves ~33% GPU memory), and compress textures (ETC2/ASTC). Avoid large contiguous allocations — they fragment the heap. Pool and reuse objects instead of allocate/free cycles.

Adaptive Quality Scaling.exp: Device capabilities vary enormously. Measure GPU fill rate, RAM, and screen resolution at startup, then set quality tiers. Use a quality profile that adjusts: shadow resolution, anti-aliasing, post-processing, texture resolution, draw distance, particle count, and LOD bias. Re-evaluate periodically and when thermal state changes. Unity's QualitySettings and Godot's OS methods support runtime quality changes.

Asset Bundles & Streaming.exp: Mobile games must manage download size and memory. Asset bundles (Unity) or resource packs (Godot) let you split content into on-demand chunks. Initial download should be under 150MB. Stream additional levels, textures, and audio on demand. Use addressable assets for runtime loading with reference counting. Cache downloaded bundles to device storage. Prioritize essential assets (first level, UI) and defer high-res textures and later levels. Use LZ4 compression for faster runtime decompression.

Responsive Layout System.exp: Mobile screens range from 320x480 (old budget) to 1440x3040 (flagship). Use anchor-based layouts that scale relative to screen edges. Avoid absolute pixel positions. Calculate UI scale based on reference resolution (typically 1080p for mobile). Handle safe areas (notch, camera cutout, status bar, gesture bar). Unity's Canvas Scaler with 'Scale With Screen Size' handles most cases. For Godot, use Control nodes with anchors. Always test on a variety of screen sizes.

Mobile UX Patterns for Games.exp: Mobile games thrive on simplicity: short sessions (3-5 minutes), clear goals, immediate feedback. Thumb zones: top = less reachable (menus, info), bottom = thumb-friendly (actions, navigation). Avoid right-edge swipe (system gesture conflict on iOS). Use touch-friendly targets (minimum 44x44pt, ideally 48x48pt). Provide visual feedback on touch (press state, animation). Use onboarding tutorials that respect player agency — let them skip or replay.

Interruptions & State Persistence.exp: Mobile games are frequently interrupted: incoming calls, notifications, app switcher, low battery. Save game state aggressively — on every significant action, not just on graceful exit. Handle OnApplicationPause (Unity) or _notification() with NOTIFICATION_APPLICATION_PAUSED (Godot). Serialize critical state (player position, score, inventory, quest progress) to persistent storage. Use auto-save with a cooldown (every 30s or on checkpoint). On resume, restore state seamlessly without reloading the entire scene.

Handling Mobile Network Conditions.exp: Mobile networks are unreliable: high latency (100-500ms cellular), packet loss, IP address changes, and frequent disconnections (tunnels, elevators). Design for offline-first with sync-on-reconnect. Use TCP for reliable state updates and UDP for real-time gameplay with interpolation/extrapolation. Implement reconnection with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). Detect connection type (WiFi vs cellular) to adjust data usage. Respect metered connections — offer low-data mode.

Offline Mode & Sync.exp: Offline-first architecture lets players continue without connectivity. Queue actions locally, sync when online. Use a local database (SQLite via Unity's SQLite plugin, or IndexedDB for web). Track a sync version per record to resolve conflicts. Last-write-wins works for simple data; CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) for complex multiplayer. Show clear indicators for online/offline state. Never block gameplay waiting for network — use optimistic updates and reconcile later.

Real-Time Multiplayer on Mobile.exp: Mobile real-time multiplayer faces latency, connection drops, and data costs. Use UDP with reliability layers (like ENET or KCP) for fast-paced games. Implement client-side prediction and server reconciliation. For turn-based games, use WebSocket with JSON payloads. Photon, Mirror (Unity), and Nakama are popular mobile netcode solutions. Matchmaking should consider ping (prefer < 100ms), skill rating, and platform (iOS vs Android cross-play). Use delta compression to minimize data per packet.

Ads Integration.exp: Mobile ads come in several formats: banner (static, low eCPM), interstitial (full-screen between levels, medium eCPM), rewarded video (player opts in for reward, highest eCPM), and native (integrated into UI). Major networks: AdMob (Google), Unity Ads, AppLovin, ironSource. Mediation platforms (AdMob Mediation, ironSource) maximize fill rate by routing to the highest-paying network. Implement ad frequency capping (max 3 interstitials per 10 minutes). Never show ads during gameplay — place them at natural breaks (level transitions, menu screens).

In-App Purchases.exp: IAPs include consumables (gems, coins, extra lives), non-consumables (remove ads, full game unlock), and subscriptions (weekly/monthly pass). Apple takes 30% (15% for small businesses under $1M). Google takes 15-30%. Use Unity IAP or a cross-platform purchase library. Always validate receipts server-side to prevent fraud. Implement a store UI that shows prices in local currency. Provide a 'restore purchases' button (required by Apple). Never make the game unplayable without IAP — monetize ethically.

Analytics & Engagement.exp: Track player behavior: session length, retention (D1/D7/D30), conversion rate, average revenue per daily active user (ARPDAU), and funnel analysis (tutorial completion → first purchase → level 5). Use Firebase Analytics, Unity Analytics, or GameAnalytics. Implement event tracking with consistent naming: level_start, level_complete, iap_purchase. Send push notifications for re-engagement (daily rewards, new content). Use A/B testing for pricing and feature changes. Respect GDPR/CCPA privacy requirements.

GPU Architecture for Mobile.exp: Mobile GPUs use tile-based deferred rendering (TBDR) — they split the frame into tiles (typically 16x16 or 32x32), process geometry per tile, then render. This differs from desktop immediate-mode GPUs. Key implications: minimize overdraw (tiles pay for hidden pixels), use fewer but larger triangles, batch draw calls, avoid alpha blending (forces multiple passes), and use power-of-two textures. Apple GPUs (A-series) are TBDR; Qualcomm Adreno uses a hybrid approach. Mali GPUs (ARM) are also tile-based.

Texture Compression & Formats.exp: Mobile texture formats: ETC2 (mandatory for OpenGL ES 3.0+ Android), ASTC (universal, best quality, supported by iOS 9+/Android 10+), PVRTC (legacy iOS), and ETC1 (old Android, no alpha). ASTC is preferred — it offers flexible bitrates (4-12 bpp) and good quality. Always generate mipmaps for 3D scenes (saves GPU memory bandwidth). Compress GUI textures too — uncompressed RGBA at 1080p = 8MB per full-screen texture. Use sprite atlases to batch UI draw calls.

Shader Optimization for Mobile.exp: Mobile shaders are constrained by instruction count (32-128 instructions), limited texture samples (8-16), and no dynamic branching on many GPUs. Use the #pragma target 3.0 minimum. Reduce precision: fixed (11-bit) for colors, half for positions/UVs, float only when necessary. Avoid pow, exp, log, sin, cos in fragment shaders (use lookup textures). Precompute lighting in vertex shaders. Use fewer lights — ideally 1 directional + 0-1 point lights. Bake lighting into lightmaps when possible.

Audio Formats & Compression.exp: OGG uses Vorbis compression for music (good quality/size), MP3 is universally supported but slightly older, AAC offers better quality than MP3 at same bitrate, ADPCM is lossless-ish and fast for short SFX. On mobile, Unity's AudioImporter lets you choose compressed (OGG) for long clips vs ADPCM for short SFX to balance memory vs CPU decode cost. Streaming loads from disk instead of RAM but adds I/O overhead.

Spatial Audio on Mobile.exp: Ambisonics captures full-sphere surround sound; HRTF filters simulate 3D direction using head-related transfer functions. iOS spatial audio leverages AirPods motion tracking for fixed-position sounds. Android spatial audio uses Google's Resonance Audio or Oboe. FMOD and Wwise provide cross-platform spatial audio with occlusion, reverb zones, and dynamic mixing channels tuned for mobile CPU budgets.

Audio Latency & Optimization.exp: iOS audio latency is minimized via AVAudioSession with category .playAndRecord and preferredIOBufferDuration (e.g. 0.005).
