Android uses Oboe or AAudio for low-latency paths. Unity's AudioMixer groups duck music under SFX, apply DSP effects (low-pass on pause), and profile via Audio Profiler. Streaming avoids loading entire clips into RAM but can stutter if I/O spikes; preload short clips as CompressedInMemory.

ARCore & ARKit Basics.exp: ARCore (Android) and ARKit (iOS) enable motion tracking, environmental understanding, and light estimation. ARCore uses visual-inertial odometry (VIO) — fusing camera imagery with IMU data. ARKit uses Visual Inertial Odometry + scene reconstruction with LiDAR on Pro devices. Both provide: plane detection (horizontal/vertical), point clouds, image tracking, object detection (ARKit 3+), and face tracking. Unity AR Foundation abstracts both APIs into a single workflow. Anchor virtual content to real-world positions using trackables.

AR Game Design Patterns.exp: AR games blend digital content with the real world. Design principles: surface alignment (content sits on tables/floors), scale matters (virtual objects should look physically sized), occlusion (hide objects behind real walls — LiDAR helps), lighting consistency (match virtual light to real environment), and persistent anchors (save object positions across sessions). User education is critical — show onboarding that demonstrates scanning surfaces and moving around. Handle low-light conditions gracefully (ARKit provides light estimation). Always provide a non-AR fallback mode.

Core ML & ML Kit.exp: Apple Core ML converts models from PyTorch/TF via coremltools for on-device inference — image classification (MobileNet), object detection (YOLO), pose estimation (OpenPose). Google ML Kit provides ready-to-use APIs for text recognition, face detection, barcode scanning, and pose detection with no custom model needed. In mobile games, use these for photo-based character creators, AR overlays, or cheater detection via screen analysis.

Unity Sentis.exp: Unity Sentis runs ONNX neural networks directly in Unity on mobile GPUs via compute shaders. Load a .sentis model asset, create a Worker (GPUCompute or CPUShader), pass input tensors via TensorFloat, execute inference, and read output tensors. Use cases: real-time pose detection for avatar mirroring, style transfer for visual effects, or AI-driven NPC behavior without server calls.

Model Optimization.exp: Quantization reduces model size and speeds inference: FP16 halves size with minimal accuracy loss, INT8 is 4x smaller but needs calibration. Pruning removes near-zero weights. Core ML conversion uses coremltools with ct.quantize_weights(). TFLite supports dynamic range, FP16, and INT8 quantization. For mobile games, prefer FP16 quantized models (<10MB) to stay under app store limits and hit 30fps inference.
Model Optimization.code:
python
import coremltools as ct
model = ct.convert("pose_model.pt",
  minimum_deployment_target=ct.target.iOS15,
  compute_precision=ct.precision.FLOAT16)
model.save("PoseModel_int8.mlpackage")

// TFLite GPU delegate
val options = Interpreter.Options()
options.addDelegate(GpuDelegate())
val interpreter = Interpreter(modelBuffer, options)

Game Controller Support.exp: MFi (Made for iPhone) controllers, Xbox Wireless, and PlayStation DualShock/DualSense pair via Bluetooth. Unity's Input System auto-detects controllers and maps to common layouts (left stick = Vector2, A/B/X/Y = button). Use Gamepad.current to poll and InputAction bindings for cross-platform prompts; detect device type to switch glyphs (e.g. 'A' on Xbox vs 'X' on PlayStation).

Gyroscope & Motion Sensors.exp: Accelerometer measures linear acceleration (g-force), gyroscope measures angular rotation rate, magnetometer acts as digital compass. Unity's Input.gyro gives attitude as a Quaternion for tilt steering (racing games), userAcceleration for step counting, and rotationRate for camera look. Must enable Input.gyro.enabled and typically set Input.compensateSensors = true for screen orientation.

Foldable & Adaptive Screens.exp: Foldable devices (Samsung Galaxy Z Fold, Pixel Fold) require handling screen continuity (activity recreates on fold), hinge angle sensor (half-fold mode for laptop-style gameplay), and display cutout (notch/punch-hole) insets. Samsung DeX and multi-window mean the game must handle arbitrary aspect ratios. Unity's Screen.safeArea gives the non-cutout rect; use OnApplicationFocus or ScreenOrientation changes to relayout.

String Management.exp: Use .po/.json/.resx files for string storage. Unity Localization package provides StringTable assets and LocalizedString variables. Plural rules handle locale-specific forms via Smart Strings. Format strings with {0} placeholders and pass variables at runtime. Set locale from system language or player preference.

RTL & Complex Scripts.exp: Arabic and Hebrew require right-to-left text rendering. TextMeshPro provides the RTL Editor for correct shaping of Arabic/Persian/Urdu. Hindi uses Devanagari script with complex ligatures — TMP handles OpenType shaping. CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) text needs appropriate fallback fonts assigned in TMP Font Asset. Set text direction via TMP_Text.isRightToLeft. Build fallback chain fonts for missing glyphs.

Cultural Adaptation.exp: Adapt content for regional sensitivity — avoid offensive imagery, flags, or political symbols. Format dates per culture: en-US uses MM/dd/yyyy, most EU uses dd/MM/yyyy. Format currency with ISO 4217 codes and locale-aware symbols ($, Euro, Yen). Set regional pricing tiers (e.g., India, Brazil, Turkey have different purchasing power). Pseudolocalization wraps strings with accents to test layout expansion.

Firebase Cloud Messaging.exp: FCM sends push notifications via Firebase. On Android 8+ you must register notification channels with importance levels. Data messages (onMessageReceived in background) vs notification messages (auto-displayed). Manage instance tokens for targeted push; subscribe to topics for group broadcasts. Unity Firebase SDK handles token registration and message forwarding to the game object.

Apple Push Notification Service.exp: APNs delivers notifications to iOS devices via device tokens. Implement UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate to handle incoming pushes. Notification Content Extensions allow custom UI within notification banners. Define notification categories with actions (accept/decline/snooze). Rich media attachments include images, video, and audio in the notification payload.

Deep Linking.exp: Android App Links (verified HTTP intents) and iOS Universal Links open your app directly from URLs. Deferred deep linking attributes installs: user clicks a link before installing, then gets routed to the correct content post-install. Firebase Dynamic Links handle this cross-platform. Handle incoming links at runtime by parsing query parameters and navigating to the relevant screen.

Google Play Games Services.exp: GPGS v2 for Unity provides sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, and Saved Games. Authenticate via PlayGamesPlatform.Instance.Authenticate. Report achievements incrementally or unlock them. Submit scores to leaderboards. Saved Games use ISavedGameClient with conflict resolution. Real-time multiplayer sends reliable/unreliable messages. Player Stats API returns session metrics.

Apple Game Center.exp: GKLocalPlayer.local.authenticateHandler triggers the sign-in dialog. Report scores via GKLeaderboard and achievements via GKAchievement. Real-time matchmaking uses GKMatchRequest and GKMatchmaker; turn-based matches use GKTurnBasedMatch. Listen for player state changes and match events. Leaderboard and achievement IDs must match App Store Connect configuration.

Cross-Platform Social Features.exp: Abstract social services behind a platform-agnostic interface so game code never calls GPGS or Game Center directly. The abstraction exposes sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, cloud saves, friend lists, and invites. Each platform (Google, Apple) implements the interface. The game logic calls the singleton SocialManager, making porting to new platforms trivial.

Battle Pass & Season Pass Design.exp: A battle pass has tiers (50-100 levels) each requiring set XP. Free track gives basic rewards; premium track (one-time purchase per season) adds exclusive skins, currency, and items. FOMO (fear of missing out) drives engagement as season-exclusive content disappears. Analytics track pass completion rate, tier drop-off, and average XP earned per day to tune progression.

Virtual Economy Balancing.exp: Define soft currency (gold, coins) earned via gameplay and hard currency (gems) from purchases. Premium currency bridges free and paid. Inflation occurs when too much currency enters the system — sinks (upgrade costs, cosmetics) drain it; faucets (quest rewards, daily login) inject it. Balance sinks vs faucets per player segment. Price virtual goods based on perceived value.

Subscription Models.exp: Apple auto-renewable subscriptions use StoreKit 2 with SKProduct. Periods: weekly, monthly, yearly. Introductory pricing (free trial, discounted period) increases conversion. Subscription groups allow users to subscribe to one of several options. Track retention via renewal rate and churn. Offer subscriber-only perks (daily bonus multiplier, exclusive items, no ads).

Code Obfuscation & Tamper Protection.exp: Protect your Unity game from reverse engineering by applying ProGuard/R8 rules to strip unused code and obfuscate managed assemblies. Use IL2CPP over Mono to convert C# to C++ before native compilation, making memory inspection far more difficult. Compute runtime integrity checks via SHA256, and detect rooted/jailbroken devices by checking for common binary paths and su binaries.

Network Security.exp: Implement SSL pinning to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks by embedding the server certificate or public key hash directly in the client. On Android use OkHttp's CertificatePinner; on iOS implement URLSession didReceiveChallenge to validate the server trust against a known key. Encrypt payloads with AES-GCM before sending, add timestamps and nonces to prevent replay attacks.

Anti-Cheat for Mobile Games.exp: Detect memory scanners by checking for suspicious process maps. Guard against speed hacks by comparing deltaTime against wall-clock time across multiple frames. Detect emulator environments by inspecting Build.FINGERPRINT, Build.HARDWARE, and Build.MODEL on Android. Encrypt and obfuscate memory values at runtime to reduce the attack surface.

Fastlane Automation.exp: Streamline your Unity mobile deployment pipeline with Fastlane lanes for building, testing, code signing, and uploading. Use match to manage iOS certificates and provisioning profiles across your team via a private Git repo. The gym action compiles your iOS .ipa, scan runs XCTests, and pilot uploads to TestFlight. For Android use gradle and supply to publish to Play Console.
Fastlane Automation.code:
// Fastlane Fastfile
lane :build_ios do |options|
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  gym(
    project: "Builds/iOS/Unity-iPhone.xcworkspace",
    scheme: "Unity-iPhone",
    export_method: "app-store"
  )
  pilot(upload: true)
end

lane :build_android do |options|
  gradle(task: "assembleRelease", project_dir: "Builds/Android/")
  supply(track: "internal",
    apk_paths: ["Builds/Android/launcher/build/outputs/apk/release/launcher-release.aab"])
end

GitHub Actions Pipelines.exp: Define reusable YAML workflows that build Unity games for both iOS and Android triggered by pushes, pull requests, or nightly runs. Use matrix strategies to test across device families and Unity versions. Cache the Library folder to cut build times by 50%. Store .ipa and .aab files as workflow artifacts, then deploy to TestFlight or Play Console via Fastlane.
GitHub Actions Pipelines.code:
# .github/workflows/unity-mobile.yml
name: Unity Mobile Build
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        target: [Android, iOS]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: Library
          key: Library-${{ matrix.target }}-${{ hashFiles('Assets/**') }}
      - name: Unity Build
        uses: game-ci/unity-builder@v4
        with:
          targetPlatform: ${{ matrix.target }}
      - name: Upload Artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: Build-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: build/${{ matrix.target }}

Automated Mobile Testing.exp: Run game-loop tests on Firebase Test Lab to validate core gameplay across hundreds of real Android devices. For iOS, automate XCUITest flows that simulate taps, swipes, and IAP purchases via Xcode Cloud or Fastlane scan. Execute Unity Test Framework tests on device by building a test runner APK/IPA. Compare screenshots per-commit against golden images to catch visual regressions.

Keyword Research & Metadata.exp: Optimize your Google Play title (30 chars), subtitle (30 chars), and short description (80 chars) to include high-volume, low-competition keywords. On iOS the keyword field (100 chars) is comma-separated. Use Sensor Tower, AppTweak, or Google Play Console keyword reports to discover competitor terms. Refresh metadata seasonally and when launching new content.
Keyword Research & Metadata.code:
// Python keyword analysis
import requests

def analyze_keywords(competitor_id, api_key):
    url = f"https://api.apptweak.io/applications/{competitor_id}/keywords.json"
    response = requests.get(url, headers={"X-AppTweak-Key": api_key})
    keywords = response.json()
    scored = [(kw["keyword"], kw["search_volume"] / max(kw["difficulty"], 1)) for kw in keywords]
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: -x[1])
    return [kw for kw, _ in scored[:20]]

Visual Assets.exp: Design an app icon that reads well at small sizes: single bold subject, vibrant colors, no text. Create screenshot templates showcasing top 3-5 gameplay moments, overlaying UI at the bottom third to avoid safe-area clipping. Produce a preview video (15-30s) that loops automatically. Use Google Play Store Listing Experiments to A/B test icons and screenshots. Localize all assets per region.

Ratings & Reviews Management.exp: Prompt users for ratings at natural engagement milestones (level complete, match win, first purchase) using SKStoreReviewController on iOS and In-App Review API on Google Play. Implement a rate limiter (max once per month) and only show on happy paths. Respond to negative reviews within 24 hours. Track rating trends per build version; investigate if dropping below 4.0 stars.

Device Testing Matrix.exp: Test on a representative device matrix covering: low-end (2GB RAM, 720p), mid-range (4GB, 1080p), high-end (8GB+, 1440p), and different GPU families (Adreno, Mali, Apple). Use Firebase Test Lab for automated testing across 50+ Android devices. For iOS, use Xcode Cloud or AWS Device Farm. Test for: crash-on-start, memory leaks after 30 minutes, thermal throttling after 15 minutes of gameplay, touch input accuracy at screen edges, notch/cutout rendering, and audio latency. Run automated UI tests with Unity Test Framework or XCTest.

App Store & Google Play Submission.exp: Google Play requires: signed AAB (Android App Bundle), store listing (icons, screenshots, feature graphic, description), content rating questionnaire, privacy policy (if collecting data), and testing track (internal → closed alpha → open beta → production). App Store requires: signed IPA via Xcode archive, App Store Connect listing (screenshots for required sizes: 6.5-inch, 5.5-inch, iPad), privacy nutrition label, and review. Common rejection reasons: crashes, broken links, placeholder content, insufficient information. Budget 1-3 business days for review.
App Store & Google Play Submission.code:
# Android AAB build and sign
# 1. Generate signed bundle
./gradlew bundleRelease

# 2. Sign with keystore
jarsigner -verbose -sigalg SHA256withRSA \
  -digestalg SHA-256 \
  -keystore my-release-key.keystore \
  app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab \
  my-alias

# 3. Verify alignment
~/Android/Sdk/build-tools/34.0.0/zipalign \
  -v 4 \
  app-release.aab \
  app-release-aligned.aab

# iOS build and upload
# 1. Build for iOS
xcodebuild -workspace MyGame.xcworkspace \
  -scheme MyGame \
  -configuration Release \
  -archivePath MyGame.xcarchive \
  archive

# 2. Export IPA
xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath MyGame.xcarchive \
  -exportPath ./ipa \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist

# 3. Upload to App Store Connect
xcrun altool --upload-app \
  -f MyGame.ipa \
  -t ios \
  -u developer@example.com

Crash Reporting & Monitoring.exp: Mobile crash reporting is essential. Unity's Cloud Diagnostics captures native crashes (iOS/Android) and managed exceptions. Firebase Crashlytics provides real-time crash reporting with symbolication (mapping minified stack traces to source). Track: crash-free session rate (target > 99.5%), ANR (Application Not Responding) rate on Android, OOM (Out of Memory) kills, and custom breadcrumbs (player was in level 3, just opened inventory). Symbolicate iOS crashes with dSYM files. Upload Android ProGuard mapping files for obfuscated stack traces.

Android Native Plugins.exp: Bridge Unity C# with Android Java/Kotlin code using AndroidJavaClass and AndroidJavaObject to call methods on the JVM. Package your Kotlin code as an AAR with dependencies declared in the Gradle file, then place it in Assets/Plugins/Android/. Extend UnityPlayerActivity or use UnityAndroidApplication to hook into the activity lifecycle. Use UnityPlayer.UnitySendMessage from Java to invoke C# methods on GameObjects.

iOS Native Plugins.exp: Expose Objective-C/Swift functionality to Unity by writing C-style function wrappers in .mm files that Unity's P/Invoke system can call. Declare [DllImport("__Internal")] extern functions in C# and implement in Objective-C using extern "C" linkage. Embed the static library (.a) or framework in Assets/Plugins/iOS/. For Swift interop, create an Obj-C bridging header that wraps your Swift classes.

Plugin Architecture & Lifecycle.exp: Design your native plugin with a singleton manager that initializes once on app start, wires up lifecycle callbacks (OnApplicationPause, OnApplicationQuit), and dispatches events back to the Unity main thread using ConcurrentQueue. Keep a weak reference to the Unity GameObject. Marshal strings and byte arrays carefully across the managed/native boundary. Wrap all native calls in try/catch.

Android Studio & SDK Setup.exp: Android Studio is the official IDE. Install via JetBrains Toolbox or direct download. SDK Manager provides platform SDKs (target Android 14/API 34 minimum), build tools, NDK (for native C/C++ code), and emulator system images. AVD Manager creates virtual devices for testing. The recommended project structure uses Gradle with Kotlin DSL. Key SDK paths: $ANDROID_HOME, NDK in $ANDROID_NDK_HOME. Use SDK command-line tools (sdkmanager) for CI environments.
Android Studio & SDK Setup.code:
# Android SDK setup (CI environment)
export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk

# Install SDK components
sdkmanager "platforms;android-34"
sdkmanager "build-tools;34.0.0"
sdkmanager "ndk;26.1.10909125"
sdkmanager "emulator"
sdkmanager "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64"

# Create AVD for testing
echo no | avdmanager create avd \
  -n test_device \
  -k "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64" \
  -d pixel_6

# Build from command line
./gradlew assembleDebug

# Install to connected device
./gradlew installDebug

Android Game Manifest & Permissions.exp: The AndroidManifest.xml configures your game: screen orientation (landscape or portrait), hardware features (android.hardware.touchscreen required), permissions (vibrate, internet, wake lock), and Google Play Services. For games, set android:hardwareAccelerated="true", disable screenshots in secure contexts, and use immersive mode to hide system UI. Declare required OpenGL ES version. For Unity, the manifest is auto-generated; overlay it via Plugins/Android/AndroidManifest.xml.
Android Game Manifest & Permissions.code:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml for Unity game -->
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.yourcompany.yourgame">
    
    <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.touchscreen" 
        android:required="true" />
    <uses-feature android:glEsVersion="0x00030000" 
        android:required="true" />
    
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE" />
    
    <application android:label="My Game"

Adaptive Icons & App Bundles.exp: Android App Bundles (AAB) are the required publishing format. They split your APK into base + configuration APKs (different densities, CPU architectures, languages). This reduces download size by 30-40%. Adaptive icons consist of a foreground layer (200x200dp) and background layer (color or gradient) — the system masks them into various shapes (circle, squircle, rounded square). Generate icons for all densities: mdpi (48x48), hdpi (72x72), xhdpi (96x96), xxhdpi (144x144), xxxhdpi (192x192). Use Android Studio's Image Asset Studio.
Adaptive Icons & App Bundles.code:
# Build Android App Bundle (AAB)
./gradlew bundleRelease

# The AAB is at:
# app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab

# Convert AAB to APK for local testing
java -jar bundletool-all.jar build-apks \
  --bundle=app-release.aab \
  --output=app-release.apks \
  --ks=my-release-key.keystore \
  --ks-pass=pass:password \
  --ks-key-alias=my-alias \
  --key-pass=pass:password

# Install to device (universal APK)
java -jar bundletool-all.jar install-apks \
  --apks=app-release.apks

Xcode & Provisioning.exp: Xcode is required for iOS development. Download from Mac App Store. Create an Apple Developer account ($99/year). Provisioning profiles and certificates authenticate your app: Development certificates (running on test devices), Distribution certificates (App Store), and Push notification certificates. Xcode manages signing automatically with 'Automatically manage signing' — it creates provisioning profiles on-the-fly. For CI, export signing certificates and provisioning profiles as files. Use fastlane match to sync signing across your team.
Xcode & Provisioning.code:
# Fastlane setup for iOS signing
# Gemfile
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "fastlane"

# Fastfile
lane :build do
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  
  build_app(
    workspace: "MyGame.xcworkspace",
    scheme: "MyGame",
    configuration: "Release",
    export_method: "app-store",
    include_bitcode: true,
    include_on_demand_resources: true
  )
  
  upload_to_app_store(
    skip_metadata: true,
    skip_screenshots: true
  )
end

# Run
fastlane build

TestFlight & App Store Connect.exp: App Store Connect manages app metadata, builds, pricing, and releases. Upload builds via Xcode Archive or Transporter app. TestFlight enables internal testing (up to 100 testers, no review) and external testing (up to 10,000 testers, requires Beta App Review). Manage versions with build numbers — each uploaded build increments. Set 'What's New' text per version. Use phased releases (7-day gradual rollout) to catch issues. Monitor crash reports and ratings in App Store Connect Analytics.
TestFlight & App Store Connect.code:

What is MongoDB.exp: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It's schema-less, horizontally scalable, and designed for modern applications with dynamic data models. Supports replica sets for HA and sharding for distributed data.

Document Model Deep Dive.exp: Documents are JSON-like structures with field-value pairs. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, nested objects, dates, ObjectIds, and more. Max document size is 16MB. Nested fields use dot notation for access.

BSON Types Deep.exp: BSON extends JSON with types: ObjectId (12-byte unique id), Date (64-bit millisecond timestamp), NumberInt/NumberLong, Decimal128 (exact precision), Binary, Regex, Code, Timestamp, and MinKey/MaxKey for comparison.
BSON Types Deep.code:
db.typesDemo.insertOne({
  _id: ObjectId(),
  intVal: NumberInt(42),
  longVal: NumberLong(9999999999),
  decVal: NumberDecimal('19.99'),
  dateVal: new Date(),
  binaryVal: BinData(0, 'S2V5cw=='),
  regexVal: /search.*term/i,
  tsVal: Timestamp({ t: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000), i: 1 })
})

MongoDB Versions & Editions.exp: MongoDB 7.0+ (latest) with improved queryable encryption, change streams, and aggregation. Editions: Community (free), Enterprise (advanced security, auditing, Ops Manager), and Atlas (cloud-managed).

Atlas & Cloud Setup.exp: MongoDB Atlas offers free M0 clusters, auto-scaling, backups, monitoring, global clusters, serverless instances, and Atlas Search. Provision via web UI, API, or Terraform.
Atlas & Cloud Setup.code:
# Create Atlas cluster via API
curl -s -u "publicKey:privateKey" \
  --digest https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v1.0/groups/{groupId}/clusters \
  -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"MyCluster","providerSettings":{"providerName":"AWS","regionName":"us-east-1","instanceSizeName":"M10"}}'

Connection Strings.exp: Standard format: `mongodb://host:port/db`. Atlas SRV format: `mongodb+srv://cluster.mongodb.net/db`. Options: retryWrites, w, readPreference, maxPoolSize, connectTimeoutMS, tls.
Connection Strings.code:
# Standard
mongodb://localhost:27017/myDB
# With auth
mongodb://user:pass@host1:27017,host2:27017/myDB?replicaSet=rs0
# Atlas SRV
mongodb+srv://myUser:myPass@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/sales?retryWrites=true&w=majority
# Pool options
mongodb://localhost:27017/myDB?maxPoolSize=50&connectTimeoutMS=5000

mongosh Scripting.exp: mongosh supports full JavaScript scripting with variables, loops, functions, and print helpers. Write scripts and load them with `load()`. The `--eval` flag runs inline expressions.

Create (insertOne / insertMany).exp: `insertOne()` inserts a single document, `insertMany()` inserts multiple in one round-trip. Each document auto-receives an `_id` (ObjectId) if not provided. `insertMany()` is ordered by default; use `{ ordered: false }` to continue on error.

Read (find / findOne).exp: `find()` returns a cursor to matching documents. `findOne()` returns the first matched doc. Filter object selects documents; projection object limits returned fields. Use `.pretty()` for formatted output in shell.

Update (updateOne / updateMany).exp: `updateOne()` updates the first matching doc. `updateMany()` updates all matching docs. Use `$set`, `$unset`, `$inc`, `$push`, `$pull`, and more. The third parameter accepts options like `upsert: true`.

Delete (deleteOne / deleteMany).exp: `deleteOne()` deletes the first match. `deleteMany()` deletes all matches. `drop()` removes the entire collection including indexes. Deletes are permanent — verify filters with `find()` first.
Delete (deleteOne / deleteMany).code:
db.users.deleteOne({ status: 'inactive' })
db.users.deleteMany({ lastLogin: { $lt: new Date('2023-01-01') } })
db.tempData.drop()
// Safe delete pattern
const filter = { status: 'pending' }
print('Docs to delete:', db.users.countDocuments(filter))
db.users.deleteMany(filter)

bulkWrite.exp: `bulkWrite()` performs multiple write operations (insert, update, replace, delete) in a single batch. Accepts an array of operation objects. Supports `{ ordered: false }` for parallel execution.

findAndModify.exp: `findOneAndUpdate()`, `findOneAndDelete()`, `findOneAndReplace()` atomically find and modify a document. Options: `returnDocument: 'after'/'before'`, `sort`, `projection`, `upsert`. Useful for queues and counters.

replaceOne.exp: `replaceOne()` replaces the entire document (except `_id`) matching the filter. Unlike `updateOne()` with `$set`, this replaces all fields. The replacement doc must not contain update operators.

Update Operators Deep.exp: `$push` adds to array. `$pull` removes matching items. `$addToSet` adds if not present. `$each` pushes multiple. `$position` inserts at index. `$slice` limits array size after push.

arrayFilters & upsert Deep.exp: arrayFilters target specific array elements for update. upsert: true creates a doc if no match is found. Combined, they enable powerful conditional updates on nested arrays.

Write Concern.exp: Write concern controls acknowledgment: `w: 0` (fire-and-forget), `w: 1` (primary acknowledged), `w: 'majority'` (majority of nodes), `w: <tag>` (custom tag set). `wtimeout` cancels if not met.

Comparison Operators.exp: `$eq`, `$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$in`, `$nin`. Combine multiple on the same field. `$in` accepts an array of values. Use `$ne` and `$nin` with indexes carefully (they scan broadly).
Comparison Operators.code:
db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 10, $lte: 100 } })
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ['Electronics', 'Books'] } })
db.orders.find({ status: { $ne: 'cancelled' }, total: { $gte: 50 } })

Logical Operators.exp: `$and`, `$or`, `$not`, `$nor`. Implicit AND is used for comma-separated conditions. Use explicit `$and` when conditions involve the same field or complex expressions.

Array Operators.exp: `$all` matches arrays containing all elements. `$elemMatch` matches docs with an array element satisfying all conditions. `$size` matches exact array length. Combine for precise array queries.

Element & Evaluation Operators.exp: `$exists` checks field presence. `$type` matches BSON type. `$expr` enables aggregation expressions in queries. `$mod` modulo match. `$regex` pattern matching.

Cursor Methods & Projection.exp: Cursors provide `.sort()`, `.limit()`, `.skip()`, `.count()`, `.forEach()`, `.map()`, `.toArray()`. Projection `{ field: 1 }` includes; `{ field: 0 }` excludes. `_id` is included by default.
Cursor Methods & Projection.code:
db.users.find({}, { name: 1, email: 1, _id: 0 })
  .sort({ name: 1 })
  .skip(20)
  .limit(10)
  .forEach(doc => print(doc.name))

// Cursor count (honors skip/limit)
db.orders.find({ status: 'shipped' }).limit(50).count()

Sort & Pagination Patterns.exp: Use `.sort()` with `.skip()`/`.limit()` for pagination (inefficient at scale). For efficient pagination, use range-based with `$lt`/`$gt` on indexed fields. Avoid large skips.

Geospatial Queries.exp: Supports GeoJSON objects (Point, LineString, Polygon). Create a `2dsphere` index for spherical queries. Operators: `$near` (sorted proximity), `$geoWithin` (within shape), `$geoIntersects` (intersects shape).

Text Search Deep.exp: `$text` query operator with `$search` performs full-text search on text-indexed fields. Supports `$language` for stemming, `$caseSensitive`, `$diacriticSensitive`. `$meta: 'textScore'` for relevance ranking.

$expr & Aggregation Variables.exp: `$expr` allows aggregation expressions in queries. `$$` references system variables (`$NOW`, `$ROOT`). `let` defines variables for use within `$expr`. Enables cross-field comparisons and computed conditions.

Index Basics.exp: Indexes speed up queries at the cost of write performance and storage. `createIndex()` creates an index. Types: single-field, compound, multikey (array), text, geospatial, hashed. Use `getIndexes()` to inspect.
Index Basics.code:
db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })
db.users.createIndex({ name: 1, age: -1 })
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1 }) // multikey (array field)
db.users.getIndexes()
// List all indexes
db.users.getIndexes().forEach(idx => printjson(idx))

Compound Indexes & ESR Rule.exp: Compound indexes support queries on multiple fields. ESR rule: Equality fields first, Sort fields next, Range fields last. Prefix matching — a compound index can serve queries on its leading fields.

Text Indexes.exp: Text indexes enable full-text search with `$text`. A collection can have only one text index (can cover multiple fields). Supports stemming, stop words, weights for field ranking, and text scoring.

Explain & Optimize.exp: `.explain('executionStats')` shows query plans, scanned docs, index usage, and timing. Look for IXSCAN (good) vs COLLSCAN (bad). `winningPlan` shows the chosen plan; `rejectedPlans` shows alternatives.

Special Index Types.exp: TTL indexes auto-delete docs after a timeout. Sparse indexes skip null fields. Unique indexes enforce uniqueness. Partial indexes index only matching docs. Hidden indexes are not used by the query planner.

Index Intersection.exp: MongoDB can use multiple indexes to satisfy a query via index intersection. Use `$or` clauses or compound queries. The query planner evaluates intersection vs compound index to pick the best plan.

Covered Queries.exp: A covered query is fulfilled entirely from the index without reading documents. All queried and projected fields must be in the index. `explain()` shows `FETCH` stage is absent for covered queries.

Index Builds & Rolling Builds.exp: Index builds can block reads/writes on the collection (foreground) or run in background. In replica sets, rolling index builds build on each member sequentially to avoid downtime. For large collections, use `createIndex()` with `{ background: true }`.

Pipeline Overview & $match / $group.exp: The aggregation pipeline processes documents through a sequence of stages. `$match` filters early (like find). `$group` groups by key and computes accumulators. Always put `$match` early.

Accumulators Deep ($first / $last / $pus.exp: `$sum` adds values. `$avg` averages. `$min`/`$max` find extremes. `$first`/`$last` get first/last doc per group (requires sort). `$push` collects into array. `$addToSet` collects unique values.

$lookup (Joins) & $unwind.exp: `$lookup` performs left outer join. `from` is the target collection, `localField` and `foreignField` define the join, `as` names the output array. `$unwind` deconstructs arrays (flattens).

$bucket & $bucketAuto.exp: `$bucket` groups documents into user-defined ranges. `$bucketAuto` auto-generates evenly-sized buckets. Both support `$output` with accumulators. Useful for histograms and distribution analysis.

$facet & $graphLookup.exp: `$facet` runs multiple sub-pipelines on the same input. `$graphLookup` performs recursive graph traversal for hierarchical data like org charts or social networks.

$merge & $out.exp: `$out` writes pipeline results to a new collection (replaces entire collection). `$merge` merges results into an existing collection with merge strategies: `replace`, `merge`, `keepExisting`, `fail`.

$unionWith & $setWindowFields.exp: `$unionWith` combines results from multiple collections (like SQL UNION). `$setWindowFields` enables window functions: `$rank`, `$denseRank`, `$rowNumber`, `$shift`, and sliding window accumulators.

Aggregation Expressions.exp: Expressions include arithmetic (`$add`, `$multiply`, `$subtract`, `$divide`, `$mod`), string (`$concat`, `$substr`, `$toLower`, `$toUpper`, `$trim`), date (`$year`, `$month`, `$dayOfMonth`, `$dateToString`), and conditional (`$cond`, `$ifNull`, `$switch`).

Embedding vs Referencing.exp: Embedding stores related data in the same document (fast reads, atomic updates). Referencing stores IDs and uses `$lookup` to join (avoids 16MB limit, reduces duplication). Prefer embedding for one-to-few, referencing for one-to-many.

One-to-One / One-to-Many / Many-to-Many.exp: One-to-one: embed or reference with unique constraint. One-to-many: embed (few) or reference (many). Many-to-many: array of references on either side or a junction collection.

Polymorphic Patterns.exp: Store different entity types in the same collection using a type discriminator field. Common for event sourcing, content management (articles, videos, podcasts), and product catalogs with shared base fields.
Polymorphic Patterns.code:
db.content.insertMany([
  {
    type: 'article',
    title: 'MongoDB Guide',
    body: 'Content...',
    tags: ['database'],
    wordCount: 1200
  },
  {
    type: 'video',
    title: 'Aggregation Tutorial',
    url: 'https://...',
    duration: 1800,
    resolution: '1080p'
  },
  {
    type: 'podcast',
    title: 'NoSQL Deep Dive',
    audioUrl: 'https://...',
    duration: 3600,
    guests: ['Alice']
  }
])
db.content.createIndex({ type: 1, createdAt: -1 })

Bucket Pattern.exp: The bucket pattern groups related data into time-based or size-based buckets. Ideal for time-series data (IoT sensor readings) — reduces document count, improves index efficiency, and enables pre-aggregation.

Computed & Pre-Aggregation Patterns.exp: Pre-compute aggregates and store them alongside or in separate collections. Use `$merge` for periodic rollups. Reduce computation at read time — ideal for dashboards, leaderboards, and trend analysis.

Document Versioning.exp: Track document versions using a version field or separate history collection. Pattern: store current doc in main collection, append versions to a history collection. Supports rollback and audit trails.

Schema Validation.exp: MongoDB supports JSON Schema validation (`$jsonSchema`) at collection level. Validate required fields, types, ranges, enums, and patterns. Use `validationLevel: 'strict' | 'moderate'` and `validationAction: 'error' | 'warn'`.

Query Profiling.exp: Set profiling level to capture slow queries. Level 0: off. Level 1: queries slower than `slowms`. Level 2: all queries. Results stored in `system.profile`. Analyze for full scans, missing indexes, and sort patterns.

Slow Query Analysis.exp: Use `explain('executionStats')` and system.profile to diagnose. Key metrics: `COLLSCAN` (bad, full collection scan), `IXSCAN` (good), `nReturned` vs `totalDocsExamined`, `executionTimeMillis`, and `docsExamined`.

mongostat & mongotop Deep.exp: `mongostat` shows real-time metrics: inserts/sec, queries/sec, page faults, % locked. `mongotop` shows read/write time per collection. Run with `--discover` for replica set monitoring.
mongostat & mongotop Deep.code:
# Real-time server stats (every 2s)
mongostat --host localhost:27017 --port 27017 2
# Fields: insert query update delete getmore command %dirty %used flushes vsize   res

# Collection-level read/write activity
mongotop 5
# Fields: ns    total    read    write

# JSON output for parsing
mongostat --host localhost:27017 --json 2

# Discovery mode for replica sets
mongostat --discover --host 'myReplSet/localhost:27017' 2

serverStatus & Operation Profiling.exp: `db.serverStatus()` provides comprehensive server metrics: connections, network, operations, memory, locks, wiredTiger cache, and repl info. `db.currentOp()` shows running operations. Kill slow ops with `db.killOp()`.

Connection Pooling.exp: Connection pooling reuses TCP connections to MongoDB. Default pool size is 100 per mongos/mongod. Monitor with `serverStatus().connections`. Tune with `maxPoolSize` and `minPoolSize` in connection string.

WiredTiger Deep & Cache Management.exp: WiredTiger is the default storage engine. It uses a cache (default 50% of RAM - 1GB, min 256MB). Manages data with B-trees and MVCC. Monitor cache hit ratio, evictions, and dirty pages via `serverStatus()`.

Replica Sets Overview.exp: Replica sets provide HA with automatic failover. Primary handles writes; secondaries replicate via oplog. Minimum 3 members (or 2 + arbiter). Use `rs.status()` and `rs.conf()` to monitor.

Election Process Deep.exp: Elections occur when primary becomes unreachable. Nodes vote using a protocol based on Raft. The node with highest priority and most up-to-date oplog wins. `settings.electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s) controls detection speed.

Oplog Size Management.exp: The oplog (local.oplog.rs) is a capped collection recording all writes. Default size: 5% of free disk (min 990MB, max 50GB). If too small, secondaries can fall behind. Resize with `replSetResizeOplog`.

Read Preference Modes.exp: Read preference controls where queries are routed: `primary` (default, strong consistency), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary` (offload reads), `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest` (lowest latency). Use with `maxStalenessSeconds`.

Delayed & Hidden Members.exp: Delayed members replicate data with a time lag (e.g., 1 hour) — protection against accidental drops/corruption. Hidden members are invisible to application queries — used for reporting, backups, or analytics workloads.

Arbiters.exp: An arbiter participates in elections but holds no data. Use to achieve odd-number voting in a 2-node replica set. Never run arbiter on the same server as a data node. Minimum recommended: 3 data nodes instead of 2+arbiter.

Replica Set Tags.exp: Tags enable custom write concern and read preference routing. Define tags per member in `rs.conf()`. Use `w: 'majority'` with tag sets to require acknowledgments from specific data centers.

Sharding Overview.exp: Sharding horizontally partitions data across shards. Components: mongos (router), config servers (metadata), shards (data). A shard key determines data distribution. Enable per-database, then per-collection.

Shard Key Strategies.exp: Hashed shard keys provide even distribution (good for monotonically increasing fields like ObjectId). Ranged shard keys support range queries but can create hotspots. Zone sharding pins data to specific shards based on key range.

Jumbo Chunks & Balancing.exp: Jumbo chunks exceed the configured chunk size (default 64MB) and cannot be split or moved. Causes: poor shard key cardinality. Balancer migrates chunks between shards. Monitor with `sh.status(true)`.

Shard Zones.exp: Shard zones allow pinning data to specific shards based on shard key ranges. Useful for data residency (GDPR), hot data on fast SSDs, cold data on cheaper storage, and multi-region deployments.
Shard Zones.code:
// Tag shards with zone names
sh.addShardTag('shard0000', 'US_East')
sh.addShardTag('shard0001', 'US_West')

// Associate key ranges with zones
sh.updateZoneKeyRange(
  'sales_db.orders',
  { region: 'NY' },
  { region: 'NZ' },
  'US_East'
)
sh.updateZoneKeyRange(
  'sales_db.orders',
  { region: 'CA' },
  { region: 'CZ' },
  'US_West'
)

// Verify zone configuration
sh.status()

Resharding.exp: Resharding changes the shard key of a collection after deployment. MongoDB 7.0+ supports live resharding without downtime. The old key remains until resharding completes. Monitor with `sh.status()`.

mongos Scaling.exp: mongos routers are stateless and can be scaled horizontally. Place mongos close to application servers. Use connection pooling and load balancers in front of multiple mongos instances for HA and throughput.
mongos Scaling.code:
# Start mongos instances
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27017
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27018

# Connection string with multiple mongos
mongodb://mongos1:27017,mongos2:27017,mongos3:27017/mydb?
  loadBalanced=true&retryWrites=true

Authentication Methods.exp: MongoDB supports SCRAM (default, password-based), x.509 (certificate), LDAP (enterprise), and Kerberos (enterprise). SCRAM-SHA-256 is the default mechanism, more secure than SCRAM-SHA-1.

Authorization & Roles.exp: Roles define permissions. Built-in: `read`, `readWrite`, `dbAdmin`, `userAdmin`, `clusterAdmin`. Create custom roles with specific actions on specific resources. Use `--auth` flag to enable.

Field Level Encryption.exp: Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) encrypts fields before they reach the server. Supports deterministic (supports queries) and random (more secure) encryption. Uses a local or remote KMS.

Audit Log.exp: Enterprise feature that logs all auth events, DDL operations, and CRUD operations. Output to console, syslog, JSON file, or BSON. Configure in mongod.conf. Essential for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI).
Audit Log.code:
# mongod.conf audit configuration
auditLog:
  destination: file
  format: JSON
  path: /var/log/mongodb/audit.log
  filter: '{"atype":{"$in":["authCheck","createCollection","dropCollection","createUser","dropUser"]}}'

# Or via command line
mongod --auditDestination file --auditFormat JSON --auditPath /var/log/mongodb/audit.log

# Parse audit logs
db.adminCommand({ getLog: 'audit' })

TLS/SSL & Network Compression.exp: Enable TLS for encrypted client-server communication. Use PEM certificates. MongoDB supports snappy, zlib, and zstd compression to reduce network bandwidth. Configure both on mongod and client side.
TLS/SSL & Network Compression.code:
# mongod.conf TLS
net:
  tls:
    mode: requireTLS
    certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/server.pem
    CAFile: /etc/mongodb/ca.pem
    allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: false

# Client connection with TLS
mongosh --tls --tlsCertificateKeyFile client.pem --tlsCAFile ca.pem \
  --host myHost --port 27017

# Connection string with TLS
mongodb://host:27017/db?tls=true&tlsCertificateKeyFile=client.pem&tlsCAFile=ca.pem

# Network compression
mongod --networkMessageCompressors snappy,zstd,zlib

IP Whitelisting & Security Checklist.exp: Bind IP to specific interfaces (not 0.0.0.0). Use firewalls, VPCs, and security groups. Enable `--auth`. Rotate users' passwords. Use SCRAM-SHA-256. Monitor with audit logs. Enable TLS everywhere.
IP Whitelisting & Security Checklist.code:
# mongod.conf security best practices
net:
  bindIp: 10.0.0.1,10.0.0.2  # NOT 0.0.0.0
  port: 27017
  tls:
    mode: requireTLS

security:
  authorization: enabled
  javascriptEnabled: false  # disable if not needed

# IP access control list
# Use iptables, AWS SG, etc:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 27017 -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 27017 -j DROP

Atlas Overview & Deployment.exp: Atlas provides fully-managed MongoDB on AWS, Azure, GCP. Free M0 cluster (512MB). Features: auto-scaling, automated backups, monitoring alerts, BI Connector, global clusters, and serverless instances.
Atlas Overview & Deployment.code:
# Create cluster via Atlas CLI
atlas clusters create myCluster --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 --tier M10 --members 3

# Get connection string
atlas clusters connectionString describe myCluster

# Create database user
atlas dbusers create --username appUser --role readWriteAnyDatabase

# Whitelist IP
atlas accessList create --ip 203.0.113.0

Atlas Search.exp: Atlas Search is built on Lucene for full-text search. Supports fuzzy matching, autocomplete, synonyms, faceted search, highlighting, and compound queries. Create indexes via web UI or API.

Atlas Data Lake & Federated Query.exp: Atlas Data Lake queries data across Atlas clusters, AWS S3, and Azure Blob Storage using the MongoDB Query API (including aggregation). No data movement — query in place with federated database instances.

Atlas App Services.exp: Atlas App Services (formerly Realm) provides serverless backend: Functions (JS on Atlas), Triggers (DB/webhook/scheduled), GraphQL API, and Data Access Rules. Enables rapid app development without managing servers.

Online Archive & Serverless Instances.exp: Online Archive automatically moves older data to cost-effective S3 storage (fully queryable). Serverless instances scale from 0 to 1M+ ops/sec without capacity planning. Pay per operation.
Online Archive & Serverless Instances.code:
# Set up online archive (via Atlas CLI)
atlas clusters onlineArchives create --clusterName myCluster \
  --db sales --collection orders \
  --dateField createdAt --archiveAfter 90

# Query archived data (transparent — same queries)
db.orders.find({ createdAt: { $lt: new Date('2023-01-01') } })

# Create serverless instance
atlas clusters create myServerless --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 \
  --tier SERVERLESS --serverlessBackupOptions enabled=true

Global Clusters & BI Connector.exp: Global clusters distribute data across geographic regions for low-latency reads/writes worldwide. BI Connector (MySQL protocol) enables Tableau, Power BI, and other BI tools to query MongoDB via SQL.
Global Clusters & BI Connector.code:
# Global cluster config (via Atlas API)
# Zone-based data distribution
atlas clusters update myCluster \
  --globalClusterConfig '{"customZoneMapping":{"US":"us-east-1","EU":"eu-west-1","APAC":"ap-southeast-1"}}'

// Connection to BI Connector (MySQL port 27016)
mysql -h mycluster.mongodb.net -P 27016 -u myUser -p

// SQL query on MongoDB collections
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) as total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customerId = c._id
WHERE o.createdAt > '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY total DESC;

MongoDB Driver Deep.exp: Official drivers (Node.js, Python, Java, Go, etc.) provide low-level database access. Key concepts: MongoClient (connection pool), Database, Collection, Cursor. Events: `commandStarted`, `commandSucceeded`, `commandFailed`.

Mongoose Deep (Middleware, Virtuals, Pop.exp: Mongoose provides schema-based modeling with middleware (pre/post hooks for save, validate, find, etc.), virtuals (computed properties), population (reference resolution), plugins, and custom validators.

Change Streams.exp: Change streams provide real-time notifications of data changes (insert, update, replace, delete, drop, invalidate). Can watch a collection, database, or entire cluster. Resumable via resume token.

Transactions.exp: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions (since 4.0). Must use replica set or sharded cluster. Session-based: start a session, execute ops within `withTransaction()`, automatic retry on transient errors.

Retryable Writes.exp: Retryable writes automatically retry write operations on network errors (not on write conflicts). Must use replica set. Enable with `retryWrites=true` in connection string. Idempotent ops are automatically retried.

mongodump & mongorestore.exp: `mongodump` creates BSON binary backups. `mongorestore` restores them. Supports `--db`, `--collection`, `--query` (filtered dump), `--gzip`, `--archive`. For consistent backups on replica sets, use `--oplog` or read from secondary.
mongodump & mongorestore.code:
# Dump entire server
mongodump --uri "mongodb://user:pass@localhost:27017" --out /backup/full

# Dump single database to gzip archive
mongodump --db myDB --gzip --archive=/backup/myDB.gz

# Dump with query filter
mongodump --db myDB --collection orders --query '{ "createdAt": { "$gte": ISODate("2024-01-01") } }' --out /backup/orders

# Point-in-time restore
mongorestore --drop --oplogReplay /backup/full

# Restore from archive
mongorestore --gzip --archive=/backup/myDB.gz --drop

Atlas Backups.exp: Atlas provides automated backups with configurable retention (1-35 days for M10+). Serverless and M0 have continuous backups. Restore via UI, API, or CLI. Supports point-in-time recovery (PITR) within the retention window.
Atlas Backups.code:
# Trigger snapshot via Atlas CLI
atlas backups snapshots create --clusterName myCluster --description "pre-upgrade backup"

# List snapshots
atlas backups snapshots list --clusterName myCluster

# Restore snapshot
atlas backups restore start --clusterName myCluster \
  --snapshotId <snapshotId> --targetProjectId <projectId>

# Enable PITR
atlas clusters update myCluster --enablePitr \
  --pitrBackupWindowDays 7

# Restore to point in time
atlas backups restore start --clusterName myCluster \
  --pointInTimeUTCMillis 1704067200000

Ops Manager & On-Premise Backups.exp: Ops Manager (Enterprise) provides automated backup, monitoring, and DB management for on-premise MongoDB. Supports continuous block-level backups with incremental snapshots, queryable backups, and point-in-time recovery.
Ops Manager & On-Premise Backups.code:
# Ops Manager backup daemon configuration
# Backup jobs configured via Ops Manager UI

# Command-line backup daemon
mongobackup --backup --destination /data/backups

# Restore from Ops Manager backup
# Via UI: Select snapshot -> Restore -> Target cluster

# Headend restore for fine-grained recovery
# 1. Download snapshot
# 2. Apply oplog
mongorestore --oplogReplay /path/to/oplog/bson

Continuous Backups & PITR.exp: Continuous backups apply oplog entries on top of snapshots for point-in-time recovery within a window. Trade-off: higher storage cost vs granular recovery. PITR allows restoring to any second within the window.
Continuous Backups & PITR.code:
# Enable continuous backup (Atlas)
atlas clusters update myCluster --enablePitr --pitrBackupWindowDays 7

# Ops Manager continuous backup
# Configure via Ops Manager UI > Project > Backup > Continuous

# Restore to a specific timestamp
mongorestore \
  --oplogFile /path/to/oplog.bson \
  --oplogLimit "1704067200:1" \
  --oplogReplay \
  /path/to/snapshot

# Validate backup integrity
mongorestore --dryRun --oplogReplay /path/to/backup

Backup Strategy & Best Practices.exp: Combine snapshot backups (mongodump/Atlas snapshots) with oplog-based continuous backup for PITR. Automate with cron/Ops Manager/Atlas. Test restores regularly. Store backups in different region. Consider compliance retention.
Backup Strategy & Best Practices.code:
# Weekly full + daily incremental cron
# crontab:
0 3 * * 0  mongodump --uri "$URI" --gzip --archive=/backups/full/$(date +%%Y%%m%%d).gz
0 3 * * 1-6 mongodump --uri "$URI" --gzip --archive=/backups/inc/$(date +%%Y%%m%%d).gz --query '{ "updatedAt": { "$gte": ISODate("'$(date -d '-1 day' +%%Y-%%m-%%d)'") } }'

# Test restore
test_restore() {
  mongorestore --gzip --archive=/backups/full/latest.gz --db test_restore
  if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Backup validated successfully"
    mongosh --eval 'db.getSiblingDB("test_restore").dropDatabase()'
  fi
}

What is MySQL.exp: MySQL is the world's most popular open-source relational database. It uses SQL for querying and is commonly used with LAMP/LEMP stacks. Known for speed, reliability, and ease of use. Owned by Oracle, with MariaDB as a popular fork.

Installing MySQL.exp: Install via package manager, official APT/YUM repos, Docker, or use XAMPP/MAMP for local dev. The mysql service must be running. Check status with systemctl. First-run setup: mysql_secure_installation.
Installing MySQL.code:
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install mysql-server-8.0
sudo systemctl start mysql
sudo mysql_secure_installation

# Docker
# docker run --name mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -d mysql:8

Connecting with mysql CLI.exp: The mysql CLI connects to a MySQL server. Options: -h host, -P port, -u user, -p password prompt. Use -e for inline queries. \q or exit to quit. Use \u db_name to switch databases.

MySQL Data Types.exp: MySQL supports many data types: INT, BIGINT, VARCHAR, CHAR, TEXT, DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, JSON, ENUM, SET, BLOB. Choose types carefully — VARCHAR(255) for short strings, TEXT for long, DECIMAL for money.
MySQL Data Types.code:
CREATE TABLE example (
  id INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 0.00,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  status ENUM('active', 'inactive') DEFAULT 'active',
  metadata JSON
);

CREATE TABLE.exp: CREATE TABLE defines a new table. Specify columns with names and types, then constraints. ENGINE=InnoDB is default (supports transactions, FK). ENGINE=MyISAM is older (full-text search, no transactions). CHARACTER SET and COLLATE control encoding.
CREATE TABLE.code:
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT,
  email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  password_hash CHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  UNIQUE KEY uk_email (email)
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4;

ALTER TABLE.exp: ALTER TABLE modifies an existing table: ADD, DROP, MODIFY, CHANGE columns, or rename table. Use ALTER to add/drop indexes, constraints, and change storage settings. Be careful with large tables — ALTER can lock the table.

DROP & TRUNCATE.exp: DROP TABLE removes the table entirely (data + structure). TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure — faster than DELETE for whole-table removal, but can't be rolled back in some engines. Use with extreme caution.

Constraints.exp: Constraints enforce data integrity: PRIMARY KEY (unique identifier), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity), UNIQUE (no duplicates), NOT NULL (required), CHECK (value validation), DEFAULT (fallback value). InnoDB supports FK constraints.
Constraints.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  total DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending',
  CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
);

SELECT.exp: SELECT retrieves rows. Use * for all columns, or list specific ones. WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT restricts rows. DISTINCT removes duplicates. AS renames columns. Use EXPLAIN to check query performance.

INSERT.exp: INSERT adds rows. INSERT INTO ... VALUES for single row, INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...), for multiple. INSERT ... SET is an alternative syntax. LAST_INSERT_ID() returns the auto-generated id. Use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for upsert.

UPDATE.exp: UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE to avoid updating all rows. LIMIT restricts how many rows to update. Use JOIN in UPDATE to update based on values in other tables. Check affected rows with ROW_COUNT().

DELETE.exp: DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE or all rows are deleted. Use JOIN to delete from multiple tables. TRUNCATE is faster for clearing all rows. Check what you'll delete first with SELECT COUNT(*).

WHERE Clause.exp: WHERE filters rows. Operators: =, !=, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL. Combine with AND, OR, NOT. Use parentheses for complex logic. LIKE uses % (any chars) and _ (single char). IN matches any value in a list.

ORDER BY & LIMIT.exp: ORDER BY sorts results (ASC ascending, DESC descending). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET skips rows (for pagination). For large pagination, use WHERE instead of OFFSET for better performance.

INNER JOIN.exp: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. Use table aliases for readability. Always prefix columns with table name/alias in JOIN queries. INNER JOIN is the most common join type.
INNER JOIN.code:
SELECT u.username, o.total, o.created_at
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';

LEFT & RIGHT JOIN.exp: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where right doesn't match. RIGHT JOIN is the opposite (rarely used — prefer LEFT JOIN). Useful for finding missing relationships.
LEFT & RIGHT JOIN.code:
-- All users, even those with no orders
SELECT u.username, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.username;

-- Find users with no orders
SELECT u.* FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

CROSS JOIN & SELF JOIN.exp: CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product (every row of A × every row of B). SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases. Used for hierarchies (employees/managers), date ranges, and adjacency lists.
CROSS JOIN & SELF JOIN.code:
-- Self join: employee hierarchy
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

-- Cross join: all combinations
SELECT p.name, s.size
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN sizes s;

UNION & UNION ALL.exp: UNION combines results from multiple SELECT queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL is faster but keeps duplicates. All SELECTs must have the same number of columns with compatible types. Column names come from the first query.
UNION & UNION ALL.code:
SELECT name, 'customer' AS type FROM customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'vendor' AS type FROM vendors
ORDER BY name;

-- Unique list across tables
SELECT email FROM users
UNION
SELECT email FROM newsletter_subscribers;

GROUP BY & HAVING.exp: GROUP BY groups rows by column values. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) compute per-group stats. HAVING filters groups (like WHERE for groups). SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY or aggregate functions.
GROUP BY & HAVING.code:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS count, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING spent > 1000
ORDER BY spent DESC;

Aggregate Functions.exp: COUNT(*): row count. COUNT(col): non-null count. SUM(col): total. AVG(col): average. MIN(col): minimum. MAX(col): maximum. GROUP_CONCAT(col): concatenates values into a string. DISTINCT inside aggregates: COUNT(DISTINCT col).
Aggregate Functions.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS unique_customers,
  SUM(total) AS revenue,
  AVG(total) AS avg_order,
  MIN(total) AS min_order,
  MAX(total) AS max_order,
  GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT status ORDER BY status SEPARATOR ', ') AS statuses
FROM orders;

ROLLUP & GROUPING.exp: WITH ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand total rows to GROUP BY results. GROUPING() distinguishes subtotal rows from regular rows. Useful for summary reports and dashboards.
ROLLUP & GROUPING.code:
SELECT
  COALESCE(region, 'ALL') AS region,
  COALESCE(product_category, 'ALL') AS category,
  SUM(amount) AS total
FROM sales
GROUP BY region, product_category WITH ROLLUP;

String Functions.exp: MySQL has powerful string functions: CONCAT (join strings), SUBSTRING (extract part), LENGTH (byte count), CHAR_LENGTH (character count), UPPER/LOWER (case), TRIM (remove spaces), REPLACE (find/replace), LOCATE (position of substring).

Date & Time Functions.exp: Key functions: NOW() (current datetime), CURDATE() (date), CURTIME() (time). DATE_FORMAT for custom formatting. DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB for arithmetic. DATEDIFF for difference. EXTRACT for parts (YEAR, MONTH, DAY).

Conditional Expressions.exp: IF(condition, true_val, false_val) — simple ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END — multi-way branching. IFNULL(val, default) — coalesce null. COALESCE(val1, val2, ..., default) — first non-null.

Index Basics.exp: Indexes speed up SELECT queries at the cost of slower INSERT/UPDATE. CREATE INDEX on frequently queried columns. PRIMARY KEY is a clustered index. UNIQUE index enforces uniqueness. Use EXPLAIN to check if queries use indexes.

EXPLAIN Query Analysis.exp: EXPLAIN shows how MySQL executes a query. Key fields: type (ALL=full scan, ref/eq_ref=index lookup), possible_keys (indexes MySQL could use), key (index actually used), rows (estimated rows examined), Extra (Using index=covered, Using filesort=bad).
EXPLAIN Query Analysis.code:
EXPLAIN SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE u.created_at > '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id
ORDER BY orders DESC
LIMIT 10;
-- Look for: type=ALL (bad), Using filesort (bad), rows (high=bad)

Slow Query Log.exp: Enable the slow query log to find performance issues. Set long_query_time (default 10s). Log queries that don't use indexes with log_queries_not_using_indexes. Analyze with mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest.

Transactions.exp: Transactions group operations as atomic units: all succeed or all roll back. START TRANSACTION / BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT creates rollback points. InnoDB supports transactions (MyISAM does not).

Stored Procedures.exp: Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. DELIMITER changes the statement delimiter. IN, OUT, INOUT parameters. Variables with DECLARE. Handlers for error handling. Reduces network traffic for complex operations.

Views.exp: Views are saved SQL queries that act like virtual tables. Simplify complex queries, add security layers (restrict columns), and provide abstraction. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents inserts/updates that don't match the view condition.
Views.code:
CREATE VIEW active_customers AS
SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE u.status = 'active'
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;

-- Use like a table
SELECT * FROM active_customers WHERE total_spent > 500;

Triggers.exp: Triggers automatically execute SQL when a table event occurs (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). BEFORE/AFTER timing. FOR EACH ROW per-row trigger. OLD/ NEW refer to row values. Useful for auditing, validation, and derived data.
Triggers.code:
CREATE TRIGGER before_user_update
BEFORE UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
SET NEW.updated_at = NOW();

-- Audit log trigger
CREATE TRIGGER after_order_insert
AFTER INSERT ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, action, record_id)
VALUES ('orders', 'INSERT', NEW.id);

JSON in MySQL.exp: MySQL has native JSON data type and functions: JSON_EXTRACT (or -> operator), JSON_UNQUOTE (or ->>), JSON_ARRAY, JSON_OBJECT, JSON_SET, JSON_KEYS, JSON_CONTAINS. Index JSON fields with generated columns.

AWS RDS for MySQL.exp: Amazon RDS for MySQL is a managed MySQL service on AWS. Automates backups, patching, failover, and scaling. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Multi-AZ for HA with synchronous standby replica. Read replicas for read scaling. Storage auto-scaling up to 64TB. Encryption at rest with KMS. Performance Insights for query monitoring.
AWS RDS for MySQL.code:
# Create RDS MySQL instance
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --engine mysql \
  --engine-version 8.4 \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --db-instance-class db.t3.medium \
  --allocated-storage 100 \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret \
  --multi-az \
  --storage-type gp3

# Create read replica
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb-ro \
  --source-db-instance-identifier mydb

# Take manual snapshot
aws rds create-db-snapshot \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --db-snapshot-identifier mydb-snapshot-pre-upgrade

AWS Aurora MySQL.exp: Amazon Aurora MySQL is AWS's cloud-native MySQL-compatible engine. Up to 5x faster than standard MySQL. Auto-scaling storage up to 128TB. 6-way replication across 3 AZs with 1/6th data written (quorum). Aurora Serverless v2 scales to zero. Global Database for cross-region replication. Backtrack rewinds DB without restore. Built-in connection pooling with RDS Proxy.
AWS Aurora MySQL.code:
# Create Aurora MySQL cluster
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --engine-version 8.0 \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-cluster \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret

# Add instance to cluster
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier aurora-instance-1 \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-cluster

# Aurora Serverless v2
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=128 \
  --db-cluster-identifier serverless-cluster

Google Cloud SQL for MySQL.exp: Cloud SQL is GCP's fully managed MySQL service. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with point-in-time recovery. High availability with regional failover across zones. Read replicas (including cross-region). Cloud SQL Proxy for secure IAM-based auth without public IP. Integrates with Vertex AI for in-database ML predictions. 30TB max storage. Private networking via VPC.
Google Cloud SQL for MySQL.code:
# Create Cloud SQL MySQL instance
gcloud sql instances create my-instance \
  --database-version MYSQL_8_4 \
  --tier db-n1-standard-2 \
  --region us-central1 \
  --root-password secret \
  --availability-type REGIONAL \
  --storage-size 100 \
  --storage-type SSD

# Connect via Cloud SQL Proxy
# ./cloud-sql-proxy INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME
# mysql -u root -p -h 127.0.0.1

# Create read replica
gcloud sql instances create my-replica \
  --master-instance-name my-instance \
  --region us-east1

Azure Database for MySQL.exp: Azure Database for MySQL is Microsoft's managed offering. Flexible Server mode: zone-redundant HA, stop/start, burstable SKUs. Supports MySQL 8.0/8.4. Automated backups with 35-day retention. Azure Private Link for VNet integration. Azure Defender for threat detection. Read replicas (up to 10) within region and cross-region. Flexible Server supports up to 16TB storage.
Azure Database for MySQL.code:
# Create Azure MySQL Flexible Server
az mysql flexible-server create \
  --name my-mysql-server \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --sku-name Standard_B1ms \
  --tier Burstable \
  --admin-user admin \
  --admin-password secret \
  --high-availability ZoneRedundancy \
  --storage-size 128 \
  --version 8.0

# Connection string
# mysql://admin@my-mysql-server:3306/mydb?ssl-mode=require

# Create replica
az mysql flexible-server replica create \
  --replica-name my-replica \
  --source-server my-mysql-server \
  --resource-group my-rg

Oracle HeatWave MySQL.exp: Oracle HeatWave is MySQL on OCI with an integrated in-memory query accelerator. HeatWave engine runs analytics directly on MySQL data — no ETL. Up to 6.5x faster than Aurora at half the cost. Built-in ML: HeatWave AutoML trains models inside the database. Lakehouse: query object storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, OCI) directly from MySQL. Consistent pricing across all global regions. Automatic in-memory caching of InnoDB buffer pool.
Oracle HeatWave MySQL.code:
# Create HeatWave MySQL on OCI
# Via OCI CLI or Console
# Shape: MySQL.Intel.32.256GB
# Storage: 10TB
# HeatWave cluster: 8 nodes

# Connect (standard MySQL protocol)
mysql -h my-instance.mysql.us-ashburn-1.oci.oraclecloud.com -u admin -p

# Load data into HeatWave (no manual loading needed)
# HeatWave auto-loads based on usage patterns

# ML inference inside MySQL
SELECT id, name,
  ML_PREDICT_ROW(
    '{"table": "customer_churn", "model": "churn_model"}',
    JSON_OBJECT('tenure', 12, 'monthly_charges', 79.99)
  ) AS churn_probability
FROM dual;

PlanetScale.exp: PlanetScale is a serverless MySQL-compatible platform built on Vitess (YouTube's MySQL sharding layer). Git-like database branching: create schema branches, test changes, deploy via deploy requests with zero-downtime. Automatic horizontal scaling via Vitess sharding. Deploy requests for schema change review. Non-blocking schema migrations using gh-ost. Point-in-time recovery. Global read replicas. Connect via standard MySQL protocol. Foreign keys limited (Vitess constraint). Free $5/mo starter plan.
PlanetScale.code:
# Install CLI
brew install planetscale/tap/pscale
# or: curl -fsSL https://cli.planetscale.com/install.sh | sh

pscale auth login

# Create database
pscale database create my-app --region us-east

# Create branch (like git branch)
pscale branch create my-app add-user-index

# Connect locally via proxy
pscale connect my-app main --port 3309
# mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3309 -u root

# Deploy request (merge schema change)
pscale deploy-request create my-app add-user-index

# Production connection string
# mysql://username:password@us-east.connect.psdb.cloud/my-app?ssl-mode=require

DigitalOcean & Aiven.exp: DigitalOcean Managed Databases: simple managed MySQL with automated backups, HA failover, monitoring. Starts at $15/mo (1 vCPU, 1GB). Aiven: multi-cloud MySQL on AWS/Azure/GCP, with BYOC option. Free tier available. PlanetScale, Aiven, and DigitalOcean offer managed MySQL outside the big 3 clouds, often simpler pricing and less lock-in.
DigitalOcean & Aiven.code:
# DigitalOcean: create via API/CLI
# doctl databases create --engine mysql --region nyc1 --size db-s-1vcpu-1gb --name my-db

# Connection
# mysql -h db-mysql-nyc1-xxxxx.db.ondigitalocean.com -u doadmin -p -P 25060 mydb

# Aiven: create via CLI
avn service create \
  --service-type mysql \
  --plan startup-4 \
  --cloud aws-us-east-1 \
  my-mysql

# Aiven connection
# mysql -h my-mysql.aivencloud.com -u avnadmin -p -P 3306

Migration to Cloud MySQL.exp: Strategies: dump-and-restore (mysqldump to cloud), logical replication, or physical migration (AWS DMS, GCP Database Migration Service, Azure DMS). For minimal downtime use CDC-based replication. Validate character sets, timezone, sql_mode differences. Plan for network latency — co-locate app and DB in same region. Use connection pooling (ProxySQL, RDS Proxy) for serverless apps.
Migration to Cloud MySQL.code:
# mysqldump migration (offline)
mysqldump -h source-host -u root -p \
  --single-transaction \
  --routines --triggers --events \
  --databases mydb > dump.sql

# Import to cloud
mysql -h cloud-host -u admin -p < dump.sql

# AWS DMS replication task (CDC, minimal downtime)
# aws dms create-replication-task \
#   --source-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:... \
#   --target-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:... \
#   --migration-type full-load-and-cdc

# Check compatibility
mysql -h cloud-host -u admin -p -e "SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'sql_mode';"
# Ensure timezone matches application expectations

Stored Procedures.exp: Stored procedures are reusable SQL blocks stored on the server. Use DELIMITER to change the statement delimiter. IN parameters pass values in, OUT returns values, INOUT does both. Variables declared with DECLARE. DECLARE ... HANDLER for error handling. A common mistake is forgetting to reset DELIMITER back to ;. Procedures reduce network traffic by executing logic server-side.

Triggers.exp: Triggers execute automatically on table events: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. BEFORE triggers validate or modify data before the operation, AFTER triggers run after. OLD refers to pre-change values (UPDATE/DELETE), NEW refers to post-change values (INSERT/UPDATE). A common mistake is creating recursive triggers (a trigger on Table A that updates Table A again). Use triggers sparingly — they're invisible to applications and can make debugging hard.
Triggers.code:
CREATE TRIGGER before_user_insert
BEFORE INSERT ON users
FOR EACH ROW
SET NEW.created_at = NOW();

CREATE TRIGGER after_order_insert
AFTER INSERT ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, action, record_id, changed_at)
VALUES ('orders', 'INSERT', NEW.id, NOW());

CREATE TRIGGER before_user_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
  INSERT INTO deleted_users SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = OLD.id;

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS before_user_insert;

Views.exp: Views are saved SELECT queries that behave like virtual tables. They simplify complex joins, restrict column access (security), and provide schema abstraction. Updatable views must map directly to a single table's columns. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents INSERT/UPDATE that would make rows disappear from the view. Views do not improve performance — they're just stored queries, not materialized (unlike materialized views in PostgreSQL).

Indexing Strategies.exp: MySQL supports BTREE (default, for =, >, <, BETWEEN, LIKE without leading %) and HASH (MEMORY engine only, for = only). Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule: index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a, a+b, a+b+c, but not b or c alone. Use EXPLAIN to verify index usage. Common mistakes: over-indexing (slows writes), indexing low-cardinality columns (e.g., gender), and not covering highly selective columns first.

Transactions & Isolation.exp: START TRANSACTION begins a transaction. COMMIT saves changes permanently. ROLLBACK undoes all changes since START TRANSACTION. SAVEPOINT creates a named rollback point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes to that point. Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (default in most DBs, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (default in MySQL/InnoDB, no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (fully isolated, slowest). Higher isolation = less concurrency. A common mistake is forgetting that DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) implicitly commit the current transaction.

User Management.exp: CREATE USER creates a new user with a host (e.g., 'user'@'localhost'). GRANT assigns privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALL PRIVILEGES. REVOKE removes privileges. FLUSH PRIVILEGES reloads the grant tables (not needed if using GRANT/REVOKE directly, but needed after manual INSERT/UPDATE on mysql.user). Common mistake: creating 'user'@'%' (any host) when only localhost is needed — a security risk. Always use strong passwords. SHOW GRANTS to inspect current privileges.

Backup & Restore.exp: mysqldump is the primary backup tool. Use --single-transaction for InnoDB consistency without locking. --routines, --triggers, --events include them. --all-databases or --databases for specific DBs. mysqlimport bulk-loads data from text files. SELECT INTO OUTFILE exports query results to a file on the server. Common mistake: forgetting --single-transaction on a live InnoDB DB (causes table locks). For large DBs, use Percona XtraBackup for physical/hot backups — mysqldump is too slow for >50GB.
Backup & Restore.code:
# Full backup of a single database
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events mydb > mydb_backup.sql

# Backup all databases
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction --all-databases > all_dbs.sql

# Backup specific tables
mysqldump -u root -p mydb users orders > users_orders.sql

# Restore a backup
mysql -u root -p mydb < mydb_backup.sql

# Restore all databases
mysql -u root -p < all_dbs.sql

# Export query result to file
SELECT id, name, email INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/users_export.csv'
  FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"'
  LINES TERMINATED BY '\n'
FROM users WHERE status = 'active';

# Bulk import from CSV
# mysqlimport --local --fields-terminated-by=',' --fields-optionally-enclosed-by='"' \
#   -u root -p mydb /path/to/users.csv

# Run from mysql CLI
# mysql> SOURCE /path/to/backup.sql;

Pages.exp: The Pages Router is the original routing system in Next.js. Pages in the pages directory automatically become routes based on their file name, with index.js mapping to the root and nested folders creating nested paths.
Pages.code:
export default function Home() { return

Hello World

; }

Routing.exp: Next.js supports dynamic routes using bracket syntax like [id].js. Links are created using the next/link component for client-side navigation with prefetching.

App Router.exp: The App Router (app directory) is the modern routing system using React Server Components by default. Routes are defined by folders with page.js files, and layouts can be nested via layout.js.

getServerSideProps.exp: getServerSideProps runs on every request on the server, fetching data before rendering the page. It is used when you need fresh data on each request or access to request-time information like cookies.

getStaticProps.exp: getStaticProps runs at build time to fetch data for static generation. The generated HTML is reused for each request, making it ideal for content that changes infrequently.

Server Actions.exp: Server Actions allow running server-side code directly from client components. They are functions defined with 'use server' that can be called via form actions or programmatically, handling mutations without building API routes.

SSR.exp: Server-Side Rendering generates HTML on each request, delivering fully rendered pages to the client. This improves SEO and initial load performance at the cost of slower response times compared to static generation.

SSG.exp: Static Site Generation pre-renders pages at build time into HTML and JSON files. These static files are served by CDN with near-instant load times, ideal for marketing pages, blogs, and documentation.
SSG.code:
export async function getStaticProps() { return { props: {} }; }
export async function getStaticPaths() { return { paths: [], fallback: 'blocking' }; }

ISR.exp: Incremental Static Regeneration allows updating static content after build without rebuilding the entire site. Pages are served from cache and regenerated in the background when the revalidation window expires.

CSR.exp: Client-Side Rendering fetches data and renders content in the browser after the initial page load. This is useful for highly interactive, user-specific dashboards where SEO is not critical.

CSS Modules.exp: CSS Modules scope styles locally to the component by generating unique class names. Files named *.module.css are automatically supported, preventing style conflicts across components.
