Tailwind.exp: Next.js integrates with Tailwind CSS out of the box. Tailwind's utility classes enable rapid styling directly in JSX, with purging of unused styles in production builds.

CSS-in-JS.exp: CSS-in-JS libraries like styled-components and Emotion work with Next.js but require configuration. The app router requires using a registry to collect styles during server-side rendering.

REST.exp: Next.js API routes let you build REST endpoints inside the pages/api directory. Each file exports functions matching HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) that receive req and res objects.

Middleware.exp: Middleware runs before every request and can modify headers, redirect users, or rewrite URLs. It is defined as middleware.ts in the root of the project and executes on the Edge runtime.

Edge Functions.exp: Edge Functions run on the Vercel Edge Network using the Edge Runtime. They provide low-latency, globally distributed execution for API routes, middleware, and server rendering.

NextAuth.exp: NextAuth.js (now Auth.js) provides a complete authentication solution for Next.js. It supports OAuth providers, email magic links, and credentials with minimal setup using the app router.

JWT.exp: JSON Web Tokens are commonly used for stateless authentication in Next.js. Tokens are signed server-side and verified on each request, often stored in httpOnly cookies for security.
JWT.code:
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';
const token = jwt.sign({ userId: user.id }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '7d' });

Session Management.exp: Session management in Next.js can use database-backed sessions or JWT-based sessions via NextAuth. The session is accessed via useSession on the client or getServerSession on the server.
Session Management.code:
import { getServerSession } from 'next-auth';
const session = await getServerSession(req, res, authOptions);

Image Optimization.exp: The next/image component automatically optimizes images with lazy loading, responsive sizes, and WebP/AVIF format conversion. Images are served via the built-in image optimizer API.
Image Optimization.code:
import Image from 'next/image';
<Image src='/hero.jpg' alt='Hero' width={1200} height={600} priority />

Fonts.exp: next/font automatically optimizes and self-hosts Google Fonts and custom fonts, eliminating external requests. It supports variable fonts and subsetting for reduced bundle size.

Bundle Analysis.exp: Next.js provides built-in bundle analysis through @next/bundle-analyzer. It generates visual reports showing the size of each JavaScript bundle and its dependencies to identify optimization targets.

Vercel.exp: Vercel is the official deployment platform for Next.js, offering zero-config deploys from Git, automatic HTTPS, edge functions, and preview deployments for every pull request.

Docker.exp: Next.js apps can be containerized with Docker for deployment on any container orchestration platform. A multi-stage Dockerfile optimizes for build speed and image size.
Docker.code:
FROM node:18-alpine AS base
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

Self-hosted.exp: Next.js supports self-hosting on any Node.js server using the standalone output mode. The standalone folder includes only production dependencies, minimizing deployment size.

Route Groups.exp: Route groups organize routes without affecting URL paths by wrapping folder names in parentheses. They are useful for separating marketing, admin, and auth sections with different layouts.

Parallel Routes.exp: Parallel routes render multiple pages simultaneously in the same layout using named slots. Each slot has its own loading and error states, enabling complex dashboard and feed layouts.

Intercepting Routes.exp: Intercepting routes overlay content from another route within the current layout using (..) syntax. They are commonly used for modal previews that render as full pages on hard refresh.
Intercepting Routes.code:
app/
  feed/
    page.tsx
    (..)photo/[id]/page.tsx  // intercepts /photo/[id] from /feed
  photo/
    [id]/page.tsx

Static Metadata.exp: The metadata object export defines page-level SEO data including title, description, Open Graph, and Twitter cards. It supports static values and template-based title generation.

Dynamic Metadata.exp: Dynamic metadata is generated with the generateMetadata function that receives route params and search params, enabling SEO data based on fetched content.

Metadata API.exp: Next.js provides a comprehensive Metadata API covering Open Graph, Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data, manifest, icons, robots, sitemaps, and alternate language links.

Turbopack.exp: Turbopack is Next.js's Rust-based incremental bundler replacing webpack in development. It provides near-instant HMR, sub-second cold starts, and incremental computation for large projects.

Partial Prerendering.exp: Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering on the same page. Static shell content is served instantly while dynamic holes stream in after rendering on the server.

Instrumentation.exp: Instrumentation hooks allow running code on server startup. The register() function in instrumentation.ts is useful for OpenTelemetry tracing, metrics setup, and infrastructure initialization.

REPL.exp: The Node.js REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) provides an interactive shell to execute JavaScript expressions in real time. It's useful for quick prototyping, debugging, and testing code snippets without creating a file.

Modules.exp: Node.js uses the CommonJS module system by default, where each file is treated as a separate module. Modules are loaded using `require()` and exports are defined via `module.exports` or `exports`.

NPM.exp: NPM is the default package manager for Node.js, used to install, manage, and publish packages. It reads `package.json` to resolve dependencies and supports semantic versioning for version control.
NPM.code:
npm init -y
npm install express
npm install --save-dev nodemon
npm uninstall express

ES Modules.exp: Node.js supports ES modules (import/export) alongside CommonJS. Use .mjs extension or set "type": "module" in package.json. ES modules support top-level await and static analysis for tree-shaking.

Global Objects.exp: Node.js provides global objects like __dirname, __filename, process, Buffer, and console that are available without importing. Each module has its own __dirname and __filename scoped to that file.

fs module.exp: The `fs` module provides both synchronous and asynchronous methods to interact with the file system. The promise-based API (`fs/promises`) is preferred for modern async code.

Path.exp: The `path` module provides utilities for working with file and directory paths. It handles path normalization, joining segments, and extracting file extension or directory components.

Streams.exp: Streams allow processing data piece by piece without loading entire files into memory. They are ideal for handling large files or real-time data like video and HTTP responses.

File Watching.exp: Node can watch files or directories for changes using fs.watch or fs.watchFile. Useful for live reload, build tools, and monitoring config file changes without restarting the process.

Callbacks.exp: Callbacks are functions passed as arguments to be executed after an async operation completes. They form the foundation of async programming in Node but can lead to deeply nested 'callback hell'.

Promises.exp: Promises represent the eventual completion or failure of an async operation, providing a cleaner chaining mechanism than callbacks. A promise exists in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected.

async/await.exp: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code. Functions declared with `async` always return a Promise, and `await` pauses execution until the Promise settles.

Event Loop.exp: The event loop is the core mechanism that enables Node's non-blocking I/O. It processes callbacks through phases: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, and close callbacks, all in a single thread.

HTTP Module.exp: The `http` module allows creating HTTP servers and clients without external dependencies. It handles low-level networking, request parsing, and response writing with a stream-based API.

Server.exp: Building an HTTP server involves handling requests and sending responses. Each request receives an IncomingMessage object and a ServerResponse object for controlling the response data and headers.

Request Handling.exp: Node.js processes requests via event emitters on the request stream. You can listen for 'data' and 'end' events to read request bodies, parse headers via `req.headers`, and inspect the URL and method.

Package Management.exp: NPM manages project dependencies defined in `package.json`. The `node_modules` folder stores installed packages, and `package-lock.json` ensures reproducible installs across environments.
Package Management.code:
npm init -y
npm install lodash
npm install --save-dev jest
npm ci
npm outdated
npm update

Scripts.exp: The `scripts` field in `package.json` defines aliases for commands that can be run via `npm run`. Pre/post hooks allow automatic script chaining, and scripts have access to `node_modules/.bin`.

Publishing.exp: Publishing packages to the npm registry requires an npm account, a unique package name, and proper versioning via `npm version`. Packages should include a README, license, and main entry point.
Publishing.code:
npm login
npm version patch
npm publish
npm version minor && npm publish
npm unpublish package@1.0.0

Workspaces.exp: NPM workspaces allow managing multiple packages in a single monorepo. Dependencies are hoisted to the root node_modules, and scripts can run across all workspaces concurrently.

NPX.exp: NPX runs npm packages without installing them globally. It's useful for one-off commands like scaffolding tools, linters, or any CLI tool that you don't need permanently.
NPX.code:
npx create-react-app my-app
npx prisma generate
npx http-server .
npx -p node@20 node --version

Buffer.exp: Buffer provides a way to work with binary data directly in Node.js. It is a fixed-size chunk of memory allocated outside the V8 heap, useful for handling raw data from files, networks, or crypto operations.

Readable/Writable.exp: Streams are classified into Readable, Writable, Duplex, and Transform types. Readable streams produce data that can be consumed via `data` events or piped to Writable streams.

Transform.exp: Transform streams are Duplex streams that can modify data during read/write operations. They are commonly used for compression, encryption, and data format conversion.

Pipeline & Finished.exp: stream.pipeline handles piping streams with automatic cleanup and error propagation. stream.finished provides a callback when a stream is no longer readable or writable.

spawn.exp: spawn launches a new process with streaming I/O. It returns a ChildProcess object with stdin, stdout, and stderr streams, ideal for long-running processes with large output.

exec.exp: exec spawns a shell and runs a command, buffering the output. It's simpler than spawn for short commands but has a 1MB output buffer limit and higher risk of shell injection.

fork.exp: fork creates a new Node.js process with an IPC channel for message passing. It is designed for offloading CPU-intensive work to separate processes while keeping communication easy.

execFile.exp: execFile is similar to exec but spawns the command directly without a shell, making it more secure. It is suitable for running binary executables with arguments and no shell interpretation.

EventEmitter.exp: EventEmitter is a core Node.js pattern for handling asynchronous events. Objects emit named events that trigger registered listener functions, enabling decoupled communication between components.

Custom Events.exp: Custom events allow building event-driven architectures. Use event names as constants to avoid typos, and leverage EventEmitter for pub/sub patterns throughout your application.

Max Listeners.exp: EventEmitter warns about memory leaks when more than 10 listeners are attached. Use setMaxListeners to increase the limit, but first investigate if listeners are being properly removed.

Error Handling.exp: Node.js uses the standard Error class and supports custom error types. Unhandled promise rejections and uncaught exceptions should be caught globally to prevent process crashes.

Debugger.exp: Node.js includes a built-in debugger accessible via `--inspect` flag, which opens a Chrome DevTools-compatible interface. The `debugger` statement creates breakpoints, and `node inspect` provides a CLI debugger.

Process.exp: The `process` object provides information about the current Node.js process, including environment variables, command-line arguments, memory usage, and exit control. It is available globally everywhere.

Profiling.exp: Node.js built-in profiler and V8 inspector help identify performance bottlenecks. Use --prof for CPU profiling and the inspector for flame graphs and heap snapshots.
Profiling.code:
node --prof app.js
node --prof-process isolated-*-v8.log > processed.txt
node --inspect app.js
# Open chrome://inspect in Chrome

Console Methods.exp: The console module provides debugging utilities beyond console.log: console.table for arrays, console.time for timing, console.trace for stack traces, and console.group for nested output.

Assert.exp: Node's built-in assert module provides basic assertion testing. While minimal, it is useful for simple checks and can be used with the built-in test runner.

Jest.exp: Jest is the most popular testing framework for Node.js with zero-config setup, built-in mocking, code coverage, snapshot testing, and watch mode.

Mocha & Chai.exp: Mocha is a flexible test framework paired with Chai for assertions. It supports BDD/TDD interfaces, async testing, and extensive plugin ecosystems.

Node Test Runner.exp: Node 18+ includes a built-in test runner (node:test) with assertion library (node:assert). It supports mocking, code coverage, and runs tests in parallel without external dependencies.

PM2.exp: PM2 is a production process manager for Node.js with load balancing, auto-restart, log management, monitoring dashboard, and zero-downtime deployments.

Environment Variables.exp: Environment variables configure Node.js apps across environments without code changes. Use dotenv for local development and process.env for runtime access.

Graceful Shutdown.exp: Production Node.js apps must handle SIGTERM gracefully, closing connections and completing in-flight requests before exiting.

Helmet.exp: Helmet secures Express apps by setting HTTP headers: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and more.

Input Validation.exp: Validate and sanitize all user input to prevent injection attacks. Use libraries like Joi, Zod, or express-validator for schema validation.

CORS.exp: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing must be configured to control which domains can access your API. Restrict origins, methods, and headers to the minimum needed.

Worker Threads.exp: Worker threads enable true multi-threading in Node.js for CPU-intensive tasks. Each worker runs in its own V8 context with isolated memory, communicating via message passing.

Cluster.exp: The cluster module allows forking multiple Node.js processes to share server load across CPU cores. The master process distributes incoming connections to worker processes via round-robin scheduling.

Performance Hooks.exp: The perf_hooks module provides performance measurement APIs similar to the Web Performance API. Use PerformanceObserver to collect timing data for monitoring and optimization.

Project Setup.exp: Nuxt 3 projects are created using the nuxi CLI. The scaffolding tool asks about desired features like package manager, UI framework, and modules, generating a ready-to-develop project structure.
Project Setup.code:
npx nuxi init my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev

Pages.exp: The pages directory in Nuxt automatically generates routes based on file structure. Each .vue file becomes a route, with index.vue as the root and dynamic routes using brackets like [id].vue.

Routing.exp: Nuxt provides <NuxtLink> for client-side navigation and <NuxtPage> for rendering matched routes. Route middleware can be defined to protect pages or redirect users based on conditions.

useFetch.exp: useFetch is the simplest way to fetch data in Nuxt 3. It automatically deduplicates requests, handles caching, and provides reactive refs for data, pending state, and error handling.

useAsyncData.exp: useAsyncData provides more control over data fetching than useFetch. It accepts a custom fetcher function and supports keys for caching, refresh intervals, and lazy loading options.

Server Routes.exp: Server routes in the server/api directory handle backend logic with h3 event handlers. They support all HTTP methods and can access request body, query parameters, and cookies directly.

Universal.exp: Universal rendering is Nuxt's default mode, combining server-side rendering with client-side hydration. The server renders HTML on first request, then Vue takes over for SPA-like navigation.
Universal.code:
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({ ssr: true })

SPA.exp: Single Page Application mode disables server-side rendering entirely. All rendering happens client-side, with the server only serving a minimal HTML shell. Useful for fully client-driven apps.
SPA.code:
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({ ssr: false })

Static Generation.exp: Static generation pre-renders all pages at build time using nuxt generate. The output is a fully static site deployable on any static hosting provider like Netlify or Vercel.

Auth.exp: The @sidebase/nuxt-auth module provides a complete authentication system for Nuxt 3. It supports multiple auth providers, session management, and middleware protection out of the box.

Content.exp: Nuxt Content is a file-based CMS that reads Markdown, JSON, and YAML files from the content directory. It provides a queryable MongoDB-like API and automatic rendering of content files.
Content.code:
// content/index.md
---
title: Hello Nuxt
---
# Welcome
<script setup>
const { data } = await useAsyncData('content', () => queryContent('/').find());
</script>

Tailwind.exp: The Nuxt Tailwind module integrates Tailwind CSS with zero configuration. It auto-imports the config, enables HMR for styles, and purges unused classes in production builds.

SEO.exp: Nuxt provides built-in SEO tools through useHead composable and the @nuxtjs/seo module. It manages meta tags, Open Graph, structured data, and sitemaps for better search visibility.

useState.exp: useState is Nuxt's built-in reactive state composable that works across server and client. It creates a singleton ref that persists across component re-renders and is serialized during SSR.
useState.code:
const counter = useState('counter', () => 0);
const increment = () => counter.value++;

Pinia.exp: Pinia is the recommended state management library for Nuxt 3. It provides a intuitive API with full TypeScript support, devtools integration, and automatic SSR hydration.

Store Patterns.exp: Nuxt stores follow the composition API pattern with defineStore. Stores can be organized by domain feature and accessed anywhere in the app via the generated composable function.

Route Middleware.exp: Route middleware in Nuxt runs before entering a route and can redirect or cancel navigation. Middleware files are placed in the middleware directory and can be applied globally or per-route.

Auth Module.exp: The nuxt-auth module provides session-based authentication with built-in login pages, OAuth support, and credential-based auth. It automatically handles token refresh and session persistence.
Auth Module.code:
const { status, signIn, signOut, data } = useAuth();
if (status.value === 'unauthenticated') signIn('github');

Vercel.exp: Deploying Nuxt to Vercel requires the Vercel preset. Vercel automatically detects the framework, optimizes serverless functions, and provides edge network distribution.
Vercel.code:
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({ nitro: { preset: 'vercel' } });

Netlify.exp: Nuxt deploys to Netlify using the Netlify preset, generating edge functions for server routes. Netlify provides automatic HTTPS, deploy previews, and form handling.

Node Server.exp: The Node server preset runs Nuxt as a standalone Node.js application. This is ideal for self-hosting on VPS, Docker containers, or traditional server environments.

Auto-imports.exp: Nuxt automatically imports composables, components, and utilities from predefined directories. Components in components/, composables in composables/, and utils in utils/ are auto-imported without explicit imports.

Layers.exp: Nuxt layers allow extending a base Nuxt project from external sources or local directories. Layers can override components, pages, composables, and configuration, enabling modular architectures.

Modules Dev.exp: Creating custom Nuxt modules allows packaging reusable functionality. Modules can modify the Nuxt configuration, add hooks, register components, and integrate with the build pipeline.

Overview.exp: Nuxt DevTools provides an in-app panel with page inspection, component tree, state editor, timeline, and module management. It is available in development with zero configuration.
Overview.code:
// Installed by default in Nuxt 3.4+
// Press Shift+Alt+D or click the DevTools icon in the bottom right corner

Pages & Components.exp: The DevTools Pages tab displays all auto-detected routes with their middleware, layout, and data dependencies. The Components tab shows the live component tree with state inspection.

Timeline & Analysis.exp: The Timeline tab records async operations, navigation events, and rendering performance. It helps identify slow API calls, excessive reactivity, and rendering bottlenecks.

Nuxt Image.exp: Nuxt Image (@nuxt/image) provides automatic image optimization with responsive sizes, format conversion to WebP/AVIF, lazy loading, and CDN provider integrations (Cloudinary, Imgix, etc).
Nuxt Image.code:
<NuxtImg src="/hero.jpg" width="1200" height="600" loading="lazy" />
<NuxtPicture src="/photo.jpg" sizes="sm:100vw md:50vw lg:400px" />

Public Assets.exp: Assets in the public/ directory are served at the root URL without processing. Assets in assets/ are processed by Vite (version-hashed, minified) and imported via ~/assets path.

Fonts.exp: Nuxt Fonts (@nuxt/fonts) automatically optimizes Google Fonts and custom fonts with self-hosting, subsetting, and fallback generation to eliminate CLS from font swaps.

Nitro Engine.exp: Nitro is Nuxt's server engine powering API routes, middleware, and SSR. It supports multiple deployment presets (Node, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare) and auto-detects the target environment.

Hybrid Rendering.exp: Hybrid rendering lets you define different rendering strategies per route: SSR, SSG, SPA, or ISR. Route rules control caching, prerendering, and rendering modes granularly.

Server Storage.exp: Nitro's server storage provides a unified key-value API across filesystem, Redis, Cloudflare KV, and other drivers. It handles session storage, cache, and file uploads without extra dependencies.

PostgreSQL History & Overview.exp: PostgreSQL began as POSTGRES at UC Berkeley in 1986, led by Michael Stonebraker. It evolved into PostgreSQL (Post-GreSQL) in 1996, emphasizing SQL compliance and extensibility. Today it is the world's most advanced open-source relational database, known for ACID compliance, MVCC, extensibility, and a vibrant community.

Installation & Configuration.exp: PostgreSQL can be installed via package managers (apt, yum, brew), Docker, or compiled from source. The main configuration file is postgresql.conf, controlling memory, logging, connections, and replication settings. After install, the postgres service must be started.
Installation & Configuration.code:
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install postgresql-16
sudo systemctl start postgresql

# Verify
pg_isready

psql Basics.exp: psql is the official interactive terminal for PostgreSQL. Connect to a database, run SQL queries, and use backslash meta-commands. Essential commands: \c to connect, \dt list tables, \d describe, \l list databases, \du list roles.
psql Basics.code:
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U myuser -d mydb

mydb=> \dt
mydb=> \d users
mydb=> \l
mydb=> \du

pgAdmin GUI.exp: pgAdmin is a popular web-based GUI for PostgreSQL. It provides visual query building, schema browsing, dashboard monitoring, and server management. The server runs as a Python/Flask app and can be accessed via browser.
pgAdmin GUI.code:
# Start pgAdmin 4 (via desktop or server mode)
pgadmin4

# Docker
# docker pull dpage/pgadmin4
# docker run -p 80:80 -e PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL=user@domain.com -e PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD=admin dpage/pgadmin4

Connection Strings & Service File.exp: PostgreSQL supports libpq connection strings (postgresql://user:pass@host:port/db) and a pg_service.conf file that stores named connection parameters for reuse. Environment variables (PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD) also configure connections.
Connection Strings & Service File.code:
# Connection string
postgresql://myuser:mypass@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=require

# ~/.pg_service.conf
[mydb]
host=localhost
port=5432
dbname=mydb
user=myuser

.pgpass & Authentication.exp: The .pgpass file stores passwords for non-interactive connections. Format: hostname:port:database:username:password. File must have 0600 permissions. psql and other libpq clients read it automatically when no password is provided.

psql Meta-Commands Deep Dive.exp: psql offers 100+ backslash meta-commands. \g executes the query buffer, \i includes a file, \o redirects output, \x toggles expanded display, \e opens an external editor, \timing shows query duration, \watch repeats a query, and \copy performs server-side data transfer.
psql Meta-Commands Deep Dive.code:
\x on            -- Expanded display
\timing on       -- Show query duration
\i queries.sql   -- Run SQL from file
\copy users TO '/tmp/users.csv' CSV HEADER
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users \watch 5

CREATE TABLE Deep Dive.exp: CREATE TABLE defines a new relation with named columns, data types, and optional constraints. Supports storage parameters (FILLFACTOR, autovacuum), WITH OIDs (deprecated), ON COMMIT behavior for temp tables, and tablespace assignment. Columns can have defaults, nullability, and compression.
CREATE TABLE Deep Dive.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL,
  customer_id INT NOT NULL,
  total NUMERIC(12,2) DEFAULT 0.00,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  notes TEXT
) WITH (FILLFACTOR = 90)
TABLESPACE fast_space;

Column Constraints.exp: Constraints enforce data integrity at the column level: NOT NULL prevents nulls, UNIQUE ensures no duplicates, DEFAULT supplies a fallback value, CHECK validates a boolean expression, and REFERENCES (foreign key) links to another table's column. Multiple constraints can stack.
Column Constraints.code:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  salary NUMERIC(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),
  dept_id INT REFERENCES departments(id),
  status TEXT DEFAULT 'active'
);

Table Constraints & EXCLUDE.exp: Table-level constraints span multiple columns: PRIMARY KEY (composite), UNIQUE (composite), FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, and EXCLUDE. EXCLUDE ensures no two rows satisfy a condition using GiST operators, useful for calendar bookings, IP allocation, and overlapping ranges.
Table Constraints & EXCLUDE.code:
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  room_id INT,
  during TSRANGE,
  booked_by TEXT,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
-- Prevents overlapping time ranges for same room

Sequences & SERIAL.exp: Sequences generate unique numeric values. SERIAL is shorthand for creating an INTEGER column with an auto-incrementing sequence. Sequences support CACHE, CYCLE, MINVALUE, MAXVALUE, and can be manipulated via nextval(), currval(), setval(), and ALTER SEQUENCE.

IDENTITY Columns.exp: GENERATED AS IDENTITY (SQL standard) replaces SERIAL. Supports BY DEFAULT (allows manual override) or ALWAYS (prevents manual override). Offers better schema introspection, no orphan sequences, and proper dependency tracking. Preferred over SERIAL in modern PostgreSQL.

GENERATED Columns.exp: Generated columns compute values from other columns. STORED means the value is computed on write and stored physically. VIRTUAL is not yet supported in PostgreSQL. Useful for derived data like full_name from first and last name, or price with tax.

Table Inheritance.exp: PostgreSQL supports table inheritance where a child table inherits all columns from a parent. Queries on the parent include child rows by default (use ONLY to exclude children). Useful for partitioning and code reuse, though modern partitioning is preferred over traditional inheritance.

Table Partitioning.exp: Partitioning splits large tables into smaller physical pieces while preserving a single logical view. Methods: RANGE (by date/id range), LIST (by discrete values), HASH (by hash of key). Partitions can be sub-partitioned, and partition pruning dramatically improves query performance.

Temporary Tables.exp: Temporary tables (prefixed with TEMP or TEMPORARY) exist only for the duration of a session or transaction. They are visible only to the creating session, stored in a temporary schema, and can have ON COMMIT DROP or ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS behavior. Useful for intermediate results.

UNLOGGED Tables.exp: UNLOGGED tables skip WAL (Write-Ahead Log) generation, making writes ~10x faster. They are NOT crash-safe — truncated or lost after an unclean shutdown. Ideal for ephemeral or cache data that can be rebuilt. Cannot be replicated via streaming replication.

Numeric Types.exp: PostgreSQL offers SMALLINT (2 bytes), INTEGER (4 bytes), BIGINT (8 bytes), NUMERIC(p,s) for exact precision, REAL (4-byte float), DOUBLE PRECISION (8-byte float), and MONEY for currency. NUMERIC is preferred for financial calculations requiring exact decimal storage without rounding errors.

Character Types.exp: CHAR(n) is a fixed-length string (blank-padded), VARCHAR(n) is variable-length with a limit, and TEXT is unlimited. PostgreSQL treats all three similarly internally — there is no performance penalty for TEXT over VARCHAR. Use CHECK if you need length constraints beyond the type itself.

Binary Data (BYTEA).exp: BYTEA stores binary strings (byte arrays). Supports hex format (\x...) and escape format. Use encode()/decode() for conversion to/from hex, base64. BYTEA is limited to 1 GB per value. For large objects >1 GB, use the large object API (lo_creat, lo_import, lo_export).

Date/Time Types.exp: PostgreSQL has DATE (no time), TIME (no date, with/without timezone), TIMESTAMP (date+time, with/without timezone), TIMESTAMPTZ (with timezone), and INTERVAL (duration). TIMESTAMPTZ stores internally as UTC and converts to session timezone on display. Use AT TIME ZONE for conversions.

Boolean & UUID.exp: BOOLEAN stores TRUE, FALSE, or NULL. Accepts 'yes'/'no', '1'/'0', 't'/'f' as input. UUID stores Universally Unique Identifiers (128-bit). The uuid-ossp or pgcrypto extension provides generation functions (gen_random_uuid()). UUIDs are ideal for distributed system primary keys.

Arrays & Composite Types.exp: Arrays store multiple values of the same type in a single column. Use array constructors or ARRAY[...] syntax. Supports multi-dimensional arrays and rich operators (@>, <@, &&). Composite types bundle multiple fields into one column, created via CREATE TYPE or inferred from table row types.

Range Types.exp: Range types represent intervals: int4range, int8range, numrange, tsrange, tstzrange, daterange. Operators include && (overlap), @> (contains), <@ (contained by), -|- (adjacent). GiST indexes on ranges enable fast exclusion constraints and overlap queries for scheduling, geofencing, and log analysis.

JSON & JSONB Deep Dive.exp: JSON stores text as-is (preserving whitespace, order, duplicates). JSONB stores a decomposed binary format (efficient indexing, no duplicates, no key order). JSONB supports GIN indexes for containment (@>), existence (?), and key/value queries. Operators: -> (json), ->> (text), #> (path), #>> (path text).

hstore Key-Value Store.exp: hstore stores sets of key-value pairs within a single column (both keys and values are strings). Requires the hstore extension. Useful for semi-structured attributes when the schema is not fixed. Operators: -> (value by key), ? (key exists), @> (contains pair), || (concatenate).

Network Address Types.exp: PostgreSQL provides inet (IPv4/IPv6 addresses), cidr (network blocks), and macaddr (MAC addresses). Built-in operators test containment (<<=, <<), sort, and compare. The ip4r extension (not built-in) adds indexed range operations for advanced network queries.

Geometric Types.exp: PostgreSQL supports geometric data types: point (x,y), line, lseg (line segment), box, path (open/closed), polygon, and circle. Operators test containment (@>), intersection (?-\||), distance (<->). GiST indexes accelerate geometric queries. Useful for GIS-like applications without PostGIS overhead.

Domain & Custom Types.exp: CREATE DOMAIN creates a reusable type based on an existing type with constraints (CHECK, NOT NULL, DEFAULT). CREATE TYPE creates a custom composite or enum type (or base type via C extension). Domains are great for business-level validation like us_zip_code, email, or positive_numeric.

SELECT Deep Dive.exp: SELECT defines the projection, FROM specifies the source, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY groups for aggregation, HAVING filters groups, ORDER BY sorts results, and LIMIT/OFFSET paginates. Execution order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> WINDOW -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
SELECT Deep Dive.code:
SELECT
  u.id,
  COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
  SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.created_at > '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id
HAVING SUM(o.total) > 100
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10;

JOIN Types.exp: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches. RIGHT JOIN is the symmetric opposite. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible. CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product of all row combinations.

LATERAL & Self Joins.exp: LATERAL allows a subquery in FROM to reference columns from preceding FROM items. Essential for top-N-per-group queries and calling set-returning functions per row. Self JOIN joins a table to itself (using aliases) to query hierarchical data like org charts or threaded comments.
LATERAL & Self Joins.code:
-- Top 3 orders per user (LATERAL)
SELECT u.name, top.*
FROM users u
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT amount, created_at FROM orders
  WHERE user_id = u.id
  ORDER BY amount DESC
  LIMIT 3
) top;

-- Self JOIN (org chart)
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

Set Operations.exp: UNION combines results of two queries, deduplicating rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates. INTERSECT returns rows present in both queries. EXCEPT returns rows from the first query not present in the second. All set operations require matching column counts and compatible data types.
Set Operations.code:
-- Active and former employees combined
SELECT name, email FROM active_employees
UNION
SELECT name, email FROM former_employees;

-- Products in both categories
SELECT product_id FROM electronics
INTERSECT
SELECT product_id FROM clearance;

-- Customers with no orders
SELECT id FROM customers
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders;

Recursive CTE.exp: WITH RECURSIVE lets a CTE reference itself. The anchor member runs first (non-recursive), then the recursive member repeatedly joins the CTE's output until no new rows are produced. Essential for tree traversal (org charts, category hierarchies), graph queries, and generating series.
Recursive CTE.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
  -- Anchor: top-level manager
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  -- Recursive: direct reports
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, t.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM org_tree ORDER BY level, name;

-- Fibonacci sequence
WITH RECURSIVE fib(a, b) AS (
  SELECT 0, 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b, a + b FROM fib WHERE b < 1000
)
SELECT a FROM fib;

Correlated Subqueries.exp: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and is re-evaluated for every row. Used in WHERE (with EXISTS, IN, comparisons), SELECT (as a scalar subquery), and HAVING clauses. Can be slower than JOINs on large datasets, but is expressive for row-by-row comparisons.
Correlated Subqueries.code:
-- Employees earning above dept average
SELECT e.name, e.salary, e.dept_id
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id = e.dept_id
);

-- Customers with recent orders
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
);

ANY, ALL, EXISTS.exp: ANY compares a value to any element in a subquery result (equivalent to IN but more flexible with operators like > ANY). ALL requires the comparison to hold for every element. EXISTS returns TRUE if the subquery has any rows. These are powerful for semi-join and anti-join patterns.

FILTER Clause for Aggregates.exp: The FILTER clause lets aggregate functions conditionally include rows without a subquery or CASE. Multiple aggregates can use different filters on the same column set. More readable and often faster than CASE-based conditional aggregation. Compatible with GROUP BY.
FILTER Clause for Aggregates.code:
SELECT
  dept_id,
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE salary > 100000) AS high_earners,
  AVG(salary) FILTER (WHERE status = 'active') AS avg_active_salary,
  SUM(bonus) FILTER (WHERE YEAR( award_date) = 2024) AS bonus_2024
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;

GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP.exp: GROUPING SETS produces multiple grouping levels in a single query. ROLLUP generates hierarchical subtotals (e.g., by year, then month, then day). CUBE produces all possible grouping combinations. The GROUPING() function identifies which level a row belongs to, preventing ambiguity with actual NULLs.
GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP.code:
SELECT dept_id, role_id, SUM(salary) AS total
FROM employees
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
  (dept_id, role_id),
  (dept_id),
  (role_id),
  ()
);

-- ROLLUP (hierarchy)
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM sale_date) AS yr,
       EXTRACT(MONTH FROM sale_date) AS mon,
       SUM(amount)
FROM sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (yr, mon);

SELECT GROUPING(yr) AS is_total FROM ...

Window Functions Deep Dive.exp: Window functions compute values across sets of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. RANK() and DENSE_RANK() assign rankings with or without gaps. NTILE(n) divides rows into n buckets. LAG()/LEAD() access adjacent rows. FIRST_VALUE()/LAST_VALUE() get window endpoints. Frame clauses (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS BETWEEN) define the sliding window.
Window Functions Deep Dive.code:
SELECT
  name, department, salary,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank,
  NTILE(4) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS quartile,
  LAG(salary, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary) AS prev_salary,
  LEAD(salary, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary) AS next_salary,
  FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS max_dept_salary,
  LAST_VALUE(salary) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC
    RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS min_dept_salary,
  AVG(salary) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary
    ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
  ) AS moving_avg
FROM employees;

INSERT ON CONFLICT (UPSERT).exp: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT handles unique/primary key violations gracefully. DO NOTHING skips the insert silently. DO UPDATE SET ... acts as an UPDATE when a conflict occurs (the UPSERT pattern). The EXCLUDED pseudo-table references the values that would have been inserted. Conflict targets can be constraint names or columns.
INSERT ON CONFLICT (UPSERT).code:
INSERT INTO users (id, email, name)
VALUES (1, 'alice@example.com', 'Alice')
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
  SET email = EXCLUDED.email,
      name = EXCLUDED.name,
      updated_at = NOW();

-- On conflict on any unique constraint
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty)
VALUES ('ABC-123', 10)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

RETURNING Clause.exp: The RETURNING clause returns values from inserted, updated, or deleted rows — similar to OUTPUT in SQL Server. Supports * or specific expressions. Works with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE. Essential for getting auto-generated keys (SERIAL, IDENTITY) without a separate SELECT.

MERGE (PostgreSQL 15+).exp: MERGE (also called upsert) conditionally inserts, updates, or deletes rows in a target table based on a source of rows. WHEN MATCHED/WHEN NOT MATCHED branches control the action. More expressive than INSERT ON CONFLICT for complex synchronization scenarios like data warehouse merges.
MERGE (PostgreSQL 15+).code:
MERGE INTO employees t
USING staging_employees s ON t.employee_id = s.employee_id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.salary <> s.salary THEN
  UPDATE SET salary = s.salary, updated_at = NOW()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (employee_id, name, salary, dept_id)
  VALUES (s.employee_id, s.name, s.salary, s.dept_id);

UPDATE with FROM.exp: UPDATE ... FROM extends standard SQL to allow joining additional tables in the UPDATE statement. Useful for updating values based on matches in another table or aggregated values. The joined table(s) appear after FROM, with conditions in WHERE to control which rows update.
UPDATE with FROM.code:
UPDATE products p
SET price = p.price * 1.1,
    updated_at = NOW()
FROM categories c
WHERE p.category_id = c.id
  AND c.name = 'Electronics';

-- Update from an aggregate
UPDATE accounts a
SET balance = a.balance + d.total
FROM (
  SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM deposits WHERE status = 'pending'
  GROUP BY account_id
) d
WHERE a.id = d.account_id;

DELETE with USING.exp: DELETE ... USING (PostgreSQL-specific) allows joining additional tables to determine which rows to delete. Similar to UPDATE FROM syntax. Useful for bulk deletes based on conditions in related tables, like purging orphaned records or cleaning up by business rules from a reference table.
DELETE with USING.code:
DELETE FROM orders o
USING customers c
WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  AND c.status = 'inactive'
  AND o.created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 year';

-- Delete duplicates
DELETE FROM products p
USING products p2
WHERE p.id > p2.id
  AND p.sku = p2.sku;

COPY for Bulk Loading.exp: COPY is the fastest way to import/export data. COPY (server-side) requires file system access on the server. \copy (psql meta-command) works client-side. Supports CSV, TEXT, and BINARY formats. HEADER skips the first line. DELIMITER specifies column separator. NULL specifies the null string.

Foreign Data Wrappers.exp: Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW) let PostgreSQL query external data sources as if they were local tables. postgres_fdw connects to remote PostgreSQL databases. mysql_fdw, mongo_fdw handle other databases. file_fdw reads flat files. CREATE FOREIGN TABLE defines the structure. IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA bulk-imports remote tables.

B-Tree Index Deep Dive.exp: B-Tree (balanced tree) is the default and most common index type. Supports =, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, and pattern matching (if left-anchored). Also handles ORDER BY and MIN/MAX efficiently. Multiple NULLs are stored together (at the front or back depending on sort order).

Hash Index.exp: Hash indexes store 32-bit hash codes of indexed values. Only support equality comparisons (=). In PostgreSQL 10+, hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe. Use them when you only need equality lookups on large, random values where B-Tree would be deeper. Generally smaller than B-Tree for simple equality.

GiST Index.exp: GiST (Generalized Search Tree) is a balanced tree structure supporting custom operator classes. Used for geometric data (@@, ~=, &&), full-text search (tsvector), range type overlap (&&), and trigram similarity (pg_trgm). Supports nearest-neighbor search (ORDER BY <-> LIMIT n).

GIN Index.exp: GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes composite values like elements within arrays, JSONB documents, tsvectors, and hstore. Excellent for containment (@>), existence (?), and full-text search queries. GIN builds fast but is slower to update. GIN can be FASTUPDATE-enabled for better write performance.

SP-GiST & BRIN Indexes.exp: SP-GiST (Space-Partitioned GiST) supports partitioned search trees (quadtrees, kd-trees) for point data, network addresses, and text. BRIN (Block Range Index) summarizes min/max values per block range. BRIN is orders of magnitude smaller than B-Tree and ideal for append-only, naturally-ordered data like time-series logs.

Bloom Filter Index.exp: The bloom extension provides Bloom filter indexes — a probabilistic data structure that tests set membership with a tunable false-positive rate. Ideal for multi-column equality queries on many columns where creating individual indexes is impractical. Supports only = queries and can have false positives.

Partial & Expression Indexes.exp: Partial indexes index only rows satisfying a WHERE clause — smaller and faster than full indexes. Expression indexes index the result of a function or expression rather than a raw column. Essential for case-insensitive lookups, computed columns, and conditional indexing of only relevant rows.

Covering Indexes & Index-Only Scans.exp: A covering index includes all columns needed by a query, allowing index-only scans that never touch the heap (table). PostgreSQL supports INCLUDE to add non-key columns to a unique or primary key index. This allows a query to be satisfied entirely from the index, dramatically reducing I/O.

Concurrent & Conditional Index Operation.exp: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index without locking the table against writes (uses extra CPU and I/O). DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY removes without blocking. REINDEX rebuilds indexes (CONCURRENTLY mode in v12+). Indexes can be marked UNUSABLE (but not yet supported in vanilla PostgreSQL — use INVALID).

EXPLAIN Deep Dive.exp: EXPLAIN shows the query plan (sequential scan, index scan, join type, etc.) with estimated costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual timing and rows. Additional options: BUFFERS (shared/local hit/read/dirtied), TIMING (enable/disable per-node timing), FORMAT JSON, and SETTINGS (showing planner parameters). Parallel plans show Workers Launched and worker timing.
EXPLAIN Deep Dive.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING, FORMAT JSON)
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > '2024-06-01'
ORDER BY o.total DESC
LIMIT 100;

-- Key metrics: startup cost, total cost, rows, width, actual time,
-- shared hit (from cache), shared read (from disk), loops

VACUUM Deep Dive.exp: VACUUM reclaims storage occupied by dead tuples and updates visibility maps. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table (exclusive lock, shrinks disk). VACUUM (without FULL) marks space for reuse but doesn't return it to the OS. VERBOSE shows detailed per-table activity. FREEZE aggressively marks tuples as frozen for anti-wraparound.

ANALYZE & Statistics.exp: ANALYZE collects table statistics (column distributions, correlation, null fractions, most-common values) used by the query planner. Run standalone or as VACUUM ANALYZE. pg_stats (system view) exposes histogram buckets, n_distinct, and correlation. Accurate statistics are critical for optimal query plans.

Autovacuum Tuning.exp: Autovacuum automatically runs VACUUM and ANALYZE based on dead tuple thresholds. Key parameters: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (triggers when dead tuples > threshold + scale * total), autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit (I/O throttling), and autovacuum_naptime. Per-table overrides via storage parameters.
Autovacuum Tuning.code:
-- Global settings in postgresql.conf
# autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50
# autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2
# autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 200
# autovacuum_naptime = 60s

-- Per-table override
ALTER TABLE busy_orders SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000,
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05
);

-- Monitor autovacuum activity
SELECT schemaname, tablename, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

pg_stat_statements.exp: pg_stat_statements tracks execution statistics for all SQL queries: calls, total_time, min/max/mean time, rows, shared hit/read/dirtied, and temp file I/O. Essential for identifying slow queries, high-frequency queries, and I/O patterns. Requires shared_preload_libraries and creating the extension.
pg_stat_statements.code:
-- postgresql.conf
# shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
# pg_stat_statements.max = 10000
# pg_stat_statements.track = all

CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements;

-- Top 10 worst queries by total time
SELECT queryid, LEFT(query, 80) AS query,
       calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time,
       shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Reset statistics
SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();

Query Tuning & Join Strategies.exp: PostgreSQL uses three join strategies: Nested Loop (good for small inner sets), Hash Join (good for large, unindexed joins), and Merge Join (good for sorted inputs). The planner chooses based on row estimates and cost parameters. Enable/disable via SET enable_hashjoin = off for debugging. Key practice: ensure proper indexes align with join and filter columns.
Query Tuning & Join Strategies.code:
-- Check join strategy
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 1000;

-- Force a specific join (for testing)
SET enable_hashjoin = off;
SET enable_mergejoin = off;

-- Tune planner
SET random_page_cost = 1.1;   -- For SSD storage (default 4.0 is for HDD)
SET effective_cache_size = '8GB';  -- Tell planner about OS cache

-- Gather feedback
SELECT relname, seq_scan, seq_tup_read, idx_scan, idx_tup_fetch
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

Memory Settings.exp: shared_buffers (typically 25% of RAM) is PostgreSQL's cache within its own memory. effective_cache_size estimates OS-level file system cache (helps planner decide index vs sequential scan). work_mem per-operation sort/hash memory (too high risks OOM, too low causes temp file spills). maintenance_work_mem for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX. wal_buffers for WAL throughput.
Memory Settings.code:
-- postgresql.conf (16 GB RAM server example)
# shared_buffers = 4GB          # 25% of RAM
# effective_cache_size = 12GB   # OS cache estimate
# work_mem = 64MB               # per sort/hash operation
# maintenance_work_mem = 1GB    # for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX
# wal_buffers = 64MB            # WAL write buffer

-- Check where sorts spill to disk
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE '%ORDER BY%';
-- Increase work_mem if many temp files created

Parallel Query Execution.exp: PostgreSQL can parallelize sequential scans, joins, aggregates, and some window functions across worker processes. Controlled by max_parallel_workers_per_gather, parallel_tuple_cost, and parallel_setup_cost. Tables can set parallel_workers storage parameter. Parallelism benefits large scans but has overhead for small queries.
Parallel Query Execution.code:
-- postgresql.conf
# max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4
# max_parallel_workers = 8
# max_worker_processes = 8

-- Enable/disable for a table
ALTER TABLE big_table SET (parallel_workers = 4);

-- Check parallel plan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(total)
FROM orders
WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- Look for: "Workers Planned: 4", "Workers Launched: 4"

PL/pgSQL Variables & Cursors.exp: PL/pgSQL is PostgreSQL's native procedural language. DECLARE defines variables (with DEFAULT or NOT NULL). %TYPE and %ROWTYPE anchor types to columns or table rows. Cursors iterate through query result sets row by row — declare, open, fetch, close. FOR loops implicitly handle cursors.

PL/pgSQL Exception Handling.exp: PL/pgSQL provides structured exception handling with BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END blocks. Caught exceptions can specify SQLSTATE or condition names (e.g., division_by_zero, unique_violation, foreign_key_violation). GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS retrieves error details. Note: exception blocks force a subtransaction, which has overhead.

SQL Functions.exp: SQL functions (LANGUAGE sql) are simple, fast, and can be inlined by the planner. Support RETURNS scalar, SETOF record/table, or single row. Can be used in FROM clauses when marked RETURNS TABLE. SQL functions have no variables, no procedural logic — just a single query (or multiple with the last one returned).

Triggers (BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF).exp: Triggers fire functions automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE. BEFORE triggers run before the operation (can modify the NEW row or prevent action). AFTER triggers run after the operation (see final values). INSTEAD OF triggers on views intercept operations entirely. FOR EACH ROW fires per row; FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once.

Column-Specific & Event Triggers.exp: Column-specific triggers fire only when specified columns are mentioned in UPDATE. Use UPDATE OF col1, col2 in the trigger definition. Event triggers (CREATE EVENT TRIGGER) fire on DDL events (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) at the database level, allowing logging or prevention of schema changes.
Column-Specific & Event Triggers.code:
-- Column-specific trigger
CREATE TRIGGER audit_salary_change
BEFORE UPDATE OF salary ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN (OLD.salary IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.salary)
EXECUTE FUNCTION log_salary_change();

-- Event trigger (DDL)
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION prevent_drop()
RETURNS EVENT_TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'Dropping tables is not allowed in this database';
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE EVENT TRIGGER block_table_drops
ON ddl_command_start
WHEN TAG IN ('DROP TABLE', 'DROP VIEW')
EXECUTE FUNCTION prevent_drop();

Trigger Functions (TG_OP, TG_TABLE_NAME).exp: Trigger functions receive automatic special variables: TG_OP (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE), TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_TABLE_SCHEMA, TG_WHEN (BEFORE/AFTER), TG_LEVEL (ROW/STATEMENT), TG_RELID, TG_NAME. OLD and NEW represent row states. A generic audit trigger uses these to log all table changes dynamically.

DO Blocks.exp: DO blocks execute anonymous PL/pgSQL (or other procedural language) code without creating a persistent function. Useful for one-off scripts, migrations, data cleanups, and administrative tasks. Can declare variables, use cursors, handle exceptions — same as a full function but nameless and immediate.

Stored Procedures (CALL).exp: Stored procedures (CREATE PROCEDURE) differ from functions: they support transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside the procedure), have no return value, and are invoked with CALL. Introduced in PostgreSQL 11. Useful for ETL pipelines, multi-step operations requiring intermediate commits, and administrative tasks.

PostGIS Extension.exp: PostGIS is the gold standard for spatial databases. It adds geometry, geography, and raster types, spatial indexes (GiST on geometry), and hundreds of functions (ST_Distance, ST_Intersects, ST_Within). Enables GIS queries, map rendering, and geospatial analytics. Requires CREATE EXTENSION postgis; then add a geometry column.

pg_stat_statements & uuid-ossp.exp: pg_stat_statements provides query execution statistics (see Performance section). uuid-ossp generates UUIDs via OSSP library (uuid_generate_v1mc, uuid_generate_v4) or use pgcrypto's gen_random_uuid() instead, which doesn't need uuid-ossp. Both extensions are simple to enable and essential for distributed IDs.

pgcrypto & citext.exp: pgcrypto provides cryptographic functions: digest(), hmac(), crypt() for password hashing, pgp_sym_encrypt()/pgp_pub_encrypt() for encryption, and gen_random_uuid()/gen_random_bytes(). citext provides a case-insensitive character string type that behaves like TEXT but comparisons are case-insensitive — ideal for email fields or usernames.

Fuzzy String Matching.exp: pg_trgm (trigram) and fuzzystrmatch (Levenshtein, Metaphone, Soundex, Double Metaphone) provide fuzzy text matching. pg_trgm creates a GIN or GiST index of 3-character substrings for fast similarity searches using %, <-> (distance), and word_similarity. Essential for search-as-you-type, deduplication, and spell correction.

unaccent & Full-Text Extensions.exp: unaccent removes diacritical marks (accents) from text, enabling accent-insensitive search. Typically combined with full-text search and an immutable function wrapping to_tsvector for GIN indexes. Also useful with citext and pg_trgm. Essential for internationalized applications (French, Spanish, German, etc.).

TimescaleDB & pg_plan_advsr.exp: TimescaleDB is a time-series extension adding hypertables (automatic partitioning by time), continuous aggregates, compression, and retention policies. pg_plan_advsr (plan advisor) analyzes slow queries and suggests index or rewriting improvements. Other notable extensions: pg_partman (partition management), pgaudit (audit logging), and hypopg (hypothetical indexes).

MVCC Internals.exp: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) allows readers never to block writers and vice versa. Each row has xmin (creating transaction ID) and xmax (deleting/expiring transaction ID). A snapshot captures active transactions at a point in time. Visibility rules determine which row versions are visible. Old versions (dead tuples) are cleaned by VACUUM.

Isolation Levels.exp: PostgreSQL supports four ANSI isolation levels, but only three distinct behaviors: Read Committed (default — sees committed data at each statement start), Repeatable Read (sees snapshot from first statement in transaction, retry on serialization failure), Serializable (detects true serialization conflicts with SSI). Higher levels reduce concurrency but increase consistency.

Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).exp: SSI is PostgreSQL's Serializable implementation. Unlike Repeatable Read, SSI detects read-write conflicts that could cause serialization anomalies (e.g., write skew). Uses predicate locks (not row locks) to track read dependencies. SSI provides true serializability at the cost of more serialization failures requiring retry logic.

Deadlock Detection.exp: PostgreSQL automatically detects deadlocks (cycles in lock wait graph). When detected, one session is aborted with ERROR: deadlock detected. The deadlock_timeout setting (default 1s) controls how often the deadlock check runs. Shorter timeouts detect deadlocks faster but use more CPU. Application code should retry on deadlock errors.

Advisory Locks.exp: Advisory locks are application-level locks managed by PostgreSQL. Session-level (pg_advisory_lock) blocks until released. Transaction-level (pg_advisory_xact_lock) auto-releases on commit/rollback. Try variants (pg_try_advisory_lock) return false immediately instead of blocking. Keyed by a single bigint or two integers. Useful for distributed job queues and rate limiting.

SKIP LOCKED & NOWAIT.exp: SKIP LOCKED (PostgreSQL 9.5+) skips rows locked by other transactions — ideal for work queues where multiple workers select jobs. NOWAIT fails immediately if a row is locked, instead of waiting. Both used with FOR UPDATE/FOR SHARE. SKIP LOCKED eliminates busy-waiting and lock contention in high-concurrency job processing.

Row Locking.exp: PostgreSQL provides row-level locking clauses on SELECT: FOR UPDATE (write lock, blocks other FOR UPDATE/FOR NO KEY UPDATE/FOR SHARE/FOR KEY SHARE), FOR NO KEY UPDATE (weaker write lock), FOR SHARE (read lock, blocks FOR UPDATE/FOR NO KEY UPDATE but not FOR SHARE), FOR KEY SHARE (weakest, blocks only FOR UPDATE). These are the foundation of pessimistic locking.

Predicate Locking.exp: Predicate locks prevent phantom reads in SERIALIZABLE isolation. Instead of row locks, PostgreSQL acquires predicate locks on index pages or whole tables that represent a query's read range. If two transactions read overlapping ranges and one writes, SSI detects the conflict. SiLockEntry view shows predicate lock state.

Roles Deep Dive.exp: Roles can be LOGIN (for user authentication), SUPERUSER (full access, needed for extension creation and system config), CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS. INHERIT means parent role's privileges are inherited. Roles can be organized in hierarchies (GRANT role TO role). Groups are just roles without LOGIN. ALTER ROLE sets per-role configuration.

GRANT / REVOKE Privileges.exp: GRANT assigns privileges (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, CREATE, CONNECT, TEMPORARY, EXECUTE, USAGE, ALL) on databases, schemas, tables, columns, sequences, functions, and procedural languages. GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA grants future tables are NOT included (use default privileges). REVOKE removes privileges. Default privileges for future objects via ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES.

Row-Level Security (RLS).exp: Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts which rows a user can see or modify based on a policy expression. Enable RLS on a table (ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), then create policies. WITH CHECK controls INSERT/UPDATE new rows. USING controls SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE visibility. BYPASSRLS role attribute exempts superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS.

Column-Level Security.exp: Column-level security restricts which columns a user can access. Implemented via column-level GRANT (GRANT SELECT(col1, col2) ON table TO role). Unprivileged columns appear as NULL in SELECT * or are rejected entirely depending on context. Often combined with views for fine-grained access control beyond simple column grants.

TLS / SSL Configuration.exp: PostgreSQL supports TLS/SSL for encrypted connections. Configure ssl = on in postgresql.conf, provide server certificate (server.crt) and private key (server.key), and optional CA (root.crt) for client certificate authentication. sslmode=require in client connection strings enforces TLS. For production, prefer verify-full sslmode with proper CA verification.
TLS / SSL Configuration.code:
-- postgresql.conf
# ssl = on
# ssl_cert_file = 'server.crt'
# ssl_key_file = 'server.key'
# ssl_ca_file = 'root.crt'
# ssl_crl_file = 'root.crl'

-- pg_hba.conf (require SSL for specific users)
# hostssl all all 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256
# hostnossl all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject

-- Client connection with SSL enforcement
postgresql://user:pass@host/db?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=ca.pem

pg_hba.conf Deep Dive.exp: pg_hba.conf controls client authentication: local (Unix socket), host (TCP/IP with or without SSL), hostssl, hostnossl. Authentication methods: trust (no password, dev only), password (plaintext), md5, scram-sha-256, cert (client certificate), ldap, pam, peer (OS user), and reject. Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins.
pg_hba.conf Deep Dive.code:
# TYPE  DATABASE  USER  ADDRESS       METHOD
local   all       all                 peer
host    all       all   127.0.0.1/32  scram-sha-256
host    all       all   ::1/128       scram-sha-256
hostssl all       all   0.0.0.0/0    cert
host    mydb      app   10.0.0.0/8   scram-sha-256
host    all       all   0.0.0.0/0    reject

# Reload config (no restart needed)
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Password Profiles & SCRAM-SHA-256.exp: PostgreSQL 10+ uses SCRAM-SHA-256 as the default password hashing mechanism (md5 still available for legacy). It's a challenge-response protocol that never sends the password in plaintext. Password expiration (valid until), password_encryption parameter, and account locking (via pg_hba.conf reject rules) provide profile-like management. Extensions like pg_password_history add rotation enforcement.

pg_dump / pg_restore.exp: pg_dump creates logical backups of a single database (plain SQL, custom, directory, or tar format). pg_dumpall backs up all databases plus global objects (roles, tablespaces). pg_restore restores from custom/directory/tar formats with parallel jobs (-j) and selective restore (-t, -n). Plain format can be restored via psql. Essential for schema migrations and data export.
pg_dump / pg_restore.code:
# Custom format (compressed, parallel restore)
pg_dump -Fc mydb > mydb.dump
pg_restore -d mydb -j 4 mydb.dump

# Plain SQL
pg_dump mydb > mydb.sql
psql mydb < mydb.sql

# Directory format (parallel dump + restore)
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 mydb -f /backup/mydb_dir/
pg_restore -d mydb -j 4 /backup/mydb_dir/

# Dump specific tables
pg_dump -t users -t orders mydb > partial.sql

# All databases
pg_dumpall > full_backup.sql

# Exclude data (schema only)
pg_dump -s mydb > schema.sql

pg_basebackup.exp: pg_basebackup creates a binary (physical) backup of the entire PostgreSQL cluster. Required for setting up streaming replication and Point-in-Time Recovery. Produces a consistent copy using WAL archiving. Supports compression (gzip, lz4, zstd), progress output, and parallel transfer with --wal-method=stream. The -X stream option includes WAL in the backup.
pg_basebackup.code:
# Full base backup with WAL streaming
pg_basebackup -D /backup/base -X stream -P -v

# With compression
pg_basebackup -D /backup/base -X stream -z -P

# For replica setup
pg_basebackup -h primary_host -D /var/lib/postgresql/data -X stream -P

# Checkpoint and label
SELECT * FROM pg_backup_label;

# Restore: copy files, create standby.signal, configure recovery settings

Continuous Archiving & WAL.exp: WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records every change to the database. Continuous archiving copies WAL segments to a safe location for PITR. Configure archive_mode, archive_command (e.g., cp to NFS or S3), and restore_command. WAL segments are 16 MB each. WAL compression (wal_compression) reduces storage. Monitor via pg_stat_archiver.

Streaming Replication.exp: Streaming replication sends WAL data from primary to standby in real time. Standby runs in recovery mode, applying WAL continuously. Hot standby allows read-only queries on standby. Configuration: wal_level >= replica, max_wal_senders >= number of replicas, primary_conninfo on standby. pg_stat_replication shows replication lag.
Streaming Replication.code:
-- Primary postgresql.conf
# wal_level = replica
# max_wal_senders = 5
# wal_keep_size = 512

-- Standby postgresql.conf
# hot_standby = on

-- Standby: standby.signal (touch file)
-- Standby: postgresql.auto.conf
# primary_conninfo = 'host=primary_host port=5432 user=replicator'

-- Create replication user
CREATE ROLE replicator WITH LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD 'secret';

-- Monitor replication
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- Check if standby
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

Synchronous Replication.exp: Synchronous replication guarantees that commits on primary are confirmed by at least one standby before reporting success. Set synchronous_standby_names to specify which standbys are synchronous (FIRST, ANY). sync_state = sync in pg_stat_replication. Provides zero-data-loss but increases commit latency. Use for critical financial or compliance workloads.
Synchronous Replication.code:
-- Primary postgresql.conf
# synchronous_commit = on
# synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (standby1, standby2)'

-- Or quorum-based (any 2 of 3)
# synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (standby1, standby2, standby3)'

-- Check sync state
SELECT application_name, sync_state, sync_priority
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- Per-session control
SET synchronous_commit = remote_write;  -- faster than 'on'

Logical Replication.exp: Logical replication publishes individual table changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) via a publication on the publisher, subscribed to on the subscriber. Unlike streaming replication, it allows selective replication (specific tables), major version upgrades, and bidirectional replication. Uses pgoutput plugin. Built on top of WAL decoding.

Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) & pg_rewin.exp: PITR restores a database to any point in time after a base backup, by replaying WAL up to the target time (recovery_target_time), transaction ID (recovery_target_xid), or named restore point. Configure recovery.conf (PG12+) or postgresql.conf recovery parameters (PG12+). pg_rewind syncs a stale replica with the new primary after a failover, enabling fast rejoin.
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) & pg_rewin.code:
-- PITR: postgresql.conf (or postgresql.auto.conf)
# restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'
# recovery_target_time = '2024-06-15 14:30:00 UTC'
# recovery_target_action = 'promote'

-- Create a named restore point on the running system
SELECT pg_create_restore_point('pre_deploy_v3');
-- Then restore with:
# recovery_target_name = 'pre_deploy_v3'

-- pg_rewind (after failover, to rejoin old primary)
pg_rewind --target-pgdata /var/lib/postgresql/16/main \
         --source-server='host=new_primary user=postgres'
-- This is much faster than rebuilding from pg_basebackup

LISTEN / NOTIFY Pub-Sub.exp: LISTEN subscribes to a notification channel. NOTIFY sends an asynchronous message (up to 8000 bytes payload) to all sessions listening on that channel. pg_notify(text, text) function sends from SQL. Used for cache invalidation, triggering application workers, and real-time UI updates without polling.

COPY Protocol Deep Dive.exp: The COPY protocol (\copy in psql, PQputCopyData in libpq) streams data between client and server. PostgreSQL 14+ supports COPY ... FROM PROGRAM (superuser only, dangerous), COPY ... WHERE for row filtering on import, and COPY ... ON_ERROR for error handling (ignore, stop). The \copy meta-command routes through the client, not the server.

Custom Aggregate Functions.exp: PostgreSQL allows creating custom aggregate functions with CREATE AGGREGATE. Define an sfunc (state transition function), stype (state type), and optionally a finalfunc (final calculation), initcond (initial condition), and combinefunc (for parallel/partial aggregation). Useful for rolling averages, statistical aggregations, or custom JSON accumulation.

Procedural Languages (PL/Python, PL/V8).exp: PostgreSQL supports multiple procedural languages via extensions. PL/Python (plpython3u) allows writing functions in Python with access to numpy, pandas, etc. PL/V8 (plv8) runs JavaScript inside PostgreSQL. PL/Tcl and PL/Perl are also available. These are powerful for data science, complex string processing, and integrating external libraries directly in SQL.
Procedural Languages (PL/Python, PL/V8).code:
-- PL/Python
CREATE EXTENSION plpython3u;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION analyze_sentiment(text TEXT)
RETURNS TEXT AS $$
  # Simple sentiment analysis example
  positive_words = ['good', 'great', 'excellent', 'happy']
  negative_words = ['bad', 'awful', 'terrible', 'sad']
  words = text.lower().split()
  pos_count = sum(1 for w in words if w in positive_words)
  neg_count = sum(1 for w in words if w in negative_words)
  if pos_count > neg_count: return 'positive'
  if neg_count > pos_count: return 'negative'
  return 'neutral'
$$ LANGUAGE plpython3u;

SELECT analyze_sentiment('This product is great and excellent!');

-- PL/V8 (requires compilation)
-- CREATE EXTENSION plv8;
-- Can use full JavaScript, including npm modules

FDW Deep Dive (file_fdw, postgres_fdw).exp: file_fdw queries CSV, text, or program output as foreign tables. Great for ad-hoc data analysis without loading data into the database. postgres_fdw connects to remote PostgreSQL, supports INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (pushdown). IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA bulk-creates foreign tables. Options include fetch_size, use_remote_estimate, and async_capable for parallel remote scans.

Table Sampling & Parallel Query Details.exp: TABLESAMPLE (BERNOULLI, SYSTEM) returns a random sample of rows. SYSTEM is faster (uses physical pages), BERNOULLI is more accurate (row-level). Percent specifies approximate sample size. REPEATABLE(seed) gives reproducible samples. For parallel queries, max_parallel_workers_per_gather controls workers per query, parallel_tuple_cost offsets overhead, and gather nodes merge worker results.

date_bin Time Bucketing.exp: `date_bin` (PostgreSQL 14+) buckets timestamps into fixed intervals. Essential for time-series aggregation: bin timestamps into 5-minute, hourly, or daily buckets. The function aligns to a specified origin. Much cleaner than manual arithmetic with EXTRACT and FLOOR. Used with GROUP BY for time-series rollups.
date_bin Time Bucketing.code:
SELECT
  date_bin('1 hour', created_at, '2024-01-01') AS bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01'
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;

-- 5-minute buckets with origin at midnight
SELECT date_bin('5 minutes', ts, TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01') AS bucket,
       COUNT(*)
FROM sensor_readings
GROUP BY bucket;

-- Equivalent to:
-- SELECT date_trunc('hour', created_at) ... for hourly
-- But date_bin supports arbitrary intervals like 7 minutes, 3 hours

-- Custom origin
SELECT date_bin('1 week', created_at, TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01') AS week_start

WAL & Checkpoint Tuning.exp: Mastering PostgreSQL 15 dedicates significant coverage to WAL tuning: wal_level (minimal, replica, logical), wal_buffers (WAL in memory), wal_writer_delay, checkpoint_timeout, checkpoint_completion_target, and max_wal_size/min_wal_size. The goal: enough WAL for crash recovery and replication, but not so much that checkpoints thrash I/O.
WAL & Checkpoint Tuning.code:
-- postgresql.conf
# wal_level = replica              # minimal, replica (default), logical
# wal_buffers = 64MB               # WAL write buffer in memory
# wal_writer_delay = 200ms         # WAL writer frequency
# wal_compression = zstd           # compress WAL (zstd, lz4, gzip)

# Checkpoint tuning
# checkpoint_timeout = 15min        # max between checkpoints
# checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9  # spread writes over 90% of interval
# max_wal_size = 8GB                # triggers checkpoint (soft limit)
# min_wal_size = 2GB                # target WAL cleanup

-- Monitor checkpoints
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;
-- checkpoints_timed vs checkpoints_req (req = too frequent)

-- WAL generation rate
SELECT wal_bytes / 1024 / 1024 AS wal_mb,
       (EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now() - stats_reset) / 3600) AS hours
FROM pg_stat_wal;

-- Checkpoint frequency
SELECT checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req,
       checkpoints_req::float / NULLIF(checkpoints_timed + checkpoints_req, 0) * 100 AS req_pct
FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;

Custom GUC Parameters.exp: PostgreSQL allows custom GUC (Grand Unified Configuration) parameters with the `custom_variable_classes` pattern. Set custom parameters in postgresql.conf or via SET. Access in PL/pgSQL via current_setting(). Useful for application-level configuration that should live in the database session, like tenant_id, application_name, or feature flags.

PL/pgSQL Profiling & Optimization.exp: Mastering PostgreSQL 15 covers PL/pgSQL performance. Key advice: minimize EXCEPTION blocks (they force subtransactions), use FOREACH over arrays, prefer SQL functions over PL/pgSQL for simple logic, avoid row-by-row processing (use set-based operations), and move expensive computations into pure SQL. Use auto_explain for logging slow PL/pgSQL executions.

pg_stat_progress Monitoring.exp: PostgreSQL provides progress reporting views for long-running operations. pg_stat_progress_vacuum (VACUUM phase, heap_blks_total/ scanned/vacuumed), pg_stat_progress_create_index (phase: building, index name, tuples), pg_stat_progress_analyze (phase, sample tuples), pg_stat_progress_basebackup, pg_stat_progress_copy. Essential for knowing how long operations will take.
pg_stat_progress Monitoring.code:
-- VACUUM progress
SELECT pid, phase, heap_blks_total, heap_blks_scanned,
       heap_blks_vacuumed, max_dead_tuples, num_dead_tuples
FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum;

-- CREATE INDEX progress
SELECT pid, command_tag, phase, lockers_total, lockers_done,
       blocks_total, blocks_done, tuples_total, tuples_done
FROM pg_stat_progress_create_index;

-- COPY progress (v14+)
SELECT pid, command_tag, phase, tuples_processed, bytes_processed
FROM pg_stat_progress_copy;

-- Combined with current query
SELECT p.pid, p.phase, a.query
FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum p
JOIN pg_stat_activity a ON p.pid = a.pid;

Install.exp: Playwright is a browser automation library supporting Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Install via npm with one command for all browsers.

Browser Context.exp: Browser contexts are isolated browser sessions with their own cookies, storage, and permissions. They enable parallel, independent test execution.
Browser Context.code:
const context = await browser.newContext({ viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 } });
const page = await context.newPage();

Config & Projects.exp: Playwright Test is configured via playwright.config.ts. Define projects for cross-browser testing, device emulation, and global setup/teardown.

Selectors.exp: Playwright selectors include CSS, XPath, text, and role-based locators. The engine auto-waits for elements to be actionable before interacting.

getByRole.exp: Role locators select elements by their ARIA role and accessible name, following best practices for accessibility and resilience.

getByText.exp: Text locators find elements by their visible text content, supporting exact matching and substring matching.

CSS.exp: CSS selectors are fast and familiar for locating elements by class, id, attribute, or structure. They support pseudo-selectors like :has.

XPath.exp: XPath selectors traverse the DOM tree with powerful path expressions, useful for complex parent-child-sibling relationships.

Filtering.exp: Locators can be filtered by text, by visibility, or by child elements. This narrows down selections without creating complex selectors.
Filtering.code:
await page.locator('button').filter({ hasText: 'Submit' }).click();
await page.locator('li').filter({ hasNotText: 'Disabled' }).click();

Click.exp: Playwright clicks scroll elements into view, wait for actionability, and dispatch real browser events. Options include force, position, and modifier keys.

Fill.exp: fill clears existing input and types new text. It dispatches input events for React and Vue change detection.

Navigate.exp: Navigation methods load URLs and wait for the page to reach a loaded state. Playwright supports back, forward, go, and reload.

Keyboard.exp: Keyboard actions simulate key presses, combinations, and typing. Special keys are accessed via page.keyboard.

Drag & Drop.exp: Playwright simulates drag and drop operations using locator.dragTo or manual mouse events for complex drag scenarios.

toHaveText.exp: toHaveText asserts that an element's text content matches expected values, with options for exact or partial matching.

toBeVisible.exp: toBeVisible checks that an element is present in the DOM, not hidden, and within the viewport. It auto-retries until timeout.

Soft Assertions.exp: Soft assertions continue test execution after failure, collecting all failures for reporting. The test fails at the end.

Negation.exp: Negation with .not allows asserting the inverse condition, such as checking an element is hidden or doesn't contain text.
