Profiling & Optimization.exp: Always profile before optimizing. Tools: cProfile, py-spy, snakeviz, pyinstrument. Common mistake: optimizing without profiling — you'll optimize the wrong things. Best practice: focus on hot spots (where time is actually spent); measure before and after each optimization; algorithmic improvements trump micro-optimizations.
Profiling & Optimization.code:
import cProfile
import pstats

def analyze():
    data = [i ** 2 for i in range(10**5)]
    total = sum(data)
    filtered = [x for x in data if x % 2 == 0]
    return sum(filtered)

# Profile
cProfile.run('analyze()', sort='cumtime')

# Visualize:
# python -m cProfile -o profile.stats my_script.py
# snakeviz profile.stats  (needs pip install snakeviz)

__slots__.exp: Reduce memory usage of classes by declaring a fixed set of attributes. Prevents __dict__ creation per instance. Common mistake: forgetting slots don't prevent adding new attributes — they just define the allowed attributes. Best practice: use __slots__ for classes with many instances (millions) to reduce memory; avoid in small-scale code.
__slots__.code:
class Point:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')  # No __dict__ per instance

    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.x, p.y)
# p.z = 5  # AttributeError: 'Point' has no attribute 'z'

# Memory comparison
import sys
class NormalPoint:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

normal_pts = [NormalPoint(i, i) for i in range(1000)]
slotted_pts = [Point(i, i) for i in range(1000)]
print(f'Normal size: {sys.getsizeof(normal_pts[0])}')
print(f'Slotted size: {sys.getsizeof(slotted_pts[0])}')

Generators vs Lists.exp: Generators produce values lazily (one at a time); lists store all values in memory. Generators save memory but have per-item overhead. Common mistake: converting a generator to a list unnecessarily — defeats the memory advantage. Best practice: use generators for large data streams and infinite sequences; use lists for small datasets and when you need random access.
Generators vs Lists.code:
import sys
import time

# Memory comparison
list_squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10**6)]
gen_squares = (x ** 2 for x in range(10**6))

print(f'List size: {sys.getsizeof(list_squares)} bytes')
print(f'Generator has no __sizeof__: ...')  # No size to measure

# Time comparison (iteration)
def time_iter(iterator):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    total = sum(iterator)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    return total, elapsed

# Note: first call creates list, second iterates generator
_, list_time = time_iter(list_squares)  # Already exists
import copy
list_copy = list_squares[:]
_, list_time = time_iter(list_copy)
_, gen_time = time_iter(x ** 2 for x in range(10**6))
print(f'List sum: {list_time:.4f}s')
print(f'Generator sum: {gen_time:.4f}s')

C Extensions (Cython & ctypes).exp: Speed up Python with C. Cython compiles Python-like code to C extensions. ctypes calls C libraries from Python. Common mistake: assuming Cython always speeds up code — pure Python with many function calls can be slower. Best practice: use Cython for numeric-heavy loops; use ctypes for calling existing C libraries; consider numpy first for array operations.
C Extensions (Cython & ctypes).code:
# Cython example (in .pyx file):
# def sum_squares(int n):
#     cdef int i
#     cdef long total = 0
#     for i in range(n):
#         total += i * i
#     return total

# ctypes: call C from Python
import ctypes

# Load libc
libc = ctypes.CDLL('libc.so.6')

# Call C's printf
libc.printf(b'Hello from C!\n')

# Or libm's sqrt
libm = ctypes.CDLL('libm.so.6')
libm.sqrt.argtypes = (ctypes.c_double,)
libm.sqrt.restype = ctypes.c_double
print(libm.sqrt(144.0))  # 12.0

timeit & Benchmarking.exp: Measure small code snippets with timeit module. Use from the command line: python -m timeit '...'. Common mistake: using time.time() for micro-benchmarks — timeit handles garbage collection and repeat counts automatically. Best practice: use timeit for micro-optimizations; use real-world data and realistic workloads for macro-benchmarks.
timeit & Benchmarking.code:
import timeit

# Compare list vs generator
list_time = timeit.timeit(
    'sum([x**2 for x in range(1000)])',
    number=10000
)
gen_time = timeit.timeit(
    'sum(x**2 for x in range(1000))',
    number=10000
)

print(f'List: {list_time:.4f}s')
print(f'Generator: {gen_time:.4f}s')

# Command line:
# python -m timeit '["a" * 100 for _ in range(100)]'
# python -m timeit -s 'data = list(range(1000))' 'sum(data)'

Memory Management & GC.exp: Python uses reference counting + cyclic garbage collector. Circular references are freed by the GC (can be slow). Use gc module to monitor/inspect. Common mistake: assuming del x frees memory immediately — it decrements the refcount; memory may not be returned to the OS. Best practice: use weakref for caching circular references; use __del__ with caution (can cause resurrection).
Memory Management & GC.code:
import gc
import sys

# Reference counting
x = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(x))  # 2 (x and getrefcount arg)

y = x
print(sys.getrefcount(x))  # 3

del y
print(sys.getrefcount(x))  # 2

# GC monitoring
gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_STATS)

# Create a cycle
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.child = None

a = Node(1)
b = Node(2)
a.child = b
b.child = a  # Cycle!

# GC will eventually collect this cycle
collected = gc.collect()
print(f'Collected: {collected} objects')

Web Scraping with BeautifulSoup.exp: Parse HTML/XML documents and extract data. Install: pip install beautifulsoup4 requests. Common mistake: not handling pagination or rate limiting — always respect robots.txt and add delays between requests. Best practice: use BeautifulSoup with a parser (lxml or html.parser); use requests.Session() for cookies/session persistence.
Web Scraping with BeautifulSoup.code:

# CSS selectors

text = soup.get_text(separator=' ', strip=True)

Selenium & Browser Automation.exp: Control real browsers for JavaScript-heavy sites and automation. Install: pip install selenium. Requires a WebDriver (ChromeDriver, GeckoDriver, or use webdriver-manager). Common mistake: not using WebDriverWait for dynamic content — elements may not be immediately available. Best practice: use webdriver-manager for automatic driver management; prefer explicit waits over implicit; use headless mode for CI.
Selenium & Browser Automation.code:
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC

Python Data Model (Dunder Methods).exp: The Python data model makes objects behave like built-in types. By implementing __getitem__, __len__, __iter__, __contains__ your objects work with for, in, slicing, and more. Fluent Python calls this 'Python's superpower'. Common mistake: implementing __len__ but not __bool__ — Python falls back to __len__ (0 = False). Best practice: implement __repr__ first (debugging), then __str__ (display), then data model methods for your domain.
Python Data Model (Dunder Methods).code:
import collections

Card = collections.namedtuple('Card', ['rank', 'suit'])

class FrenchDeck:
    ranks = [str(n) for n in range(2, 11)] + list('JQKA')
    suits = 'spades diamonds clubs hearts'.split()

    def __init__(self):
        self._cards = [Card(rank, suit) for suit in self.suits
                       for rank in self.ranks]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._cards)

    def __getitem__(self, position):
        return self._cards[position]

deck = FrenchDeck()
print(len(deck))       # 52
print(deck[0])         # Card(rank='2', suit='spades')
print(choice(deck))    # random card (needs from random import choice)
print(deck[:3])        # first 3 cards
print(Card('Q', 'hearts') in deck)  # True

__getattr__ & __setattr__.exp: __getattr__ called when normal lookup fails. __setattr__ called on every assignment. Fluent Python warns: __setattr__ is tricky — must call super() to avoid recursion. Common mistake: infinite recursion via self.x = val in __setattr__. Best practice: use __setattr__ for validation; prefer @property for individual attributes.

__call__ & Callable Objects.exp: Make instances callable via __call__. Used for decorators, factories, strategies. Fluent Python shows this for function-like objects with state. Common mistake: overusing __call__ when a method is clearer. Best practice: use __call__ for objects representing a single action (callbacks, factories).

Descriptors.exp: Descriptors control attribute access via __get__, __set__, __delete__. Examples: @property, classmethod, staticmethod. Fluent Python calls descriptors 'the most important tool for framework builders'. Common mistake: descriptors only work as class attributes — instance-level assignment disables them. Best practice: use __set_name__ (3.6+) to auto-generate storage attribute names.

Metaclasses.exp: Metaclasses are classes of classes — intercept class creation via __new__/__init__. Use cases: ORMs, registries, class validation. Fluent Python says 'metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% should ever use'. Common mistake: using a metaclass when a class decorator suffices. Best practice: prefer class decorators; keep metaclasses single-purpose.

ABC Advanced (subclasshook).exp: ABCs support virtual subclasses via register() and __subclasshook__(). Virtual subclasses are recognized by isinstance() without inheritance. Fluent Python shows this for duck typing with safety. Common mistake: registering too many virtual subclasses slows isinstance checks. Best practice: prefer collections.abc over custom ABCs; use __subclasshook__ for protocol-like behavior.

Operator Overloading Advanced.exp: Python supports a fixed set of operator methods: __add__, __radd__, __iadd__, __eq__, __lt__, etc. Fluent Python emphasizes returning NotImplemented (not raising) for unsupported types. Common mistake: forgetting __hash__ when defining __eq__. Best practice: use @total_ordering to fill in missing comparisons; always return NotImplemented for unsupported operands.

Context Managers Advanced.exp: Beyond basic with: contextlib.contextmanager (generator-based), ExitStack (dynamic cleanup), suppress (ignore exceptions), redirect_stdout. Fluent Python covers these in depth. Common mistake: using @contextmanager without try/finally — cleanup won't run on exception. Best practice: always wrap yield in try/finally; use ExitStack for dynamic contexts.
Context Managers Advanced.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager, ExitStack, suppress
import tempfile, os

@contextmanager
def atomic_write(filepath):
    tmp = tempfile.mktemp(dir=os.path.dirname(filepath))
    try:
        yield tmp
        os.rename(tmp, filepath)
    except:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise

with suppress(FileNotFoundError):

Best practice: use async/await for new code; understand the coroutine model for framework-level work.

def averager():
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    while True:
        term = yield
        if term is None:
            return total / count if count else 0
        total += term
        count += 1

coro = averager()
next(coro)
print(coro.send(10))
print(coro.send(20))

df['rolling_7d'] = df['value'].rolling(window=7).mean()
df['rolling_30d'] = df['value'].rolling(window=30).mean()

# Shift for lag features
df['lag_1'] = df['value'].shift(1)
df['lag_7'] = df['value'].shift(7)
df['diff'] = df['value'].diff()

Unsupervised Learning.exp: Extract hidden patterns from unlabeled data. Clustering (K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical) groups similar points. Dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) projects high-dim data to 2/3D for visualization and noise reduction. Common mistake: assuming clusters exist — always validate with silhouette score.
Unsupervised Learning.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Generate blobs
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=4, n_features=10, random_state=42)

# Standardize
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# K-Means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=42, n_init=10)
labels = kmeans.fit_predict(X_scaled)
print(f'K-Means Silhouette: {silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels):.3f}')

# DBSCAN
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=1.5, min_samples=5)
db_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_scaled)
n_clusters = len(set(db_labels)) - (1 if -1 in db_labels else 0)
print(f'DBSCAN clusters: {n_clusters}, noise: {list(db_labels).count(-1)}')

# PCA for visualization
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print(f'Explained variance: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.2%}')

plt.scatter(X_pca[:, 0], X_pca[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='viridis', alpha=0.6)
plt.title('K-Means clusters (PCA projection)')
plt.show()

# t-SNE
tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=42)
X_tsne = tsne.fit_transform(X_scaled)
plt.scatter(X_tsne[:, 0], X_tsne[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='viridis', alpha=0.6)
plt.title('K-Means clusters (t-SNE projection)')
plt.show()

Prompt Engineering.exp: Craft inputs to guide LLM outputs. Components: system prompt (role/constraints), user prompt (task), few-shot examples. Techniques: chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning), zero-shot chain-of-thought ('Let's think step by step'), structured outputs (JSON mode). From Hands-on LLM: systematic prompt iteration is key to reliable LLM apps.
Prompt Engineering.code:
from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

def classify_sentiment(texts):
    # Few-shot prompt with examples
    examples = [
        {'role': 'user', 'content': 'I love this product!'},
        {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'positive'},
        {'role': 'user', 'content': 'This is terrible.'},
        {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'negative'},
    ]
    messages = [{
        'role': 'system',
        'content': 'Classify sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral.'
    }]
    messages.extend(examples)
    messages.append({'role': 'user', 'content': texts[0]})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model='gpt-4o-mini',
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Chain-of-thought for reasoning
def solve_math(problem):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model='gpt-4o-mini',
        messages=[
            {'role': 'system', 'content': 'Solve step by step.'},
            {'role': 'user', 'content': f'{problem}\nLet\'s think step by step.'}
        ]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).exp: RAG grounds LLM responses in external knowledge: chunk documents, embed chunks, store in vector DB, retrieve relevant chunks at query time, generate with context. From Hands-on LLM: chunk size, overlap, embedding model, and retrieval top-k are critical hyperparameters.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI
import os

# 1. Chunk and embed documents
docs = ['Python is a programming language.', 'LLMs are large language models.']
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
doc_embeddings = model.encode(docs)

# 2. Query and retrieve
def retrieve(query, k=1):
    query_emb = model.encode([query])
    scores = np.dot(doc_embeddings, query_emb.T).squeeze()
    top_k = np.argsort(scores)[-k:][::-1]
    return [docs[i] for i in top_k]

# 3. Generate with context
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

def rag_query(query):
    context = '\n'.join(retrieve(query))
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model='gpt-4o-mini',
        messages=[
            {'role': 'system', 'content': 'Answer using the provided context.'},
            {'role': 'user', 'content': f'Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}'}
        ]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

print(rag_query('What are LLMs?'))

Data Collection for AI (Web Scraping Pip.exp: Collect training/evaluation data via web scraping. Use requests + BeautifulSoup for static pages, Playwright/Selenium for JS-heavy sites. From oxylabs-ai-studio: build robust pipelines with retry, caching, proxy rotation, and structured output schemas.
Data Collection for AI (Web Scraping Pip.code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

def scrape_page(url, selectors):
    headers = {'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'}
    try:
        resp = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
        resp.raise_for_status()
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        print(f'Error fetching {url}: {e}')
        return None

    soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'html.parser')
    data = {}
    for key, selector in selectors.items():
        if el := soup.select_one(selector):
            data[key] = el.get_text(strip=True)
    return data

# Pipeline with caching
CACHE_DIR = Path('./scrape_cache')
CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def scrape_pipeline(urls, selectors, delay=1):
    results = []
    for url in urls:
        cache_file = CACHE_DIR / f'{hash(url)}.json'
        if cache_file.exists():
            with open(cache_file) as f:
                results.append(json.load(f))
            continue

        data = scrape_page(url, selectors)
        if data:
            with open(cache_file, 'w') as f:
                json.dump(data, f)
            results.append(data)
        time.sleep(delay)  # rate limiting
    return results

Embeddings & Vector Databases.exp: Vector databases store and search embedding vectors by similarity (cosine, dot product, L2). Chroma is lightweight and local; Pinecone/Qdrant are production-grade. Chunk documents, embed with sentence-transformers, index in vector DB, retrieve by semantic similarity. Common mistake: using wrong distance metric for your embedding model.
Embeddings & Vector Databases.code:
import chromadb
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

# Initialize Chroma
client = chromadb.Client()
collection = client.create_collection(name='docs')

# Embedding model
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')

docs = [
    'Python is a high-level programming language',
    'Vector databases store embeddings for similarity search',
    'Transformers revolutionized NLP with attention mechanisms',
    'Pandas is a data manipulation library for Python'
]

# Embed and store
embeddings = model.encode(docs).tolist()
collection.add(
    embeddings=embeddings,
    documents=docs,
    ids=[f'doc{i}' for i in range(len(docs))]
)

# Query
query = 'data manipulation tools'
query_emb = model.encode([query]).tolist()
results = collection.query(query_embeddings=query_emb, n_results=2)
for doc in results['documents'][0]:
    print(f'- {doc}')

print(f'Collection count: {collection.count()}')

LangChain & LlamaIndex.exp: Frameworks for building LLM applications: document loading, chunking, embedding, retrieval, chains, agents. LangChain is modular with many integrations; LlamaIndex excels at data indexing/retrieval. Common mistake: over-abstraction — start with direct API calls, add frameworks when complexity demands it.
LangChain & LlamaIndex.code:
from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
import os

# 1. Load and chunk documents
loader = TextLoader('README.md')
docs = loader.load()
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)

# 2. Create vector store
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name='all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)

# 3. Create RAG chain
llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini', temperature=0)
qa_chain = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm=llm,
    retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={'k': 3})
)

# 4. Query
response = qa_chain.invoke({'query': 'What is this project about?'})
print(response['result'])

# LlamaIndex equivalent
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader
documents = SimpleDirectoryReader('.').load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
response = query_engine.query('What is this project about?')
print(response)

AI Safety & Alignment.exp: Build responsible AI: content filtering, bias detection, adversarial robustness, jailbreak prevention. Techniques: RLHF/DPO for alignment; prompt injection detection; output guardrails; red-teaming. Common mistake: relying solely on system prompts for safety — use layered defenses. JSX.exp: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML and allows you to write markup inside your components. It gets transpiled to React.createElement calls under the hood by tools like Babel.

Components.exp: Components are reusable, self-contained pieces of UI that can be either function-based or class-based. Modern React favors functional components with hooks.

Props.exp: Props (short for properties) are read-only inputs passed to components from their parent. They enable parent-to-child communication and make components configurable.

useState.exp: useState is a hook that adds local state to function components. It returns a stateful value and a function to update it, triggering a re-render when called.

useEffect.exp: useEffect lets you perform side effects in function components such as data fetching, subscriptions, or DOM manipulation. The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs.

useRef.exp: useRef returns a mutable ref object whose .current property persists across renders without causing re-renders. It's commonly used to access DOM elements directly.

useContext.exp: useContext consumes a context value created by React.createContext, allowing deep prop drilling to be avoided. It re-renders the component when the context value changes.

useReducer.exp: useReducer is an alternative to useState for complex state logic involving multiple sub-values or when the next state depends on the previous one. It follows the reducer pattern from Redux.

useMemo.exp: useMemo memoizes the result of an expensive computation, recomputing only when its dependencies change. Use it to optimize performance by avoiding unnecessary recalculations.

CSS Modules.exp: CSS Modules scope CSS class names locally by default, preventing naming collisions across components. Files are imported like JavaScript objects and class names are accessed as properties.

Styled Components.exp: Styled Components is a CSS-in-JS library that lets you write actual CSS inside your JavaScript using tagged template literals. It automatically handles vendor prefixing and scoping.

Tailwind.exp: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first framework providing low-level classes for rapid UI building. It pairs well with React through class composition and tools like clsx for conditional classes.
Tailwind.code: <div className="flex items-center p-4 bg-blue-500 text-white rounded-lg">

Controlled Forms.exp: In controlled forms, form elements derive their value from React state and update via onChange handlers. This gives React single source of truth for form data and enables validation.

React Router.exp: React Router is the standard routing library for React apps, enabling navigation between views while keeping the UI in sync with the URL. It supports nested routes, params, and lazy loading.

Jest.exp: Jest is a delightful JavaScript testing framework with zero configuration, built-in assertions, mocking, and code coverage. It's the default test runner in Create React App.

React Testing Library.exp: React Testing Library builds on top of DOM Testing Library and encourages testing components from the user's perspective. It queries rendered output rather than testing implementation details.

Cypress.exp: Cypress is an end-to-end testing framework that runs in the browser, providing real-time reloads, time travel debugging, and automatic waiting. It's ideal for integration and E2E tests.

Code Splitting.exp: Code splitting breaks your bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. React.lazy and Suspense make code splitting declarative and easy to implement.

Lazy Loading.exp: Lazy loading defers loading of non-critical resources until they are needed. Combined with Suspense, it shows a fallback UI while the lazy component loads asynchronously.

Memoization.exp: React.memo is a higher-order component that prevents re-rendering when props haven't changed. useCallback memorizes callback functions to maintain referential equality across renders.

Redux.exp: Redux is a predictable state container with a single store, immutable updates via pure reducers, and actions dispatched to trigger state changes. The Redux Toolkit simplifies boilerplate significantly.

Zustand.exp: Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API, no boilerplate, and support for middleware. It's ideal for projects that need simple global state without Redux overhead.

Context API.exp: Context API provides a built-in way to share values across the component tree without prop drilling. It's best suited for low-frequency updates like theme, locale, or auth state.

useTransition.exp: useTransition marks state updates as non-urgent transitions, keeping the UI responsive during expensive re-renders. The isPending flag shows a loading state without blocking user input.

useDeferredValue.exp: useDeferredValue lets you defer re-rendering a non-urgent part of the tree. The deferred value lags behind the real value, allowing urgent updates (like input typing) to stay responsive.

RSC Basics.exp: React Server Components run exclusively on the server, never sent to the client. They reduce bundle size by keeping heavy dependencies server-side and can directly access databases and file systems.

Server Actions.exp: Server Actions are async functions that run on the server, invoked from client components. Use 'use server' to mark them, enabling direct mutations without building API routes.

Error Boundaries.exp: Error Boundaries catch JavaScript errors in their child component tree, displaying a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. Class components with componentDidCatch are required.

Error Recovery.exp: Use key props to reset error boundaries. Changing the key unmounts and remounts the component tree, clearing the error state without a full page refresh.

Portals.exp: Portals render children into a DOM node outside the parent component's hierarchy, useful for modals, tooltips, and dropdowns that need to escape overflow or z-index clipping.

TypeScript with React.exp: TypeScript with React provides type safety for props, state, hooks, and event handlers. Use generic types for useState, useRef, and forwardRef for stricter typing.

Installation.exp: Redis can be installed via package managers, compiled from source, or run via Docker. The default configuration listens on port 6379 and stores data in memory with optional persistence to disk.
Installation.code:
# Install on Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install redis-server

# Run via Docker
docker run --name my-redis -p 6379:6379 -d redis

# Verify installation
redis-server --version
redis-cli ping
# Output: PONG

Data Types.exp: Redis supports Strings, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes, Bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, Streams, and Geospatial indexes. Each type has optimized commands for specific use cases and data access patterns.
Data Types.code:
SET stringkey "hello"
LPUSH listkey "a" "b" "c"
SADD setkey "member1" "member2"
ZADD zsetkey 1 "one" 2 "two"
HSET hashkey field1 "value1" field2 "value2"
TYPE stringkey
# Output: string

CLI.exp: The `redis-cli` command-line interface connects to Redis servers for interactive or scripted use. It supports command execution, monitoring, slow log analysis, and server administration with built-in help.
CLI.code:
redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1 "Alice"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET user:1
"Alice"
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO server
127.0.0.1:6379> MONITOR
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG GET 10

SET/GET.exp: Strings are the most fundamental Redis data type, capable of storing text, numbers, or binary data up to 512MB. SET stores a key-value pair, GET retrieves it, and commands like `SETNX` help with distributed locks.
SET/GET.code:
SET welcome "Hello Redis"
GET welcome
# Output: "Hello Redis"

SETNX lock:resource "locked"
# Output: (integer) 1 - key was set

SETEX session:token "abc123" 3600
# Sets with 1 hour TTL

MSET key1 "val1" key2 "val2"
MGET key1 key2

INCR.exp: Redis provides atomic increment/decrement operations that are essential for counters, rate limiting, and real-time analytics. Commands like `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, and `INCRBYFLOAT` operate on string values holding numbers.
INCR.code:
SET counter 0
INCR counter
# Output: (integer) 1
INCRBY counter 5
# Output: (integer) 6
DECR counter
# Output: (integer) 5
GET counter
# Output: "5"

INCRBYFLOAT price 10.50

Expiry.exp: TTL (Time To Live) automatically removes keys after a specified duration. `EXPIRE`, `TTL`, and `PERSIST` manage key lifetimes. Expiry is crucial for caching, temporary tokens, and session management.
Expiry.code:
SET cache:page "/home" 
EXPIRE cache:page 60
# Or set with expiry inline:
SETEX cache:api 300 "{\"data\": []}"

TTL cache:page
# Output: (integer) 58 - seconds remaining

PERSIST cache:page
# Remove TTL

SET key "value" EX 10 NX
# Set if not exists with 10 second expiry

LPUSH/LPOP.exp: Lists are ordered sequences of strings, efficient for queue and stack implementations. LPUSH adds to the left, RPUSH adds to the right; LPOP and RPOP remove and return elements from either end.
LPUSH/LPOP.code:
LPUSH queue "task3" "task2" "task1"
# List: task1, task2, task3

RPUSH queue "task4"
# List: task1, task2, task3, task4

LPOP queue
# Output: "task1" - removes from left

LLEN queue
# Output: (integer) 3

LRANGE queue 0 -1
# Output: "task2", "task3", "task4"

BRPOP queue 0
# Blocking pop - waits indefinitely

SADD.exp: Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. SADD adds members, SREM removes them, SMEMBERS returns all members, and SISMEMBER checks existence. Sets are ideal for tagging, deduplication, and relations.
SADD.code:
SADD tags:post:1 "javascript" "node" "redis"
SADD tags:post:2 "python" "redis" "database"

SMEMBERS tags:post:1
# Output: "javascript", "node", "redis"

SISMEMBER tags:post:1 "redis"
# Output: (integer) 1

SCARD tags:post:1
# Output: (integer) 3 - set cardinality

SPOP tags:post:1 1
# Remove and return 1 random member

Union/Intersect.exp: Set operations enable powerful data analysis: SUNION combines sets, SINTER finds common elements, and SDIFF finds differences. These are used for recommendations, permissions, and social features.
Union/Intersect.code:
SUNION tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "javascript", "node", "redis", "python", "database"

SINTER tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "redis" (common tag)

SDIFF tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "javascript", "node"

SINTERSTORE common:tags tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Store intersection in new set

HSET.exp: Hashes store field-value pairs within a single key, ideal for representing objects. They provide memory-efficient storage with commands for individual field CRUD, bulk operations, and field counting.
HSET.code:
HSET user:100 name "Alice" email "alice@example.com" age 30

HGET user:100 name
# Output: "Alice"

HGETALL user:100
# Output: name, Alice, email, alice@example.com, age, 30

HMSET user:101 name "Bob" email "bob@example.com"
HEXISTS user:100 age
# Output: (integer) 1

HINCRBY user:100 age 1
# Output: (integer) 31

HDEL user:100 age

ZADD.exp: Sorted Sets associate each member with a numeric score, maintaining order by score. ZADD adds or updates members, ZRANGE retrieves by rank, and ZRANK gets position. Perfect for leaderboards and priority queues.
ZADD.code:
ZADD leaderboard 100 "Alice" 85 "Bob" 95 "Charlie"

ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 WITHSCORES
# Output: Bob(85), Charlie(95), Alice(100)

ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES
# Output: Alice(100), Charlie(95), Bob(85) - top 3

ZSCORE leaderboard "Alice"
# Output: 100

ZRANK leaderboard "Alice"
# Output: (integer) 2 - 0-indexed rank

ZINCRBY leaderboard 10 "Bob"
# Output: 95

Ranking.exp: Sorted Sets excel at real-time leaderboards with atomic score updates, range queries, and pagination. Combined with aggregation commands like ZCOUNT and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, they handle ranking systems efficiently.
Ranking.code:
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
# Top 10 players

ZCOUNT leaderboard 80 100
# Count players with scores between 80-100

ZREVRANK leaderboard "Alice"
# Rank from high to low

ZREMRANGEBYRANK leaderboard 0 -11
# Keep only top 10, remove rest

ZUNIONSTORE weekly 2 week:1 week:2 WEIGHTS 0.5 0.5
# Combine two weeks' scores with weighting

RDB.exp: RDB (Redis Database) performs point-in-time snapshots at configurable intervals. It creates compact single-file backups, ideal for disaster recovery, but may lose data written between snapshots.
RDB.code:
# redis.conf
save 900 1          # Snapshot if ≥1 key changed in 900s
save 300 10         # Snapshot if ≥10 keys changed in 300s
save 60 10000       # Snapshot if ≥10000 keys changed in 60s

# Manual snapshot
redis-cli SAVE
redis-cli BGSAVE

# RDB file location
dir /var/lib/redis
dbfilename dump.rdb

AOF.exp: Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write operation for durability. It provides finer-grained persistence than RDB with fsync policies (every write, every second, or OS-controlled) and can be rewritten to compact.
AOF.code:
# redis.conf
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec     # fsync once per second
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# Manual rewrite
redis-cli BGREWRITEAOF

# Check AOF status
INFO persistence

Backup/Restore.exp: Redis backup involves copying RDB/AOF files, or using `redis-cli --rdb` for live snapshots. Restore requires stopping the server, placing the backup file correctly, and restarting. SLAVEOF enables replication-based recovery.
Backup/Restore.code:
# Backup
redis-cli --rdb /backups/dump-$(date +%Y%m%d).rdb

# Or copy from data directory
cp /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb /backups/

# Restore
systemctl stop redis
cp /backups/dump.rdb /var/lib/redis/
chown redis:redis /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb
systemctl start redis

# Restore from AOF
redis-cli --aof /backups/appendonly.aof

Channels.exp: Pub/Sub implements the publish-subscribe messaging pattern where publishers send messages to channels without knowledge of subscribers. SUBSCRIBE listens on channels, PUBLISH sends messages, and UNSUBSCRIBE stops listening.
Channels.code:
# Terminal 1 - Subscriber
redis-cli
SUBSCRIBE notifications
# Waiting for messages...

# Terminal 2 - Publisher
redis-cli
PUBLISH notifications "New user registered"
PUBLISH notifications "Order #1234 shipped"

# Terminal 1 receives:
# 1) "message"
# 2) "notifications"
# 3) "New user registered"

Pattern Subscribe.exp: PSUBSCRIBE enables subscription to channels matching a glob-style pattern. This allows listening to multiple related channels (e.g., `user:*`, `orders:*`) with a single subscription for efficient message routing.
Pattern Subscribe.code:
# Subscribe to all order-related channels
PSUBSCRIBE orders:*

# Subscribe to user events
PSUBSCRIBE user:* event:*

# Publisher
PUBLISH orders:created "{id: 123, total: 99.99}"
PUBLISH orders:shipped "{id: 123, tracking: '1Z999AA10123456784'}"
PUBLISH user:registered "{id: 456, name: 'Charlie'}"

# Pattern matching: orders:* matches both orders:created and orders:shipped

PUNSUBSCRIBE orders:*

Messaging.exp: Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no message persistence; subscribers only receive messages sent after subscription. For reliable messaging, use Redis Streams which support consumer groups, acknowledgment, and message history.

Sentinel.exp: Redis Sentinel provides high availability through automatic failover, monitoring, notifications, and service discovery. A Sentinel cluster monitors master/replica instances and promotes a replica when the master fails.
Sentinel.code:
# sentinel.conf
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2
sentinel auth-pass mymaster yourpassword
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000

# Start sentinel
redis-sentinel /etc/redis/sentinel.conf

# Check status
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL masters
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL replicas mymaster

Cluster Mode.exp: Redis Cluster automatically shards data across multiple nodes using hash slots (0-16383). Each node handles a subset of slots, providing horizontal scalability and automatic rebalancing when nodes are added or removed.
Cluster Mode.code:
# Create cluster with 6 nodes (3 masters, 3 replicas)
redis-cli --cluster create \
  127.0.0.1:7000 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 \
  127.0.0.1:7003 127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 \
  --cluster-replicas 1

# Connect to cluster
redis-cli -c -p 7000

# Check cluster info
CLUSTER INFO
CLUSTER NODES
CLUSTER KEYSLOT "mykey"

Sharding.exp: Hash slots distribute keys deterministically: `HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384`. Client-side sharding is also possible for simpler setups, but Redis Cluster handles routing transparently with MOVED redirections.

Caching.exp: Redis caching improves application performance by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Common patterns include cache-aside (lazy loading), write-through, and TTL-based expiry with automatic cache invalidation.

Rate Limiting.exp: Redis enables efficient distributed rate limiting using INCR with TTL. The sliding window algorithm tracks request counts per time window, and the token bucket algorithm offers more flexible rate control.

Session Store.exp: Redis is an ideal session store for distributed applications because of its speed, built-in TTL, and atomic operations. `connect-redis` or `ioredis-session` replace the default in-memory session store for persistence across restarts.

Queues.exp: Redis Lists provide the foundation for lightweight job queues. `LPUSH` + `BRPOP` implement reliable FIFO queues with blocking pops. Bull and Kue are popular Node.js queue libraries built on Redis.

Routing.exp: Remix uses a file-based routing system in the app/routes directory. Each file represents a route segment, with dot and folder conventions creating nested URL structures automatically.

Nested Routes.exp: Nested routes in Remix allow multiple components to render on the same URL. The parent route's layout wraps child routes through the <Outlet /> component, enabling complex UI hierarchies.

Layouts.exp: Layout routes use the special app/root.tsx file and route-specific layout.tsx files. Layouts wrap child routes and persist across navigation, preventing full page re-renders.

loader.exp: Loaders are server-side functions that fetch data before rendering a route. They run on every request, returning data that becomes available to the component via the useLoaderData hook.

useLoaderData.exp: useLoaderData returns the typed data from the nearest route loader. It provides type safety when used with TypeScript and the typeof loader generic pattern.

params.exp: Params give access to dynamic segments from the URL pattern. They are available in loaders and actions via the params argument, matching the bracket syntax in the route filename.

action.exp: Actions handle form submissions and data mutations on the server. They run on POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE requests and can return data, redirects, or errors to the client.

Form.exp: The <Form> component submits data without JavaScript by default. When JS loads, it progressively enhances to use fetch, providing optimistic UI and pending states without full page reloads.
Form.code:
import { Form } from '@remix-run/react';
<Form method='post'>
  <input name='title' />
  <button type='submit'>Create</button>
</Form>

useFetcher.exp: useFetcher allows submitting actions or loading data without navigational transitions. It is ideal for non-blocking interactions like add-to-cart buttons or inline search suggestions.
useFetcher.code:
const fetcher = useFetcher();
<fetcher.Form method='post' action='/api/cart'>
  <button type='submit'>Add to Cart</button>
</fetcher.Form>

Request/Response.exp: Remix embraces Web Fetch API standards. Loaders and actions receive native Request objects and return Response objects, making routes portable across server environments.

Headers.exp: Headers in Remix can be set at the route level for caching, security, and content negotiation. The headers export controls both document and resource route responses.

Cookies.exp: Remix provides a cookies API that integrates with the Web Fetch standard. Cookies are created, read, and written using the cookie utilities from @remix-run/node.

ErrorBoundary.exp: ErrorBoundary catches unexpected rendering errors in a route. When an error is thrown, Remix renders the closest ErrorBoundary instead of the default component, showing a fallback UI.

CatchBoundary.exp: CatchBoundary handles expected error responses from loaders and actions. It receives the thrown Response object, allowing different UI for 404, 403, and other status codes.

Links.exp: Remix manages CSS through the links export, which adds link tags to the document head. This enables route-level CSS loading and automatic cleanup when navigating away.

Route Styles.exp: Route styles in Remix support both traditional CSS files and CSS-in-JS solutions. CSS files can be imported in links functions, with automatic scoping via CSS Modules.

Tailwind.exp: Remix supports Tailwind CSS through the conventional PostCSS setup. The @tailwind directives are processed during build, generating optimized CSS with unused class purging.

Fly.io.exp: Fly.io is the recommended deployment target for Remix, offering global edge regions and effortless scaling. Remix apps deploy as Docker containers running close to users worldwide.

Vercel.exp: Vercel supports Remix via the @remix-run/vercel adapter. It automatically optimizes serverless functions and delivers assets through Vercel's edge network.

Netlify.exp: Netlify deploys Remix apps using the Netlify adapter, providing serverless functions for the Remix server and global CDN for static assets via Netlify Edge.

Cloudflare.exp: The Cloudflare Workers adapter runs Remix on Cloudflare's edge network. It uses Workers KV for sessions and Durable Objects for real-time state.

Resource Routes.exp: Resource Routes return non-HTML content such as JSON, images, PDFs, or sitemaps. They handle requests without rendering a component, functioning as pure API endpoints within the routes system.

WebSockets.exp: Real-time features in Remix are achieved through WebSocket integrations. While Remix does not include WebSockets natively, it pairs well with libraries like Socket.io or PartyKit.

Caching.exp: Remix leverages HTTP caching extensively. The headers export allows setting Cache-Control headers per route, and loaders can implement conditional requests with ETags for efficient revalidation.

Remix Vite Plugin.exp: Remix now ships as a Vite plugin for faster builds, HMR, and streamlined configuration. The vite.config replaces remix.config with a familiar Vite API and automatic React Fast Refresh.

Plugin Configuration.exp: The Remix Vite plugin accepts options for server entry, routes directory, future flags, and build output. It integrates with other Vite plugins like Tailwind and MDX for a unified build pipeline.

HMR & Fast Refresh.exp: Vite-powered HMR updates Remix route components in milliseconds without losing page state. React Fast Refresh preserves component state across edits, dramatically improving the dev feedback loop.

createCookieSessionStorage.exp: Cookie session storage encodes session data directly in encrypted cookies, suitable for small payloads. It requires no database and is the simplest session strategy for Remix apps.

createSessionStorage.exp: createSessionStorage allows custom backing stores (database, Redis) for larger session data while using a cookie only for the session ID. This scales beyond cookie size limits.

Flash Messages.exp: Flash messages are one-time session values that are cleared after being read, ideal for success or error notifications after form submissions. They use the session's flash method.

Typed Loader Data.exp: useLoaderData infers the return type of the route's loader using typeof loader. This provides end-to-end type safety from the server to the client without manual type definitions.

Typed Actions.exp: useActionData provides type-safe access to action return values. Combine with typeof action for compile-time checking of error messages, form data, and mutation results.

serialize Type.exp: Remix's SerializeFrom type unwraps Promise and Response types from loaders, providing a cleaner type for client-side hooks when the loader uses async patterns.

JSX.exp: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML and is compiled to React.createElement calls. It allows writing UI components declaratively in React Native.

Components.exp: Components are reusable building blocks in React Native, defined as functions returning JSX. They accept props and manage their own state using hooks.

StyleSheet.exp: StyleSheet provides a way to define styles with performance benefits through abstraction. It validates and optimizes style objects, and styles are only sent to native once.

Expo CLI.exp: Expo is the recommended framework for building React Native apps. It provides managed workflows, over-the-air updates, and access to native APIs without Xcode or Android Studio.
Expo CLI.code:
npx create-expo-app my-app
cd my-app
npx expo start
# Press i for iOS, a for Android, w for web

View.exp: View is the fundamental container component supporting flexbox layout, styling, touch handling, and accessibility. It maps to UIView on iOS and View on Android.

Text.exp: Text is the only component that renders text in React Native. It supports nesting, styling, and event handling like onPress.

Image.exp: Image displays images from local assets, network URLs, or data URIs. It requires explicit dimensions when loading from network sources.

ScrollView.exp: ScrollView is a scrolling container for multiple components and views. It loads all content upfront and is best for smaller amounts of content.

Pressable.exp: Pressable is the modern touch handling component that provides feedback for different press states. Use instead of TouchableOpacity for more control.
Pressable.code:
<Pressable onPress={handlePress} style={({ pressed }) => [{ opacity: pressed ? 0.5 : 1 }]}>
  <Text>Press me</Text>
</Pressable>

Modal & StatusBar.exp: Modal presents content on top of the app, useful for alerts and forms. StatusBar controls the device status bar appearance per screen.

React Navigation.exp: React Navigation is the standard navigation library for React Native apps, providing stack, tab, and drawer navigators with native transitions.

Stack.exp: Stack navigator manages a navigation stack where screens are pushed and popped. It provides native-like transitions and header customization.

Tab.exp: Tab navigator provides bottom or top tab navigation with icons and labels. Each tab maintains its own navigation state for independent back stacks.

Drawer.exp: Drawer navigator creates a side menu that slides in from the left, supporting nested navigators and custom drawer content.

Expo Router.exp: Expo Router provides file-based routing similar to Next.js. Files in the app/ directory automatically become routes with support for layout files and deep linking.

Fabric.exp: Fabric is the new rendering system that uses JSI (JavaScript Interface) instead of the Bridge. It enables synchronous communication and better performance for UI updates.

TurboModules.exp: TurboModules replace the old Native Modules system, allowing lazy loading of native modules and efficient type-safe communication via JSI.

JSI.exp: JavaScript Interface (JSI) enables direct, synchronous communication between JavaScript and native code without the Bridge. It eliminates the serialization overhead of the old architecture.

useState.exp: useState is a React hook that adds local state to functional components, returning a state variable and a setter function.
useState.code:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
<Button title="Press" onPress={() => setCount(count + 1)} />

AsyncStorage.exp: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value storage system for persisting data across app restarts on both iOS and Android.

Zustand.exp: Zustand is a minimal state management library with a hook-based API. It works well in React Native for global state without boilerplate.

MMKV Storage.exp: MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage by Tencent. It's significantly faster than AsyncStorage and ideal for performance-critical persistence.

Animated API.exp: React Native's built-in Animated API provides declarative animations using Animated.Value and timing/spring configurations. It drives animations natively on the UI thread.

Reanimated.exp: Reanimated provides gesture-driven animations that run entirely on the UI thread using worklets. It enables smooth 60fps animations for complex interactions.

Gesture Handler.exp: Gesture Handler replaces PanResponder with native gesture processing. It supports pan, pinch, rotation, tap, long press, and custom gesture compositions.

fetch.exp: The Fetch API provides a native way to make HTTP requests in React Native. It returns promises and supports JSON, text, and binary responses.

Axios.exp: Axios is a promise-based HTTP client with interceptors, automatic JSON parsing, and request cancellation. It provides a cleaner API than fetch.

React Query.exp: React Query (TanStack Query) manages server state with automatic caching, refetching, pagination, and optimistic updates.

WebSocket.exp: WebSocket enables full-duplex real-time communication over a persistent TCP connection, ideal for chat apps, live updates, and gaming.
WebSocket.code:
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://example.com/socket');
ws.onmessage = (e) => console.log(e.data);

Camera.exp: React Native Camera provides device camera access with support for photos, videos, barcode scanning, and custom camera UI.
Camera.code:
import { Camera } from 'react-native-camera';
<Camera ref={ref => setCamera(ref)} type={Camera.Constants.Type.back} />

Location.exp: Geolocation APIs provide device location through GPS or network positioning, supporting high-accuracy and background location tracking.

Push Notifications.exp: Push notifications allow sending alerts to user devices even when the app is closed. Firebase Cloud Messaging is the standard solution.
Push Notifications.code:
import messaging from '@react-native-firebase/messaging';
const token = await messaging().getToken();

FlatList.exp: FlatList efficiently renders large lists by virtualizing rows, recycling components, and rendering only visible items. It supports headers, footers, and pull-to-refresh.

Optimization.exp: React Native optimization includes using PureComponent, useMemo, avoiding inline functions in render, and minimizing re-renders with React.memo.

Hermes.exp: Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine optimized for React Native, reducing app startup time, memory usage, and APK/IPA size.

InteractionManager.exp: InteractionManager schedules tasks to run after animations or navigation transitions complete, preventing dropped frames during critical UI updates.

Skia.exp: React Native Skia provides a high-performance 2D graphics canvas for custom drawing, image manipulation, and complex animations using the Skia graphics library.
Skia.code:
import { Canvas, Circle, Group } from '@shopify/react-native-skia';

<Canvas style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <Circle cx={100} cy={100} r={40} color='blue' />
</Canvas>

CodePush.exp: CodePush enables over-the-air JavaScript bundle updates without going through the App Store review process, allowing instant bug fixes and small feature updates.

AppState.exp: AppState tracks whether the app is in foreground, background, or inactive state. Use it to pause/resume timers, network requests, and animations.

iOS.exp: iOS deployment requires an Apple Developer account, Xcode configuration, and provisioning profiles. The app is archived and uploaded via Xcode or Transporter.

Android.exp: Android deployment generates a signed APK or AAB using keystore credentials. The build is created with Gradle and uploaded to the Play Console.

EAS Build.exp: Expo Application Services (EAS) Build compiles and signs your app in the cloud without requiring Xcode or Android Studio installed locally.
EAS Build.code:
npm install -g eas-cli
eas login
eas build --platform all

What is Rust.exp: Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, speed, and concurrency. It guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector through its ownership system and zero-cost abstractions.

Rust Syntax Basics.exp: Rust uses `fn` for functions, `let` for variables, and macros with `!`. Semicolons end expressions, blocks use curly braces. `main` is the program entry point. Statements vs expressions distinction is key.

Variables & Mutability.exp: Variables are immutable by default. Use `mut` to make them mutable. `const` for compile-time constants. Shadowing redeclares a variable with `let`, allowing type changes.

Scalar Types.exp: Four scalar types: integers (i8-u128, i64, usize), floats (f32, f64), bool, char. Integer overflow wraps in release, panics in debug. Underscores improve readability: `1_000_000`.

rustup & Toolchains.exp: rustup manages Rust toolchains. Switch between stable, beta, nightly. `rustup target add` for cross-compilation. `rustup component add` for tools. `rustup show` displays active toolchain.
rustup & Toolchains.code:
# shell commands
$ rustup install nightly
$ rustup default stable
$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
$ rustup component add rust-src

Cargo Basics.exp: Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo check`, `cargo clean`. Cargo.toml defines metadata and dependencies.
Cargo Basics.code:
# shell commands
$ cargo new my_project --bin
$ cd my_project
$ cargo add serde --features derive
$ cargo run --release
$ cargo check

rustfmt.exp: rustfmt auto-formats code according to style guidelines. `cargo fmt` formats the whole project. `rustfmt --check` verifies formatting in CI. Configure with `rustfmt.toml`.
rustfmt.code:
# shell commands
$ cargo fmt
$ rustfmt --check src/main.rs
# rustfmt.toml
max_width = 100
edition = "2021"

Clippy.exp: Clippy is Rust's linter with 550+ rules. `cargo clippy` catches common mistakes, non-idiomatic code, and performance pitfalls. `#[allow(clippy::...)]` silences specific lints.
Clippy.code:
# shell commands
$ cargo clippy
$ cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic
$ cargo clippy --fix

rust-analyzer.exp: rust-analyzer provides IDE support: code completion, goto-definition, type hints, inlay hints, rename, diagnostics. LSP server used by VS Code, Neovim, Emacs, and Zed.

if / else if / else.exp: Conditions must be `bool` — no truthy/falsy coercion. `if` is an expression, assignable with `let`. All arms must return the same type. Blocks evaluate to their last expression.

Loops (loop, while, for).exp: `loop` repeats forever until `break`. `while` loops on a condition. `for` iterates over iterators. `for (0..n)` is range syntax. Use `continue` to skip to next iteration.

Pattern Matching (match).exp: `match` is Rust's powerful pattern matching. Arms must be exhaustive. Patterns can bind, match ranges (`..=`), use `|` for alternatives, and guards with `if`.

if let.exp: `if let` combines `match` for a single pattern, ignoring others. Useful with `Option`, `Result`, and enums. Reduces boilerplate when only one arm matters.

while let.exp: `while let` repeatedly matches a pattern until it fails. Common with iterators, `Option`-producing functions, and mutable borrow patterns.

Labeled Break & Continue.exp: Loop labels (`'label`) disambiguate nested loops. `break 'label` exits the named loop. `continue 'label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop.

Loop Returning Values.exp: `loop` can return a value with `break value`. `break` with no value returns `()`. Useful for retry logic or initializing values from fallible operations.

Ownership Rules.exp: Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. Ownership can be moved. This guarantees memory safety without GC.

Move Semantics.exp: Assigning or passing a value moves ownership unless the type implements `Copy`. Stack-only types (integers, bools, floats, chars, tuples of Copy types) are copied.

Borrowing & References.exp: References borrow values without taking ownership. `&T` (immutable, shared). `&mut T` (mutable, exclusive). References must never outlive their referent.

Borrow Rules Deep.exp: At any time: either one mutable reference, or any number of immutable references. References must always be valid. The borrow checker enforces this at compile time.

Split Borrows.exp: Rust allows borrowing different fields of a struct simultaneously. The borrow checker tracks borrows at the field level, enabling mutable access to disjoint fields.

Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL).exp: NLL makes the borrow checker smarter: borrows end when they're last used, not at the end of the scope. This reduces friction with the borrow checker significantly.

Slices.exp: Slices are dynamically-sized views into contiguous sequences. `&str` is a string slice. `&[T]` is an array slice. They are fat pointers (ptr + length) and never own data.

Interior Mutability.exp: Interior mutability allows mutating data through shared references. Provided by `Cell<T>` (Copy types, no threads), `RefCell<T>` (runtime borrow checking, no threads), and `Mutex<T>` (thread-safe).

RefCell & Borrow Checking at Runtime.exp: RefCell enforces borrow rules at runtime — panics on violation. `borrow()` returns `Ref<T>`, `borrow_mut()` returns `RefMut<T>`. Useful when the compiler can't verify correctness.

Function Declaration.exp: Functions use `fn` with snake_case naming. Parameters require type annotations. Return type is `-> Type`. The last expression in a block is implicitly returned. Early return with `return`.

Methods & Associated Functions.exp: Methods are functions defined in `impl` blocks with a `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` parameter. Associated functions (like constructors) don't take `self` and are called with `::`.

Closures.exp: Closures are anonymous functions that capture their environment. `||` syntax. Traits: `Fn` (immutable capture), `FnMut` (mutable capture), `FnOnce` (consume capture). Each closure has a unique type.

Diverging Functions & Never Type.exp: `!` (never type) indicates a function that never returns. `panic!()`, `loop {}`, `todo!()`, `unreachable!()` all diverge. Used in match arms that must match any type.

Function Pointers.exp: `fn(T) -> U` is a function pointer type, not a closure. Cannot capture environment. Useful for callbacks and FFI. Coerces from closures that don't capture.

Where Clauses.exp: `where` clauses specify trait bounds after the function signature. More readable for complex generics. Same semantics as inline bounds. Required for some complex bound patterns.

Higher-Order Functions.exp: Functions can take closures as parameters using generic bounds. Iterator adapters like `map`, `filter`, `fold` enable functional pipelines. Combinators compose nicely.

Tuples.exp: Tuples group values of different types. Fixed length. Destructure with pattern matching or index syntax `.0`, `.1`. Unit tuple `()` is the empty tuple, representing absence of value.

Arrays.exp: Arrays have fixed length `[T; N]`. Stored on stack. Bounds-checked at runtime. Slices `&[T]` borrow array elements. `[0; 100]` creates an array filled with the same value.

Vectors.exp: `Vec<T>` is a growable heap-allocated array. Use `vec![]` macro. Amortized O(1) push. `Vec::with_capacity(n)` pre-allocates. `drain`, `retain`, `splice` are powerful methods.

Strings (&str vs String).exp: `&str` is a borrowed string slice (UTF-8). `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer. `&str` to `String` via `.to_string()` or `String::from()`. Strings are not `Index` due to UTF-8.

Structs.exp: Structs define custom data with named fields. Use `impl` blocks for methods. Field init shorthand when variable matches field name. Struct update syntax `..other` fills remaining fields.

Tuple Structs.exp: Tuple structs have unnamed fields accessed by position. Newtype pattern wraps a single type. Good for type safety without field name overhead. `struct Wrapper(T)`.

Unit Structs.exp: Unit structs have no fields — act as markers or flags. Zero size. Useful for implementing traits without data, or as phantom types with `PhantomData`.

Enums.exp: Enums define sum types with variants. Variants can hold data (tuple or struct). `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are the most common enums. `match` enforces exhaustive handling.

Generics.exp: Generics abstract over types, enabling code reuse. Monomorphization generates specialized code per concrete type at compile time. Type parameters are declared with `<T>`.

Traits.exp: Traits define shared behavior (like interfaces). Types implement traits with `impl Trait for Type`. Traits can provide default method implementations. Must be in scope to use methods.

Derive Macros.exp: `#[derive(...)]` auto-implements common traits: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default, PartialOrd, Ord. Saves boilerplate and ensures correctness.

Supertraits.exp: Supertraits express that one trait extends another. `trait A: B` means types implementing A must also implement B. Used with `where Self: SuperTrait` for method access.

Trait Objects & dyn Trait.exp: Trait objects enable dynamic dispatch via vtable. `dyn Trait` is unsized — must be behind a pointer (`&dyn Trait`, `Box<dyn Trait>`). Objects must be object-safe (no generic methods, no Self by value).

impl Trait Syntax.exp: `impl Trait` in argument position is like a generic. In return position, it returns an opaque type implementing Trait. Cannot return multiple types. Useful for returning closures/iterators.

Associated Types.exp: Associated types define placeholder types within a trait. One implementation per type — unlike generics which allow multiple impls. Used extensively in Iterator, Deref, and operator traits.

Blanket Implementations.exp: Blanket impls implement a trait for all types satisfying bounds. `impl<T: Display> ToString for T {}` is a blanket impl. They allow adding methods to all types meeting criteria.

Trait Bounds & where Clauses.exp: Trait bounds constrain generics. Multiple bounds: `T: Clone + Debug`. `where` clauses improve readability. `impl Trait` as shorthand. `?Sized` opts out of the implicit Sized bound.

Result & Option.exp: `Result<T, E>` for recoverable errors. `Option<T>` for nullable values. `?` operator propagates errors. `unwrap()` and `expect()` extract values or panic. `ok_or()` converts Option to Result.

The ? Operator.exp: `?` unwraps `Result` or `Option`, returning early on error/None. Converts error types via `From` trait. Only works in functions returning Result, Option, or types implementing `FromResidual`.

Panic & Unrecoverable Errors.exp: `panic!()` unwinds the stack (or aborts with `panic = "abort"`). Use for unrecoverable states. `unwrap`, `expect`, `unreachable!()`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()` all panic on use.

Custom Error Types.exp: Implement `std::error::Error` for custom errors. Requires `Display` + `Debug`. `source()` method for error chaining. `Box<dyn Error>` for type-erased error handling.

thiserror Crate.exp: thiserror derives `std::error::Error` with minimal boilerplate. Supports `#[error("...")]` for Display, `#[source]` for error chaining, and `#[from]` for automatic From impls.

anyhow / eyre Crates.exp: anyhow provides `Result<T, anyhow::Error>` for application-level error handling. `bail!()` and `ensure!()` macros. Context method `.context()`. eyre is a similar alternative with better error reports.

Error Chaining.exp: Errors chain via `source()` or `.context()`. The `?` operator auto-converts via `From`. Libraries define specific error types; apps use anyhow/eyre. `Error::source` iterates the chain.

Result Combinators.exp: `map`, `map_err`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `ok`, `err`, `transpose` — these combinators transform Results without explicit match.

Vec.exp: `Vec<T>` is the primary sequence type — growable, heap-allocated, contiguous. Amortized O(1) push/pop. O(n) insert/remove. `with_capacity` pre-allocates. `drain`, `splice`, `retain` for advanced operations.

VecDeque.exp: `VecDeque<T>` is a double-ended queue with O(1) push/pop at both ends. Ring buffer internally. Use for queue/sliding window patterns. `make_contiguous()` for slice access.

HashMap & HashSet.exp: `HashMap<K, V>` stores key-value pairs with O(1) average lookup. `HashSet<T>` is a set of unique values. Both require keys to implement `Hash + Eq`. `entry()` API handles insert-or-update.

BTreeMap & BTreeSet.exp: `BTreeMap` / `BTreeSet` maintain sorted order with O(log n) operations. Keys must implement `Ord`. Use when order matters or for range queries. `range()` returns entries within bounds.

BinaryHeap.exp: `BinaryHeap<T>` is a max-heap priority queue. O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop. Use `Reverse<T>` for min-heap. `into_sorted_vec()` drains in order.

LinkedList.exp: `LinkedList<T>` is a doubly-linked list. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Split/append operations. Generally slower than Vec/VecDeque due to cache behavior. Use for heavy splitting.

Box<T> (Heap Allocation).exp: `Box<T>` allocates on the heap. Used for recursive types (linked lists), trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`), and large data moved infrequently. Derefs to `&T` / `&mut T`.

Rc<T> (Reference Counting).exp: `Rc<T>` enables shared ownership within a single thread. `Rc::clone()` increments reference count. `strong_count` / `weak_count`. `Weak<T>` prevents cycles. Use `Arc` for threads.

Arc<T> (Atomic RC).exp: `Arc<T>` is `Rc` + atomic reference counting — thread-safe. `Arc::clone()` is atomic. Pair with `Mutex<T>` for mutable shared state. `Arc<[T]>` for shared slices.

Cell<T> & RefCell<T>.exp: `Cell<T>` provides interior mutability for Copy types (no borrow checking — just copy in/out). `RefCell<T>` provides interior mutability for any type, checking borrows at runtime.

Cow (Clone-on-Write).exp: `Cow<'a, B>` abstracts borrowed vs owned data. `Cow::Borrowed(&str)` / `Cow::Owned(String)`. Call `.to_mut()` to get mutable access, cloning if borrowed. Ideal for read-mostly APIs.

Pin<T>.exp: `Pin<T>` ensures a value is never moved again. Required for self-referential structs and async generators. `Pin<&mut T>` / `Pin<Box<T>>`. Unsafe to construct. Foundation of async Rust.

Drop Order.exp: Variables drop in reverse declaration order. Struct fields drop in declaration order. `std::mem::forget` skips Drop. `ManuallyDrop` controls Drop. Nested values: outer drops first, then inner.

Mutex, RwLock, Condvar.exp: `Mutex<T>` guards shared data across threads. `RwLock<T>` allows concurrent reads / exclusive writes. `Condvar` blocks threads until a condition is met. `PoisonError` on panic.

Channels (mpsc).exp: `std::sync::mpsc` provides multi-producer, single-consumer channels. `Sender` clones for multiple producers. `Receiver` has `recv`, `try_recv`, `iter`. `crossbeam` offers multi-consumer variants.

Modules & Paths.exp: `mod` declares a module. Files and directories mirror modules. `pub` controls visibility. `super` / `crate` / `self` keywords for paths. `pub(crate)` restricts to crate.

Re-exports.exp: `pub use` re-exports items at a different path, making them part of the public API. Useful for flattening module hierarchies and renaming. `pub(crate) use` for internal re-exports.

Nested Modules & File System.exp: Modules can be nested inline or in files. `mod foo;` looks for `foo.rs` or `foo/mod.rs`. `mod foo { ... }` for inline. The 2018 edition uses the `foo.rs` convention.

Cargo.toml & Crate Types.exp: Crate types: `bin` (binary), `lib` (library), `cdylib` (C-compatible dynamic lib), `staticlib`, `proc-macro`. `edition` field selects Rust edition. `[profile.*]` for optimization settings.
Cargo.toml & Crate Types.code:
[package]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
[lib]
crate-type = ["lib", "cdylib"]
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true

Dependencies & Features.exp: Dependencies from crates.io, git, or path. `features` enable conditional compilation. `default-features = false` to opt out. `[target.'cfg(...)'.dependencies]` for platform-specific deps.

Workspaces.exp: Workspaces manage multiple crates in one project. Shared `target/` and `Cargo.lock`. Members listed in `[workspace]`. `cargo build -p specific-crate` to build a single member.

Conditional Compilation.exp: `#[cfg()]` gates code on target, feature, or OS. `cfg!()` is a runtime boolean. `#[cfg_attr(...)]` conditionally applies attributes. `cfg(test)` gates test-only code.

Basic Lifetime Annotations.exp: Lifetimes (`'a`) annotate how long references are valid. Prevent dangling references. The borrow checker validates lifetimes at compile time. Elision rules handle common patterns automatically.

Lifetime Elision Rules.exp: Three elision rules: 1) each input reference gets its own lifetime. 2) with one input lifetime, output gets that lifetime. 3) with `&self`/`&mut self`, output gets self's lifetime. These cover 95%+ of cases.

'static Lifetime.exp: `'static` references live for the entire program. String literals have type `&'static str`. `Box::leak` produces `&'static mut`. Const items are effectively static.

Lifetime Bounds & Subtyping.exp: `'a: 'b` means 'a outlives 'b (is a subtype of 'b). Required when one lifetime must strictly outlive another. Common in structs and complex function signatures.

Higher-Ranked Trait Bounds (HRTB).exp: HRTBs with `for<'a>` express that a bound must hold for all lifetimes. `Fn(&i32)` is sugar for `for<'a> Fn(&'a i32)`. Required for trait objects and closure bounds.

Variance.exp: Variance describes how lifetimes compose: `&'a T` is covariant in 'a, `&'a mut T` is invariant in 'a, `fn(T) -> U` is contravariant in T. `Cell<T>` makes T invariant. Important for type safety.

Lifetime Coercion.exp: Rust coerces shorter lifetimes to longer ones when safe. `&'a T` coerces to `&'b T` if `'a: 'b`. String `&str` to `&str` with shorter lifetime. Occurs implicitly at coercion sites.

NLL Deep.exp: NLL (Non-Lexical Lifetimes) allows borrows to end before the scope ends. Two-phase borrows let reborrowing during method calls. The borrow checker uses a location-aware analysis.

async/await Basics.exp: `async fn` returns a `Future`. `.await` polls the future to completion. Futures are lazy — they do nothing until awaited or polled. An executor is required to drive futures.

Tokio Runtime Deep.exp: Tokio provides a multi-threaded (work-stealing) or single-threaded runtime. `#[tokio::main]` attribute sets up the runtime. Key components: reactor (I/O events), scheduler (tasks), timers.

Async Traits.exp: Async traits require nightly or workarounds. `async-trait` crate desugars to `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`. Upcoming native async traits in Rust will remove this overhead.

select! & join! Macros.exp: `tokio::select!` waits on multiple futures, completing when the first finishes. `futures::join!` awaits multiple futures concurrently. `try_join!` returns on first error.

join_all / FuturesUnordered.exp: `futures::future::join_all` awaits a collection of futures, returning all results. `FuturesUnordered` polls a set of futures, yielding results as they complete — ideal for dynamic workloads.

Async Streams.exp: `Stream` trait is the async version of `Iterator`. `StreamExt` provides `next()`, `map`, `filter`, `fold`. `tokio_stream` and `futures` libraries. `async-stream` macro creates streams.

Pin Projection.exp: Pin projection allows safely accessing fields of a pinned struct using `pin_project` or `pin_utils`. Critical for self-referential async state machines. `#[pin_project]` attribute handles the unsafe parts.

Async Sync Primitives.exp: Tokio provides async-aware synchronisation: `Mutex` (hold across .await), `RwLock`, `Semaphore`, `Barrier`, `Notify`, `watch`, `broadcast` channels. Never hold a std::sync::Mutex across .await.

Raw Pointers.exp: `*const T` and `*mut T` are raw pointers with no safety guarantees. Can be null, dangling, or aliased. Dereferencing requires `unsafe`. Create from references with `as *const T`. Used for FFI and perf.

Unsafe Functions & Blocks.exp: `unsafe fn` marks an unsafe function that callers must wrap in `unsafe {}`. `unsafe` blocks opt into: deref raw pointers, call unsafe fns, access mutable statics, implement unsafe traits.

Calling C (FFI).exp: `extern "C"` declares functions from C libraries. `#[link(name = "...")]` links native libs. `#[no_mangle]` prevents name mangling. `unsafe` to call. `libc` crate provides C type aliases.

#[repr(C)] & repr Attributes.exp: `#[repr(C)]` lays out struct fields like C (no reordering). `#[repr(transparent)]` wraps a single field with same layout. `#[repr(packed)]` removes padding. `#[repr(align(n))]` sets alignment.

no_std & Global Allocator.exp: `#![no_std]` removes the standard library for embedded/kernel targets. Use `core` and `alloc` crates. `#[global_allocator]` replaces the default allocator. `alloc_error_handler` for OOM.

#[link] & extern Blocks.exp: `#[link(name = "foo", kind = "static")]` links native libraries. `extern "C"` (or "system", "stdcall") blocks declare foreign functions. `#[link_name = "actual_name"]` overrides the symbol name.

Exposing Rust to C (cdylib).exp: `#[no_mangle]` with `extern "C"` exposes Rust functions to C. `CString` creates null-terminated strings. `Cargo.toml` needs `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]`. FFI-safe types only.

Builder Pattern.exp: Builder pattern constructs complex objects with many optional parameters. Methods return `&mut Self` or `Self` for chaining. `build()` consumes the builder and produces the final value.

RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initializa.exp: RAII ties resource lifetime to scope. Files, locks, and memory are released in `Drop`. `MutexGuard`, `File`, `Box` all use RAII. Cannot forget to release — the compiler handles it.

Newtype Pattern.exp: Wrap a single type in a tuple struct for type safety and trait impls. Zero-cost abstraction — the wrapper is optimized away. Used for units, IDs, and implementing external traits on external types.

Deref Pattern & Deref Coercion.exp: Implementing `Deref<Target=U>` allows smart pointers to behave like references. `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, `Arc<T>` all deref to their inner type. `DerefMut` for mutable deref. Chains `.` auto-derefs.

Drop Order in Composed Types.exp: Struct fields drop in declaration order. Tuple fields drop in index order. Slices/vectors drop elements front-to-back. Closures drop their captures when the closure drops.

Typestate Pattern.exp: Typestate encoding uses the type system to enforce state transitions. Methods consume the current state and return the next. Invalid transitions are compile-time errors. Common in builders and protocols.

Unit Tests.exp: Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Test functions are annotated with `#[test]`. Assert with `assert!`, `assert_eq!`, `assert_ne!`. `#[should_panic]` for expected panics.

Integration Tests.exp: Integration tests live in `tests/` directory at crate root. Each file is a separate crate. They test the public API only. `cargo test --test integration_test_name` runs a specific file.

Doc Tests.exp: Doc tests are code blocks in `///` or `//!` docs. Run with `cargo test`. Code blocks with ` ``` ` are compiled and run. ` ```ignore ` skips compilation. ` ```no_run ` compiles but doesn't run.

Test Organization & Attributes.exp: `#[cfg(test)]` only compiles test modules. `#[test]` marks a test. `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. `#[ignore]` skips a test. `#[bench]` for benchmarks (nightly). `cargo test -- --nocapture` for stdout.

Benchmarks.exp: `cargo bench` runs benchmark functions with `#[bench]` (nightly). Or use the `criterion` crate (stable). Criterion measures time, generates reports, and detects performance regressions.

Property Testing with proptest.exp: proptest generates many random inputs to verify properties. `proptest!` macro defines strategies. `#[proptest]` is an alternative. Checks invariants hold for all inputs. Finds edge cases.

Mocking & Test Doubles.exp: Mock objects simulate dependencies. `mockall` crate generates mock types from trait definitions. `#[automock]` for single methods. Use with dependency injection for isolated tests.

Declarative Macros (macro_rules!).exp: `macro_rules!` matches patterns and generates code. Metavariables: `$expr`, `$ty`, `$ident`, `$stmt`, `$pat`, `$tt`. Repetition with `$()*`, `$()+`, `$()?`. Hygiene prevents name collisions.

Macro Patterns & Designators.exp: Designators: `block`, `expr`, `ident`, `item`, `lifetime`, `literal`, `meta`, `pat`, `path`, `stmt`, `tt`, `ty`, `vis`. `tt` (token tree) is the most flexible — matches any single token group.

Procedural Macros (proc-macro).exp: Procedural macros operate on the token stream. Three kinds: `#[derive]`, attribute-like `#[...]`, function-like `name!()`. Defined in proc-macro crates. `proc_macro::TokenStream` as input/output.

Derive Macros.exp: Derive macros automatically implement traits. Custom derive macros use `#[proc_macro_derive(Name)]`. Generate impl blocks. The `syn` crate parses token streams. `quote` crate generates output tokens.

Attribute Macros.exp: Attribute macros customize items they annotate. `#[proc_macro_attribute]` receives the attribute arguments and the annotated item tokens. Used for `#[tokio::main]`, `#[async_trait]`, etc.

Debugging Macros.exp: `cargo expand` (cargo-expand) shows macro expansion output. `log_syntax!()` prints tokens during expansion. `trace_macros!()` logs all macro invocations. `stringify!()` converts to string.

What is Spring.exp: Spring is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications. Spring Boot simplifies Spring development with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Key modules: Spring Core (DI/IoC), Spring MVC (web), Spring Data (databases), Spring Security (auth), Spring Cloud (microservices). Spring Boot's opinionated defaults reduce boilerplate while remaining configurable. Convention over configuration with auto-configuration classes. Starter POMs bundle related dependencies.
What is Spring.code:
<!-- pom.xml - Spring Boot starter -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.0</version>
    </parent>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>demo</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
