                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

// Main application class
package com.example.demo;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// Run: mvn spring-boot:run
// Or: java -jar target/demo-1.0.0.jar

Project Structure.exp: Spring Boot projects follow a layered architecture. Typical structure: controller (REST endpoints), service (business logic), repository (data access), model/entity (domain objects), dto (data transfer objects), config (configuration classes), exception (custom exceptions), util (utilities). Resources folder contains application.yml, static files, and templates. The @SpringBootApplication main class is typically at the root package. Package structure by feature or by layer.
Project Structure.code:
src/
├── main/java/com/example/demo/
│   ├── DemoApplication.java
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── SecurityConfig.java
│   │   └── SwaggerConfig.java
│   ├── controller/
│   │   └── UserController.java
│   ├── service/
│   │   ├── UserService.java
│   │   └── impl/UserServiceImpl.java
│   ├── repository/
│   │   └── UserRepository.java
│   ├── model/
│   │   └── User.java
│   ├── dto/
│   │   ├── UserRequest.java
│   │   └── UserResponse.java
│   └── exception/
│       ├── GlobalExceptionHandler.java
│       └── ResourceNotFoundException.java
└── main/resources/
    ├── application.yml
    ├── static/
    └── templates/

Configuration.exp: Spring Boot externalizes configuration via application.properties or application.yml. YAML is more readable for hierarchical config. Profile-specific files: application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml. Active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Custom properties with @ConfigurationProperties (type-safe). @Value for simple injection. Environment variables override properties. Random values with ${random.int}. Command-line args override file properties. Spring Cloud Config for centralized config.

Spring IoC.exp: Inversion of Control (IoC) is Spring's core - the container manages object creation and wiring. Annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController register beans. @Autowired injects dependencies (by type). @Primary resolves conflicts when multiple beans of same type. @Qualifier specifies exact bean. @Bean for explicit declaration in @Configuration classes. @Scope controls bean lifecycle (singleton, prototype, request, session). @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy for lifecycle callbacks.

REST Controllers.exp: @RestController combines @Controller + @ResponseBody for REST APIs. Request mapping annotations: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping. Extract data with: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader. @Valid for request validation. ResponseEntity for full HTTP response control. @ExceptionHandler for controller-level exception handling. @InitBinder for custom data binding.

Exception Handling.exp: Global exception handling with @ControllerAdvice. @ExceptionHandler for specific exceptions. Custom error response DTO for consistent API errors. HTTP status code mapping: 400 (bad request), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 500 (internal error). Field-level validation errors with MethodArgumentNotValidException. ResponseEntityExceptionHandler provides default Spring exceptions.

JPA Entities.exp: Spring Data JPA simplifies database access. Entities are POJOs with @Entity annotation. @Table customizes table name. @Id + @GeneratedValue for primary keys. @Column for column customization. Relationships: @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany. @JoinColumn for foreign key. Cascade types: ALL, PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE. Fetch types: LAZY (default for collections), EAGER. @Embeddable for value objects. @Enumerated for enums. @PrePersist/@PreUpdate for lifecycle callbacks.

Spring Data Repositories.exp: Spring Data JPA generates implementations at runtime. Extend JpaRepository<T, ID> for full CRUD. Custom query methods via method naming: findBy, findByFieldNameContaining, findByFieldNameBetween, countBy, existsBy. @Query for custom JPQL/SQL. @Modifying + @Transactional for update/delete. Specifications for dynamic queries. Projections for partial data. @EntityGraph for eager fetching. Pageable for pagination.

Building REST APIs.exp: Spring Boot makes building REST APIs straightforward. Use @RestController with request mappings. Content negotiation via produces/consumes. HATEOAS with links for discoverability. Versioning via URL, header, or content type. CORS with @CrossOrigin or global config. HTTP method support: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove). @Valid for request body validation. DTOs to decouple API from entities.

API Documentation.exp: Springdoc OpenAPI generates API documentation automatically. Add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui dependency. Access at /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs. Customize with @OpenAPIDefinition, @Info, @Tag, @Operation, @ApiResponse. Group APIs with GroupedOpenApi. Spring Boot 3.x uses springdoc v2. Configuration via application.yml. OAuth2 security scheme definition. Request/response examples with @Schema.
API Documentation.code:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>2.3.0</version>
</dependency>

// Custom OpenAPI config
@Configuration
public class OpenApiConfig {
    @Bean
    public OpenAPI customOpenAPI() {
        return new OpenAPI()
            .info(new Info()
                .title("User API")
                .version("1.0.0")
                .description("REST API for user management"))
            .addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement()
                .addList("bearerAuth"))
            .components(new Components()
                .addSecuritySchemes("bearerAuth",
                    new SecurityScheme()
                        .type(SecurityScheme.Type.HTTP)
                        .scheme("bearer")
                        .bearerFormat("JWT")));
    }
}

// Controller annotations
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
@Tag(name = "Users", description = "User management endpoints")
public class UserController {
    @Operation(summary = "Get user by ID", description = "Returns a single user")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Found the user")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "User not found")
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
}

# application.yml
springdoc:
  swagger-ui:
    path: /swagger-ui.html
  api-docs:
    path: /v3/api-docs

Spring Security.exp: Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common attacks. Add spring-boot-starter-security dependency. Core concepts: SecurityFilterChain (filter pipeline), AuthenticationManager (auth processing), UserDetailsService (user lookup), PasswordEncoder (password hashing). @EnableMethodSecurity for method-level security with @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured. CSRF protection (enabled by default for non-REST, disable for REST APIs with stateless JWT). CORS, headers, and exception handling configured in SecurityFilterChain bean.

JWT Authentication.exp: JWT (JSON Web Token) is commonly used for stateless REST API authentication. Flow: User logs in with credentials, server validates and returns JWT token, client sends token in Authorization header on subsequent requests, server validates token on each request. Use io.jsonwebtoken (jjwt) library. JWT contains claims (sub, iat, exp, roles). Access tokens (short-lived) and refresh tokens (long-lived) pattern. Blacklist for token revocation.

Spring Boot Testing.exp: Spring Boot provides comprehensive testing support. @SpringBootTest for integration tests. @WebMvcTest for controller layer (loads only web beans). @DataJpaTest for repository layer (in-memory DB). @MockBean for mocking dependencies. TestRestTemplate or MockMvc for HTTP testing. @TestContainers for real database integration tests. AssertJ for fluent assertions. Test slices reduce startup time by loading only relevant beans.

Actuator & Monitoring.exp: Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready monitoring and management endpoints. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency. Key endpoints: /health (app health), /info (app info), /metrics (metrics), /env (environment), /loggers (logging levels), /httptrace (HTTP trace), /beans (all beans), /mappings (route mappings). Custom health indicators, metrics with Micrometer, and info contributors. Expose via HTTP or JMX. Integrate with Prometheus/Grafana for monitoring.
Actuator & Monitoring.code:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,env,loggers,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
      show-components: when-authorized
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}

// Custom health indicator
@Component
public class DatabaseHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            if (conn.isValid(1000)) {
                return Health.up().withDetail("database", "PostgreSQL").build();
            }
            return Health.down().withDetail("reason", "Connection timeout").build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down(e).build();
        }
    }
}

// Custom metrics
@Component
public class CustomMetrics {
    private final Counter userCreatedCounter;

    public CustomMetrics(MeterRegistry registry) {
        userCreatedCounter = Counter.builder("users.created")
            .description("Number of created users")
            .register(registry);
    }

    public void incrementUserCreated() {
        userCreatedCounter.increment();
    }
}

Profiles & Logging.exp: Spring profiles activate different configurations per environment. Use @Profile on beans or profile-specific YAML/properties files. Set active profiles via spring.profiles.active. Logging with Logback (default). Configure levels per package: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG. Logback-spring.xml for advanced config. Logstash encoder for JSON logging (ELK stack). Distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing + Zipkin. Structured logging for better observability.
Profiles & Logging.code:
# application.yml - logging
logging:
  level:
    com.example: DEBUG
    org.springframework: INFO
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG
  pattern:
    console: "%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n"
    file: "%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n"
  file:
    name: logs/app.log
    max-size: 10MB
    max-history: 7

# logback-spring.xml - advanced
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
        <file>logs/app.log</file>
        <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.TimeBasedRollingPolicy">
            <fileNamePattern>logs/app-%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.log</fileNamePattern>
            <maxHistory>30</maxHistory>
        </rollingPolicy>
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE" />
        <appender-ref ref="FILE" />
    </root>

    <springProfile name="dev">
        <logger name="com.example" level="DEBUG" />
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <logger name="com.example" level="WARN" />
    </springProfile>
</configuration>

Spring Cloud.exp: Spring Cloud provides tools for building microservices. Service discovery with Netflix Eureka or Consul. API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway. Load balancing with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer. Circuit breakers with Resilience4j. Distributed configuration with Spring Cloud Config. Distributed tracing with Micrometer + Zipkin. Event-driven communication with Spring Cloud Stream. Feign/WebClient for inter-service HTTP calls. Centralized logging with ELK stack.

WebFlux.exp: Spring WebFlux provides reactive programming support for non-blocking, event-driven applications. Built on Project Reactor (Mono and Flux types). Reactive MongoDB, Cassandra, R2DBC for databases. WebClient for non-blocking HTTP calls. Reactive WebSockets. Functional endpoints with RouterFunctions. Backpressure handling. Better scalability for I/O-bound applications with fewer threads. Netty is the default embedded server for WebFlux.

What is SQLite.exp: SQLite is a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration SQL database engine. It's the most widely deployed database in the world — embedded in browsers, phones, IoT devices. The entire database is a single file. No separate server process needed.
What is SQLite.code:
sqlite3 --version
# SQLite 3.45.1

-- Open/create database
sqlite3 mydb.db
-- .databases
-- .quit

Installing SQLite.exp: SQLite comes pre-installed on macOS and most Linux distros. On Windows, download from sqlite.org. Or use a package manager: apt, brew, or compile from source. The sqlite3 CLI tool is all you need.
Installing SQLite.code:
# Linux
sudo apt install sqlite3

# macOS
brew install sqlite3

# Verify
sqlite3 --version

# Python (bundled)
python3 -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)"

SQLite CLI Basics.exp: The sqlite3 CLI is the main interface. Dot-commands start with . (not SQL). Key commands: .tables, .schema, .databases, .import, .output, .mode, .dump, .quit. SQL statements end with ;.
SQLite CLI Basics.code:
sqlite3 mydb.db

sqlite> .tables
sqlite> .schema users
sqlite> .mode column
sqlite> .headers on
sqlite> SELECT * FROM users;
sqlite> .quit

SQLite Data Types.exp: SQLite uses dynamic typing: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB. Type affinity (flexible): INTEGER affinity for whole numbers, REAL for floats, TEXT for strings, BLOB for binary. BOOLEAN stored as INTEGER 0/1. No separate DATE type — use TEXT, INTEGER (Unix), or REAL (Julian).
SQLite Data Types.code:
CREATE TABLE sample (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  age INTEGER,
  salary REAL,
  photo BLOB,
  is_active INTEGER DEFAULT 1, -- boolean
  created TEXT DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

-- Check types with typeof()
SELECT typeof(42), typeof(3.14), typeof('hello'), typeof(x'deadbeef');

SQLite Limitations.exp: No concurrent writes (single writer, shared lock). No user management/authentication. 64-bit ROWID limit (~9 quintillion rows). 140TB max DB size (pragma page_size * max_pages). Limited ALTER TABLE (DROP COLUMN was added in 3.35, but no MODIFY COLUMN).

CREATE TABLE.exp: CREATE TABLE defines a table. Column constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK. SQLite auto-creates INTEGER PRIMARY KEY as ROWID alias (auto-increment). WITHOUT ROWID tables use the PRIMARY KEY as the B-tree key.

ALTER TABLE.exp: SQLite supports limited ALTER TABLE: RENAME TABLE, RENAME COLUMN (3.25+), ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+). Cannot MODIFY, ALTER, or ADD CONSTRAINT after creation. Workaround: create new table, copy data, drop old, rename.

DROP & TRUNCATE.exp: DROP TABLE removes the table entirely. SQLite has no TRUNCATE TABLE — use DELETE FROM without WHERE. For large tables, DROP and recreate with same schema, or use DELETE and VACUUM to reclaim space.

Constraints & Foreign Keys.exp: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enables FK enforcement (off by default!). Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY. ON DELETE/UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT, NO ACTION.

SELECT.exp: SELECT retrieves rows. Support for WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING. SQLite's LIMIT/OFFSET syntax is standard. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to check optimization.

INSERT.exp: INSERT adds rows. Standard VALUES syntax. Multi-row INSERT supported (3.20+). INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR ROLLBACK / INSERT OR ABORT / INSERT OR FAIL / INSERT OR IGNORE for conflict handling. last_insert_rowid() returns the auto-generated id.

UPDATE.exp: UPDATE modifies existing rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports UPDATE FROM (joins in UPDATE) since 3.33. No LIMIT in UPDATE — use a subquery or WHERE with ROWID.

DELETE.exp: DELETE removes rows. Always use WHERE. SQLite supports DELETE FROM JOIN USING (since 3.35) and RETURNING clause (3.35+) to return deleted rows.

WHERE & Filtering.exp: Standard WHERE operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, GLOB, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL. LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII. GLOB uses Unix wildcards (*, ?). Combine with AND, OR.

ORDER BY & LIMIT.exp: ORDER BY sorts results. NULLs sort first by default (change with NULLS FIRST/LAST). LIMIT restricts row count. OFFSET for pagination. For efficient pagination, use WHERE on indexed column instead of OFFSET.

String Functions.exp: SQLite has practical string functions: || for concatenation, LENGTH, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTR, REPLACE, TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM, INSTR (find substring), LIKE/GLOB, || for concatenation. No CONCAT() — use ||.

Date & Time Functions.exp: SQLite has no date/time storage type. Use TEXT (ISO-8601), INTEGER (Unix timestamp), or REAL (Julian day). Functions: date(), time(), datetime(), strftime(), julianday(). strftime uses C-style format strings.

Conditional & Math Functions.exp: IIF(condition, true_val, false_val) — ternary. CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END for multi-way. IFNULL(val, default) replaces NULL. COALESCE returns first non-null. Math: ABS, ROUND, RANDOM, TOTAL, AVG, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX.

Transactions.exp: SQLite has full ACID transactions. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. SAVEPOINT for nested transactions (savepoints). IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE transaction types control locking. WAL mode allows concurrent reads during a write.

Views & Triggers.exp: Views: saved queries acting as virtual tables. CREATE VIEW, DROP VIEW. Triggers: automatic SQL execution on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. BEFORE/AFTER and INSTEAD OF (for views). FOR EACH ROW (only option — no FOR EACH STATEMENT).
Views & Triggers.code:
CREATE VIEW active_users AS
SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE status = 'active';

-- Trigger for updated_at
CREATE TRIGGER update_timestamp
AFTER UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE users SET updated_at = datetime('now') WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

-- Audit trigger
CREATE TRIGGER log_deletes
AFTER DELETE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log(table_name, action, record_id)
  VALUES ('orders', 'DELETE', OLD.id);
END;

Indexes & Performance.exp: CREATE INDEX speeds up queries. Types: single-column, composite, UNIQUE, partial (WHERE clause), DESC. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows query execution. ANALYZE collects statistics for better query planning. Use WHERE clause indexes.

Full-Text Search (FTS5).exp: SQLite's FTS5 extension provides full-text search. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE using fts5. MATCH for searching. Supports stemming, ranking (bm25), prefix queries, and content tables (external content).

JSON Support.exp: SQLite has JSON functions: json_extract, json_set, json_remove, json_array, json_object, json_each (table function), json_type. The -> and ->> operators work like MySQL. Use json_valid to check JSON validity.

WAL Mode & Concurrency.exp: WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) allows concurrent readers during a write. PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL. Better performance for many reads + occasional writes. Checkpoint moves WAL content to main DB. PRAGMA synchronous controls durability vs speed.

VACUUM & Maintenance.exp: VACUUM rebuilds the database file, reclaiming space and defragmenting. AUTO_VACUUM is incremental but less effective. PRAGMA auto_vacuum = 1 enables incremental vacuum. PRAGMA integrity_check verifies database health.

SQLite with Python.exp: Python's sqlite3 module is part of the standard library. No external dependencies. Connection, cursor, execute, commit, close pattern. Use ? placeholders for parameterized queries (never f-strings!).
SQLite with Python.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('mydb.db')
c = conn.cursor()

c.execute('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users
             (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT)''')

# Parameterized query (safe)
c.execute('INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?)',
          ('Alice', 'alice@example.com'))
conn.commit()

# Fetch
c.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', ('Alice',))
print(c.fetchone())

conn.close()

SQLite with Node.js.exp: Use better-sqlite3 (synchronous, fast) or sql.js (WASM, browser-compatible). better-sqlite3: prepare, run, get, all, iterate. No async — synchronous is fine for SQLite's speed.

SQLite with Go.exp: Use mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO) or modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go). Standard database/sql interface. Placeholder: ?. WAL mode for concurrency.
SQLite with Go.code:
package main

import (
  "database/sql"
  _ "github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3"
)

func main() {
  db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite3", "mydb.db")
  defer db.Close()

  db.Exec("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")

  tx, _ := db.Begin()
  stmt, _ := tx.Prepare("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)")
  stmt.Exec("Alice")
  stmt.Exec("Bob")
  tx.Commit()

  rows, _ := db.Query("SELECT id, name FROM users")
  for rows.Next() {
    var id int
    var name string
    rows.Scan(&id, &name)
  }
}

SQLite in Browsers.exp: sql.js compiles SQLite to WebAssembly for in-browser use. Also: OPFS (Origin Private File System) with SQLite WASM builds from sqlite.org. Great for offline-first apps, demos, and tools.

CLI Tips & Tricks.exp: The sqlite3 CLI is powerful: .mode for output (column, csv, json, html), .headers on/off, .output file, .import for CSV loading, .dump for backup, .read for script execution, .timer for timing.
CLI Tips & Tricks.code:
# Working with CSV
.mode csv
.headers on
.import data.csv mytable

# JSON output
.mode json
SELECT * FROM users;

# Export to file
.output output.txt
SELECT * FROM users;
.output stdout

# Backup
.output backup.sql
.dump
.output stdout

# Load and run script
.read setup.sql

# Timing
.timer on

Window Functions.exp: Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique number, RANK() allows ties with gaps, DENSE_RANK() allows ties without gaps. LEAD() accesses the next row's value, LAG() accesses the previous row's value. OVER() defines the window; PARTITION BY splits into groups, ORDER BY orders within each group. SQLite has supported window functions since version 3.25. A common mistake is forgetting ORDER BY inside OVER for functions that depend on order (like ROW_NUMBER).
Window Functions.code:
SELECT
  id,
  name,
  amount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rank,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM sales;

-- Per-group ranking
SELECT
  department,
  employee,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees;

-- LEAD and LAG (compare with previous/next row)
SELECT
  date,
  amount,
  LAG(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY date) AS prev_day,
  LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS next_day,
  amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS day_change
FROM daily_sales;

CTEs & Recursive Queries.exp: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) use WITH to define a named subquery that can be referenced multiple times. WITH RECURSIVE allows self-referencing CTEs for traversing hierarchical or graph data. The recursive CTE has two parts: the anchor (initial rows, no recursion) and the recursive member (references the CTE itself). Must use UNION ALL. SQLite limits recursion depth with PRAGMA recursive_triggers and an internal max depth of 1000 (configurable). Common mistake: forgetting the UNION ALL between anchor and recursive members.
CTEs & Recursive Queries.code:
-- Simple CTE
WITH sales_summary AS (
  SELECT department, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM sales GROUP BY department
)
SELECT * FROM sales_summary WHERE total > 10000;

-- Recursive CTE: generate numbers 1 to 10
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 1           -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 10  -- recursive
)
SELECT * FROM numbers;

-- Recursive CTE: directory tree
CREATE TABLE directories (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_id INTEGER REFERENCES directories(id)
);

WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM directories WHERE parent_id IS NULL  -- root
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.id, d.name, d.parent_id, t.depth + 1
  FROM directories d
  JOIN tree t ON d.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM tree ORDER BY depth, name;

-- Recursive CTE: Fibonacci sequence
WITH RECURSIVE fibonacci(a, b, n) AS (
  SELECT 0, 1, 1  -- anchor: F1=0, F2=1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b, a + b, n + 1
  FROM fibonacci WHERE n < 20
)
SELECT a AS fib_number FROM fibonacci;

Full-Text Search (FTS5).exp: FTS5 is SQLite's full-text search extension. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts5 creates the search index. MATCH performs the search. Supports prefix queries (*), phrase queries ("in double quotes"), and NEAR proximity searches. The bm25() function ranks results. FTS5 can use an external content table (content=) to avoid duplicating data. Use snippet() to get highlighted excerpts. Common mistake: forgetting that FTS5 is an extension that may not be available in all builds (check with PRAGMA compile_options).

Triggers.exp: Triggers in SQLite run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. BEFORE and AFTER control timing. INSTEAD OF triggers are used on views (since views aren't directly updatable). FOR EACH ROW is the only option (no FOR EACH STATEMENT). OLD.column and NEW.column access row values. Use RAISE(ABORT, 'message') to cancel an operation. Common mistake: triggers that recursively fire (Table A trigger updates Table A, firing the trigger again) — SQLite stops at recursion depth limit.

Views & Indexes.exp: Views encapsulate complex queries as virtual tables. Indexes speed up lookups at the cost of write speed. Partial indexes index only rows matching a WHERE condition — saves space and improves speed for filtered queries. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether indexes are being used. The WITH clause can be used inside views. Common mistake: assuming a view with ORDER BY guarantees order (it doesn't — wrap in SELECT ... FROM (view) ORDER BY). Always use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify index usage.

WAL Mode & Journaling.exp: SQLite has two journaling modes: DELETE (default) and WAL (Write-Ahead Logging). DELETE mode: changes go to a rollback journal, readers and writers block each other. WAL mode: changes are appended to a separate WAL file, readers can read the old DB while a write is in progress — much better concurrency. Checkpoints merge the WAL into the main DB (automatic or manual). WAL is faster for most workloads. Trade-off: WAL requires more file descriptors and is slightly worse for very large transactions. PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL is safe with WAL and faster than FULL. Common mistake: not setting WAL mode in applications with concurrent reads.
WAL Mode & Journaling.code:
-- Check current journal mode
PRAGMA journal_mode;

-- Enable WAL mode (once per database, persists)
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;

-- Manual checkpoint (force WAL flush to main DB)
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint;
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);  -- checkpoint and truncate WAL

-- Performance pragmas for WAL mode
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;      -- safe with WAL, faster than FULL
PRAGMA cache_size = -64000;       -- 64MB page cache
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;       -- wait 5s before locking error

-- Other journal modes
PRAGMA journal_mode = DELETE;     -- default, rollback journal
PRAGMA journal_mode = MEMORY;     -- fast but not durable
PRAGMA journal_mode = OFF;        -- no journaling (risk of corruption)

-- WAL file management (.wal and .shm files appear alongside DB)
-- To safely move a DB in WAL mode, first run: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);

JSON Support.exp: SQLite has robust JSON support since 3.9.0. json_extract() extracts values, json_set() updates values, json_remove() deletes keys. The -> and ->> operators (3.38+) provide shorthand: -> returns JSON, ->> returns SQL text/integer/real. json_each() expands a JSON array into rows (table function). json_group_array() aggregates values into a JSON array. json_group_object() aggregates into a JSON object. Common mistake: assuming JSON values in TEXT columns are validated — SQLite does not validate JSON on insert unless you use a CHECK(json_valid(data)) constraint.

Reactivity.exp: Svelte's reactivity is compiler-driven: assignments to variables automatically trigger DOM updates without a virtual DOM or manual state management. The compiler instruments variable assignments to invalidate dependencies.

Templates.exp: Svelte templates extend HTML with {expression} bindings, {#if} blocks, {#each} loops, and {#await} for promises. The template syntax is concise and compiles to highly optimized imperative DOM operations.

Logic.exp: Svelte provides logic blocks ({#if}, {:else if}, {:else}) and loops ({#each}, {:else}) within templates. Loops support destructuring and index tracking without special directives.

Props.exp: Props in Svelte are declared with the export keyword inside a component script, allowing parent components to pass data. Props can have default values and are reactive when reassigned.

Slots.exp: Slots allow parent components to inject content into a child's layout. Named slots and slot props enable flexible component composition and scoped content distribution.

Events.exp: Svelte uses the createEventDispatcher helper to forward custom events from child to parent components. DOM events are bound directly with on: directives like on:click.

Writable.exp: Writable stores are the most basic store type, providing set, update, and subscribe methods. They allow cross-component state sharing without prop drilling and auto-subscribe in Svelte templates.
Writable.code:
import { writable } from 'svelte/store';
export const count = writable(0);

Derived.exp: Derived stores compute values from one or more dependent stores, updating automatically when their sources change. They support transformations and can produce derived writable stores.

Custom Stores.exp: Custom stores encapsulate logic by wrapping the store primitives and exposing a controlled API. They hide implementation details while providing the same subscribe contract for template binding.

onMount.exp: onMount is the most commonly used lifecycle function, executing after the component is first rendered. It's ideal for data fetching, DOM measurements, and cleanup via returned teardown functions.

beforeUpdate.exp: beforeUpdate runs before the DOM is updated after state changes, making it useful for reading the DOM before Svelte patches it. It's the counterpart to afterUpdate.

afterUpdate.exp: afterUpdate runs after the DOM has been updated following state changes, suitable for DOM measurements or scrolling to newly rendered elements. It fires after every component update.

onDestroy.exp: onDestroy registers a callback that runs when a component is unmounted, making it the right place for cleanup like clearing timers, unsubscribing from stores, or canceling network requests.

Tweened.exp: Tweened stores smoothly interpolate numeric values over time, creating animated transitions between states. They support configurable easing functions and interpolation durations.
Tweened.code: const progress = tweened(0, { duration: 400, easing: cubicOut });

Spring.exp: Spring stores simulate physics-based animations using stiffness, damping, and mass parameters. They create natural-feeling motion that responds dynamically to changing target values.

Transitions.exp: Svelte's built-in transitions (fade, slide, scale, fly) and custom transition functions provide declarative enter/exit animations. They work with the transition: directive and support in/out modifiers.

Animations.exp: Svelte's animate: directive enables FLIP-based animations for list reordering, automatically calculating position changes and animating elements to their new positions smoothly.

Actions.exp: Actions are Svelte's approach to integrating with DOM elements imperatively, similar to use:action. They receive the element and optional parameters, returning lifecycle methods like destroy for cleanup.

Context API.exp: The context API allows passing data to a component and all its descendants without prop drilling. setContext and getContext are scoped to the component tree, not globally like stores.

Special Elements.exp: Svelte provides special elements like <svelte:body>, <svelte:head>, <svelte:window>, and <svelte:options> for declaring side effects and configuration directly in templates.

Routing.exp: SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where each +page.svelte file in src/routes creates a route. Dynamic parameters are captured with [bracket] notation in directory names.

Endpoints.exp: Endpoints are server-only API routes defined as +server.js files exporting request handlers. They handle GET, POST, PUT, DELETE requests and return JSON or other responses.

SSR.exp: SvelteKit renders pages server-side by default, generating HTML on the server for fast initial loads and SEO. SSR can be disabled per route or globally for fully client-rendered apps.

Vitest.exp: Vitest integrates seamlessly with SvelteKit projects for fast unit and integration testing with Vite-powered HMR, Jest-compatible API, and native ESM support.

Playwright.exp: Playwright is the recommended E2E testing framework for SvelteKit, providing cross-browser automation, network interception, and component testing across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

$state.exp: Svelte 5 introduces runes, explicit reactivity markers prefixed with $. $state replaces let-based reactivity and works outside .svelte files, making .svelte.ts files possible for shared state.
$state.code:
<script>
  let count = $state(0);
  function increment() { count++; }
</script>
<button onclick={increment}>{count}</button>

$derived.exp: $derived computes values from $state dependencies and updates automatically. Unlike the store-based derived, it works in any .svelte or .svelte.ts file with no setup wrapper.

$effect.exp: $effect runs a callback whenever its reactive dependencies change, consolidating lifecycle and reactivity into one primitive. The returned teardown function handles cleanup on re-run or destroy.

$props.exp: $props replaces the export let pattern for component props in Svelte 5. It accepts a default object and returns reactive bindings that update when the parent re-renders.

$bindable.exp: $bindable marks a prop as eligible for two-way binding using bind: in the parent. It provides a default value and enables the parent-child sync pattern without manual event dispatching.

Snippet Blocks.exp: Snippets are reusable template fragments defined with {#snippet name} and rendered with {@render name}. They accept parameters and can be passed between components as first-class template values.

Snippet Props.exp: Snippets passed as props allow parent components to inject template content into children, replacing slot-based composition with a more explicit and type-safe pattern.

Children Snippet.exp: The implicit children snippet captures default content between component tags. It provides a cleaner alternative to the default slot for wrapping content in layout components.

Project Setup.exp: Create a new SvelteKit project with the CLI, choosing from demo app, skeleton project, or minimal setup. The project includes Vite, TypeScript, ESLint, and Prettier out of the box.
Project Setup.code: npx sv create my-app && cd my-app && npm install

Routing.exp: SvelteKit uses filesystem-based routing where files in src/routes map to URL paths. +page.svelte files define pages, +layout.svelte wraps nested routes, and dynamic params use [bracket] directories.

Layouts.exp: Layout components wrap child routes with shared UI like headers and footers. Nested layouts inherit from parent layouts, and +layout.js can run data loading for an entire route segment.

load.exp: The load function runs before a page or layout renders, fetching data on the server during SSR and on the client during client-side navigation. It returns data passed to the page as $page.data.

Page Data.exp: Page data from load is available in +page.svelte via $page.data. Data is typed automatically when using TypeScript, and re-fetched reactively when load dependencies change via depends().

Layout Data.exp: Layout load functions in +layout.js combine data for all child routes using merge strategies, accessible from any child page or layout. This is ideal for fetching shared resources like user profiles.

GET.exp: GET handlers in +server.js return data from the server, typically JSON. They receive request event with params, url, fetch, and locals, making them ideal for API routes.

POST.exp: POST handlers accept request bodies for creating resources, validating input, and returning appropriate status codes. They're used for REST APIs and can handle multipart uploads.

API Routes.exp: API routes in SvelteKit are server-only endpoints defined alongside pages, sharing the same filesystem routing. They can use server-side secrets and databases without exposing them to the client.

Form Actions.exp: Form actions handle POST form submissions with progressive enhancement, running on the server to mutate data and return validation errors or success responses without JavaScript required.

Rendering Modes.exp: SvelteKit supports SSR (default), prerendering (SSG), and CSR modes configurable per route or globally. SSR renders on the server on each request, SSG pre-builds static HTML at build time.
Rendering Modes.code:
export const ssr = true;
export const prerender = 'auto';

Prerendering.exp: Prerendering generates static HTML files at build time for routes that don't need server data, suitable for marketing pages and blogs. Prerendered routes can be served from CDN with zero server cost.

CSR.exp: Client-side rendering skips server rendering entirely, loading the page as a shell and fetching data on the client. Useful for authenticated dashboard pages or apps that need minimal server load.
CSR.code:
export const ssr = false;
export const csr = true;

Session Management.exp: SvelteKit sessions can be managed with cookies, JWTs, or server-side stores accessible via the event.locals object in hooks. Authentication libraries like Lucia or Auth.js integrate seamlessly with the hooks pattern.

Cookies.exp: SvelteKit provides a cookies API in server contexts for reading, setting, and deleting cookies with configurable options for path, maxAge, secure, httpOnly, and sameSite.

OAuth.exp: OAuth authentication flows are handled server-side using endpoints or form actions, redirecting users to providers and exchanging authorization codes for tokens. Libraries like Lucia provide OAuth adapters.

Adapters.exp: Adapters configure SvelteKit for deployment on various platforms by transforming the build output. Each adapter optimizes for the target platform's capabilities and constraints.

Vercel.exp: The Vercel adapter deploys SvelteKit apps to Vercel's serverless edge network with automatic CDN caching, ISR, and serverless function support for dynamic routes.
Vercel.code:
import adapter from '@sveltejs/adapter-vercel';

export default { kit: { adapter: adapter() } };

Netlify.exp: The Netlify adapter deploys to Netlify's platform with serverless functions, split testing, and form handling. It supports on-demand builders for incremental static regeneration.
Netlify.code:
import adapter from '@sveltejs/adapter-netlify';

export default { kit: { adapter: adapter() } };

Node.exp: The Node adapter creates a standalone Node.js server for traditional hosting environments. It produces a single output with middleware support, ready for PM2 or Docker deployment.
Node.code:
import adapter from '@sveltejs/adapter-node';

export default { kit: { adapter: adapter() } };

Hooks.exp: Hooks are server-side middleware that intercept every request in handle, or module-level functions like handleError and handleFetch. They enable session management, redirects, and error tracking.

Params.exp: Params matchers validate and transform dynamic route parameters before load runs, preventing invalid requests from reaching data loading logic. Built-in matchers include int, uuid, and custom matchers.

Error Handling.exp: SvelteKit provides structured error handling with error/is-error utility, custom error pages (+error.svelte), and the handleError hook for logging and monitoring integration.
Error Handling.code:
import { error } from '@sveltejs/kit';

if (!post) throw error(404, 'Post not found');

Client Navigation.exp: SvelteKit integrates with the View Transition API for smooth page transitions on client-side navigation. The onNavigate lifecycle runs before navigation, enabling transition setup.

Cross-document Transitions.exp: Cross-document view transitions work across full page loads by defining @view-transition CSS rules. SvelteKit handles the JavaScript enhancement for seamless cross-page animations.

Element-level Transitions.exp: Individual elements can have their own view-transition-name for independent animation. Paired with the View Transition API, elements morph smoothly between pages without layout shifts.

$env/static/private.exp: $env/static/private provides build-time environment variables accessible only on the server. These are inlined at build time and reserved for secrets like API keys and database URLs.
$env/static/private.code:
import { API_KEY, DATABASE_URL } from '$env/static/private';
// Only importable in server files (+page.server.js, +server.js, hooks.server.js)

$env/static/public.exp: $env/static/public exposes build-time environment variables prefixed with PUBLIC_ to both client and server code. These are safe for the browser and inlined during build.
$env/static/public.code:
import { PUBLIC_API_URL } from '$env/static/public';
// Accessible in any file (client or server)

$env/dynamic.exp: $env/dynamic/private and $env/dynamic/public load environment variables at runtime instead of build time. Dynamic env vars are useful when the same build deploys to multiple environments.
$env/dynamic.code:
import { env } from '$env/dynamic/public';
// Runtime resolution: env.PUBLIC_API_URL

data-sveltekit-preload-data.exp: Link options control prefetching behavior. data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover" starts loading data when the user hovers over a link, reducing perceived navigation time.

data-sveltekit-reload.exp: data-sveltekit-reload forces a full page navigation instead of client-side routing, useful when the target page uses different global CSS or needs a clean JavaScript context.

data-sveltekit-keepfocus.exp: data-sveltekit-keepfocus preserves the currently focused element across navigation, improving accessibility for keyboard users on single-page applications.

What is Swift.exp: Swift is Apple's modern programming language for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and beyond. It combines the performance of compiled languages with the expressiveness of scripting languages. Open-sourced in 2015.

Swift Syntax.exp: Swift uses `var` for mutable variables, `let` for constants. No semicolons needed. Parentheses around conditions are optional. Braces are required for all control flow.

Variables & Constants.exp: `let` declares constants (immutable binding). `var` declares variables (mutable). Type inference is common, but types can be annotated explicitly. Swift is type-safe with no implicit conversions.
Variables & Constants.code:
let maxItems = 100
var counter = 0
var name: String = "Alice"
var isActive = true
print("\(name), \(counter), \(isActive)")

Basic Types.exp: Swift's fundamental types: Int, Double, Float, Bool, String, Character. Collection types: Array, Set, Dictionary. All types are strongly inferred and strictly checked at compile time.
Basic Types.code:
let pi: Double = 3.14159
var count: Int = 42
let done = false
let items: [Int] = [1, 2, 3]
print("\(pi) \(count) \(done) \(items)")

Xcode & Playgrounds.exp: Xcode is the official IDE for Swift development. Playgrounds provide interactive coding environments with live results, timeline views, and inline visualization of values.

Swift Versions.exp: Swift evolves rapidly. Swift 5.9 introduced macros and parameter packs. Swift 5.10 completed actor isolation. Swift 6 enhances concurrency safety and enables strict concurrency checking by default.
Swift Versions.code:
#if swift(>=5.9)
print("Using Swift 5.9+")
#else
print("Older Swift version")
#endif

Swift REPL & Format.exp: Swift has an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) for quick experimentation. `swift format` auto-formats code. `swiftc` compiles directly. Run with `swift` in terminal.

Type Inference.exp: Swift infers types from literal values and expressions. The compiler deduces the type without explicit annotations. Inference works across function returns, closures, and complex expressions.
Type Inference.code:
let pi = 3.14159        // inferred as Double
let count = 42          // inferred as Int
let message = "Hello"  // inferred as String
let result = count * 2  // inferred as Int
print(type(of: pi))      // Double

Type Safety.exp: Swift is a type-safe language. Every value has a known type at compile time. Type mismatches produce compiler errors, preventing runtime type errors. No implicit type conversions.
Type Safety.code:
let value: Int = 42
// let invalid: String = value  // ERROR: cannot convert
let converted = String(value)   // explicit conversion
print(converted)

Tuples.exp: Tuples group multiple values into a single compound value. Values can be accessed by position (.0, .1) or by name. Tuples are value types useful for returning multiple values.

Type Aliases.exp: `typealias` creates an alternative name for an existing type. Improves code readability and abstracts complex types like closures or generic types.

Numeric Types.exp: Swift offers Int (signed), UInt (unsigned), Int8/16/32/64, Float (32-bit), Double (64-bit), and CGFloat. Use `.random(in:)` for randomization. Overflow trapping prevents silent truncation.
Numeric Types.code:
let a: Int8 = 100
let b: UInt = 42
let pi: Float = 3.14159
let precise: Double = 3.14159265358979
let dice = Int.random(in: 1...6)
let masked = a &+ 50  // overflow addition &+
print(dice)

Booleans & Characters.exp: Bool has `true` and `false`. Character is a single Unicode grapheme cluster. `String` is a collection of Characters. Use toggle() to flip a Bool value.
Booleans & Characters.code:
var isOn = true
isOn.toggle()
print(isOn)  // false

let star: Character = "⭐️"
let chars: [Character] = ["H", "e", "l", "l", "o"]
print(String(chars))

Any & AnyObject.exp: `Any` can represent any type (including functions and optionals). `AnyObject` represents any class instance. Avoid using these in favor of generics and protocol types for type safety.

if / else.exp: `if` and `else` work as expected. Conditions must be Bool expressions (no truthiness). Swift supports `if let` for optional binding and `if case` for pattern matching.

switch.exp: `switch` supports pattern matching, ranges, tuples, value binding, and where clauses. No implicit fallthrough — use `fallthrough` explicitly. Must be exhaustive with `default` or all cases covered.
switch.code:
let value = 3
switch value {
case 1:
    print("one")
case 2...5:
    print("two to five")
case let n where n % 2 == 0:
    print("even")
default:
    print("other")
}

for-in & while.exp: `for-in` iterates over sequences, ranges, and collections. `while` loops on a condition. `repeat-while` guarantees at least one execution. Use `break` and `continue` for flow control.

if case & guard let.exp: `if case` pattern-matches without a full switch. `guard let` unwraps optionals with early exit, reducing nested `if-let` blocks. `guard` must transfer control (return, break, throw).

for where.exp: `for where` filters loop iterations inline. Combines iteration with condition without nesting an `if` inside the loop body.

Labeled Statements.exp: Labels identify loops and switch statements for precise `break` and `continue` control. Useful for breaking out of nested loops.

Availability Check.exp: `#available` checks API availability at runtime. `@available` marks declarations with minimum platform versions. Guard against using unavailable APIs on older OS versions.

#warning & #error.exp: `#warning` emits a compiler warning. `#error` emits a compiler error, preventing compilation. Useful for TODOs, reminders, and blocking incomplete code from shipping.

Function Declaration.exp: Functions use `func` keyword. Parameters have argument labels (external) and parameter names (internal). `_` omits the external label. Return type with `->`. Functions are first-class types.

Closures.exp: Closures are anonymous function literals. Syntax: `{ (params) -> ReturnType in body }`. Trailing closure syntax omits parameter labels. Shorthand: `$0`, `$1`. Closures capture surrounding context.

inout Parameters.exp: `inout` parameters allow functions to modify variables passed as arguments. Use `&` prefix when calling. The parameter is copied-in, modified, and copied-out (copy-in copy-out).
inout Parameters.code:
func swapValues(_ a: inout Int, _ b: inout Int) {
    let temp = a
    a = b
    b = temp
}

var x = 10
var y = 20
swapValues(&x, &y)
print(x, y)  // 20, 10

@discardableResult.exp: `@discardableResult` suppresses the unused-result compiler warning. Use when a function performs work through side effects and the result is optional to consume.

autoclosure.exp: `@autoclosure` wraps an expression in a closure automatically, delaying evaluation until called. Useful for short-circuiting, lazy evaluation, and assertion-style APIs.

Operator Functions.exp: Custom types can implement operators as static functions. Precedence groups define evaluation order. Define both prefix/postfix/infix and assignment variants.

Variadic Parameters.exp: Variadic parameters accept zero or more values of the same type. Use `...` after the type. Inside the function, the parameter is an array. Only one variadic per function.

Nested Functions.exp: Functions can be defined inside other functions. Nested functions capture variables from the enclosing scope (closures). Useful for helper logic that is only relevant within a single function.

Optional Basics.exp: Optionals represent values that may be nil. `Type?` is syntactic sugar for `Optional<T>`. Unwrap with `!` (force), `if let`, `guard let`, or nil-coalescing `??`.

Optional Chaining.exp: Optional chaining (`?.`) safely accesses properties and methods on optional values. Returns nil if any link in the chain is nil. Can be chained multiple levels deep.

map & flatMap on Optionals.exp: Optionals conform to map/flatMap. `map` transforms an optional's value if non-nil, preserving nil. `flatMap` flattens nested optionals. Chains transformations without unwrapping.

Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals.exp: IUOs (`Type!`) automatically force-unwrap when accessed. Used for properties that start nil but are set before use (e.g., IBOutlets). Safer to use regular optionals in new code.

Nil Coalescing Deep.exp: `??` unwraps an optional with a default value. `??` can chain multiple fallbacks. Combine with ternary and `?:` for concise optional handling.
Nil Coalescing Deep.code:
let name: String? = nil
let nickname: String? = nil
let display = name ?? nickname ?? "Guest"
print(display)  // Guest

let values: [Int?] = [nil, 1, nil, 2]
let flat = values.compactMap { $0 }
print(flat)  // [1, 2]

Optional Pattern Matching.exp: Optionals integrate with switch-case pattern matching. Match `.some` and `.none` directly, or use optional pattern `let x?`. Works with `if case` and `for case`.

Arrays.exp: Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Type-safe and grow dynamically. Methods: append, insert, remove, map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, first, last.
Arrays.code:
var items = [1, 2, 3]
items.append(4)
items.insert(0, at: 0)
let doubled = items.map { $0 * 2 }
let evens = items.filter { $0 % 2 == 0 }
print(items)
print(doubled)
print(evens)

Sets.exp: Unordered collections of unique values. `Set<Element>`. Efficient membership testing with `contains`. Set operations: union, intersection, subtracting, symmetricDifference.
Sets.code:
let a: Set = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let b: Set = [3, 4, 5, 6]
print(a.union(b).sorted())
print(a.intersection(b).sorted())
print(a.subtracting(b).sorted())
print(a.contains(3))

Dictionaries.exp: Key-value collections with hashable keys. `[Key: Value]`. Access and modify with subscript. `updateValue(_:forKey:)` returns optional old value. Use `default` subscript for safe access.
Dictionaries.code:
var scores: [String: Int] = [:]
scores["Alice"] = 100
scores["Bob"] = 85
scores["Alice"] = 95
for (name, score) in scores {
    print("\(name): \(score)")
}
print(scores["Charlie", default: 0])

Slice.exp: Array slices are lightweight views into portions of an array. They share memory with the original. Use Array(slice) to create a new array. Preserves indices of the original.
Slice.code:
let numbers = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let slice = numbers[1...3]
print(slice)           // [1, 2, 3]
print(slice.startIndex) // 1
print(Array(slice))    // [1, 2, 3]

let prefix = numbers.prefix(3)
let suffix = numbers.suffix(2)
print(Array(prefix))   // [0, 1, 2]

Lazy Sequences.exp: `lazy` defers computation until elements are accessed. Avoids creating intermediate arrays. Chain multiple transformations efficiently with lazy evaluation.

anySatisfy & allSatisfy.exp: `allSatisfy` checks if every element meets a condition. `contains(where:)` checks if any element matches. `first(where:)` finds the first match.
anySatisfy & allSatisfy.code:
let numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
print(numbers.allSatisfy { $0.isMultiple(of: 2) })  // true
print(numbers.contains { $0 > 5 })                   // true
print(numbers.first { $0 > 5 } ?? 0)                 // 6
print(numbers.firstIndex { $0 == 6 } ?? -1)          // 2

reduce into.exp: `reduce(into:)` accumulates into a mutable result (usually a collection). More efficient than `reduce` for building arrays/dictionaries since it avoids copying.
reduce into.code:
let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let grouped = numbers.reduce(into: [String: [Int]]()) { dict, n in
    let key = n.isMultiple(of: 2) ? "even" : "odd"
    dict[key, default: []].append(n)
}
print(grouped)

let squares = numbers.reduce(into: [Int]()) { $0.append($1 * $1) }

zip & sequence.exp: `zip(_:_:)` pairs elements from two sequences into tuples (stops at shortest). `sequence(first:next:)` and `sequence(state:next:)` generate infinite/lazy sequences.

Structs Deep.exp: Structs are value types. They receive automatic memberwise initializers. Properties can have observers (willSet, didSet). Mutating methods can modify self. Copy on write for performance.

Classes Deep.exp: Classes are reference types. Support inheritance, deinitializers, and multiple references to the same instance. ARC manages memory. Use `===` for identity comparison.

Properties & Observers.exp: Stored properties hold values. Computed properties calculate on access. Property observers willSet/didSet watch changes. lazy properties initialize on first access.

Mutating Methods.exp: Value types cannot modify their properties in methods by default. Mark methods `mutating` to allow self-modification. Mutating methods can reassign self entirely.

Static Subscript.exp: Types can have static subscripts, enabling type-level subscript access. Useful for registry patterns, default values, and lookup tables.

Subclass Deep.exp: Classes support single inheritance. Override methods with `override` keyword. `final` prevents overriding. `super` accesses parent. `required` init ensures subclasses implement it.

Convenience & Required Init.exp: `convenience init` calls another init (delegating). `required init` forces subclasses to implement it. `failable init?` returns nil. `designated init` is the primary initializer.

@objc & Dynamic.exp: `@objc` exposes Swift declarations to Objective-C runtime. Required for target-action patterns, KVO, and some UIKit APIs. `dynamic` enables method swizzling via ObjC dispatch.

Protocols.exp: Protocols define blueprints of methods, properties, and requirements. Structs, classes, and enums can adopt protocols. Protocols can have default implementations via extensions.

Extensions.exp: Extensions add functionality to existing types. Add computed properties, methods, initializers, subscripts, and protocol conformance. Cannot override existing or add stored properties.

Protocol Composition.exp: Protocol composition combines multiple protocols into a single requirement using `&`. A type must conform to all composed protocols. Use with type annotations and generic constraints.

Associated Types Deep.exp: Associated types (`associatedtype`) define placeholder types within protocols. Concrete types are resolved by the conforming type. Use `where` clauses for additional constraints.

Conditional Conformance.exp: Types can conform to protocols only under certain conditions using `extension: where`. Enables powerful composability like Array: Equatable only when Element: Equatable.

Opaque Types.exp: `some` keyword hides the concrete return type while preserving protocol conformance. The compiler knows the concrete type. Enables abstraction without generics at the call site.

Existential Types.exp: `any` keyword creates an existential box for protocol types. Unlike `some` (opaque), `any` can hold any conforming type at runtime with a performance cost of the existential container.

Default Implementations.exp: Protocol extensions provide default method implementations. Conforming types can override or use the default. Combine with constrained extensions for conditional defaults.

Enum Basics.exp: Enums define a common type for a group of related values. Can have methods, computed properties, and initializers. Cases are first-class values.

Associated Values.exp: Enum cases can carry associated values of any type. Each case can have different associated types. Enables tagged unions and the Result pattern.

Indirect Enums.exp: `indirect` enables recursive enums where a case references the enum itself. Required for recursive data structures like lists and trees. Mark individual cases or the whole enum.

CaseIterable.exp: `CaseIterable` protocol auto-generates an array of all enum cases. Access via `AllCases`. Works for enums without associated values. Useful for menus, pickers, and iteration.

@unknown default.exp: `@unknown default` handles future enum cases without breaking exhaustive switches. The compiler warns if all known cases are not covered. Use alongside explicit cases.

Raw Values.exp: Enums can have raw values of String, Character, Int, or floating-point types. Raw values are unique per case. Auto-increment for Int if unspecified. Access with `.rawValue`.

do / try / catch.exp: Errors are thrown with `throw` from `Error` conforming types. `try` calls throwing functions. `do/catch` handles errors. Catch specific cases before generic. `defer` runs cleanup on scope exit.

try? & try! Deep.exp: `try?` converts throwing expressions to optional (nil on error). `try!` disables error propagation, crashing on failure. Use `try?` for optional handling, `try!` only when guaranteed.

Result Type.exp: `Result<Success, Failure>` captures either a success value or error as a value. Useful for async callbacks, composeable error handling, and mapping over errors.

Throwing Properties.exp: Properties can throw errors by delegating to throwing functions in their getter. Computed properties marked with `get throws` (Swift 5.9+).

Throwing Subscripts.exp: Subscripts can throw errors (Swift 5.9+). Access elements with `try` when the subscript can fail. Useful for safe collection access beyond bounds.

rethrowing.exp: `rethrows` indicates a function only throws if its closure parameter throws. The function itself never throws directly. Enables higher-order functions that preserve throw behavior.

Defer.exp: `defer` schedules code to execute when the current scope exits, regardless of errors or early returns. Multiple defers execute in reverse order (stack-like).

Custom Errors.exp: Custom error types conform to the `Error` protocol (or `Swift.LocalizedError`). Use enums with associated values for structured error information.

Generic Functions.exp: Generic functions work with any type. Type parameters (`<T>`) represent placeholders. Type constraints (`where T: Equatable`) restrict allowed types. Swift infers type parameters at call sites.

Generic Types.exp: Generic types like `Array<T>` work with any element type. Define custom generic structs, classes, and enums with type parameters. Methods can add their own generic parameters.

Generic Where Clauses.exp: `where` clauses add constraints to generic parameters and associated types. Specify conformance, inheritance, and equality relationships between types.

Constrained Extensions.exp: Extensions on generic types can be constrained with `where` clauses. Methods and properties inside constrained extensions are only available when the constraints are met.

Phantom Types.exp: Phantom types are generic parameters not used in the struct's stored properties. They add type-level state without runtime overhead. Enforce invariants at compile time.

Type Erasure.exp: Type erasure wraps a concrete generic type into an abstract type, hiding the generic parameter. Common patterns: AnySequence, AnyPublisher. Implement via a box/wrapper class.

KeyPaths.exp: Key paths (`\Type.property`) provide type-safe references to properties. `WritableKeyPath` for mutable access. Useful for functional programming, sorting, and binding.

Dynamic Member Lookup.exp: `@dynamicMemberLookup` enables dot-syntax access to arbitrary properties via a `subscript(dynamicMember:)` method. Useful for JSON handling, scripting, and DSLs.

Result Builders.exp: Result builders (formerly function builders) construct complex values from a block of statements. Power SwiftUI's DSL, AttributedStringBuilder, and custom DSLs.

@propertyWrapper Deep.exp: Property wrappers encapsulate getter/setter logic. Custom wrappers use `@propertyWrapper` with `wrappedValue`. `projectedValue` provides additional API via `$` prefix.

Codable & JSON Deep.exp: `Codable` (Encodable & Decodable) auto-generates serialization. Custom keys with `CodingKeys` enum. Custom encoding/decoding via `encode(to:)` and `init(from:)`.

Regex.exp: Swift 5.7+ introduces native regex literals `/pattern/`. `Regex<Output>` type with type-safe captures. Use `firstMatch`, `wholeMatch`, and `matches` for matching.

Opaque vs Existential.exp: `some` (opaque) preserves concrete type identity at compile time. `any` (existential) boxes the type at runtime. Some types work for return values; any types work for heterogeneous collections.

Opaque Parameter Types.exp: Swift 5.7+ allows `some` in function parameter position (like `some View`). Equivalent to a generic parameter with a protocol constraint but written more concisely.

async/await.exp: Swift's structured concurrency uses async functions and await calls. async functions can suspend and resume, freeing the thread. Building block for all modern Swift concurrency.

Actors Deep.exp: Actors protect mutable state with actor isolation. Only one task accesses actor state at a time. `nonisolated` for methods that don't access actor state. `isolated` parameters for cross-actor calls.

Task Groups.exp: Task groups create structured concurrency trees. Tasks added run in parallel. Group collects all results before returning. `withThrowingTaskGroup` for throwing tasks.

async let.exp: `async let` launches a child task that runs concurrently with the current task. All async let bindings must be awaited before the enclosing scope exits.

MainActor.exp: `@MainActor` ensures code runs on the main actor (main thread). Mark types, functions, or closures. `await` required when calling from non-main context.

Global Actors.exp: Global actors provide shared concurrency isolation across types. Define with `@globalActor`. All properties/methods of an actor-isolated type share the same executor.

Sendable.exp: `Sendable` protocol guarantees a type is safe to share across concurrency domains. Value types are implicitly Sendable. Classes must be final with immutable state or use actor isolation.

AsyncSequence Deep.exp: AsyncSequence provides asynchronous iteration over values over time. `AsyncStream` creates custom async sequences. `AsyncAlgorithms` package adds zip, merge, combineLatest.

Task Local Values.exp: Task-local values propagate through the async task hierarchy. Scoped to specific task trees. Useful for logging context, request IDs, and configuration that follows async flow.

ARC Deep.exp: Automatic Reference Counting manages memory for class instances. Each strong reference increments the count. Deallocation happens at zero. `deinit` for cleanup. Retain cycles prevent deallocation.

Strong Reference Cycles.exp: Strong reference cycles (retain cycles) occur when two instances hold strong references to each other. Memory is never reclaimed. Use `weak` or `unowned` to break cycles.

unowned vs weak Deep.exp: `weak` references auto-nil when object deallocates, always optional. `unowned` assumes object lives at least as long, non-optional (crash on access after dealloc). Use weak for optional relationship, unowned for guaranteed co-lifetime.

Closure Capture Lists.exp: Closures capture references strongly by default. Capture lists `[weak self]` or `[unowned self]` break retain cycles with closures. Use weak for escaping closures to avoid cycles.

@NSCopying.exp: `@NSCopying` copies the property value on assignment using the NSCopying protocol. Ensures the instance holds its own copy rather than sharing mutable reference.

Memory Layout.exp: `MemoryLayout` provides the size, alignment, and stride of any type. Useful for understanding struct packing, interop with C, and performance optimization.
Memory Layout.code:
struct Point {
    var x: Double
    var y: Double
}

print(MemoryLayout<Int>.size)         // 8
print(MemoryLayout<Int>.stride)       // 8
print(MemoryLayout<Int>.alignment)    // 8

print(MemoryLayout<Point>.size)       // 16
print(MemoryLayout<Point>.stride)     // 16

print(MemoryLayout<Bool>.size)        // 1
print(MemoryLayout<Bool>.stride)      // 1

print(MemoryLayout<Int?>.size)        // 9 (Optional enum with associated)

Package.swift.exp: SPM uses Package.swift manifest. Define targets, dependencies, products in a declarative Swift DSL. `// swift-tools-version: 5.9` declares the manifest version.

Package Structure.exp: Standard SPM layout: Sources/PackageName/*.swift, Tests/PackageNameTests/*.swift, Package.swift at root. Resources in Sources/PackageName/Resources/. Use `.target(name:resources:)` to declare.
Package Structure.code:
MyPackage/
└── Package.swift
└── Sources/
│   └── MyPackage/
│       └── Core.swift
│       └── Resources/
│           └── data.json
└── Tests/
    └── MyPackageTests/
        └── CoreTests.swift

Binary Targets.exp: Binary targets distribute pre-compiled frameworks (e.g., Firebase, Sentry). Reference remote .xcframework URLs or local paths. SPM downloads and links the binary.

SPM Plugins.exp: Swift Package Manager plugins extend build processes. Build Tool Plugins run before compilation (code gen, linting). Command Plugins run on-demand (formatting, documentation).

Macro Targets.exp: Swift macros generate code at compile time. SPM 5.9+ supports macro targets. Macros reduce boilerplate and can introspect code at compile time.

Build Settings.exp: SPM supports Swift compiler flags, linker flags, C settings, and preprocessor macros per target and configuration. Conditionally apply with `.when(platforms:, configuration:)`.

SPM Commands.exp: Key SPM commands: `swift build`, `swift test`, `swift run`, `swift package generate-xcodeproj`, `swift package --version`. Resolution info with `swift package show-dependencies`.
SPM Commands.code:
# Terminal commands:
# swift build              # Build package
# swift test               # Run tests
# swift run <target>       # Run executable
# swift package clean      # Clean build artifacts
# swift package resolve    # Resolve dependencies
# swift package show-dependencies  # Show dependency tree
# swift package plugin --list     # List available plugins

POP Principles.exp: Protocol-Oriented Programming is a core Swift paradigm (from The Swift Programming Language): start with a protocol, provide default implementations via extensions, use protocol inheritance and composition. Prefer protocols over superclasses for flexibility.

Protocol Inheritance & Composition.exp: Protocols can inherit from multiple protocols (unlike classes). Protocol composition `&` combines requirements. Use `AnyObject` protocol for class-only protocols. From The Swift Programming Language.

Protocol Extensions & Defaults.exp: Protocol extensions provide default implementations, computed properties, and methods. Constrained extensions (`where`) add capabilities only when specific conditions are met. This powers Swift's standard library.

Empty Protocols (Marker).exp: Empty protocols mark types with a semantic property without requiring methods. `Sendable`, `Codable`, `Hashable` are examples. Combined with constrained extensions and generics.

Self Requirements.exp: Protocols can use `Self` to reference the conforming type. `Equatable` uses Self for ==. `Identifiable` uses Self for ID. Useful for type-safe comparison, copying, and factory patterns.

Access Control.exp: Swift's access levels: `open` (subclassable outside module), `public` (visible outside module), `internal` (default, module-wide), `fileprivate` (file scope), `private` (declaration scope). Use the most restrictive level possible.

URLSession & Networking.exp: Swift's URLSession provides async HTTP networking. `data(from:)` for GET requests, `upload(for:from:)` for POST. Combine with Codable for type-safe JSON parsing. From Hacking with Swift.

Custom ViewModifier & Animation.exp: Custom `ViewModifier` encapsulates reusable view styling. Combine with `withAnimation` for animated transitions. From Hacking with Swift's practical SwiftUI patterns.

Date & Time Handling.exp: Swift provides `Date`, `DateFormatter`, `Calendar`, `DateComponents`, and `DateInterval`. Use `RelativeDateTimeFormatter` for human-readable relative dates. From Hacking with Swift.

SwiftUI Preferences & Custom Layout.exp: Preferences pass data from child to parent views in SwiftUI. `PreferenceKey` aggregates values. `GeometryReader` for layout calculations. From Hacking with Swift's advanced SwiftUI coverage.

UIKit Integration with SwiftUI.exp: SwiftUI can wrap UIKit views via `UIViewRepresentable` and `UIViewControllerRepresentable`. Bridge UIKit delegates, data sources, and target-action patterns. From Hacking with Swift.

View Protocol.exp: SwiftUI views conform to the `View` protocol. The `body` computed property describes the view hierarchy. Views are lightweight value types describing UI.

Modifiers.exp: Modifiers configure views. Each modifier returns a new view. Order matters. Common modifiers: .padding(), .font(), .foregroundColor(), .frame(), .background(), .clipShape(), .shadow().

@State.exp: `@State` creates mutable state within a view. SwiftUI automatically updates the view when state changes. Use `private` access. State is owned by the view's storage.

@Binding.exp: `@Binding` creates a two-way connection to a source of truth owned by a parent view. Use `$` prefix to pass binding. Child views read/write through the binding.

@Observable.exp: SwiftUI 6+ uses `@Observable` macro for observable objects (replacing `ObservableObject`). SwiftUI tracks property reads and only updates views when observed properties change.

@Environment.exp: `@Environment` reads values from the view's environment. System environments: colorScheme, locale, managedObjectContext, dismiss. Custom environments via `.environment()` modifier.

StateObject & ObservedObject.exp: `@StateObject` creates and owns a reference-type observable object. `@ObservedObject` observes an object owned elsewhere. `@StateObject` ensures the object lives across view recreation.

Lists & Navigation.exp: `List` renders scrollable rows. `NavigationStack` enables push navigation. `NavigationLink` links to detail views. Use `\.self` for identifiable data or custom Identifiable conformance.

Utility-First.exp: Tailwind's utility-first approach uses small, composable classes for styling directly in HTML. Instead of writing custom CSS, you combine utilities like flex, text-center, and p-4 to build designs.

Setup.exp: Tailwind is installed via npm and configured through tailwind.config.js. The PostCSS plugin processes the CSS directives, scanning your source files for class usage to generate the final stylesheet.
Setup.code:
npm install -D tailwindcss postcss autoprefixer
npx tailwindcss init -p

Configuration.exp: The tailwind.config.js file controls content paths, theme extensions, variants, and plugins. Custom values can extend the default theme without overriding the complete design system.

Flexbox.exp: Tailwind provides comprehensive flexbox utilities including flex-direction, justify-content, align-items, and flex-wrap. Responsive variants allow different flex behaviors at each breakpoint.

Grid.exp: Tailwind's grid utilities enable CSS Grid layouts with grid-cols, grid-rows, and gap classes. Items can span multiple columns or rows using col-span and row-span utilities.

Spacing.exp: Spacing in Tailwind uses a consistent scale for margin, padding, and gap classes. The scale ranges from 0 to 96, with values like p-4 (1rem), mx-auto (auto margins), and gap-8 (2rem).
Spacing.code: Spaced content

Sizing.exp: Width and height utilities follow the spacing scale plus fractional and viewport values. Classes like w-full, h-screen, max-w-7xl, and min-h-screen handle common sizing needs.

Font.exp: Tailwind provides font-family, font-size, font-weight, and font-style utilities. Classes like font-sans, text-lg, font-bold, and italic compose to create typographic styles.
Font.code:

Text.exp: Text utilities cover alignment, decoration, transform, and overflow. Truncation, line-clamping, and text wrapping classes handle common text layout challenges.
Text.code:

Alignment.exp: Tailwind's text alignment and vertical alignment classes work alongside flex and grid for precise text positioning. Text can be aligned left, center, right, or justified.

Lists.exp: List style utilities control markers, position, and indentation. Tailwind provides list-none, list-disc, list-decimal, and list-inside/list-outside for ordered and unordered lists.

Custom Colors.exp: Custom colors are added through the theme.extend.colors configuration. Tailwind generates shades from 50 to 900 automatically, or you can define exact hex values for each shade.

Color Palette.exp: Tailwind's default palette includes eight color families (gray, red, yellow, green, blue, indigo, purple, pink) each with 11 shades. Colors are applied via bg-*, text-*, border-*, and ring-* utilities.
Color Palette.code: Colored element

Dark Mode.exp: Dark mode is enabled via the darkMode config option. The dark: prefix applies styles only when dark mode is active, either via class strategy or media query.

Breakpoints.exp: Tailwind uses five default breakpoints: sm (640px), md (768px), lg (1024px), xl (1280px), and 2xl (1536px). Breakpoint prefixes conditionally apply styles at specific viewport widths.
Breakpoints.code: Responsive text size

Mobile-First.exp: Tailwind follows a mobile-first approach where unprefixed utilities apply to all screen sizes. Larger screen overrides use breakpoint prefixes like md: or lg: to modify the base styles.

Responsive Patterns.exp: Common responsive patterns include stacking on mobile and side-by-side on desktop, hiding/showing elements per breakpoint, and adjusting spacing or typography across viewports.

Desktop sidebar

Buttons.exp: Tailwind buttons combine padding, colors, borders, and hover states. Focus rings ensure accessibility, and disabled states convey inactive buttons with reduced opacity.
Buttons.code:
<button class='px-6 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-blue-700 focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 disabled:opacity-50'>
  Click me
</button>

Cards.exp: Cards are built with rounded corners, shadows, padding, and dividers. Tailwind's utility classes compose to create consistent card components with header, body, and footer sections.
Cards.code:
Card Title

Modals.exp: Modals use fixed positioning, backdrop overlays, and z-index utilities. Transitions and transforms create smooth open/close animations using Tailwind's transition utilities.
Modals.code:
Modal Title

Forms.exp: Form elements are styled with consistent padding, borders, and focus states. Tailwind provides form-specific classes for inputs, selects, textareas, checkboxes, and radio buttons.
Forms.code:
<input class='w-full px-4 py-2 border border-gray-300 rounded-md focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500' />
<select class='block w-full mt-1 rounded-md border-gray-300 shadow-sm'>
  <option>Option 1</option>
</select>

Custom Plugins.exp: Tailwind plugins allow adding new utilities, components, or base styles programmatically. Plugins use the addUtilities, addComponents, addBase, and matchUtilities API functions.

Directives.exp: Tailwind's CSS directives (@tailwind, @apply, @layer, @config) control how styles are generated and applied. @apply inlines utility classes into custom CSS, while @layer organizes styles.

Functions.exp: Tailwind provides theme(), screen(), and other CSS functions. theme() accesses design tokens from the config, while screen() generates media query strings for custom CSS.

PurgeCSS.exp: Tailwind automatically removes unused CSS in production by scanning content files. The content array in config specifies the paths to scan, resulting in dramatically smaller CSS bundles.

JIT Mode.exp: Just-in-Time mode (now default in v3) generates styles on-demand as you author HTML. This eliminates unused CSS entirely, enables arbitrary values like top-[117px], and speeds up builds.
JIT Mode.code: Arbitrary values in JIT mode

Bundle Size.exp: Tailwind's production builds typically result in CSS files under 10KB after purging. The built-in minification and tree-shaking ensure only the utilities you actually use end up in the final bundle.
Bundle Size.code:
# Check bundle size
npx tailwindcss -i ./src/input.css -o ./dist/output.css --minify
# Typical result: 3-10KB

HCL Syntax.exp: HCL is Terraform's declarative language for defining infrastructure. Blocks define resources, providers, and variables in a human-readable format.
